en: The Kūrma Purāṇa— 1.
Now begins the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa,
the Pūrvavibhāga (First Section).
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then proclaim victory.
Having paid homage to the immeasurable Viṣṇu in the form of the Tortoise,
I shall fully proclaim this Purāṇa which was spoken by the Source of the Universe.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the great ṛṣis of Naimiṣa questioned the sinless Sūta Romaharṣaṇa regarding the meritorious Purāṇa-saṃhitā.
O Sūta of great intelligence, you have properly served the Blessed One Vyāsa, the foremost among those who know Brahman, for the sake of the meaning of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
O Blessed One, because all the hairs on your body stood on end at his words, you are indeed called Romaharṣaṇa, "the Hair-raiser," after Dvaipāyana.
In ancient times, the Lord himself,
the Master Vyāsa, spoke to you alone in order to proclaim the Puranic compendium of the sages.

For you, O Hari, the Supreme Person, were manifested through your own partial incarnation at the Svāyambhuva sacrifice on the day of the Soma-pressing, which had been spread out, in order to proclaim the *Saṃhitā*.
Therefore, we ask you, O master who are expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas: you ought to tell us the ancient and supreme Kūrma Purāṇa.
Having heard the words of the sages, Sūta, the best of those versed in the Purāṇas,
bowed mentally and spoke to his guru, the son of Satyavatī.
Romaharṣaṇa said:
Having paid homage to Hari, the source of the universe, who has assumed the form of a tortoise,
I shall relate this divine, purifying narrative from the Purāṇas.
Having heard which, even one who has committed evil deeds may go to the supreme goal;
one should never speak this meritorious discourse to an atheist.
One should recite this narrative, uttered directly by Nārāyaṇa himself, to a twice-born man who is faithful, tranquil, and righteous.
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.
The first is the Brāhma Purāṇa, then the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava,
the Śaiva, the Bhāgavata, the Bhaviṣya, and the Nāradīyaka.
Then the Mārkaṇḍeya, the Āgneya, and the Brahmavaivarta;
likewise the Laiṅga, the Vārāha, the Skānda, and the Vāmana. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.14)
The Kaurma, the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and immediately after that the Vāyavīya;
the eighteenth is designated as that known by the name Brahmāṇḍa.
O twice-born ones, having heard in brief these eighteen Purāṇas spoken by the sages, which are distinct from one another.
The first was spoken by Sanatkumāra; after that, the Nārasiṃha;
the third is designated as the Skānda, which was indeed narrated by Kumāra.
The fourth is called the Śivadharmākhya, spoken directly by Nandīśa;
after that is the wonderful one spoken by Durvāsas, and beyond that, the one spoken by Nārada.
The Kāpila, the Mānava, and likewise that which was proclaimed by Uśanas;
the Brahmāṇḍa, the Vāruṇa, and also the one called the Kālikā. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.19)
Likewise, the Māheśvara, the Sāmba, the Saura which contains a collection of all purposes, the other one spoken by Parāśara, the Mārīca, and that called Bhārgava. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.20)
This, however, is the fifteenth Purāṇa, the supreme Kaurma;
it exists in four parts, meritorious according to the divisions of its Saṃhitās.
The four meritorious Saṃhitās—the Brāhmī, Bhagavatī, Saurī, and Vaiṣṇavī—are proclaimed to bestow virtue, merit, worldly prosperity, and liberation. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.22)
This Brahma-saṃhitā is commensurate with the four Vedas;
its number of verses here amounts to six thousand.
Wherein, O lords of sages, the entire majesty of dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation is known as Brahman, the Supreme Lord.
Primary creation and secondary creation, the genealogies and the periods of the Manvantaras,
the history of the dynasties, and the divine, meritorious, incidental narratives.
This [Purāṇa] should be upheld by righteous Brahmins and others whose minds are tranquil;
I shall now set it forth in detail, as it was told of old by Vyāsa.
For the sake of the nectar of immortality, the deities, together with the Daityas and Dānavas,
made Mount Mandara their churning rod and churned the Ocean of Milk.
Then, while that [ocean] was being churned, the god Janārdana, in the form of a tortoise,
supported Mount Mandara out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
And the gods and the great seers, headed by Nārada,
praised the Lord upon seeing the imperishable Viṣṇu assuming the form of a tortoise as their witness.
In that interval, the goddess Śrī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, appeared;
the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, took her as his own.
Bewildered by the splendor of the unmanifest Viṣṇu, the great sages headed by Nārada, together with Śakra, spoke these words to Śrī: KūrmP_1.1.31.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Nārāyaṇa, who pervades the universe:
who is this large-eyed goddess? Tell me truly as I ask you.
Having heard their words at that time, Viṣṇu, the crusher of the Dānavas,
looked toward the sinless goddess and [the sages] headed by Nārada, and spoke.
This is that supreme power, consisting of me and having the nature of Brahman;
it is my beloved, infinite Māyā, by which this world is deluded.
By this very [power], O best of the twice-born, I delude the entire world— including gods, asuras, and humans— I swallow it up and I emit it forth.
Having understood and scrutinized the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their coming and going,
they cross over this vast [ocean of existence] after realizing the Self.
Presiding over portions of her, the twice-born gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, became possessed of power; this [power] of mine is all-encompassing.
This very one, the source of the entire world, whose nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas),
was born from me long ago in the Śrī-kalpa as the dweller in the lotus.
Four-armed, with conch, discus, and lotus in her hands, endowed with auspiciousness,
she shines like ten million suns, enchanting all embodied beings.
Neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor humans, nor even the Vasus,
nor any other embodied beings on earth are capable of crossing over this illusion.
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, the sages said to Viṣṇu:
"O lotus-eyed one, tell us: if indeed throughout the three periods of time, who is it that crosses over that Māyā created by the gods, which is so difficult to conquer?"
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, who is worshipped by hosts of sages, spoke to the sages:
"There is a preeminent among the twice-born known as Indradyumna."
In a previous birth, this king was unassailable even by Śaṅkara and others;
having seen me established in the form of a tortoise and having himself heard the divine Purāṇic compendium from my own mouth, he placed the lords of sages at his head. (KūrmP 1.1.43)
Having realized that Brahmā, Mahādeva, and the other gods abide within my power by virtue of their own respective powers, he has come to me alone for refuge.
Then, having been addressed by me, you shall go to the womb of a Brahmin;
known as Indradyumna, you will remember your former birth.
O sinless one, I shall impart to you that most secret knowledge which is beyond the reach of all beings, even of the gods;
having obtained this knowledge of mine, you shall enter into me alone at the end.
"Stay there upon the earth with another portion of yourself, remaining well-guarded;
when the Vaivasvata interval has passed, you shall enter me for the sake of our purpose."
Having bowed to me and gone to his city, he protected the earth;
then, when the time came, he passed away and, by the power of time, went to Śvetadvīpa along with me.
O best of sages, having enjoyed those Vaiṣṇava pleasures inaccessible even to yogins,
he was born again in a brahmin family by my command.
Having known me, who am called Vāsudeva, wherein the two imperishables—
knowledge and ignorance, whose forms are hidden— are situated, they know that as the supreme Brahman.
He propitiated the Supreme Lord, the refuge of all beings,
through vows, fasts, observances, golden offerings, and the gratification of Brahmins.
Blessed by Him, offering salutations to Him, established in Him, and devoted to Him,
he worshipped Mahādeva, who dwells within the hearts of yogins.
As he was thus engaged, the supreme, divine form arising from Viṣṇu revealed its true nature to him at one time.
Having seen [her], he bowed his head to the beloved of the blessed Lord Viṣṇu,
and after praising her with various hymns, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Irindadyumna said:
"Who are you, O goddess of large eyes, auspicious one marked with the signs of Viṣṇu?
Tell me now truly what your nature is."
Having heard those words of his, the very gracious Sumaṅgalā,
smiling and remembering Viṣṇu, spoke these kind words to the Brāhmaṇa.
The sages and the gods, led by Śakra, do not see me;
I am the singular Māyā whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, and I am the supreme one composed of that.
Upon careful reflection, no difference exists between me and Nārāyaṇa;
I am composed of that, the Supreme Brahman, he is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord.
For those who perceive me here as the Supreme Lord, the refuge of all beings,
through knowledge and the yoga of action, I do not prevail over them.
Therefore, being devoted to the yoga of action, worship the Infinite One through knowledge— He who is without beginning or end— and thereby you shall attain liberation.
Thus addressed, that highly intelligent Indradyumna, the best of sages,
bowed his head to the Goddess and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke again.
"How can that Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, who is eternal, partless, and infallible, be known? O Goddess, O Supreme Mistress, tell me this."
Then, having been addressed thus by the brahmin, the goddess dwelling in the lotus said to that sage: "Nārāyaṇa himself will grant you knowledge. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.63)
Then, having touched the prostrate sage with both hands and remembering Viṣṇu, who is higher than the highest, he vanished right there.
He too, with supreme meditative absorption, sought to behold Nārāyaṇa and propitiated Hṛṣīkeśa, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him.
Then, after a long time had passed, Nārāyaṇa himself appeared, the great yogin clad in yellow garments, who is identical with the universe.
Seeing the Lord Viṣṇu, the imperishable Self, approaching,
he knelt upon the ground and praised the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Indradyumna said:
O Lord of Sacrifice, Acyuta, Govinda, Mādhava, Ananta, Keśava, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa; salutations to You, the Soul of the Universe. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.68)
Homage be to you, the ancient Hari, whose form is the universe,
the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction, and possessed of infinite power.
Salutations to you who are devoid of qualities; salutations to you whose self is partless and stainless. Salutations to you, the Puruṣa; salutations to you whose form is the universe.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, to Viṣṇu, the source of the universe;
salutations to you who are devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and who are attainable through knowledge.
Salutations to you who are changeless; salutations to you who are beyond all conceptual proliferation.
Let there be salutations to you who are devoid of both difference and non-difference, whose very form is bliss.
Homage to Tārā, the peaceful one; homage to you whose self is unimpeded;
homage again and again to you of infinite form, who are yourself formless.
Salutations to you, the ultimate reality; salutations to you who transcend illusion.
Salutations to you, the supreme lord, the Brahman, the supreme self.
Homage be to you, the most subtle; homage to you, Mahādeva.
Homage to Śiva, the pure; homage to you, the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
Everything has been created by you alone; you alone are the supreme goal.
You are the father of all beings, and you are the mother, O Puruṣottama.
You are the imperishable, supreme abode, pure consciousness, the partless void;
the unmanifest support of all, infinite, and beyond darkness.
They perceive the Supreme Self alone by means of the lamp of knowledge;
I take refuge in that form of yours, which is the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
To him who was thus praising, the Blessed One, the soul of all beings and the creator of all beings,
then touched [him] with both hands, as if smiling.
As soon as he was touched by the Blessed Viṣṇu,
that bull among sages came to know the supreme reality exactly as it is, through His grace.
Then, with a joyful mind, having prostrated before Janārdana—
the unswerving one, clad in yellow garments, whose eyes are like blossoming lotuses— he spoke.
O Supreme Person, by your grace, knowledge that has Brahman as its sole object—which bestows the attainment of supreme bliss—has undoubtedly arisen within me. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.82)
Homage to you, O Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the Creator!
O Lord of Yoga, O Pervader of the World, tell me: what shall I do? (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.83)
Having heard the words of Indradyumna, Mādhava Nārāyaṇa spoke these words with a smile, for the benefit of the entire world.
The Blessed Lord said:
For men who observe the conduct prescribed for their caste and stage of life, the Great Lord Maheśvara is to be worshipped through knowledge and the yoga of devotion, and not otherwise.
Having understood that supreme reality, as well as my manifestation, the cause and effect,
and my active engagement, one who seeks liberation should worship the Lord.
Having abandoned all attachments and knowing the world to be composed of illusion, contemplate the non-dual Self; you shall behold the Supreme Lord.
O Brahmin, understand from me as I describe the threefold cultivation (bhāvanā):
one among them has me as its object, the second relies upon the manifest (vyakta),
and the other cultivation is known as the Brahma-cultivation, which transcends the qualities (guṇātiga).
Then, the wise man should cultivate one of these meditations;
if he is incapable, he should resort to the first—such is the Vedic revelation.
Therefore, with every effort, being devoted to that and making it your supreme goal, propitiate the Lord of the Universe; through that, you shall attain liberation.
Indradyumna said:
What is that supreme reality? What is your manifestation, O Janārdana?
What is the effect, what is the cause, who are you, and what is your activity?
The reality higher than the highest is the supreme Brahman, one and immutable;
it is eternal bliss, self-luminous, imperishable, and beyond darkness.
His sovereignty is that which is eternally celebrated as his manifestation (vibhūti);
the world is his effect, while the unmanifest is his cause—pure and imperishable.
For I am the supreme Lord, the inner witness of all beings;
my activity is proclaimed as the agency over creation, preservation, and destruction.
Having understood all this in its entirety as it truly is with your inner being, O twice-born one,
you should then properly worship the Eternal One through the yoga of action.
Indradyumna said:
What are those duties of the castes and stages of life by which the Supreme is propitiated?
And what is that divine knowledge, established in the threefold contemplation?
How was this world created in the beginning, and how is it withdrawn again?
How many creations are there in the world, as well as lineages and Manvantaras?
What are their measures, and what are the purifying vows?

"Tell me now, O lotus-eyed one, everything exactly as it is: the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the locations of the sun and other celestial bodies, the length and breadth of the earth, how many continents (*dvīpa*), oceans, mountains, and rivers there are."
Śrī Kūrma said: Thus addressed by him, O best of sages, I then spoke everything in its entirety and exactly as it is, out of a desire to show grace to my devotees.
Having explained all of this that I was asked by the twice-born,
and having shown favor to that brahmin, I vanished right there.
That best of the twice-born, purified by his inner disposition and composed in mind, worshipped the Supreme One according to that very method prescribed by me.
Having abandoned affection for sons and others, free from the pairs of opposites and without possessions,
having renounced all actions, he takes recourse in supreme dispassion.
Having perceived the Self within the self, and having realized the entire universe within his own self,
he attained the final realization of Brahman, which is preceded by the Imperishable.
He attained the supreme yoga by which he perceives the One,
that which those desiring liberation long for— those who are sleepless and have conquered their breath.
Then, on one occasion, the lord of yogis went through the sky alone— by the power of his mastery over yoga— to the Mānasottara mountain to see the imperishable Brahmā, as directed by the Sun.
An unsurpassed celestial chariot, radiant as the sun, appeared;
the hosts of gods, gandharvas, and apsarases followed after it.
Seeing the lord of yogis on the path, others—siddhas and brahmin seers—proceeded along.
Then, having gone to the mountain, he entered that place worshipped by the gods,
frequented by yogis, where the Supreme Person resides.
Having reached that supreme abode, which possesses a splendor equal to ten thousand suns,
he entered the inner palace of the gods, which is difficult for others to approach.
He meditated upon the supreme refuge of all embodied beings,
the god who is without beginning or end, the God of gods, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
Then, from that [lotus], the light of the Supreme Self appeared;
in its midst, he beheld the primordial Person, the supreme state.
A great mass of splendor, inaccessible to those who hate the knowers of Brahman,
four-faced, with noble limbs, and adorned with rays of light.
Seeing that yogi standing before him with a prostration,
the Lord, the soul of the universe, went out to meet him himself and embraced him.
Then, from the body of that best of the twice-born as he was embraced by the Lord,
a great radiance emerged and entered the solar orb—
that pure and stainless state known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Where the blessed Hiraṇyagarbha dwells, the consumer of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors—
that is the primordial gateway of yogins, established in the Vedāntas;
it is composed of the splendor of Brahman, glorious, and the ultimate goal of the wise.
As soon as he was seen by the Blessed One, the sage, composed of light,
beheld the divine splendor— tranquil, all-pervading, and auspicious.
One's own self is the imperishable void, that supreme station of Viṣṇu;
it is the blissful, immovable Brahman, that abode of the Supreme Lord.
Having become the self of all beings and established in supreme sovereignty,
he attained his own abode, which is known as liberation and is imperishable.
Therefore, remaining with every effort established in the ordinances of caste and stage of life,
and having resorted to the final state of being, the wise man should cross over Māyā and Lakṣmī.
Sūta said:
Having been thus addressed by Hari, Nārada and the other great ṛṣis,
all together with Śakra, questioned the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
The sages said:
O God of gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, Lord Nārāyaṇa, stainless one!
Tell us in its entirety that which was previously spoken by you. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.120)
"O you who pervade the universe, this Śakra, your friend, is desirous of hearing from the brahmin Indradyumna the knowledge concerning dharma and other such matters."
Then that Blessed One Viṣṇu, Janārdana in the form of a tortoise,
the god who had gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala), was [approached] by Nārada and other great sages.
Being questioned, he proclaimed the entire, supreme *Kūrma Purāṇa* in the presence of the King of the Gods; that I shall now relate to you.
O Brahmins, listening to the Purāṇas and especially narrating them brings wealth, fame, long life, merit, and bestows liberation upon men.
Having heard even a single chapter, one is liberated from all sins;
or by hearing even a single episode, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
This supreme Purāṇa, the Kaurma, was spoken by the God of gods in the form of a tortoise; it should be faithfully accepted by the twice-born.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Pūrvavibhāga of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
The venerable Kūrma said: "Listen, all you sages, to that which is for the welfare of the world, about which I have been asked."
Everything that is about to be spoken by me was previously told to Indradyumna.
The Purāṇa, which bestows merit upon men and proclaims the dharma of liberation, is augmented by the deeds of those who have been, those who are, and those who will be. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.2)
"I was formerly the god Nārāyaṇa; there is nothing higher than me. Having resorted to the couch of the serpent, I was enjoying a vast sleep. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.3)
Then, having awakened at the end of the night, I reflected upon creation;
thereupon, O best of sages, a sudden clarity arose within me.
Then the four-faced Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was born;
in the meantime, at that time, anger arose from some cause.
O tigers among sages, there the god Maheśvara was born from the Self as Rudra, the son of Krodha, trident-bearing and three-eyed;
resembling the sun in brilliance, he appeared as if destroying the three worlds. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.6)
Then the goddess Śrī appeared, with large lotus-like eyes,
beautiful in form, gentle of countenance, and enchanting to all embodied beings.
She possessed a pure smile and was most serene; she was auspicious and the abode of greatness.
She was endowed with divine splendor and adorned with celestial garlands.
Nārāyaṇī, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the imperishable primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti),
sat down by my side, filling this space with her own radiance.

Having seen her, the Blessed Brahmā, the Lord of the World, said to me: "O Mādhava, employ this beautiful-formed one for the delusion of all beings, so that this vast creation of mine may increase. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.10)
Thus addressed, I spoke to the goddess Śrī as if laughing:
"O Goddess, having deluded this entire universe—including gods, asuras, and humans—cast it down into the cycle of worldly existence by my command. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.11)
Keep far away from those who are devoted to the yoga of knowledge, who are self-controlled, most firmly established in Brahman, exponents of Brahman,
free from anger, and dedicated to truth.
Avoid from afar those Brahmins who are meditative, free from possessiveness, tranquil, righteous, masters of the Vedas, reciters of mantras, and ascetics.
Keep far away from those Brahmins who have severed all doubts through their knowledge of the Vedas and Vedānta, and who are devoted to the great sacrifices.
Those who worship Maheśvara, the God of gods, with prayers, gold offerings,
Vedic study, and ritual sacrifices— avoid them with great effort from afar.
Keep far away from those pure ones who are endowed with the yoga of devotion, whose minds are offered to the Lord,
and who delight in breath control and other such practices.
Avoid those whose minds are fixed on the *praṇava*, who are devoted to the recitation of the *Rudra*, who study the *Atharvaśiras*, and who know the Dharma. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.17)
What need is there for much speaking here? Do not delude those who protect their own dharma and are devoted to the worship of the Lord, acting on my command.
Thus impelled by me, Mahāmāyā, the beloved of Hari, acted according to my instruction; therefore, one should worship Lakṣmī.
The consort of the Blessed One, when worshipped, bestows abundant prosperity, nourishment, intelligence, fame, and strength; therefore, one should worship Lakṣmī.
Then, by my command, that Blessed One Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, created all beings, both moving and unmoving, just as before.
By means of the science of yoga, he created Parīci, the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha.
These nine are the sons of Brahmā, Brahmins who are the best of Brahmins; they alone are exponents of the Veda, while Marīci and the others are the practitioners.
The omnipresent Lord, the Grandfather, created the Brāhmaṇas from his mouth, the Kṣatriyas from his arms,
the Vaiśyas from his two thighs, and the Śūdras from his feet.
For the accomplishment of sacrifice, Brahmā indeed created [the castes] with the exception of the Śūdra;
for from them, sacrifice shone forth for the protection of all the Vedas.
The Ṛg-veda, Yajur-veda, Sāma-veda, and likewise the Atharva-veda, are the innate form of Brahman; this is his eternal, undecaying power.
The divine speech, without beginning or end,
was emitted by the Self-Existent One in the beginning as consisting of the Vedas, from which all activities proceed.
Therefore, the wise man does not take delight in whatever other treatises exist upon this earth; by that, he is born as a heretic.
That which was ordained of old by the sages, the foremost knowers of the meaning of the Vedas, should be known as the supreme dharma; it is not established in other scriptures.
Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all of them are declared to be fruitless after death, resulting in the ultimate state of darkness.
In a former kalpa, all creatures that were born were free from all afflictions;
they were pure in their inner hearts and always devoted to their own duties.
Then, O tigers among sages, by the power of time, passion, hatred, and other such qualities arose among them— an unrighteousness that obstructed their own dharma.
Consequently, that innate accomplishment (siddhi) did not arise in them to any great extent;
instead, their other accomplishments at that time consisted merely of passion (rajas).
When those [arts] had been entirely exhausted by the course of time,
they once again established the means of livelihood through trade and the manual skills born of labor;
then the omnipresent Brahmā ordained their means of subsistence through work.
In the beginning, Svāyambhuva Manu, the seer of dharma, proclaimed the laws;
O twice-born ones, he was an incarnation of Prajāpati himself, sent forth by Brahmā.
Having heard those laws from his mouth, Bhṛgu and the others then spoke them forth.
Sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, receiving gifts, teaching, and studying—these are the six duties of the best of the twice-born, O Brāhmaṇas. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.36)
Giving, study, and sacrifice are the duties of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya;
for the Kṣatriya, punishment and warfare are prescribed, while for the Vaiśya, agriculture is commended.
For Śūdras, the means of accomplishing dharma is solely the service of the twice-born;
likewise, their livelihood consists of manual crafts, and according to dharma, they may also perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices.
Then, while the social classes were established, he established the stages of life:
the householder, the forest-dweller, the mendicant, and the student.
The maintenance of the sacred fires, service to guests, sacrifice, charity, and worship of the gods—
this, O best of sages, is the duty of the householder in brief.
Subsisting on roots and fruits, the study of sacred texts, austerity,
and the equitable distribution [of what one has]— this is the dharma of forest-dwellers.
Subsisting on alms, observing silence, austerity, meditation especially,
right knowledge, and detachment— this is considered the duty of a mendicant.
Begging for alms, service to the teacher, Vedic study,
the performance of twilight rituals, and the tending of the sacred fire— this is the duty of those in the stage of the religious student (brahmacārin).
O best of the twice-born, the Lotus-born One declared that the practice of celibacy is common to those living as students, forest-dwellers, and mendicants.
Approaching one's own wife only during her fertile period and not at other times—
except on the forbidden lunar days— is declared to be the celibacy (*brahmacarya*) of a householder.
Therefore, from the very moment of conception until birth, one must act with vigilance;
O best of Brahmins, he who fails to do so becomes a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā).
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, the performance of śrāddha rites, the honoring of guests,
and likewise the worship of the deities— this is the supreme duty of the householder.
One who has gone to another country or whose wife has died should kindle the domestic fire (vaivāhya) every evening and morning according to the prescribed rule.
Of the three stages of life, the householder is said to be the source;
the others depend upon him, therefore the householder’s stage is superior.
The single stage of life belongs to the householder, as seen in the Vedic revelation;
therefore, the state of the householder alone should be known as the sole means for accomplishing dharma.
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness;
however, one should not practice even righteousness if it is contrary to the whole world.
For from dharma wealth is born, and from dharma desire arises;
dharma alone leads to liberation; therefore, one should take refuge in dharma.
Dharma, artha, and kāma are considered the threefold aggregate (trivarga) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa):
sattva, rajas, and tamas; therefore, one should take refuge in dharma.
Those established in *sattva* go upward; those characterized by *rajas* remain in the middle;
and those characterized by *tamas*, abiding in the conduct of the lowest quality, go downward. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.54)
In that [state] where both wealth and pleasure are established in accordance with Dharma,
one becomes happy in this world and, after death, is fit for infinity.
From dharma liberation is born; from artha desire is produced.
Thus, the relationship between the means and the goal has been demonstrated within the fourfold system.
The man who knows this and practices the greatness of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
is fit for infinity.
Therefore, having abandoned both wealth and pleasure, one should take refuge in dharma;
for the exponents of Brahman say that everything is born from dharma.
By means of Dharma, the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—is sustained;
this is that power of Brahmā, O best of the twice-born, which is without beginning or end.
Dharma is attained through action and through knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, one should practice the yoga of action accompanied by knowledge.
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which is engaged (pravṛtta) and that which is withdrawn (nivṛtta).
That which is preceded by knowledge is withdrawn; that which is otherwise is engaged.
But by practicing that which is characterized by cessation, one goes to that supreme state;
therefore, that which is characterized by cessation should be practiced, for otherwise one will wander again in saṃsāra.
Forbearance, self-control, compassion, charity, freedom from greed,
renunciation, as well as straightforwardness, lack of malice, and likewise following the sacred fords.
Truthfulness, contentment, faith in the hereafter, devotion, restraint of the senses, worship of the deities, and especially the honoring of Brāhmaṇas; KūrmP_1.2.64.
Non-violence, pleasant speech, absence of backbiting, and freedom from guile—
Manu declared this to be the summary of the Dharma for the four castes.
The station of Prajāpati is ordained for Brāhmaṇas who perform their duties;
the station of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who do not flee in battles.
The station of the Maruts belongs to the Vaiśyas who follow their own duty;
that of the Gandharvas belongs to those of the Śūdra caste who subsist by service.
The very place that is prescribed for the eighty-eight thousand sages who have drawn up their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) is also the abode of those who dwell with their teacher (guruvāsin).
The place that is remembered as belonging to the Seven Sages is indeed for the forest-dwellers;
the station of the Prājāpatya order has been declared by the Self-Existent One to belong to householders.
That is the station of Hiranyagarbha, from which those ascetics who have controlled their minds, who have renounced all attachments, and whose vital energy is drawn upward, do not return again.
The immortal abode of yogis, known as the void, is the supreme syllable;
it is the blissful domain of Īśvara, that ultimate limit, and that highest goal.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, O slayer of the enemies of the gods, O destroyer of Hiraṇyākṣa!
Four stages of life (āśramas) have been proclaimed, yet for yogins, one alone is spoken of."
The venerable Kūrma said:
Having renounced all actions and having resorted to unwavering meditative absorption,
the yogin who remains motionless— he is the true renunciant, not the fifth kind.
Indeed, the twofold nature of all the stages of life (āśramas) is shown in the revealed scripture (Śruti):
the student (brahmacārin) is either the temporary student (upakurvāṇa) or the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) who is intent upon Brahman.
He who, having studied the Vedas according to the prescribed rules, enters the householder stage of life is to be known as an *upakurvāṇaka*; one who remains until death is a *naiṣṭhika*.
The householder may be of two kinds: the indifferent and the practitioner.
That householder who is diligent in supporting his family is the practitioner.
Having discharged the three debts and renounced wife, wealth, and so forth,
he who wanders alone and remains indifferent is one intent on liberation.
He who performs austerities in the forest, sacrifices to the gods, offers oblations,
and is devoted to the study of the Vedas is considered a forest-dwelling ascetic.
He who, having been excessively emaciated by austerity, becomes intent on meditation,
should be known as a renunciant (sāṃnyāsika) established in the forest-dweller stage of life (vānaprasthāśrama).

The mendicant who is constantly devoted to the practice of yoga, who desires to ascend [to liberation], and whose senses are conquered, proceeds toward knowledge; he is called one who has attained the supreme state.
But he who delights only in the Self, who is eternally content and a great sage,
perfected in right vision— he is called a yogi, a mendicant.
Some are renunciants of knowledge, others are renunciants of the Vedas, and some are renunciants of action; these are the three kinds of supreme seekers.

The yogi is to be known as being of three kinds: the materialist (bhautika), the follower of Sāṃkhya, and the third, who is declared to be one belonging to a religious order (āśramin) established in the supreme yoga.
The first contemplation (bhāvanā) is in the former [system], while the contemplation on the Imperishable (akṣara-bhāvanā) is in Sāṃkhya;
and in the third [system], the final contemplation is declared to be that of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvarī).
Therefore, understand this: there are four stages of life (āśramas) in all the Vedic scriptures; a fifth is not established.
Having thus created the castes and stages of life, the stainless God of gods, the soul of the universe, said to Dakṣa and the others: "Create various kinds of progeny."
At the word of Brahmā, the sons Dakṣa and others, the best of sages,
created all progeny, beginning with gods and humans.
Thus this Blessed One, Brahmā, is established in the capacity of the Creator;
I indeed shall protect this [universe], and the wielder of the trident will withdraw it.
Three forms are proclaimed— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
arising from the union of the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas with the Supreme Self.
They are mutually devoted to one another, for they depend upon each other for their livelihood;
bowing to one another, these supreme lords sport together in play.
The Brāhmī, the Māheśvarī, and likewise the Akṣarabhāvanā—
these three meditations, O twice-born ones, are constantly present in Rudra.
The first contemplation on the Imperishable proceeds toward me incessantly;
the second is declared to be the contemplation on the Imperishable of the divine Brahmā.
I and Mahādeva are not distinct from the perspective of ultimate reality;
having divided himself by his own will, that Lord remains as another.
In order to create the entire triple world, including gods, asuras,
and humans, the Puruṣa, who is beyond the unmanifest, attained the state of Brahman.
Therefore, Brahmā, Mahādeva, and Viṣṇu, the supreme Lord of the Universe,
are remembered as the three bodies of that one Lord alone, manifested according to the requirements of his purpose.
Therefore, with every effort, they should be saluted and worshipped diligently,
if one desires that imperishable state known as liberation which is attained without delay.

Endowed with devotion and joined with joy, one should worship with a sincere disposition, according to the dharma prescribed for one's caste and stage of life, throughout one's entire lifetime by means of a solemn vow.
O twice-born ones, among the four stages of life (āśramas), this Vaiṣṇava stage has been duly described; the Brāhma and the Hara stages constitute the other three.
Constantly wearing their respective insignia and affectionate toward those who are devoted to them,
one who is dedicated to the knowledge of Brahman should meditate upon and worship these [deities].
For all devotees of Śambhu, the unsurpassed liṅga should be fashioned on the forehead as a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with white sacred ash.
But he who has taken refuge in the god Nārāyaṇa, the supreme state,
should always apply a trident on his forehead with fragrant waters.
Those who have taken refuge in Brahmā, the supreme lord and seed of the universe,
should always wear a sectarian mark (tilaka) upon their foreheads.
That which is beginningless, the source of all beings, and the very soul of time— by wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) through its application above and below, that [Self] becomes sustained.

That which is Pradhāna, consisting of the three guṇas and having the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, certainly becomes [the bearer of the trident] by holding the trident; of this there is no doubt.
This white orb of the sun, consisting of Brahmanic splendor,
truly becomes the established station of the Lord when the tilaka is applied.
Therefore, for the three classes of devotees, the mark of the trident, the auspicious sectarian mark (*tilaka*),
and the triple-ash mark (*triyāyuṣa*) should be applied according to the prescribed ritual.

One who has conquered the senses, who is peaceful, self-controlled, and has subdued anger, and who knows the ordinances for the castes and stages of life, should sacrifice, offer oblations into the fire, mutter prayers, and give gifts. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.107)
Thus, with a concentrated mind, one should serve the gods for as long as life lasts;
he soon attains their immovable state.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The sages said:
"The four castes and likewise the four stages of life have been pointed out by the Blessed One."
Now, O Lord, tell us the sequence of our stages of life (āśramas).
The venerable Kūrma said:
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—these stages of life (āśramas) are declared to follow this very sequence; otherwise, it would be for a specific reason.
Having produced knowledge and discernment and having attained supreme detachment,
one should indeed go forth into the life of a celibate student if one desires the highest goal.
Having taken a wife according to the prescribed rites, he should otherwise worship with various sacrifices and procreate sons; if he becomes dispassionate, he may renounce the world.
Without having performed sacrifices according to the prescribed rules, and likewise without having procreated a son,
a wise twice-born man should not abandon the life of a householder to take up renunciation.
Then, if due to the force of dispassion he does not venture to remain at home,
the wise and best of the twice-born may renounce right there, even without having performed the [final] sacrifices.
Otherwise, having worshipped with various sacrifices, he should dwell in the forest;
and having performed austerities through the practice of yoga, if he becomes dispassionate, he should renounce.
Having entered the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), one should not enter a house again;
likewise, a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) does not go to the forest, nor does a seeker (sādhaka) practice celibacy (brahmācarya).
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, or alternatively the Āgneyī,
a learned twice-born householder may renounce from the forest, as enjoined by the Śruti.
Even if he is unable to perform the acts of *homa* and *yajña*,
a twice-born man who is blind, lame, poor, or dispassionate should renounce the world.
Detachment is prescribed for all who wish to undertake renunciation;
indeed, he who desires to perform renunciation while lacking detachment falls from his state.
Alternatively, a twice-born man endowed with faith, properly engaged in even a single stage of life until his death, is fit for immortality.
One who has acquired wealth through righteous means, who is tranquil, devoted to the knowledge of Brahman, and constantly protects his own dharma, is fit for immortality. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.3.13)
Having entrusted all actions to Brahman, free from attachment and devoid of desire, one who acts with a serene mind attains that supreme state. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.3.14)
That which is to be given is given by Brahman; it is offered to Brahman;
and it is Brahman itself that is given—this is the supreme offering to Brahman.
"I am not the doer; Brahman alone performs all this in such a manner.
This is declared by the seers who perceive the truth to be the 'offering unto Brahman' (brahmārpaṇa)."
"May the eternal Lord Īśa be pleased by this action;
he constantly performs this supreme offering to Brahman with his intellect. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.3.17)
Or else, one should perform the renunciation of the fruits of actions unto the Supreme Lord;
this too they call the unsurpassed offering to Brahman.
Whatever obligatory action is performed by the wise man as a mere duty, free from attachment—that action shall even grant liberation. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.3.19)
Otherwise, even if a twice-born man should perform rites constantly, if he does not renounce the fruits, he is bound by those very fruits. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.3.20)
Therefore, having abandoned with every effort the fruit dependent on action, even an ignorant person should perform action; he shall attain the supreme state without delay.
By means of ritual action, sin—both of this life and of former lives—is destroyed;
the mind attains clarity, and through that, Brahman is realized.
From knowledge conjoined with action, right yoga is born;
and knowledge conjoined with action arises free from defects. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.3.23)

Therefore, devoted to whichever stage of life he may be, one should perform all actions with every effort for the sake of pleasing the Lord; thus one shall attain the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).
Having attained supreme knowledge and the state of actionlessness through its grace,
one who is solitary, free from possessiveness, and tranquil is liberated even while living.
One beholds the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Great Lord, who is eternal bliss and devoid of appearance; one attains dissolution into that very state. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.3.26)
Therefore, with a serene intellect, one should constantly practice the yoga of action for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord; thus one attains that eternal state. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.3.27)
All this fourfold stage of life (cāturāśramya) has been declared to you as supreme;
for no human being attains perfection by transgressing it.
Thus ends the third chapter in the first section of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Having heard the complete rule for the stages of life (āśrama), the sages were delighted in their hearts.
Having paid homage to Hṛṣīkeśa, they spoke these words again:
The sages said:
"Everything concerning the four stages of life has been excellently explained by you;
now we wish to hear how the world comes into being."
From what has all this been born, and into what will it go to its dissolution? And who is the controller of all things? Tell me, O Supreme Person. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.4.3)
Having heard the words of the sages, Nārāyaṇa, assuming the form of a tortoise,
spoke with a profound voice concerning the origin and dissolution of all beings.
The venerable Kūrma said: Maheśvara is supreme, unmanifest, the eternal fourfold manifestation,
infinite, immeasurable, the controller, and facing in all directions.
That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, consisting of both being and non-being,
is what the seekers of truth call Pradhāna and Prakṛti.
It is devoid of smell, color, taste, sound, and touch;
it is undecaying, stable, imperishable, eternal, and established within its own self.
The source of the world, the great element, the supreme, eternal Brahman—
the great body of all beings, presided over by the Self.
Without beginning or end, unborn, subtle, composed of the three qualities, the source and the place of dissolution, beyond the present, and unknowable— Brahman existed in the beginning.
When the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) has been established in that Self, the Puruṣa,
it should be known as the primordial dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya), lasting until the emergence of the universe once again.
This night is said to be Brahma’s, and the day is declared to be his creation;
yet for him there is neither day nor night, for these are merely figurative designations.
At the end of the night, he who is the beginning of the world, himself without beginning,
consisting of all beings, unmanifest, the inner controller, and the supreme Lord, awoke.
Having swiftly entered both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, Maheśvara,
the Supreme Lord, agitated them by means of his supreme yoga.
Just as intoxication affects men and women, or as the spring breeze does,
so too did he, possessing a yogic form, enter [them] for the sake of agitation.
O Brahmins, that very Supreme Lord is both the agitator and the object of agitation;
through contraction and expansion, he remains even in the state of primordial matter (pradhāna).
From the primordial Pradhāna being agitated, and likewise from the ancient Puruṣa,
the Great Seed (mahadbīja) appeared, consisting of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa.

The Great Self, Intellect, Brahmā, Supreme Awakening, Renown, the Lord, Wisdom, Fortitude, Memory, and Consciousness—it is from this that [all these] are said to have originated. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.4.17)
The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi characterized by Tamas—
this threefold ego (ahaṅkāra) indeed arose from the Mahat.
Egoism and self-conceit are known as the agent and the thinker;
it is called the self (ātman), the person (pudgala), and the living being (jīva), from which all activities proceed. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.4.19)
From the ego (ahaṅkāra) were born the five elements and the subtle essences (tanmātrāṇi);
likewise, the sense organs and the gods—this entire world is his offspring.
The mind is said to be born from the unmanifest; it is recorded as the first transformation, by which that [self] becomes an agent and perceives the elements and so forth. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.4.21)
From the *vaikārika* ego (ahaṅkāra) arose the *vaikārika* creation;
from the *taijasa* [ego] the sense organs arise, and the ten deities are *vaikārika*.
The eleventh there is the mind (*manas*), which by its own quality partakes of both natures;
from this Bhūtādi proceeded the creation of the gross elements and the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), and from them, living beings were born.
But the *bhūtādi*, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of sound;
from that, space (*ākāśa*) arose, characterized by sound and possessing vacuity.
But space, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of touch;
from that, wind arises, and touch is considered its quality. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.4.25)
And Vāyu, undergoing transformation, indeed created the subtle element of form;
light is produced from Vāyu, and it is said to have form as its quality.
And the light, undergoing transformation, emitted the subtle element of taste;
from that, the waters came into being, which serve as the support for that taste.
And the waters, undergoing transformation, produced mere fragrance;
from that, the aggregate (saṃghāta) is born, and fragrance is considered its quality.
Space, which consists of sound alone, enveloped that which consists of touch alone;
from that, the twofold wind arose, having the nature of both sound and touch.
As he likewise enters into form, both qualities—sound and touch—are added;
thus fire becomes threefold, possessing sound, touch, and form.
Entering into sound, touch, form, and taste alone,
water should therefore be known as having four qualities and being essentially composed of taste.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell enter into it;
therefore, earth is called "gross" among the elements because it possesses these five qualities.
They are known as the specific qualities (viśeṣa) because they are tranquil, terrible, and deluded;
through their mutual interpenetration, they sustain one another.
These seven high-souled beings, due to their mutual dependence,
were unable to create progeny without coming together in their entirety.
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest (avyakta),
those [principles] beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Simultaneously produced like a bubble upon water,
that vast egg, resting upon the waters, arose from the subtle elements.
In that [egg], the accomplishment of the task of the Supreme Lord occurs;
having emerged from the elemental egg, he is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) designated as Brahmā.
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa.
He is the original creator of all beings; as Brahmā, he existed at the beginning.
They call him the Puruṣa, the Haṃsa, who stands beyond Pradhāna;
the eternal Hiraṇyagarbha, Kapila, whose form is the Vedic meters.
The spinal cord of that Supreme Self became Meru, the mountains became his placenta,
and the oceans were the amniotic fluid of that Supreme Self.
Within that egg was the entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans;
it contained the moon and the sun with the stars and planets, together with the wind.
The egg is surrounded on the outside by waters ten times its size,
and those waters are in turn surrounded on the outside by fire ten times their size.
Fire, possessing tenfold [the quality] of its predecessor, is enveloped on the outside by wind;
wind is enveloped by space, and space is enveloped by the source of the elements (bhūtādi).
Likewise, the origin of the elements (bhūtādi) is enveloped by the Great One (mahat), and the Great One is enveloped by the Unmanifest (avyakta).
These worlds belong to the Great Self (mahātman), who presides over all the principles (tattva).
There dwell men who have become one with that [Self], firmly established;
they are lords possessing the nature of yoga, as well as others who contemplate the principles of reality.
The omniscient ones, whose passion has been stilled and whose minds are eternally joyful,
[perceive that] this cosmic egg is enveloped by these seven elemental coverings.
O twice-born ones, this much can be said: this is the profound Māyā;
this is the primary effect which has been described by me as the seed;
"this is the supreme form of Prajāpati"—such is the Vedic revelation.
This entire cosmic egg, together with its seven levels of worlds,
is the second body of that supreme deity Parameṣṭhin.
The venerable Lord Brahmā, born from the golden egg, is Hiraṇyagarbha;
those who know the meaning of the Vedas declare him to be the third form of the Blessed One.
Another form of that very wise one consists of the quality of rajas;
as the four-faced Lord, he engages in the creation of the world.

And having himself resorted to the quality of *sattva*, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe and the Soul of the Universe who faces all directions, protects everything that has been created. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.4.51)
At the time of the end, the Lord himself, the Supreme Ruler who is the soul of all,
resorts to the quality of darkness and, as Rudra, withdraws the universe.
Though he is one, this Great God is established in three ways; though devoid of qualities and untainted, he abides through the qualities of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
He exists as one, as two, as three, and again as many.
The Lord of Yoga creates and transforms bodies by his own sport, endowing them with various forms, actions, appearances, and names.
For the very benefit of his devotees, he himself devours [the world] again;
having divided himself threefold, he proceeds through the three periods of time,
specifically creating, devouring, and observing.
Because he creates and then favors all beings, and again devours them—
since his nature consists of the *guṇas* throughout the three periods of time— he is therefore called the One.
In the beginning, that eternal Hiraṇyagarbha manifested;
because he is the primordial source, he is known as Ādideva, and because he is unborn, he is remembered as Aja.
Because he protects all creatures, he is remembered as Prajāpati;
and among the gods, he is remembered as Mahādeva, the Great God.
He is remembered as Brahmā because of his vastness; he is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) because of his transcendence;
and he is designated as Īśvara because of his mastery and because he is himself unmastered.
Because Hari is all-pervading, he is the Sage (Ṛṣi); because he takes away everything, he is the All-Remover (Sarvahara);
and because he is unproduced and prior to all, he is remembered as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū).
Because he is the path (ayana) for men (nara), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
he is Hara because he removes (haraṇa) the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), and he is called Viṣṇu because of his all-pervading power (vibhutva).
The Blessed One is remembered as "Aum" because he is all-knowing;
he is the omniscient one because of his universal knowledge, and he is the All since he consists of everything.
He is Śiva because he is pure, and he is the All-pervasive Lord (Vibhu) because he is omnipresent;
he is celebrated as the Savior (Tāraka) because he delivers one from all sufferings.
What need is there for much speaking here? The entire world consists of Brahman;
yet the Supreme Lord sports, divided into manifold distinctions.
Thus, O Brahmins, this primary creation has been briefly described by me as being devoid of prior intelligence; now learn of the creation of Brahmā.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The glorious Kūrma said:
"O best of the twice-born, such is the calculation of time for the self-existent one who has manifested."
It cannot be fully described even by oneself over many years.
In brief, the calculation of time is conceived as two *parārdhas*;
that indeed is the supreme time (*paraḥ kālaḥ*), at the end of which the world is re-absorbed.
By his own measure, his lifespan is recorded as one hundred years;
that is called a *parā*, and half of that is designated as a *parārdha*.
O best of the twice-born, fifteen *nimeṣas* are known as one *kāṣṭhā*;
thirty *kāṣṭhās* make one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* constitute the duration of one *muhūrta*.
A human day and night is said to consist of that same number of muhūrtas;
a month, consisting of two fortnights, consists of that same number of days and nights.
By those six [months] a solstice (*ayana*) is formed; two solstices constitute a year (*varṣa*).
The southern and the northern [solstices]: the southern solstice is the night of the gods, and the northern is their day.
The four yugas, known as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, consist of twelve thousand divine years; learn now their respective divisions.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga; its dawn (sandhyā) and its twilight (sandhyāṃśa) each last for as many hundreds of years.
The *saṃdhyā* periods consist of three hundred, two hundred, and one hundred [verses] respectively;
from that, the *kṛta-saṃdhyā* period consists of six hundred [verses], excluding its own *saṃdhyā* portion.

Therefore, in the knowledge of time, the durations of the Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are proclaimed as three, two, and one thousand years respectively, excluding the transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśaka). (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.5.10)
This [period] is calculated as twelve thousand years plus a little more;
seventy-one times that is said to be the interval between Manus (Manvantara).
O Brahmins, during one day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus:
all those beginning with Svāyambhuva, followed by those beginning with Sāvarṇika.
By those lords of men, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its mountains—
is indeed to be protected for a full thousand yugas.
By means of a single Manvantara, all intermediate periods (Antaras) are indeed explained;
there is no doubt that a Kalpa is likewise explained by means of a [single] Kalpa.
One day of Brahmā is a kalpa, and his night is held to be of the same duration;
the wise say that a kalpa consists of a thousand cycles of the four yugas.
O best of the twice-born, three hundred and sixty such kalpas constitute one year of Brahmā;
they know that a hundred of those years is called Parārdha.
At its conclusion, there is the dissolution of all principles (tattvas) into their own cause, which is primordial nature (prakṛti);
therefore, this is called by the wise the "primal reabsorption" (prākṛta-pratisaṃcara).
The dissolution of the triad of Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Īśāna into primordial nature (prakṛti) is proclaimed; and by the conjunction of time, their re-emergence occurs once again.
In this way, Brahmā, the elements, Vāsudeva, and Śaṅkara are created by Time alone; he himself devours them again.
This Blessed One is beginningless, infinite, undecaying, and immortal;
because he is omnipresent and independent, this Maheśvara is the self of all.
"There are many Brahmās, Rudras, and others such as Nārāyaṇa;
for the Lord Īśa alone is Time and the Seer—so says the Śruti. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.5.21)
O twice-born ones, one half of Brahmā’s lifespan, consisting of a parārdha, has already passed;
likewise, this is currently his eighth kalpa.
The seventh past kalpa is called Pādma by the wise;
the Vārāha kalpa now prevails, and I shall describe its details in detail.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The glorious Kūrma said:
There was a single, terrible ocean, undifferentiated and consisting of darkness.
Everything, beginning with the calm winds, is not perceived as anything at all.
Then, when that single ocean had arisen and all things moving and stationary had perished,
Brahmā appeared, possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, golden-hued and beyond the senses,
known as Brahmā Nārāyaṇa, then slept upon the waters.

And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa, the god whose nature is Brahman, the source and the dissolution of the world: KūrmP_1.6.4: "They cite this verse here concerning Nārāyaṇa, the god whose nature is Brahman, the origin and the end of the universe."
"Water was formerly called 'nārā' by name," so says the Śruti;
since it was his place of resort (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Having passed a period of night equal to a thousand yugas, at the end of that night,
he assumes the state of Brahmā for the purpose of creation.
Then, having discerned through inference that the earth was submerged within those waters, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) desired to effect its extraction.
Assuming the beautiful form of the Boar during his water-sports, he is invincible even to the minds of others; he is composed of speech and is known as Brahman.
For the sake of lifting up the earth, he entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) and,
supporting himself by his own power, the Uplifter of the Earth raised her up with his tusk.
Having seen the earth resting upon the tip of his tusk,
the Siddhas and Brahman-sages dwelling in the world of Janas praised Hari, whose prowess is renowned.
The sages said:
"Salutations to you, the God of gods, to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
to the Ancient Puruṣa, the Eternal, and the Victorious. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.6.11)
Salutations to you, the self-existent, the creator who knows all things;
salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, the ordainer, the supreme self.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu, the source of the universe,
the divine Nārāyaṇa, who acts for the welfare of the gods.
Homage be to you, O four-faced one, who bear the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the sword;
homage again and again to the one who is the self of all beings and the immovable pinnacle.
Homage to the secret essence of the Vedas; homage to you, the source of the Vedas!
Homage to the pure Buddha; homage to you, whose form is primordial wisdom!
Salutation be to the one whose form is bliss, the witness of the worlds;
salutation to the infinite and immeasurable one, both the effect and the instrument.
Salutations to you who consist of the five elements; salutations to the self of the five elements.
Salutations to the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti); salutations to you whose form is māyā.
Homage be to you, the Boar; homage to you in the form of the Fish;
homage to you who are attainable through yoga; homage to you, the Attractor (Sakarṣaṇa).
Salutations to you, the three-formed one, who possesses the three abodes and divine splendor;
salutations to the perfected one, the worshipful one, who manifests the three qualities.
May there be darkness for Him who has the color of the sun; salutations to You, the lotus-born one!
Salutations to the formless and the formed; repeated salutations to Mādhava!
Everything created by you alone shall return to dissolution in you;
protect this entire world, for you are the protector, the refuge, and the ultimate resort. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.6.21)
Thus praised by Sanaka and the others, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu,
the Sovereign in the form of the Boar, bestowed his grace upon them.
Then, having brought the earth to its proper state, the lord of the earth,
Prajāpati, released his form while retaining it within his mind.
Above that flood of water, she stands like a great ship;
and because her body is so vast, the earth does not undergo submersion.
Having leveled the earth, he then gathered all the mountains that had been burnt during the previous dissolution; thereafter, he set his mind upon the creation.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
The venerable Kūrma said: As he was contemplating creation at the beginning of the Kalpas, just as before—
A creation consisting of darkness (tamas) appeared, not preceded by conscious intent.
Darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, and that which is called blinding darkness—
this fivefold ignorance manifested from the Great Self.
The creation of that conceited one who was meditating existed in five states;
it was enveloped by darkness and covered by the world-seed and the cosmic egg.
Those who have hair on their bodies, who are without luster, rigid, and devoid of consciousness—
these are called the Mukhya-nagas, and that is remembered as the Mukhya-sarga (the primary creation).
Seeing that creation to be unsuccessful, the Lord conceived another;
as he was meditating, a creation consisting of animals (tiryak-strotas) came forth.
Because it flows horizontally, it is therefore known as the "horizontal stream" (tiryak-srotas);
those who follow it, O twice-born ones, are renowned as cattle and other animals that tread upon the wrong path.
Knowing that [creation] also to be ineffective, he indeed created another creation;
it is called "upward-stream" (ūrdhva-srotas), the divine creation characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
Abounding in happiness, they are unobstructed both internally and externally;
luminous within and without by their very nature, they are designated as "gods."
Then, as he was meditating upon the truth with unwavering intent, there emerged from that Unmanifest the "downward-stream" (arvāk-srotas), which is the means for spiritual realization.
And those humans are proclaimed to be abundant in light, yet dominated by darkness (tamas), excessive in passion (rajas), intense in suffering, and endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva).
Having seen that [creation], the unborn Lord conceived of another creation;
as he meditated upon that creation, the creation beginning with the *bhūta* (the unevolved) came into being.
All of them were without possessions and delighted in sharing; furthermore, those beginning with the Bhūtas are proclaimed to be without food and without moral discipline.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, these five creations have indeed been described.
The first creation is to be known as that of Mahat, which belongs to Brahmā;
the second, however, is the creation of the subtle elements (tanmātras), which is remembered as the creation of the gross elements (bhūtas).
The third creation, however, is known as the Vaikārika or Aindriyaka;
thus is this Prākṛta creation, which has arisen without prior conscious intent.
The fourth is the primary creation (mukhyasarga), for the primary beings are known as the stationary (sthāvara);
that which is called the transverse-stream (tiryakstrotas) is the fifth, consisting of those born of animal wombs (tiryagyoni).

Likewise, the sixth creation of the gods is recorded as that of the *ūrdhvasrotas* (those whose stream flows upward); thereafter, the seventh creation is that of the *avākśrotas* (those whose stream flows downward), which is the human race.
The eighth creation is proclaimed as the elemental (bhautika), consisting of the elements and so forth;
the ninth is the primal (kaumāra) creation, which is both natural (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta).
O best of sages, the first three creations were natural and not preceded by conscious intent; from the primary creation onwards, however, they proceed with conscious intent.
In the beginning, Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, indeed created from his own mind his mental sons who were equal to himself:
Sanaka, Sanātana, and likewise Sanandana,
as well as Ṛbhu and Sanātkumāra, even before [the other beings].
These five Brahmin yogins, established in supreme detachment and with their minds fixed on the Lord, directed no thought toward creation.
When they were thus indifferent toward the creation of the world, Prajāpati suddenly became deluded by the illusion of the supreme Lord Māyin.
The great sage Nārāyaṇa, the supreme yogi who delights the minds of yogis, awakened his son, who was like the illusion of the world.
Thus instructed by him, the Soul of the Universe performed supreme austerity;
though he was performing that penance, the Blessed One did not attain anything.
Then, after a long time, anger arose from his suffering;
from the eyes of him who was possessed by anger, drops of tears fell.
From his forehead, which was furrowed with a frown, the Supreme Lord Mahādeva emerged— the blue-and-red one who is the refuge of all.
He alone is the Blessed Lord, the eternal mass of splendor,
whom the wise perceive as the Supreme Lord abiding within their own selves.
Having recollected the syllable Oṃ and having bowed with palms joined in reverence, the Blessed Brahmā said: "Create these various kinds of progeny."
Having heard these words, the blessed Śaṅkara, whose vehicle is dharma, the auspicious one,
created by his mind Rudras equal to himself—
wearing their hair in matted locks, free from affliction, three-eyed, and blue-and-red in hue.
The Blessed Brahmā said to him: "Create subjects endowed with birth and death. He replied: "I shall not create subjects possessed of death and old age;
O Lord of the World, you yourself create such inauspicious subjects."
Having then restrained Rudra, the Lotus-born One created all those who possess pride regarding their respective stations; listen as he speaks of them.
Water, fire, the intermediate space, heaven, wind, earth,
as well as rivers, oceans, mountains, trees, and even creepers.
The lava-s, kāṣṭhā-s, kalā-s, muhūrta-s, days, nights,
half-months, months, solstices, years, yugas, and so forth.
Having created those who pride themselves on their status, he then created the *sādhakas*:
Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Dharma, and Saṃkalpa. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.7.33)
From his breath the god Brahmā created Dakṣa, from his eye Marīci,
from his head Aṅgiras, and from his heart Bhṛgu.
From his two ears, the Grandfather of all the worlds produced the one named Atri through determination, as well as Dharma from determination, and Saṃkalpa from Saṃkalpa.
From Udāna he likewise [beheld] Pulastya, and from Vyāna the sage Pulaha;
from Apāna he beheld the composed Kratu, and from Samāna, Vasiṣṭha.
Thus these practitioners and householders were created by Brahmā;
assuming human form, they set the Dharma in motion.
Then, desiring to create the fourfold [world]— the gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans— he joined his own self to these waters.
In the Prajāpati of disciplined soul, the quality of darkness (tamas) became predominant;
from that, his sons, the Asuras, were first born from his hindquarters.
Having created the Asuras, the Supreme Person cast off that body;
and that body, once cast off by him, immediately became night,
because it was preponderant with darkness (tamas) and because living beings slept during it.
The Lord assumed another body consisting of pure sattva;
from the mouth of that playing deity, the gods were born.
That body was also abandoned by him, and the day became filled with living beings;
therefore, the gods, endowed with righteousness, worship that day.
Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of *sattva*;
as he regarded it as his father, the Pitṛs were born from him.
Having created the ancestors, the Creator of the Universe then cast off that body as well;
that discarded body immediately became the twilight (sandhyā).
Therefore, day belongs to the gods, and night to those who hate the gods;
between the two, the form of the ancestors, the twilight (sandhyā), is most venerable.
Therefore, all the gods and asuras, as well as the Manus and human beings,
being disciplined, then worship that intermediate form [of the Lord] which exists between night and day.
Brahmā assumed another body consisting of the quality of rajas;
from that, his sons were born, humans enveloped by rajas.
The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) also quickly abandoned that body immediately;
O brahmins, it became the moonlight which is designated as the morning twilight.
Then, O best of the twice-born, that Blessed Brahmā,
having attained that form consisting primarily of *tamas* and *rajas*, joined it once again.
In that darkness, there were born to him Rākṣasas overcome by hunger;
his sons were powerful night-stalkers, consisting mostly of the qualities of Tamas and Rajas.
Serpents, yakṣas, as well as rākṣasas and gandharvas were born;
thereafter, the Lord created others who were possessed by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
Having created birds from his vital energy (*vayas*), he produced goats from his chest;
he created other animals from his mouth and fashioned cows from his belly.

From his feet were born horses along with elephants, donkeys, gayals, deer, camels, mules, antelopes, and other species; and from his body hair grew medicinal herbs that bear both fruits and roots. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.7.53)
From his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatrī, the Ṛg-veda, the Trivṛt-sāman, the Rathantara, and the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices.
From his southern mouth, he emitted the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh metre, the fifteen-fold Stoma, the Bṛhat Sāman, and likewise the Uktha.
From his western mouth, he created the Sāman chants, the Jāgata meter, the seventeen-fold Stoma, the Vairūpa, and the Atirātra sacrifice.
From his northern mouth, he created the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvāṇa, the Āptoryāmaṇa, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Svarāja.
High and low beings were born from his limbs as Prajāpati Brahmā was indeed creating the emanation of progeny.
Having created the fourfold creation— consisting of gods, sages, ancestors, and humans—
he then created all beings, both stationary and moving.
Yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, and likewise auspicious apsarases; nāgas, kinnaras, and rakṣasas; birds, cattle, wild animals, and serpents;
the imperishable and the perishable—the dual nature of both the stationary and the moving.
Whatever actions those beings performed in a previous creation,
those very same actions they encounter again and again as they are created anew.

Whether violent or non-violent, mild or cruel, righteous or unrighteous, truthful or false—conditioned by those very qualities, they enter into them; therefore, each finds pleasure in that which accords with their own nature.
The Creator himself ordains the diversity among the great elements, the sense objects, and physical forms, as well as the specific functions of those elements.
In the beginning, that Great Lord fashioned from the very words of the Veda the names and forms of all beings, as well as the expansion of their activities.
The Unborn One bestows upon those born at the end of the night exactly those names belonging to the Ṛṣis and those visions found in the Vedas.
Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle,
so too do those very same things reappear at the beginnings of the Yugas.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The glorious Kūrma said:
"In this manner, all beings were created, both the immobile and the mobile."
And when the offspring created by that wise one did not increase, KūrmP_1.8.1.
Enveloped by the quality of darkness (tamas), Brahmā then grieved in distress;
thereafter, he applied his intellect toward the determination of the goal.
Then he beheld within himself the limiting power of *tamas*,
which exists by its own nature, having veiled both *rajas* and *sattva*.
Thereafter, that darkness was dispelled by the Rajas joined with the Sattva;
indeed, when that darkness was driven back, a pair was produced.
O Brahmins, because of the practice of unrighteousness and violence characterized by inauspiciousness,
Brahmā then cast off that radiant body of his.
He divided his body again into two parts; with one half he became a man, and with the other half a woman. The Lord, the Puruṣa, created Virāj from that man.
And he created a beautiful woman named Śatarūpā, a yoginī;
she remained pervading both heaven and earth by her own greatness.
Endowed with the power of yogic sovereignty and possessed of both knowledge and realized wisdom,
he who became the son of the Unmanifest-born Puruṣa was Virāj.
The divine Manu Svāyambhuva became that Puruṣa, the Sage;
and that goddess, known as Śatarūpā, having performed most difficult austerities, [became his consort].
She followed after Manu alone, the son of Brahmā and her husband;
and from him, Śatarūpā gave birth to two sons.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were born, along with two most excellent daughters; Manu gave one of those daughters to Dakṣa as a wife.
Then Prajāpati Mānasa took Ruci as his wife;
from that Mānasa Ruci, a beautiful pair was born of Ākūti: Yajña and Dakṣiṇā, by whom the world was nourished. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.8.12)
From the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the sacrifice, twelve sons were born;
they are known as the Yāma gods in the Svāyaṃbhuva interval.
And likewise, Dakṣa begot twenty-four daughters through Prasūti; learn their names correctly. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.8.14)
Faith, Fortune, Fortitude, Contentment, Nourishment, Intelligence, Action, as well as Wisdom, Modesty, Body, Peace, Success, and Fame as the thirteenth.
Dharma accepted the auspicious daughters of Dakṣa as his wives;
from among them, eleven younger sisters with beautiful eyes remained.
Khyāti, Satya, Sambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā, as well as Santati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.8.17)
Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, as well as the sage Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu, who is the knower of the supreme dharma. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.8.18)
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Vahni, and the Pitṛs—these best of sages received the daughters beginning with Khyāti in due order. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.8.19)
Lust is known as the son of faith; pride is said to be the son of Lakṣmī;
restraint is the son of fortitude, and contentment is said to be the son of satisfaction.
From Puṣṭi was born Lābha, as well as Medhāputra and Śruta;
from Kriyā were born Daṇḍa and Samaya as sons.
From Buddhi was born her son Bodha, and likewise Apramāda was born; from Lajjā came her son Vinaya, and from Vapus came Vyavasāya.
Kṣema was born as the son of Śānti, and likewise Sukha and Siddhi were born; Yaśas was the son of Kīrti—these are the sons of Dharma.
Harṣa was the son of Kāma, and Devānanda was born from him;
thus has this creation of Dharma, which results in happiness, been proclaimed.
For from Adharma, Hiṃsā (Violence) was indeed born, as well as her son Nikṛti (Deceit) and Anṛta (Untruth).
From Nikṛti and Anṛta were born Bhaya (Fear) and Naraka (Hell).
Māyā and Vedanā indeed formed a couple;
then, out of fear, Māyā gave birth to Death (Mṛtyu), the destroyer of beings.
Then from Raurava were born Feeling and Folly;
furthermore, Suffering was born, and from Death arose Disease, Old Age, Sorrow, Thirst, and Anger.
For all these are known to be overcome by suffering and characterized by unrighteousness;
they have neither wife nor son, for they are all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
"Thus this creation characterized by darkness (tāmasa) was born, which regulates dharma.
O best of sages, I have described this emanation to you in brief."
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Pūrvavibhāga of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having heard these words, Nārada and the other great sages—
Having bowed down to Viṣṇu, the bestower of boons, they, filled with doubt, questioned him.
The sages said:
"O Janārdana, the creation of the primary beings and others has been described by you.
Now, you ought to dispel this doubt of ours."
How did that Blessed Lord Īśa, the primordial progenitor and wielder of the Pināka bow,
become the son of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest?
And how did the Blessed One come to know that Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, was born from an egg as the Lord of all beings? You should tell us this here.
The venerable Kūrma said: Listen, all you sages, to how Śaṅkara, of immeasurable splendor,
became the son of Brahmā and how he came to possess the state of being born from a lotus.
At the conclusion of the past kalpa, the three worlds were shrouded in darkness;
everything was a single ocean, where there were no gods and no sages.
There, in a solitary and undisturbed place, the divine Nārāyaṇa,
the Supreme Person, reclined upon his serpent-couch and fell asleep.
Having become thousand-headed, he is thousand-eyed and thousand-footed;
he is thousand-armed, the omniscient one, contemplated by the wise.
