Clad in yellow garments, large-eyed, resembling a dark blue cloud,
possessed of great majesty, the soul of yoga, he is the abode of the hearts of yogins.
Once, while he was asleep, there appeared from his navel for the sake of sport a divine, wonderful,
stainless lotus, the essence of the three worlds.
Extending for a hundred yojanas, resembling the rising sun,
it is meritorious, filled with divine fragrance, and endowed with a pericarp and filaments.
While the wielder of the Śārṅga bow remained in that state for such a very long time,
the blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha approached that place.
The Soul of All, deluded by his illusory power (māyā), raised that eternal one up with his hand and spoke these sweet words: KūrmP_1.9.13.
"In this terrible, solitary, and darkness-enveloped single ocean, who are you that lie here alone? Tell me, O bull among men."
Having heard those words of his, the one whose banner is Garuḍa smiled and spoke to the god Brahmā in a voice as deep as a thundercloud: Kūrma Purāṇa 1.9.15.
"O, O Nārāyaṇa, know me to be the god Nārāyaṇa, the source and dissolution of the worlds, the great Lord of Yoga, the Supreme Person."
Behold within me the entire universe, including you, O Grandfather of the worlds,
together with the mountains and great continents, surrounded by the seven oceans.
Having spoken thus, Hari, the Great Yogi, though already knowing, addressed the Creator Brahmā, asking, "Who are you? KūrmP 1.9.18.
Then the Lord Brahmā, the master and treasury of the Vedas, smiling,
replied with gentle words to the lotus-eyed one.
I am the sustainer and the ordainer, the self-existent Great-Grandfather;
the entire universe is established in me alone, for I am Brahmā, whose face is turned in every direction.
Having heard these words, the Blessed Viṣṇu, whose prowess is truth,
then took leave and entered the body of Brahmā through his yogic power.
Having seen this entire triple world, including the gods, asuras, and humans,
within the belly of that deity, he was filled with wonder.
Then, having emerged from his mouth, the blessed Ajātaśatru, whose abode is the king of serpents, spoke to the Grandfather.
O bull among men, you too should likewise enter these worlds today and behold these various wonders, which are eternally enchanting. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.9.24)
Then, having heard those heart-gladdening words and having rejoiced in them,
Kuśadhvaja entered once more into the belly of the Lord of Śrī.
He of true prowess beheld those very worlds situated within the womb;
yet, though he wandered about, he did not see the end of the divine Hari.
Then all the gates were closed by the high-souled Janārdana; thus, Brahmā could find no opening at the navel.
There, having entered by the power of yoga, that four-faced one born from the golden egg assumed his own form from the lotus.
Seated upon a lotus, possessing a splendor like the interior of a lotus,
the Lord Brahmā is self-born, the source of the universe, and the Grandfather.
Recognizing himself as the Lord of All and the supreme state,
he addressed the Puruṣa Viṣṇu with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
"What have you done now out of a desire for victory over yourself? I alone am powerful; who indeed could withstand me? (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.9.31)
Having heard these words of Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds, Hari Nārāyaṇa spoke these sweet words in a conciliatory manner.
"You are the sustainer and the creator, the self-existent great-grandfather;
it was not through the influence of envy that the doors were closed to me."
But this is solely for the sake of sport, not with the desire to cause you harm;
for who would wish to harm the Grandfather, the God of gods? (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.9.34)
"You must not understand this otherwise; you are to be honored by me in every way.
Whatever noble lineage of yours has been taken away by me, [I restore it]."
And for this reason, O Brahman, may you become my son,
renowned as Padmayoni, for the sake of my pleasure, O you who pervade the universe.
Then that Blessed Lord, having granted the boon to the wearer of the diadem (Arjuna) and having attained incomparable joy, spoke again to Viṣṇu.
You are the soul of all, the infinite, the supreme lord of all;
you are indeed the inner self of all beings, the eternal Supreme Brahman.
I am indeed the Self of all worlds, the Great Lord of the universe;
all this is composed of me alone; I am Brahmā, the Supreme Puruṣa.
Indeed, there exists no other supreme lord of the worlds than us two;
the single form is divided into two, as Nārāyaṇa and Pitāmaha.
Thus addressed by him, Vāsudeva said this to Brahmā:
"This vow of yours will lead to your own destruction."
Do you not see the Lord of Yoga, the imperishable sovereign of Brahmā, the lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa? I know him to be the Supreme Lord.
Go for refuge to that very Brahman, the Great Lord, who is without beginning or end, whom the lords of yogis and even the followers of Sāṃkhya do not perceive. KūrmP 1.9.43.
Then, enraged, Brahmā spoke to Keśava, whose eyes resemble lotuses:
"Surely you do not know yourself to be that supreme, imperishable [Brahman]."
"Brahmā is the one Self of all worlds, the supreme state;
indeed, there exists no other Supreme Lord of the worlds besides us two."
"Abandoning this excessive sleep, behold your own self!
Hearing those words born of his anger, Viṣṇu spoke.
"Do not speak thus, O auspicious one; do not speak ill of the Great-Souled One. Nothing is unknown to me, O Brahmin; I do not speak otherwise. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.9.47)
But, O Brahmin, the supreme illusion of the Lord,
which arises from the Self and is the cause of all particularities, deludes you.
Having spoken thus much, the Blessed Viṣṇu became silent,
having realized that supreme reality, his own self as Maheśvara.
Then, from somewhere, Hara— the immeasurable self and supreme lord of all beings—
manifested himself in order to bestow his grace upon Brahmā.
With an eye on his forehead, infinite, adorned with a circle of matted locks, the Blessed One holds a trident in his hand; he is the supreme treasury of splendors.
Wearing a divine, vast, and most wondrously formed garland, strung with the planets along with the sun, moon, and stars, which hung down to his feet.
Having seen that Lord Īśāna, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
was utterly deluded by his *māyā*, and he addressed him who was clothed in yellow garments.
"O Janārdana, who is this infinite person, trident-bearing and three-eyed, a mass of splendor and immeasurable soul, who approaches? (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.9.54)
Having heard those words of his, Viṣṇu, the crusher of demons,
beheld the Lord God blazing within the pure waters.
Having understood that supreme state of the Lord, which consists of the contemplation of Brahman,
the Blessed One rose and spoke to the Grandfather, the God of gods.
This god is Mahādeva, self-luminous and eternal;
without beginning or end, inconceivable, the great Lord of the worlds.
Śaṅkara, Śambhu, Īśāna, the Self of All, the Supreme Lord,
the Sovereign of Beings, the Yogi, Maheśa, the Immaculate, Śiva.
He is the Ordainer and the Disposer, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa;
him the ascetics, purified by the state of Brahman, behold.
Becoming Time, Mahādeva—the solitary, partless Śiva—creates this entire universe, protects it, and likewise withdraws it. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.9.60)
"He who is eternal appointed you as Brahmā in the beginning and bestowed the Vedas upon you; that very Śaṅkara is now approaching."
And know me, O Great-Grandfather, as another eternal form of this very [Brahman], the source of the universe, designated by the name Vāsudeva.
"Do you not see the Lord of Yoga, the imperishable Sovereign of Brahman?
Let there be divine vision for you, by which you shall behold that Supreme."
Then, having regained his divine vision through Śiva, Viṣṇu, the grandfather of the worlds,
perceived the Supreme Lord standing before him.
Having obtained that supreme divine knowledge,
the great-grandfather sought refuge in that very god, his father Śiva.
Having recollected the syllable *oṃ* and steadied himself by means of his own self,
he praised the God with the *Atharvaśiras*, his hands joined in reverence.
The Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, being thus praised by Brahmā,
attained supreme delight and spoke as if smiling.
"You are equal to me, of this there is no doubt, because you are my devotee;
I myself created you long ago, imperishable one, for the purpose of creating the world."
"You are indeed my own self, the primordial person, born from my body.
Choose a boon, O Soul of the Universe; I am the giver of boons to you, O sinless one."
Having heard the words of the God of gods, the lotus-born Brahmā looked at Viṣṇu, the Supreme Being, and after bowing down, spoke to the bull-bannered Śiva.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Great God, Consort of Ambikā,
I desire you alone as my son, or a virtuous being equal to you.
O Mahādeva, I am deluded by your subtle māyā;
O Śiva, I do not know your supreme nature as it truly is.
O Lord, you alone are the brother, mother, father, and friend of your devotees;
be gracious, for I have come to you for refuge and bow at your lotus feet.
Having heard his words, the bull-bannered Lord of the World then spoke, looking toward his son Janārdana.
"O dear son, I shall do whatever has been requested by the Blessed One;
O sinless one, divine and sovereign consciousness shall arise within you."
"You alone have been appointed as the primordial creator of all beings;
therefore, O Lord of Gods, O Grandfather of the World, act accordingly through me."
"This Nārāyaṇa Ananta is my own supreme body;
he shall be your lord, Hari, who provides for your security and well-being."
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord, with a joyful soul, touched the god Brahmā with both hands and addressed Hari with these words.
"I am entirely satisfied with your devotion, O you who pervade the universe!
Choose a boon; for in the ultimate sense, we two are not distinct."
Then, having heard the words of the god, Viṣṇu, who pervades the entire universe,
looked upon the four-faced one and spoke with a gracious voice.
This alone is the boon to be praised: that I behold the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self; may my devotion be fixed upon you. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.9.81)
Having said "So be it," Mahādeva spoke again to Viṣṇu:
"You are the performer of every task; I am merely the presiding deity."
All this is composed of you and composed of me; of this there is no doubt.
You are the moon and I am the sun; you are the night and I am the day.
You are primordial nature (prakṛti) and the unmanifest (avyakta), and I am indeed the person (puruṣa);
you are knowledge (jñāna) and I am the knower (jñātṛ); you are illusion (māyā) and I am the Lord (īśvara).
You are the power whose nature is knowledge, and I am the Lord who possesses that power;
I, who am the God entirely devoid of parts, am also that supreme Nārāyaṇa.
The yogins who discourse upon Brahman perceive you through a state of oneness. O Soul of the Universe, no yogin shall reach me without taking refuge in you;
protect this entire world, including its gods, asuras, and humans.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, who is without beginning and who has deluded the distinctions between beings through his own māyā,
departed for that state which is devoid of birth, old age, and destruction.
The one abode is unmanifest, possessing infinite power.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the first section of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
The venerable Kūrma said:
When the Lord Maheśvara had departed for his own abode, the Grandfather (Brahmā) [remained].
He resorted to that very same immense lotus that had arisen from his navel.
Then, after a long time, two great asuras of incomparable prowess, the brothers Madhu and Kaiṭabha, arrived there.
Possessed by great wrath, those two with bodies like massive mountains emerged from the ears of the god of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Seeing that they had arrived, the unborn and all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa said:
"You ought to slay these two asuras, who are thorns to the three worlds."
Having heard those words of his, the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa commanded two men to slay them both.
O twice-born ones, by his command a great battle took place between those two [demons] and the two [deities];
Viṣṇu slew Kaiṭabha, and Jiṣṇu slew Madhu.
Then Hari, his mind filled with affection, addressed these sweet words to the Grandfather, the Lord of the World, who was seated upon the lotus throne.
"O Lord, descend from the lotus as you are being requested by me;
I am not able to bear you, for you are heavy and composed of radiant energy."
Then, having descended and entered the body of the wielder of the discus, the Soul of the Universe,
becoming one with Viṣṇu, spoke the Vaiṣṇavī sleep.
Then that one known as Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, possessing a thousand heads and eyes and bearing the conch, discus, and mace, slept upon the waters.
Having experienced for a long time the bliss of the Supreme Self—
beginningless, endless, non-dual, and designated as Brahman— he realizes his own self.
Then, at dawn, the four-faced god, having become absorbed in yoga and having resorted to the Vaiṣṇava state, emitted a creation of that same nature.
In the beginning, the Lord created Sananda and Sanaka,
as well as Ṛbhu, Sanatkumāra, and that eternal one who was born first.
Freed from the delusion of dualities and established in supreme detachment,
they realized the ultimate reality and set their minds no longer upon creation.
When they were thus indifferent toward the creation of the world, the Grandfather (Brahmā) became indeed bewildered in mind by the illusory power (māyā) of the Supreme Lord.
Then Janārdana, the Ancient Being, whose form is the universe,
spoke to his son, the lotus-born [Brahmā], for the sake of destroying delusion.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Lord, have you not forgotten the eternal god Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident,
who declared himself to be your son?"
Having regained consciousness from Govinda, the lotus-born Grandfather,
desiring to create progeny, performed a most difficult penance.
As he was thus performing austerities, nothing at all came to pass;
then, after a long time, anger arose from his suffering. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.10.19)
From the eyes of him who was possessed by anger, drops of tears fell;
from those drops of tears, beings and pretas likewise came into existence.
Seeing all those born of his tears, Brahmā reproached himself;
and the Lord Prajāpati, overcome with anger, gave up his life-breaths.
Then Rudra, consisting of vital breath, emerged from his mouth,
resembling a thousand suns and like the fire at the end of an eon.
The God of gods, Śiva himself, wept with a loud and terrible cry.
Then Brahmā said to him as he was weeping, "Do not weep;
because of this weeping, you shall attain fame in the world as Rudra. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.10.23)
The Grandfather of the worlds gave seven other names, eternal wives and sons, and the stations for these eight.
Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Bhīma, Ugra, and Mahādeva—these indeed are the seven names. (KūrmP 1.10.25)
The Sun, water, the earth, fire, wind, space,
the initiated Brāhmaṇa, and the Moon— these are the eight forms (mūrtis).
To those who meditate upon and bow down to Rudra in these places,
the eight-bodied god grants the supreme state.
Suvarcalā, likewise Umā, Vikeśī, and Śivā;
Svāhā, the Quarters (Diśas), Dīkṣā, and Rohiṇī—these are the wives.
Śanaiścara, Śukra, Lohitāṅga, Manojava,
Skanda, Sarga, Santāna, and Budha are remembered as their sons.
Such is the Blessed One, the God of gods, Maheśvara;
having abandoned the duty of progeny and sensual desire, he has resorted to dispassion.
Having absorbed the Self into the Self and established himself in the state of the Lord,
he drank that imperishable Brahman, the eternal, supreme nectar.
Commanded by Brahmā to "create progeny," the blue-and-red Śiva created through his mind Rudras who were like himself.
[He saw] those with matted hair, free from fear, blue-throated, bearers of the Pināka bow,
holding tridents in their hands, destroyers of the Ṛṣṭi weapon, full of great bliss, and three-eyed.
The Lord beheld hundreds of millions upon millions of all-knowing ones, free from passion, liberated from old age and death, and mounted upon great bulls.
Having seen those various stainless Rudras, blue-and-red in hue and liberated from old age and death, the Guru addressed Hara.
O Lord, do not create such offspring as these who are exempt from death;
O Lord of Beings, create others who are subject to birth and death.
Then the Blessed One, the subduer of desire, said to Kapardin:
"I have no such creation; you yourself create these inauspicious beings."
From that time forward, that god did not produce inauspicious offspring;
for his mind being withdrawn by those very Rudras who were his own sons, he remained as Sthāṇu (the motionless one).
Thus, the state of being Sthāṇu came to belong to that trident-bearing God of gods.
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forbearance, fortitude, the power of creation, self-awareness, and indeed the power of presiding; Kūrma Purāṇa 1.10.39.
These ten indeclinables always abide in Śaṅkara;
he alone is the manifest Pinākin, the Supreme Lord Śaṅkara.
Then the blessed Brahmā, his eyes wide with joy, beheld the three-eyed god together with his mind-born sons.
Having understood with the eye of knowledge the supreme divine nature,
he placed his joined palms upon his head and praised the sole Lord of the worlds.
Brahmā said:
Homage be to you, O Mahādeva; homage to you, O Supreme Lord!
Homage to the divine Śiva; homage to you who are the embodiment of Brahman.
Homage be to you, the Great Lord; homage to the peaceful one, the cause;
homage to the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the sovereign of Yoga.
Homage to Kāla, to Rudra, to the great devourer, to the wielder of the trident;
homage to the one who holds the *pināka* bow in his hand, to the three-eyed one—salutations again and again!
Salutations to you, the triple-formed one; to you, the progenitor of Brahmā;
to the sovereign lord of the knowledge of Brahman; to the bestower of the knowledge of Brahman.
Homage to the secret essence of the Vedas; homage to you, the Death of Death!
Homage to the quintessence of the heart of the Vedānta; homage to the embodiment of the soul of the Vedas! (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.10.47)
Homage to the Buddha, the pure one; homage to you, the teacher of yogins, who are surrounded by various beings whose sorrows have been abandoned.
Homage to the God who is the friend of Brahman, homage to the Lord of Brahman;
homage to the three-eyed God, homage to you, the Supreme Being. *Kūrma Purāṇa* 1.10.49.
Salutations to you, the sky-clad one; salutations to you, the shaven-headed one who bears a staff;
salutations to you, who are free from beginningless impurity and are accessible through knowledge.
Homage to Tārā, the sacred ford; homage to the cause of the perfection of yoga; homage to you who are attainable through the Dharma and accessible through yoga. KūrmP_1,10.51.
Salutations to you who are free from conceptual proliferation; salutations to you who are without appearance.
Salutations to you, the Brahman of universal form, the Supreme Self.
By you alone was everything created; in you alone does all abide;
by you the entire universe, consisting of the world and beginning with primordial matter (pradhāna), is withdrawn, O you who are composed of the universe.
You are the Lord, Mahādeva, the Supreme Brahman, Maheśvara,
Parameṣṭhin, Śiva, the Peaceful One, the Partless Puruṣa, and Hara.
You are the imperishable, the supreme light; you are time, the Supreme Lord;
you alone are the infinite Puruṣa, as well as Pradhāna and Prakṛti.
I bow to you, who are designated as Brahman, whose form consists of earth, water, fire, air, ether, and indeed ego-consciousness.
I bow down to that Virāj, whose head became the sky, whose feet were the earth, whose arms were the quarters,
and whose belly was the ether.
Salutation to that one whose nature is the Sun, who eternally consists of the splendor of Brahman, who heats the universe while illuminating the quarters with his own rays.
Salutation to that one whose self is fire, who eternally carries the oblation to Rudra with his body composed of splendor,
and the ancestral offering to the hosts of ancestors.
Salutations to Him who is the essence of Soma, who constantly nourishes the entire universe by His own splendor and is drunk by the hosts of deities.
Salutations to you, whose nature is wind, who sustains all beings and always moves within them; salutations to that Māheśvarī Śakti of yours.
Salutations to Him whose nature is the four-faced one, who, abiding within His own self, creates this entire universe in accordance with the karma of each being.
Salutation to that Soul of the Universe, who, pervading the entire world through his illusory power (māyā), reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa by means of the yoga of self-realization.
Salutation to that Śeṣa, the support of all, who constantly bears upon his head the cosmic egg consisting of the fourteen worlds.
Salutation to that one whose nature is Rudra, who, having drunk the supreme bliss at the end of all things before the sole divine witness, dances with infinite majesty.
I bow to that Lord, the witness of all, who stands as the controller within all beings; I bow to him who is your very body.
Salutation to that Self of Yoga, whom those who are free from indolence, have conquered their breath, are contented, and possess equal vision, perceive as light while practicing yoga.

Salutation to that Self in the form of Knowledge, by which the yogi, whose impurities are utterly destroyed, crosses over illusion— illusion which is boundless and whose further limits cannot be reached.
I take refuge in that Supreme Reality, that Supreme Lord, whose light makes this non-dual world shine, which is beyond darkness, and whose very form is that [Reality]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.10.69)
I take refuge in you, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord— eternal bliss, supportless, partless, and the supreme Śiva.
Having thus praised Mahādeva, Brahmā, permeated by his being,
stood with palms joined in reverence, bowing down and chanting the eternal Brahman.
Then Hara, the Great God, bestowed upon him supreme divine yoga,
sovereignty, the true nature of Brahman, and dispassion.
Touching him with his two most beautiful hands, the Lord himself, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him,
spoke after bestowing grace upon the Grandfather.
"O Brahmin, that which was requested by you—that I become your son—has all been done by me; now create the manifold world."
O Brahmin, though I am the partless Supreme Lord, I am divided threefold under the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, according to the qualities of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
You, my eldest son, were fashioned for the purpose of creation from my very right limb,
while Puruṣottama was formed from my left limb.
Then, from the region of the heart of that Śambhu, the god of gods, this Rudra was born; I am his other body.
O Brahman, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the causes of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
though he is one, Śaṅkara remains established by his own will, having divided himself.
Likewise, my other forms are created by my illusory power (māyā);
however, Mahādeva is by his very nature formless, absolute, and pure.
Beyond these is the God who is the threefold form, the supreme body;
the Maheśvarī, the three-eyed one, who always bestows peace upon yogins.
Know me, O Grandfather, to be her very supreme form,
endowed with eternal sovereignty, wisdom, splendor, and yoga.
Therefore, having become Time (Kāla) and presiding over the quality of darkness (tamas), I swallow everything; no one else shall overcome me by means of that darkness.
Whenever you constantly meditate upon me, O Lotus-born one,
at that very moment my presence shall be with you, O sinless one.
Having spoken thus and paid homage to Brahmā, his guru,
Hara vanished in an instant along with his mind-born sons.
Having likewise resorted to yoga,
the Lord known as Nārāyaṇa, the Prajāpati, created the manifold world just as in former times.
By means of the science of yoga, he created Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha.
"These nine Brahmās are established as such in the Purāṇas;
all of them are equal to Brahmā, being practitioners who proclaim the Brahman."
He [taught] volition, dharma, and the eternal duties of the ages (yuga-dharmas),
as well as all those who pride themselves on their stations, just as it was told to you previously.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first section of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The glorious Kūrma said:
Having thus created Parīkṣit and the others, the Grandfather, the God of gods, [proceeded].
Together with his mind-born sons, he performed supreme austerity.
As he was thus performing penance, from his mouth there emerged the three-eyed Lord Rudra, the sovereign, bearing a trident in his hand and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction.
Having a body half-female and half-male, difficult to behold and exceedingly terrifying,
Brahmā said, "Divide yourself," and then vanished out of fear.
Thus addressed, he divided himself into two: femininity and then masculinity;
and he further divided that masculinity into ten parts and then again into one.
These eleven Rudras, the lords of the three worlds, beginning with Kapālīśa, O brahmins, have been described; they were appointed to the service of the gods.
That Lord, the God, divided womanhood in many ways through forms that were gentle or fierce, peaceful or unpeaceful, and dark or light.
These indeed are the renowned powers (vibhūtayaḥ) and energies (śaktayaḥ) on earth known by the wise as Lakṣmī and others, by which the Lord of Śaṅkara pervades the universe.
Having divided herself from the omnipresent Śaṅkara,
the mistress of the city approached the Grandfather at the command of Mahādeva.
The Blessed Brahmā said to her, "Become the daughter of Dakṣa.
By his command, she appeared before that Prajāpati.
By the command of Brahmā, he gave that goddess Satī to Rudra;
and Rudra, the wielder of the trident, received her from Dakṣa as his very own.
Having censured Prajāpati, that supreme goddess Satī, in due course of time,
became the daughter of Himavat through Menā.
And that best of mountains also gave Pārvatī to Rudra for the welfare of all the gods, of the three worlds, and of himself as well.
She is this very Goddess Maheshvari, whose body is half that of Shankara;
she is Shiva, Sati, and Haimavati, saluted by both gods and demons.
All the gods, together with Indra, perceive her incomparable power;
the sages know it, as does Śaṅkara himself, or Hari.
O Brahmins, this has been told to you: how Parameṣṭhin became the son [of Brahmā], how Brahmā was born from the lotus, and [how] Śaṅkara of immeasurable splendor [attained his state].
Sūta said:
Having thus heard what was spoken by Viṣṇu in the form of a tortoise, the sages once again bowed down to Hari.
The sages said:
"Who is this blessed goddess who forms half the body of Śaṅkara?
Tell us who ask you truly: who is Śivā, Satī, and Haimavatī?"
Having heard those words of the sages, the Great Yogin, the Supreme Person, meditated upon his own supreme state and replied.
The venerable Kūrma said: In ancient times, this most beautiful secret knowledge was spoken by the Grandfather (Brahmā) on the summit of Mount Meru; it is to be kept especially concealed.
This supreme Sāṃkhya of the Sāṃkhyas is the highest knowledge of Brahman;
it is the sole means of liberation for living beings submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
That power of Maheśvara, whose form is knowledge and who is intensely longing [for it],
known as Vyoman, the supreme goal— she is considered to be Haimavatī.
Śivā is all-pervading, infinite, beyond the qualities (guṇas), and perfectly partless;
she abides as both one and many, and is intensely devoted to the nature of knowledge.
Non-different from that partless reality, she abides by its splendor;
she is both innate and rooted in Him, as stainless as the radiance of the sun.
The single Śakti of Maheśvara, through association with manifold limiting adjuncts,
sports in his presence in both supreme and inferior forms.
She performs all this; this world is her effect.
The wise declare that for the Lord there is neither effect nor instrument.
The four powers of the Goddess abide as her very own nature;
hear from me, O best of sages, how they exist through her presiding influence.
Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti are remembered as the fourfold manifestation;
therefore, the Supreme Lord is called the God of the Fourfold Array (Caturvyūha).
By this supreme [knowledge], O Lord, the God enjoys the bliss of his own self;
and in all four Vedas, Maheśvara exists as the fourfold form.
Her sovereignty, however, is great, incomparable, and established from time immemorial;
it is infinite because of her connection with Rudra, the Supreme Self.
This very goddess is the sovereign of all, the impeller of all beings;
she is called the Blessed Time, Hari, Prāṇa, and Maheśvara.
In him this entire world is woven, both warp and woof;
he is celebrated by the exponents of the Vedas as Time, Fire, Hara, and Rudra.
Time creates all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
All are subject to Time; Time is not subject to anyone.
Pradhāna, Puruṣa, the principle (tattva), Mahat, and Ahaṅkāra—
these other principles were entered by the yogin through Time.
His power, known as Māyā, is the source of the entire world; by means of it, the Lord, the master of illusion, the Supreme Person, causes this universe to revolve.
This very power, whose essence is *māyā*, is multiform and eternal;
it perpetually manifests the universal form of the Great Lord.
Furthermore, three other primary powers were created by that God:
the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the power of vital breath (prāṇa-śakti).
O best of Brahmins, the possessors of all powers were created by means of Māyā alone; and that Māyā, O lords, is beginningless and infinite.
Māyā, whose essence is all-pervading power, is difficult to ward off and difficult to transcend;
the wielder of Māyā is the Lord of all powers, Time, the maker of time, and the Sovereign.
Time creates everything, for Time alone indeed withdraws all;
Time sustains the universe, and this world is dependent upon Time. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.39)
Having obtained the presence of the God of gods, the Supreme Lord,
the Infinite One, the Sovereign of all, Śambhu, the Lord whose nature is Time.
Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Māyā—thus does Māyā proceed;
she is one, all-pervading, infinite, absolute, partless, and auspicious.
Śakti is one, and Śiva alone is called the possessor of Śakti;
all other possessors of Śakti arise from the totality of Śaktis.

Those yogins who contemplate reality declare that, from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is a distinction between power and the possessor of power; yet they perceive their non-distinction as well.
The goddess Girijā is the power (śakti), while Śaṅkara is the possessor of power (śaktimat);
this distinction is declared in the Purāṇa by those who discourse on Brahman.
The Goddess Viśveśvarī, devoted to Maheśvara as her husband, is called the object of enjoyment; the Blessed One, Kapardin Nīlalohita, is called the enjoyer. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.45)

The Lord Śaṅkara, the God who is the Master of All, is called Mantṛ (the Thinker) and Manmathāntaka (the Destroyer of Desire); and from the perspective of inquiry, the Goddess Īśānī is both Mati (Intellect) and Mantavyā (the Object of Thought).
O Brahmins, all this which arises from the Power (Śakti) and the Possessor of Power (Śaktimat) is proclaimed in all the Vedas by the sages who perceive the ultimate reality.
This supreme, divine majesty of the Goddess has been revealed;
it is determined by the exponents of Brahman within all the Vedas and Vedāntas.
Yogins behold that supreme state of the Great Goddess—unique, all-pervading, subtle, immovable, unshakable, and eternal. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.49)
Yogis behold that supreme state of the Great Goddess— the blissful, imperishable Brahman, which is absolute, partless, and transcendent.
The reality that is higher than the highest, eternal, auspicious, and immutable—
that supreme state of the Goddess is merged within the infinite primordial nature (prakṛti).
Auspicious, stainless, pure, devoid of qualities, and free from duality—
that supreme state of the Goddess is the object of the realization of the Self.
This very [devotion], resting upon the Lord, is the nurse and the creator for those desiring supreme bliss;
it destroys all the torments of saṃsāra.
Therefore, one seeking liberation should take refuge in Pārvatī, the Supreme Goddess,
who is the self-nature of all beings and whose essence is Śiva.
And having obtained Śarvāṇī as his daughter after performing very difficult austerities,
he went with his wife to Śara to see the supreme goddess Pārvatī.
Seeing that beautiful-faced girl being born by her own will, Menā, the wife of Himavat, spoke thus to the Lord of Mountains: Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.56.
Menā said:
"Behold this girl, O King, whose face resembles a lotus;
she was born through our ascetic penance for the welfare of all living beings."
He too, having then seen his daughter— who resembled the rising sun, wore her hair in a braided coil, had four faces and three eyes, and was exceedingly lovely— [beheld her].
Eight cubits tall and large-eyed, adorned with the crescent moon as her ornament,
she is both devoid of qualities and possessed of qualities, manifest in person yet free from the distinction between existence and non-existence.
Bowing his head to the ground, overwhelmed by her splendor and filled with fear, he spoke with palms joined in reverence to that Supreme Goddess: KūrmP_1,11.60.
Himavat said:
"Who are you, O goddess of large eyes, marked with the parts of the moon?
I do not know you, my child; tell me truly as I ask you."
Having heard the words of the lord of mountains, that Supreme Goddess, the bestower of fearlessness upon yogis, then addressed the great mountain: (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.62)
The Goddess said:
"Know me to be the supreme Śakti, who rests upon the Supreme Lord—
non-dual, imperishable, and one, whom those seeking liberation behold."
I am indeed the Self of all beings, the auspicious one dwelling within all;
I am the embodiment of eternal sovereignty and wisdom, the impeller of everything.
"O you of infinite and boundless majesty, who carry one across the ocean of saṃsāra!
I grant you divine vision; behold my sovereign form. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.65)
Having said this much and having bestowed his wisdom upon Himavat,
he himself revealed his own divine form, that of the Supreme Lord.
A sphere of light resembling ten million suns, undisturbed,
enriched with thousands of garlands of flames, and comparable to hundreds of fires of cosmic destruction.
With fangs formidable and difficult to withstand, adorned with a circle of matted locks,
holding an excellent trident in his hand, he was of terrible form and fearsome.
Tranquil, with a gentle countenance, endowed with infinite wonders,
marked by the beauty of a crescent moon, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Wearing a crown, with a mace in his hand, adorned with anklets,
and clad in divine garlands and garments, he was anointed with divine perfumes and unguents.
He who bears the conch and the discus, the desirable one, three-eyed and clad in animal hide,
situated within the cosmic egg and outside the cosmic egg, external and internal, the supreme.
Consisting of all powers, pure, possessing all forms, and eternal,
his lotus feet are being worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and the lords of yogins.
He beheld the Supreme Lord standing, pervading everything, with hands and feet extending everywhere, and eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
Having seen such a supreme, divine form of Māheśvara,
the king was both overcome with fear and filled with joy in his heart.
Having established his self within the Self and recollecting the syllable *oṃ*,
he praised the Supreme Goddess with her eight thousand names.
Himavat said:
"Śivomā is the supreme power, infinite, partless, stainless,
peaceful, belonging to Maheśvara, eternal, everlasting, and the supreme imperishable."
Inconceivable, absolute, infinite, the self of Śiva, the supreme self,
beginningless, imperishable, pure, the self of the gods, all-pervading, and immovable.
Abiding beyond the distinction of one and many, transcending illusion, perfectly pure,
the Great Goddess of Maheśvara, the true Mahādevī, the stainless one.

The power of consciousness (cicchakti), which abides within all things and is intensely longing, is Nandā; she is the knowledge (vidyā) that is the self of all, whose form is light, and who is the immortal syllable. // KūrmP 1.11.79 //
She is peace, the foundation of all, cessation that bestows immortality;
she has the sky as her form, merges into the sky, is supported by the sky, and is the infallible, immortal goddess.
Without beginning or end, unfailing, the causal self, the source of all parts;
she is the first-born sacrifice, the navel of immortality, resting within the Self.
The beloved of the Lord of Life, the Mother, the slayer of the great Mahiṣa;
the Mistress of Life, whose form is life itself, the Sovereign of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
She is the source of all powers and arts, the moonlight that is the abode of heaven's majesty;
she is the controller of all effects and the sovereign of the lords of all beings.
She is beginningless, the unmanifest cave, great bliss, and eternal;
she has space as her womb, she is established in yoga, and she is the sovereign of the great lords of yoga.

Mahāmāyā is exceedingly difficult to satisfy; she is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the sovereign (īśvarī), the womb of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), the totality, and the source from which all powers arise.

The power of life-force (*prāṇaśakti*), the science of breath (*praṇavidyā*), the Yoginī, the supreme digit (*kalā*), is the far shore of *saṃsāra*, difficult to restrain, difficult to perceive, and difficult to attain. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.86)
Possessing great power and difficult to overcome, she is born from the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti);
her manifestation is without beginning or end, she exists for the sake of others, and she is the friction-stick for the fire of the Puruṣa.
She brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution; she is difficult to describe and hard to transcend;
she is the source of sound, composed of sound, known as *nāda*, and having *nāda* as her very form.

She transcends both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa), yet she consists of the essence of both primordial matter and the individual soul; she is ancient, composed of consciousness, the beginning of all beings, and takes the form of the Supreme Person (puruṣa).
The inner self of all beings, immutable and designated as the Great Puruṣa,
transcends birth, death, and old age, and is endowed with all powers.
The power of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña-śakti) is all-pervasive, undivided, entering into primordial matter (pradhāna), characterized by the unmanifest, and free from impurity.
The cave of primordial nature (prakṛti) is undivided from beginningless illusion, consisting of the three principles;
it arises from the Great Illusion (mahāmāyā), is characterized by darkness (tāmasī), belongs to the Puruṣa, and is eternal.
Consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, she is black, red, and white;
she is the progenitress, beyond action yet the mother who generates all that is to be done, eternally characterized by the nature of giving birth.

She is free from creation and dissolution; she possesses the natures of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal; she contains the Brahman within her; she is the twenty-fourth [tattva]; she is the lotus-navelled one, whose essence is Acyuta.
She is the lightning-like, eternal womb, the mother of the world, and the beloved of the Lord;
she is the support of all, possessed of a great form, and endowed with all sovereign powers.
She is multiform, containing the great embryo within her, following the will of the Lord of the Universe;
she is most exalted, the source of Brahman, and manifested from Mahālakṣmī.
Abiding in the center of the great celestial palace, having itself as its own cause, the Great Sleep is indeed the ultimate,
subtle ignorance common to all.
The Goddess, who deludes men, possesses infinite forms and infinite abodes;
she exists in manifold shapes and is devoid of the three periods of time.
Born from Brahmā, she is the form of Hari, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
she is the mother of Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu, known as Brahmā, and she rests upon Brahmā.
Manifest, the first-born of Brahmā, the Great One whose form is knowledge,
whose nature consists of dispassion, sovereignty, and dharma— this embodiment of Brahman resides in the heart;
she is the source of the waters, self-existent manifestation, born of the mind, and arisen from the fundamental principles.
Īśvarāṇī, Śarvāṇī, she who forms half the body of Śaṅkara,
Bhavānī, Rudrāṇī, Mahālakṣmī, and Ambikā.
Born from Maheśvara, she bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
she is the sovereign of all, worthy of worship by all, and her mind is eternally joyful.
Bowed to by Brahmā, Indra, and Upendra, she follows the will of Śaṅkara;
seated upon half the throne of Īśvara, she is the devoted wife of Maheśvara.
Once meditated upon, she dries up the entire ocean;
Pārvatī, the daughter of Himavat, is the bestower of supreme bliss.
Rich in virtues, born of yoga, worthy, the embodiment of knowledge,
and radiant— Sāvitrī, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, and Śrī abide upon the chest of Ananta.
She whose abode is the lotus, the Mudrā, Yoganidrā, the destroyer of the gods' foes;
she is Sarasvatī, the embodiment of all knowledge, the eldest in the world, and the most auspicious.
The goddess of speech, the bestower of boons, she who is to be spoken, fame, the accomplisher of all aims;
the mistress of yogis, the knowledge of Brahman, the great knowledge, most beautiful. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.107)
The secret science, the science of the self, and the science of dharma cultivated within one's own being;
Svāhā, Viśvaṃbharā, Siddhi, Svadhā, Medhā, Dhṛti, and Śruti.
She is Nīti (Right Conduct), Sunīti (Good Policy), Sukṛti (Virtuous Action), Mādhavī, Naravāhinī;
she is Ajā (the Unborn), Vibhāvarī (the Radiant Night), Saumyā (the Gentle One), Bhoginī (the Enjoyer), and Bhogadāyinī (the Bestower of Enjoyment).
Śobhā, Vaṃśakarī, Lolā, Mālinī, Parameṣṭhinī,
Trailokyasundarī, Ramyā, Sundarī, and Kāmacāriṇī.
She is of great majesty, established in the essence of being, the crusher of the great buffalo;
she wears a garland of lotuses, removes all evil, is multicolored, and has a face adorned with a crown.
Niryantrā, Yantravāhasthā, Nandinī, Bhadrakālikā, Ādityavarṇā, and Kaumārī, who rides upon a noble peacock. KūrmP_1.11.112.
Niryantrā, Yantravāhasthā, Nandinī, Bhadrakālikā, Ādityavarṇā, and Kaumārī, who rides upon a noble peacock; KūrmP 1.11.113.
Seated upon a bull-throne, fair-complexioned Mahākālī is worshipped by the gods;
she is Aditi, the disciplined Raudrī, the womb of the lotus, and she whose vehicle is a bird.
Virūpākṣī, Lelihānā, the dweller in Mahāpura;
she of great fruit and faultless limbs, the fulfiller of desires, Vibhāvarī.
She who wears a crown of various jewels, who destroys the suffering of those who bow before her,
Kauśikī, the attractor, Night, and the destroyer of the afflictions of the thirty gods.
She is multiform, beautiful, deformed, and devoid of form;
she is the alleviator of the distress of her devotees, the auspicious one who destroys the very nature of worldly existence.
The song of the Sāmaveda is devoid of qualities, eternally manifest, essence-less, and shameless; it is glorious and has its abode within the body of Bhava.
Dīkṣā is the radiant Vidyādharī who strikes down Mahendra;
she is the knowledge that transcends all and bestows all accomplishments.
She is beloved by the Lord of All, she is Tārkṣyā, she dwells within the ocean;
she is stainless, without support, eternally perfected, and free from affliction.
She is the wish-fulfilling cow, the one of vast womb, the wise, and the destroyer of delusion;
she is free from conceptual construction, free from fear, disciplined, and the bestower of discipline.
The goddess of gods, Manonmanī, rich with thousands of garlands of flames,
is the Great Bhagavatī Durgā, born from Vāsudeva.

She is the sister of Mahendra and Upendra, accessible through devotion, both transcendent and immanent; she is knowledge and the object of knowledge, beyond old age, the domain of the Vedānta, and the ultimate goal.
She is the sacrificial fee, the burner, and that which is to be burned; she is saluted by all beings.
She is the power of yoga-illusion, the knower of manifestations, the great illusion, and the most exalted one.
The twilight is the source of all that arises; it is the bending of the Brahma-tree, the emergence of the sprout from the seed, the Great Power, and the Great Intellect.
She is Fame, Wisdom, Consciousness, and Awareness; she reclines upon the great lord of serpents;
she is the Transformation, the Auspicious One, the Teacher, and she is served by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas.
Vaiśvānarī, Mahāśālā, Devasenā, Guhapriyā,
Mahārātri, Śivānandā, Śacī, and Duḥsvapnanāśinī.
She is the object of sacrifice, the one worthy of worship, the sustainer of the world, difficult to comprehend, and possessed of beautiful form;
she is the Mother of the Cave, the source of the qualities (*guṇa*), the great sacred seat, and the daughter of the Wind-god.
She who dwells within the fire that carries the oblations, born from the fire that carries the oblations;
she is the source of the world, the mother of the world, transcending birth, death, and old age.
She is the mother of intelligence, the intelligent one, dwelling within another person;
she is the swift one, established in meditative absorption, three-eyed, and stationed in heaven.
The Mother of all senses and the mind, dwelling in the heart of all beings,
she is the Vidyā that carries one across saṃsāra, the dissolution of the mind for those who proclaim Brahman.
She is Brahmāṇī, the Great One (Bṛhatī), the Vedic (Brāhmī), who has become Brahman, the fire-pit of worldly existence;
she is the golden one, the Great Night, who causes the revolution of saṃsāra.
Sumālinī, Surūpā, Bhāvinī, Tāriṇī, Prabhā, Unmīlanī, Sarvasahā, and Sarvapratyayasākṣiṇī. // KūrmP_1,11.133 //
She is exceedingly gentle, with a face like the moon, and her mind is intent on the *tāṇḍava* dance;
she is purity that effects the purification of the inner being and destroys the three impurities.
She is beloved by the world, the embodiment of the universe, the triple-formed one, and the refuge of immortality;
she is without support, without food, and not born from the sprouts of the forest.
With the moon in her hand, of variegated limbs, wearing a garland and holding a lotus,
she knows the ordinances of the higher and the lower, and is the progenitor of the Great Beings.

The beloved of the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara), she is Knowledge (Vidyā) herself; she has a tongue like lightning, has conquered all fatigue, consists of knowledge, possesses a thousand eyes, and is the daughter of the Thousand-faced One.
The thousand-rayed one, established in goodness, resting in the station of Maheśvara;
she is the purifier, composed of truth, all-pervading, radiant, and the awakener of the lotus.
She who has Mahāmāyā as her support, she who is worthy of honor, she who is delightful to Mahādeva,
the Fortune of the Sky, she whose chariot is a lion, and she who possesses immeasurable splendor while shining forth.
Vīreśvarī, seated upon a celestial chariot, the sorrowless one who destroys grief;
the unstruck sound (Anāhatā), the coiled energy (Kuṇḍalinī), the lotus-like one who dwells within the lotus.
She is eternal bliss, eternal fame, and the abode of all beings;
she is the goddess of speech, a portion of Brahman, beyond all parts, yet the source of all parts.
She is the glory of Brahman, the heart of Brahman, and the beloved of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
she is the power of space, the power of action, the power of knowledge, and the supreme goal.
She is the agitator, the binder, the one to be divided, and she who is devoid of both difference and non-difference;
she is undivided yet established in a non-different form, the bearer of the lineage, and the one who carries away the lineage.
The secret power (Guhyashakti) transcends the qualities (gunas), is eternal, and faces in every direction;
she is the sister, the consort of the Lord, the totality, and the maker of time.
She is the All-Knowing, the Auspicious in Every Way, Beyond the Secret, the Source of the Cave,
the Ritual Procedure, the Mother of Yoga, the Gaṅgā, and the Sovereign of the Lord of the Universe.
Kapilā, Kāpilā, the beloved Kanakābhā, Kalāntarā,
Puṇyā, Puṣkariṇī, Bhoktrī, and Purandaras-purassarā.
She is the nourisher, the bestower of supreme sovereignty and prosperity, adorned with divine splendor;
she is the source of the five Brahmans and her form is the ultimate reality itself.
Dharmodayā, Bhānumatī, Yogijñeyā, Manojavā,
Manoharā, Manorakṣā, Tāpasī, and Vedarūpiṇī.
She is the power of the Vedas, the mother of the Vedas, the illuminator of Vedic knowledge;
she is the sovereign of the lords of yoga, the Mother, the Great Power, whose nature is mind.
Viśvāvasthā, Viyanmūrti, Vidyunmālā, Vihāyasī, Kiṃnarī, Surabhī, Vandyā, Nandinī, and Nandivallabhā. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.150)
Bhāratī is supreme bliss, the divider of the higher and the lower;
she is endowed with all weapons, desirable, and the sovereign of the Lord of Desire.
Acintyā, Acintyavibhavā, Hṛllekhā, Kanakaprabhā, Kūṣmāṇḍī, Dhanaratnāḍhyā, Sugandhā, and Gandhāyinī. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.152)
Born from the foot of Trivikrama, holding a bow in her hand, the source of auspiciousness,
exceedingly difficult to attain, the guardian of wealth and other treasures, fortunate, and with tawny eyes— [she is Śrī].
Śānti, Prabhāvatī, Dīpti, and Paṅkajāyatalocanā—
these are considered the primordial cows born from the heart-lotus, who delight in battle.
Satkriyā, Girijā, Śuddhā, Nityapuṣṭā, Nirantarā, Durgā, Kātyāyanī, Caṇḍī, Carcikā, and Śāntavigrahā. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.155)
She is golden-hued, the night, the activator of the machine of the universe,
she who dwells on Mount Mandara, Śāradā, and she who wears a garland of gold.
She is the garland of jewels, the womb of jewels, the earth that crushes all worlds;
she has a lotus-face, resembles a lotus, and is eternally content, born from the nectar of immortality.
Shaking [all things] yet herself unshakable, the mother of Sūrya, the Dṛṣadvatī,
sister of Mahendra, worthy of honor, most excellent, and proud of her boon-granting power.
She is auspicious, the lotus-born, the beautiful one, composed of the five elements, and the bestower of boons;
she is to be addressed as the Sovereign of Boons, worthy of worship, invincible, and difficult to transcend.
Kālarātri, of great velocity, the beloved of Vīrabhadra, the benefactor;
Bhadrakālī, the Mother of the World, who bestows auspiciousness upon her devotees. (Kūrmapurāṇa 1.11.160)
Karālā, Piṅgalākārā, Nāmabheda, Mahāmadā, Yaśasvinī, and Yaśodā—these are the six who traverse the paths. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.161)
Śaṅkhinī, Padminī, Sāṃkhyā, the one who sets in motion Sāṃkhya-yoga, Caitrā, she who has ascended the year, the fulfiller of the world, and Indrajā.
The enemy of Śumbha, established in the sky-farers, with a neck like a conch, fond of strife;
she who has the bird as her banner, mounted upon a bird, most worthy of honor, and the supreme garlanded one.
Dwelling on the path of sovereignty, she is dispassionate and seated upon Garuḍa;
Jayantī is the delightful cave of the heart, established in the abyss as the leader of the Gaṇas.
She is the one whose will is accomplished, who abides in equanimity, and who bestows all higher knowledge;
she is the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age and the supreme secret Upaniṣad. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.165)
Niṣṭhā, Dṛṣṭi, Smṛti, Vyāpti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Kriyāvatī, Viśvā, Amareśvarī, Īśānā, Bhukti, Muktī, Śivā, and Amṛtā. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.166)
She is Lohitā, Sarpamālā, Bhīṣaṇī, Vanamālinī;
she is Anantaśayanā, none other than she who gave birth to Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
She is Nṛsiṃhī, the destroyer of the Daityas, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
she is born from Saṃkarṣaṇa and takes refuge at the feet of Ambikā.
She of the great flame, she of the great form, she of the beautiful form, the granter of all desires;
she of the excellent luster, she of the beautiful breasts, Gaurī, the bestower of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Dwelling between the eyebrows, she is the eastern [direction], the fire-drill for the Ancient Puruṣa;
she is the bestower of great sovereignty, the central one, lotus-eyed, and equanimous.
The first [form] has eighteen arms and the luster of the petals of a blue lotus;
she is seated upon the seat of all powers (Śaktis) and is free from both merit and demerit.
Devoted to dispassion and knowledge, she is without light and devoid of sense organs;
she is the support for various deep mysteries and dwells in the eternal abode.
Sthāneśvarī is devoid of worldly joy, bearing the trident and the boon-granting gesture;
she is the embodiment of all deities, the goddess, the supreme deity,
the mother of the Gaṇas, the daughter of the Mountain, and the slayer of Niśumbha.
She is without color, devoid of color, and colorless; she is born from the seed-syllable.
She possesses infinite colors, yet remains non-dual; she is the bringer of auspiciousness, with a tranquil mind.

She who is without lineage, who possesses all lineages, the protectress, whose form is secret, who is supreme in virtues; she who is the cow, who is fond of cows and the products of the cow, she who is metaphorical, and who is saluted by the Lord of the Gaṇas.
She consists of truth alone, she is faithful to truth, she is the three junctions of time, yet free from all junctions;
she is the basis of all doctrines, she is number, and she arises from the union with number.
She is called the Innumerable and the Immeasurable, empty, born of a pure lineage,
the source of the Bindu and Nāda, the beloved of Śambhu, and radiant as the moon.
She is free from attachment, devoid of division, delightful, and the destroyer of Madhu;
she is great fortune, the source of prosperity, and established on the far shore beyond darkness.
The Mother of the three principles is threefold, abiding in the most subtle state;
she is beyond tranquility, beyond impurity, changeless, and without support.
She is named Śivā, the abode of the mind, whose very nature is the knowledge of Śiva;
she is the creator of Daityas and Dānavas, the mother of Kaśyapa, and the one who brings about the end of time.
She is the source of the scriptures, the embodiment of ritual action, and the revealer of the four aims of life;
she is Nārāyaṇī, the origin of men, the moonlight, and the bearer of the *liṅga*.

The passionate Lalitā, whose nature bestows both supreme and non-supreme glory, possesses a majesty born from the ultimate limit; she is the mare of the submarine fire and the one with beautiful eyes.
Subhadrā, Devakī, Sītā, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
she was high-minded, the mother of Manyu, and born from the great wrath.
Amṛtyu, Amṛtā, Svāhā, Puruhūtā, Puruṣṭutā,
Aśocyā, Bhinnaviṣayā, and Hiraṇyarajatapriyā.
Golden, silver, and made of gold, adorned with golden ornaments,
it shines brilliantly, is difficult to comprehend, and bestows the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
The Great Sleep is the source of awakening; she is the deity of truth, long-necked and hump-backed, dear to the heart, the giver of peace, and the increaser of peace.
She is the progenitor of the powers such as Lakṣmī and others, the instigator of the circle of powers (śakticakra),
the mother of the three powers, the one who is born, and she who is completely victorious over the six waves of existence.
Sudhāmā, Karmakaraṇī, she whose nature is the fire at the end of the age,
Saṃkarṣaṇī, the sustainer of the world, the source of desire, and the wearer of the diadem.
She is Aindrī, saluted by the three worlds; she is Vaiṣṇavī, the supreme sovereign;
she is the beloved of Pradyumna, self-restrained, possessing a double gaze and three eyes.
Madotkaṭā, Haṃsagati, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍavikramā,
Vṛṣāveśā, Viyanmātā, and Vindhyaparvatavāsinī.
She whose abode is the Himavat and Meru mountains, who dwells on Mount Kailāsa,
the daughter of the slayer of Cāṇūra, she who knows the principles of policy, and who can assume any form at will.
She has bathed in the vows of Vedic knowledge, is virtuous in conduct, and subsists on air;
she is the beloved of Vīrabhadra, a heroine born from Mahākāla.
The beloved of the Vidyādharas, the perfected one, the form of the Vidyādharas,
the nourisher, the remover, the purifier, the sustainer, and the all-encompassing.
Mātṛkā, born from Manmatha, the lotus-born one, fond of her vehicle,
Karīṣiṇī, whose speech is nectar, and she who is intent upon playing the lute.
Sevitā, Sevikā, Sevyā, Sinīvālī, Garutmatī,
Arundhatī, Hiraṇyākṣī, Mṛgāṅkā, and Mānadāyinī.
Vasupradā, Vasumatī, Vasordhārā, Vasundharā,
Dhārādharā, Varārohā, and Varāvarasahasradā.
Śrīphalā, Śrīmatī, Śrīśā, Śrīnivāsā, Śivapriyā,
Śrīdharā, Śrīkarī, Kalyā, and she whose body is half that of Śrīdhara.
She possesses infinite vision, she is noble, the sovereign of the world, the beloved of the Giver of Wealth;
she is the slayer of the hosts of Daityas, Siṃhikā, whose vehicle is the lion.
Suṣeṇā, Candranilayā, Sukīrti, Chinnasaṃśayā, Rasajñā, Rasadā, Rāmā, Lelihānā, and Amṛtastravā. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.199)
Ever-arisen, self-luminous, and eager, she is the giver of life to the dead;
she is the Goddess of Speech with a vajra-staff, a vajra-tongue, and a vajra-body.
She is auspiciousness itself, the auspicious one, the garland, the soiled one, and the remover of impurity;
she is the celestial musician, the goddess of the Garuḍas, the daughter of the Moon, and the beloved of Kambala and Aśvatara.
Saudāminī, who brings joy to the people, whose face is furrowed with a frown,
who holds a *karṇikāra* flower in her hand, who is the girdle of the earth, and who took away the life-breath of Kaṃsa.
Yugandharā, Yugāvartā, Trisaṃdhyā, Harṣavardhanī, Pratyakṣadevatā, Divyā, Divyagandhā, and Divāparā. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.203)
Seated upon the throne of Śakra is the consort of Śakra, a virtuous woman seated upon a corpse;
she is beloved, preeminent, cherished by the learned, and worshipped by both the disciplined and the undisciplined.
Śatarūpā, Śatāvartā, Vinatā, Surabhi, Surā,
Surendramātā, Sudyumnā, Suṣumnā, and Sūryasaṃsthitā.
She is worthy of contemplation and well-established; she is cessation that has reached the further shore of knowledge.
She is skilled in the meaning of the treatises on Dharma; she is the knower of Dharma who conveys the Dharma.
She is the fashioner of dharma and adharma; she bestows auspiciousness upon the righteous;
she is the power of dharma, composed of dharma, yet beyond dharma, possessing all dharmas.
She is the one who is other than phenomena, the cloud of Dharma, preceded by Dharma, the bringer of wealth;
she is the instructor of Dharma, whose self is Dharma, accessible through Dharma, and the upholder of the earth.
The form of Śākalā is the bearer of the skull, her body fashioned from the creative arts;
she is liberated from all powers, yet she is the ultimate refuge for the locus of all powers.
She is all, the sovereign of all, subtle, most subtle, and the embodiment of knowledge; she is the mistress of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the sole witness of Mahādeva;
she is Sadāśivā, whose form is space, whose form is the universe, yet who is formless.
Having thus praised Him with a thousand names, that mountain Himavat, bowing down again with a fearful heart and with palms joined in reverence, spoke this: KūrmP_1.11.211.
O Supreme Goddess, this divine form of yours is terrible;
having now seen it, I am afraid—show me another form.
Having been addressed thus by that mountain, the goddess Pārvatī withdrew [her form] and again displayed another, her own true nature.
Resembling the petals of a blue lotus, possessing the fragrance of a blue lotus,
with two eyes and two arms, he is gentle and adorned with dark-blue locks of hair.
With the soles of his lotus feet red and his sprout-like hands deeply crimson,
he was glorious, radiant with a tilaka mark upon his broad and well-rounded forehead.
Adorned with ornaments on all his beautiful limbs, he was exceedingly delicate;
upon his chest, he wore a large garland fashioned of gold.
With a gentle smile and beautiful, well-shaped lips, accompanied by the tinkling of anklets,
his divine face was serene— the abode of infinite majesty.
Having beheld such a form, the best of mountains,
casting off his fear and with a joyful heart, spoke to the Supreme Goddess.
Himavat said:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic toil has become fruitful, since you, the unmanifest one, have appeared before my very eyes in person, being well-pleased."
The entire world was created by you; from primordial matter (pradhāna) to its end, it rests within you.
O Goddess, it dissolves into you alone, and you alone are the supreme goal.
Some call you alone the primordial nature (prakṛti), beyond even nature;
others, who know the supreme truth, call you Śiva, O refuge of Śiva.
In you there arose Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Mahat, Brahmā, as well as Īśvara;
and Avidyā, Niyati, Māyā, Kalā, and so forth, by the hundreds.
For you are that supreme power, infinite and most excellent;
liberated from all distinctions, yet the innate foundation of all distinctions.
Presiding over you, O Mistress of Yoga, Mahādeva Maheśvara creates and transforms the entire universe, beginning with primordial matter (pradhāna).
United with you alone, O Goddess, the Lord experiences his own bliss;
you alone are supreme bliss, and you alone are the bestower of bliss.
You are the imperishable, the supreme ether, the great light, stainless,
auspicious, all-pervading, subtle, the supreme Brahman, and eternal.
O Goddess, you are Śakra among all the gods, you are Brahmā among those who know Brahman;
you are Vāyu among the powerful, and you are Kumāraka among the yogins.
Among the sages you are Vasiṣṭha, and among those who know the Vedas you are Vyāsa;
among the followers of Sāṃkhya you are the divine Kapila, and among the Rudras you are Śaṅkara.
Among the Ādityas you are Upendra, and among the Vasus you are Pāvaka;
among the Vedas you are the Sāmaveda, and among the meters you are the Gāyatrī.
Among the sciences, you are the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), the supreme goal among all goals;
you are *māyā* among all powers, and you are time (*kāla*) among those who reckon.
The syllable Oṃ is the foremost of all secret syllables, the best of the twice-born among all castes,
the householder’s stage among the stages of life, and Maheśvara among all lords.
Among men, you alone are the Supreme Person (Puruṣa) dwelling in the hearts of all beings;
O Goddess, among all the Upaniṣads, you are called the Secret Upaniṣad.
You are the lord of the kalpas and of the ages, including the Kṛta age itself;
you are the sun among all paths, and, O Goddess, you are Sarasvatī among all speech.
You are Lakṣmī among those of beautiful form; you are Viṣṇu among the masters of illusion;
you are Arundhatī among virtuous women; and you are Suparṇa among those who fly.
Among hymns, you are the Puruṣasūkta; among Sāmans, you are the Jyeṣṭhasāman;
among prayers to be recited, you are the Sāvitrī; and among Yajus formulas, you are the Śatarudriya.
Among mountains you are Mahāmeru; among serpents you are Ananta. You are the supreme Brahman of all, for everything indeed consists of you.
Form is devoid of all remaining parts, beyond the range of the senses, stainless, of a single nature,
without beginning, middle, or end, infinite, and primordial.
I bow to that Truth which is beyond darkness.
Those who have ascertained the meaning through the knowledge of Vedānta behold that very source of the world,
which is pure bliss and designated by the syllable Om.
I take refuge in that very form.
Residing within all beings without exception,
it is the cause of the union and separation of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa); consisting of light, it is devoid of birth and destruction.
I bow down to that form which is designated as Prāṇa.
Devoid of beginning and end, the self-nature of the world, existing as something distinct yet beyond primordial nature (prakṛti),
your very being is immutable and unmanifest in form.
I bow to the form designated as Puruṣa.
The Pradhāna is the support of all, the ordainer of the entire world, omnipresent, devoid of birth and destruction,
subtle, manifold, and composed of the three qualities.
I am born from you, whose form is devoid of division.
Your primordial, great form as the Self of the Puruṣa exists in the state of Prakṛti, the seed consisting of the three guṇas, endowed with sovereignty, wisdom, dispassion, and virtue.
O Goddess, I bow to that form endowed with [all these qualities].
This world, consisting of fourteen realms, resting upon the waters,
possessing manifold divisions, having the Puruṣa as its sole lord,
and permeated by infinite beings— [all this has been created] by you.
I am born as form, known as the cosmic egg of the world.
The one primordial source consisting of all Vedas without exception, which has filled the distinctions of the worlds with its own splendor,
the cause of the three times, known by the name Raṇameṣṭhi.
I bow to that form situated within the solar disc.
The ancient Puruṣa, with a thousand heads, infinite power, and a thousand arms,
was lying there likewise within the waters.
I bow down to the form known as Nārāyaṇa.
With fangs formidable, worshipped by the thirty gods, having a form like the fire at the end of an eon,
and being the cause of the destruction of the entire cosmic egg of beings—
I bow to your form known as Time.
Resplendent with a thousand hoods,
being worshipped by the foremost of the serpent lords,
Janārdana was reclining, fast asleep, upon his body.
I am born as your form, known by the name Śeṣa.
The one with unimpeded sovereignty, the three-eyed one,
who knows the essence of the bliss of the nectar of Brahman, the sole survivor at the end of the age, dancing in heaven— him [I salute].
I have been born as your form known by the name Rudra.
O Goddess, your lotus-feet are free from sorrow, stainless, and pure; they are worshipped by gods and asuras,
exceedingly tender, and vast and beautiful.
I bow to this form of yours; I bow to you.
Oṃ, homage to you, O Great Goddess; homage to you, O Supreme Sovereign.
Homage to the Blessed Mistress, to Śivā; to you, repeated salutations. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.250)
I am composed of you, I have you as my support, and you alone are my refuge;
I go to you alone for shelter—be gracious, O Supreme Goddess!
"There is no one equal to me in the world, whether among the gods or even the Dānavas;
for my daughter has become the Mother of the World through her ascetic penance."
"This goddess was indeed your mother, the daughter of a father;
she is Menā, the mother of the entire world. Oh, the weightiness of merit! (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.253)
Protect me always, O Queen of the Immortals, together with Menā;
I bow at your lotus feet and go for refuge to you, Śivā.
"Oh, how great is my fortune through this union with the Great Goddess!
Command me, O Great Goddess, O Śaṅkarī; what shall I do?"
Having spoken these words, the Lord of the Himālaya mountain then stood by her side with palms joined in reverence, gazing intently at Girijā.
Then, having heard his words, she who is the source of the world spoke with a smile to her father, remembering her husband Paśupati.
The Goddess said:
Listen, O best of mountains, to this supreme secret within the domain of the Lord, an instruction practiced by those who discourse on Brahman.
That supreme, wondrous, divine form of mine which was seen by me directly—
endowed with all powers, infinite, and the supreme impeller.
Tranquil, with a concentrated mind, free from hypocrisy and egoism,
being established in that and intent upon that, go to that alone for refuge.
But by means of unswerving devotion, O dear one, having taken refuge in that supreme state,
worship Him alone at all times with all sacrifices, austerities, and gifts.
Behold that very [reality] with the mind; meditate upon it and recite its mantra.
By my instruction, O sinless one, I shall destroy your cycle of worldly existence.
I indeed swiftly deliver those devotees who are intent on me and established in the yoga of the Lord from this ocean of saṃsāra.
"O best of mountains, I am indeed attained by you through meditation, the yoga of action, devotion, and knowledge; not otherwise, even by ten million ritual acts."
Constantly perform for the sake of liberation the duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti according to one's caste and stage of life, together with the knowledge of the supreme self.
From Dharma devotion is born; through devotion the Supreme is attained.
Dharma, consisting of sacrifice and other rites, is considered to be that which is proclaimed by the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Dharma is not born from anything else; for dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
Therefore, one who desires liberation and seeks dharma should take refuge in the Veda, which is my own form.
This very supreme, ancient power of mine, known as the Veda,
proceeds at the beginning of creation in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
And for the sake of protecting those very Vedas,
the unborn Lord then created the Brāhmaṇas and the other [castes], and assigned them each to their respective duties.
For those who do not perform that dharma created by Brahmā for that purpose,
he ordained the hells, beginning with Tāmisra, beneath them.
There is no scripture other than the Veda that expresses the dharma;
he who takes delight in anything else is not to be conversed with by the twice-born.
Whatever various treatises are seen in this world that contradict the Śruti and Smṛti, their foundation is indeed characterized by darkness (tāmasī).
The Kāpāla, Pañcarātra, Yāmala, Vāma, and Ārhata—
these and other such [systems] are intended for the purpose of delusion.
Those who delude human beings here through their application to false scriptures—
these scriptures were created by me for their delusion in another birth.
Those men who perform with diligence that Vedic rite which is prescribed by those most proficient in the meaning of the Vedas— they are indeed dear to me.
Out of compassion for the social classes (varṇas), Virāṭ himself,
at my command, formerly declared the dharmas to the sages as Svāyambhuva Manu.
And having heard that supreme Dharma from his mouth, other sages as well composed treatises on Dharma for the purpose of establishing the Dharma.
When those [teachings] have thus disappeared at the end of the ages, the great seers will,
by the command of Brahmā, restore them in age after age.
O King, eighteen Purāṇas were indeed narrated by Vyāsa at the command of Brahmā; in them, Dharma is firmly established.
Furthermore, other Upapurāṇas were indeed narrated by his disciples;
in every age, the author of all these is one who knows the treatises on Dharma.
Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, and Chandas,
as well as Jyotiḥśāstra, Nyāyavidyā, and Mīmāṃsā, constitute the supplementary sciences (upabṛṃhaṇa).
Thus, O best of beings, these fourteen branches of knowledge are declared along with the four Vedas; dharma is not found elsewhere.
Thus, at my command, Manu, Vyāsa, and others establish this supreme dharma of the Grandfather until the dissolution of all beings.
When the dissolution has arrived, at the end of the supreme [cycle], all those who have perfected their selves enter the supreme state together with Brahmā.
Therefore, with every effort, one should resort to the Veda for the sake of dharma;
knowledge conjoined with dharma shall illuminate the supreme Brahman.
But those who, having abandoned all attachments, have come to me alone for refuge and always worship with devotion, established in the sovereign yoga; KūrmP 1.11.286.
Compassionate toward all beings, peaceful, self-controlled, free from envy,
devoid of pride, wise, ascetics of praised vows— [these are the ones who should be honored].
With their minds fixed on me and their lives dedicated to me, they delight in the discourse of my knowledge—
whether they be renunciants, householders, forest-dwellers, or celibate students.
For those who are constantly devoted to this, I shall soon dispel all the darkness arising from the principle of illusion (māyātattva) by means of the lamp of knowledge.
Having thoroughly shaken off all darkness through that single knowledge, those who consist of me are eternally blissful; they are not born again and again in saṃsāra.
Therefore, in every way, my devotee who is intent upon me should worship me alone everywhere, accompanied by Menā.
If you are unable to meditate upon my imperishable sovereign form,
then take refuge in my manifest form, which begins with Time.
O dear one, whatever form may come within the range of my mind,
become established in that, intent upon that, and devoted to the worship of that.
But that form of mine which is partless, pure consciousness alone, auspicious, entirely free from all limiting adjuncts, infinite, immortal, and supreme— KūrmP_1.11.294.
That supreme state is attainable through knowledge alone, without hardship;
those who perceive only knowledge enter into me alone. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.295)
Those whose intellects are absorbed in That, whose very selves are That, who are established in That, and for whom That is the supreme goal—
having shaken off all impurities through knowledge— they go to the state from which there is no return.
O King of kings, without taking refuge in me, that supreme, stainless state of nirvāṇa cannot indeed be attained; therefore, go to me for refuge.
O Great King, by worshipping me as one, as distinct, or even as both, you shall thereafter go to that supreme state.
O King of kings, that reality which is inherently pure and auspicious cannot be known without taking refuge in me; therefore, go to me for refuge.
Therefore, you should worship with diligence that imperishable, eternal, formless, and sovereign form; by doing so, you will cast off bondage.
Through action, mind, and speech, propitiate Śiva everywhere and at all times with devotion; then you shall go to that state.
Deluded by my māyā, they do not indeed perceive that reality—
the supreme Maheśvara, unborn, auspicious, without beginning or end.
Abiding as the self-nature of all beings, the support of all, stainless,
eternal bliss, without appearance, devoid of qualities, and beyond darkness.
Brahman is non-dual, immovable, partless, and devoid of phenomenal expansion;
it is self-cognizable yet unknowable by others, established in the supreme ether.
Constantly enveloped by my subtle Māyā and by darkness,
they are born again and again in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
O King, that Brahman must indeed be sought through unswerving devotion and through perfect knowledge, for the sake of liberation from the bondage of birth.
Having abandoned egoism, envy, desire, anger, possessiveness,
and attachment to unrighteousness, he remained established in dispassion.
Having perceived oneself in all beings and all beings in oneself,
and having beheld the Self by means of the self, one is fit for becoming Brahman.
Having become one with Brahman, with a serene self, and bestowing fearlessness upon all beings,
he shall attain supreme, exclusive devotion to the Lord.
He beholds that supreme reality, the Lordly Brahman devoid of parts;
liberated from the entire cycle of worldly existence, he abides solely in Brahman.
For this Maheśvara, the supreme Śiva, is the foundation of Brahman—
the infinite and immutable One who has his own self as his support.
O King, for the sake of liberation from the entire cycle of worldly existence, constantly take refuge in the Lord through the yoga of knowledge, the yoga of action, or the yoga of devotion.
This secret instruction has been given to you by me, O Lord of the Mountain;
having examined all of this thoroughly, you should act as you wish.
"Indeed, having been requested by the gods, I was born from the Supreme Lord after censuring my father Dakṣa, who was a reviler of Maheśvara."
For the sake of establishing the Dharma and for the purpose of propitiating you,
she was born from the body of Menā and has taken refuge in you alone as her father.
By the command of the god Brahmā, the Supreme Self,
you shall yourself bestow me upon Rudra at the assembly of the self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*).
And because of that connection, O King, all those gods together with Vāsava pay homage to you, my dear; indeed, Śaṅkara is well-pleased with you.
Therefore, with every effort, know me as being within the sphere of the Lord;
having fully worshipped the divine Īśāna, go for refuge to him who is the worthy protector.
Thus addressed by the goddess of gods, the Lord of the Mountains, the Blessed One,
bowed his head to the goddess and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke again.
O Great Goddess, explain to me in detail the supreme Māheśvara Yoga,
as well as the knowledge of the Self and its yoga, and the means of accomplishment.
The Lord explained to him this supreme knowledge, the unsurpassed yoga of the Self,
exactly as it is, along with its means of accomplishment in detail.
Having heard from the lotus-face of the Mother of the World that supreme knowledge, Giriṇdra, who is honored by the world, became once again intent upon yoga.
And by virtue of his great fortune, he gave the virtuous Pārvatī to Maheśa at the command of Brahmā and in the presence of the gods.
He who reads this chapter, which proclaims the majesty of the Goddess, with devotion in the presence of Śiva, being pure and permeated by that very spirit; KūrmP_1,11.324.
Freed from all sins and endowed with divine yoga,
having transcended the world of Brahmā, he shall attain the abode of the Goddess.
And whoever recites this hymn in the presence of Brāhmaṇas with a concentrated mind is liberated from all sins by the Goddess.
Having known and honored the Supreme Goddess as residing within the orb of the sun, one should recite the eight thousand names of the Goddess that have been proclaimed.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, endowed with the yoga of devotion,
he should call to mind the supreme state of the Goddess, the supreme state of Maheśvara.
With a mind focused on nothing else, the twice-born should recite [the mantra] constantly until death;
having regained mindfulness at the time of his end, he attains the supreme Brahman.
Or else, by the power of his previous impressions, he is born as a Brahmin in a pure family of Brahmins, having obtained the knowledge of Brahman.
Having attained that supreme, divine Yoga belonging to the Supreme Lord,
and having become tranquil and all-pervading, one shall attain union with Śiva.
Furthermore, one should offer oblations with each of the names during the three daily libations;
