thus, one is liberated from the afflictions caused by Pūtanā and others, as well as from the defects of the seizing spirits (grahas).
Desiring prosperity, one who has worshipped the goddess Pārvatī according to the prescribed rite should recite [the mantra] daily, without weariness, for the duration of a year.
Having worshipped Śambhu, the three-eyed one, at his side with devotion,
one obtains great fortune through the grace of Mahādeva.
Therefore, with every effort, the twice-born should indeed recite the Thousand Names of the Goddess for the sake of dispelling all sins. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.11.335)
O Brahmins, the supreme majesty of the Goddess has been recounted as an incidental matter;
hereafter, learn of the creation of progeny by Bhṛgu and the others.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the first part of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
From Bhṛgu and Khyāti was born Lakṣmī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, the two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are the sons-in-law of Meru.
Āyati and Niyati were the two daughters of the high-souled Meru;
they became the wives of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and from them two sons were born.
Prāṇa, Mṛkaṇḍu, and from Mṛkaṇḍu came Mārkaṇḍeya;
likewise, the son of Prāṇa was the radiant one named Vedaśiras.
From Marīci also was born Paurṇamāsī,
who gave birth to a daughter and four sons, all endowed with every auspicious mark.
Tuṣṭi, Jyeṣṭhā, Vṛṣṭi, Kṛṣṭi,
and Apaciti were [the daughters], while Virajas and Parva were the two sons of Paurṇamāsī.
Kṣamā, however, gave birth to sons for the progenitor Pulaha:
Kardama, who was most excellent, and Sahiṣṇu, the best of sages.
In the same way, Anasūyā bore to Atri a younger son whose impurities were shaken off by asceticism, as well as other sons who were likewise stainless.
Smṛti, the daughter of Aṅgiras, gave birth to Soma, Durvāsas, and the yogi Dattātreya, all endowed with auspicious marks.
The blessed lord Pulastya affectionately procreated Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati upon Dattātri.
In a previous birth during the Svāyambhuva interval, he was known as Agastya;
likewise, his daughter was named Vedabāhu, and by name she was Sannati.
The progeny of Kratu gave birth to sixty thousand sons;
they were all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas) and are known as the Bālakhilyas.
And Vasiṣṭha likewise begot seven sons upon Urjā,
as well as a daughter with lotus-like eyes, endowed with all splendor.
Rajoha, Ūrdhvabāhu, Savana, Anagha, Sutapas, and Śukra— these were the seven sons of great power.
O twice-born ones, that fire which is of the nature of Rudra and is the son of Brahmā—
Svāhā obtained from him three noble sons of great power.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci—these are the three fires.
Pavamāna is produced by friction, while Pāvaka is known to be of lightning origin.
That sun which blazes is known as the pure fire;
from their lineage, there were forty-five others.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, Śuci, and he who is their father—
these are proclaimed to be the forty-nine fires.
All are declared to be ascetics, all are entitled to shares in sacrifices;
they are remembered as being of the nature of Rudra, their foreheads marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra).
The ancestors of Brahmā are recorded as being both those who have not performed sacrifices and those who have;
they are established in two groups: the Agniṣvāttas and the Barhiṣads. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.12.19)
From them, Svadhā gave birth to Sūtā, Menā, and likewise Vaitaraṇī;
both of them, O best of sages, were exponents of the Vedas and practitioners of yoga.
Menā gave birth to Maināka and likewise to Krauñca, his younger brother;
from Himavat was born Gaṅgā, the sole purifier of all the worlds.
By the power of the fire of his own yoga, he obtained the goddess Maheśvarī as his daughter;
thus has the supreme majesty of the Goddess been related as it was previously told.
This lineage of the offspring of Dakṣa’s daughters has been explained by me to you today; now learn of the creation of Manu.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the first division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
"Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were the two sons of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu."
Śatarūpā gave birth to two who were knowers of dharma and possessed of great heroism.
Then, Uttānapāda had a son named Dhruva,
who was devoted to the god Nārāyaṇa and attained the highest station.
From Dhruva, Śambhu gave birth to Śliṣṭi and Bhavya as her two wives.
Succhāyā bore five stainless sons to Śliṣṭi.
At the word of Vasiṣṭha, the queen performed very difficult austerities and propitiated the Supreme Person Viṣṇu, Janārdana, at Śālagrāma.
Ripu, Ripuñjaya, Vipra, Vṛkala, and Vṛṣatejas—
these pure ones were devoted to Nārāyaṇa and protectors of their own dharma.
The Bṛhatī bore to Ripu a son, Cakṣuṣa, who possessed all splendor. He begot Cākṣuṣa Manu upon Puṣkariṇī,
the daughter of the high-souled Vīraṇa Prajāpati, in the land of Vīraṇī.
Ten sons of great majesty and immense heroism were born to Naḍvalā,
the daughter of the Prajāpati Vairāja.
Ūru, Pūru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavāk, Śuci,
Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, Sudyumna, and Abhimanyuka.
From her thighs, the daughter of Agni gave birth to six sons of great strength:
Aṅga, Sumanas, Svāti, Kratu, Aṅgiras, and Śiva.
From his body Vena was born later, and from Vena was born the son of Vena (Bainya),
who is renowned as Pṛthu, the mighty protector of subjects.
By whom the earth was formerly milked for the sake of the welfare of living beings,
at the command of Brahmā, together with the highly powerful Indra, the lord of the gods.
In former times, at the extensive sacrifice of Vena’s son performed by the Grandfather (Brahmā),
the Sūta Paurāṇika was born as Hari himself in a manifested form.
O best of sages, know me as the expounder of all scriptures, the knower of dharma, and the lover of virtue; I am that ancient and eternal one who appeared in the past.
In this Manvantara, the Puruṣa Hari himself, as Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana,
graciously caused me to hear this Purāṇa in former times.
But those Sūtas who were born in my lineage, being excluded from the Vedas,
had the narration of Purāṇas as their livelihood by the command of Brahmā.
That son of Vena, Pṛthu, was a performer of sacrifices, true to his word, and a master of his senses;
he was a sovereign emperor of great splendor and a protector of his own dharma.
From his very childhood, he possessed devotion toward Nārāyaṇa;
having reached Govardhana Hill, he performed austerities with his senses subdued.
Pleased by his ascetic penance, the Lord Dāmodara himself— the deity who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace— approached the king and spoke.
"Righteous, endowed with beauty, and the best among all wielders of weapons—
by my grace, these two shall undoubtedly become your sons.
Having said this once, Hṛṣīkeśa returned to his own nature.
Vainya also, maintaining unwavering devotion toward Madhusūdana according to the Vedic injunctions,
protected his own kingdom with justice.
Not long after, O slender-limbed one, his wife Sucismitā gave birth to Khikaṇḍana,
Havirdhāna, and Antardhāna.
A son named Śikhaṇḍana was born, renowned as Suśīla;
he was righteous, endowed with beauty, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Having studied the Vedas according to the prescribed rules and remaining steadfast in dharma through austerity,
that knower of dharma, by the power of his good fortune, set his mind upon renunciation.
Having performed his service at sacred fords and being established in sacred study and austerity,
he once went to the slopes of the Himalayas, which are frequented by perfected beings.
There he beheld the forest named Dharmapada, which bestows the accomplishment of dharma; it is accessible to yogins but inaccessible to those who hate the knowers of Brahman.
There flows the most meritorious, pure river named Mandākinī,
endowed with groves of lotuses and water-lilies, and adorned by the hermitages of the Siddhas.
On its southern bank, filled with joy, he beheld a beautiful and most meritorious hermitage, frequented by lords of sages and yogis.
Having bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he worshipped Mahādeva with flowers such as lotuses and water-lilies.
Having meditated upon Īśāna situated within the sun and placing his joined palms to his head,
he gazed at the radiant one and praised the Supreme Lord.
He [worshipped] Giriśa with the Rudrādhyāya, with the life-story of Rudra,
and with various other hymns dedicated to Śambhu originating from the Vedas.
Then, in the meantime, he saw the great sage named Śvetāśvatara approaching, the most excellent among the great Pāśupatas.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, clad in a loincloth for covering, his body emaciated by asceticism, and wearing a white sacred thread; KūrmP_1,13.32.
Having concluded his praise of Śambhu, his eyes clouded with tears of joy,
he bowed his head at the Lord’s feet with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words.
I am blessed,
I am favored, since today I have seen in person the Lord of Sages, the Blessed One, the Master of Yoga, the foremost among those who know yoga.
"Oh, how great is my fortune! My ascetic penances have borne fruit.
What shall I do? I am your disciple; protect me, O sinless one! (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.13.35)
Then, having shown favor to King Suśīla, who was endowed with virtuous conduct,
he accepted him as a disciple— he whose defilements had been worn away by ascetic penance.
Having caused the wise one to perform the entire rite of renunciation,
he then bestowed upon him divine knowledge and the vow prescribed in his own Vedic branch.
That essence of all the Vedas, which liberates from the bonds of Paśu,
is known as the Final Stage (Antyāśrama), practiced by Brahmā and the other gods.
Having looked upon his disciples— those Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas dwelling in that hermitage who were devoted to the practice of celibacy— he spoke.
Having studied the branch set forth by me, yogins here dwell in repose,
meditating upon Mahādeva, the partless Śiva.
Here the Lord Mahādeva, the Blessed Īśa, taking delight together with Umā, dwells out of compassion for his devotees.
In this regard, in former times, Nārāyaṇa himself, the sustainer of the entire world, propitiated Mahādeva out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.13.42)
In this very place, having propitiated the Lord Īśāna, the deity even of the gods,
the gods and dānavas attained great perfection.
In this very place, in former times, the sages beginning with Marīci beheld Maheśvara and,
through the power of their asceticism, obtained eternal knowledge.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, endowed with the yoga of austerity, should remain constantly with me; from that, you shall attain perfection.
Having spoken thus and meditated upon the god who wields the Pināka bow, the lord of brahmins duly imparted the great mantra for the accomplishment of his own purpose.
The meritorious rite beginning with "Agnir" was promulgated by the sages; it pacifies all evils, is the essence of the Vedas, and bestows liberation.
At his word, King Suśīla, endowed with faith,
became a manifest Pāśupata and devoted himself to the study of the Vedas.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits,
he was peaceful, self-controlled, having conquered anger, and had taken recourse to the discipline of renunciation.
Likewise, Havirdhāna begot a virtuous son in the south-eastern direction named Prācīnabarhis, who was a master of the science of archery (dhanurveda).
Prācīnabarhis, the son of Bhaga and the best among all wielders of weapons,
begot ten sons upon the daughter of the Ocean.
Those renowned kings, the Pracetasas, of celebrated luster,
having studied their own Veda, were devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
From the ten Pracetas and through Māriṣā,
the illustrious Prajāpati Dakṣa was born— he who was formerly the son of Brahmā.
But that Dakṣa, having engaged in a dispute with the wise Rudra Maheśvara, was cursed by Rudra and became the son of Pracetas.
Seeing Dakṣa approaching his house, Mahādeva Hara himself offered him the worship due to him.
Then, possessed by darkness and seeking honor for which he was unworthy, that son of Brahmā went home in anger.
Once, when Satī had arrived at her own home, Dakṣa, being deeply distressed,
censured her along with her husband and reviled her in anger.
Other sons-in-law are superior to you, the wife of our Lord, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
you too, being the daughter of an unworthy man, depart from our house just as you came.
Having heard those words of his, that goddess, the beloved of Śaṅkara,
reviled her father Dakṣa and consumed herself by means of her own self.
Having prostrated before the Lord of Creatures, her husband who is clad in animal skins,
that daughter of Himavat became gratified by his ascetic penance.
Having learned of this, the Lord Rudra, Hara, the remover of the distress of those who seek refuge, became enraged; he went to Dakṣa’s house and cursed him.
O Brahmin, having cast off this body, you— born of a lineage of Kṣatriyas and deluded in mind— will procreate a son upon your own daughter.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva went to Mount Kālāsa;
and Svāyambhuva Dakṣa, in the course of time, became Prācetasa.
Thus has all this been told to you concerning the creation of Svāyambhuva Manu up to Dakṣa; for those who hear it, it is the destroyer of sin.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Pūrvavibhāga of the Ṣaṭsāhasrī Saṃhitā of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa.
The residents of Naimiṣa said:
[Tell us] of the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rakṣasas.
O Sūta, tell me in detail of the origin [of these] during the Vaivasvata interval.
O one of great intelligence, what did that King Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, who was previously cursed by Śambhu, do? We wish to hear this now.
Sūta said:

I shall declare that which was spoken by Nārāyaṇa concerning the continuity of the previous kalpa—the detailed account of the creation of beings, bound to the three periods of time, which destroys sin. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.14.3)
O King, that Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, who had previously been cursed by Śambhu,
reviled him out of old enmity and worshipped Bhava at Gaṅgādvāra.
And all the gods, together with Viṣṇu, were summoned for their shares;
and all the eminent sages arrived along with all the other seers.
Having seen the entire assembly of gods arrived without Śaṅkara,
the brahmin-sage named Dadhīca then spoke to the son of Pracetas:
Dadhīca said:
"Why is that Lord Rudra— who is followed by the commands of all beings from Brahmā down to the Piśācas— not worshipped according to the prescribed rite at this time?"
Dakṣa said:
"Indeed, in all sacrifices, no share has been assigned for Śaṅkara; nor are there mantras for him together with his wife, and thus he is not worshipped."
Smiling, the great sage, who is himself composed of all knowledge, spoke these words in anger to Dakṣa in the hearing of all the gods.
Dadhīca said:
Having indeed known Śaṅkara, who is the source from which all beings proceed and who is their supreme lord, he is worshipped with all sacrifices.
For this Śaṅkara Rudra— the destroyer, Hara, characterized by darkness (tamas),
naked, skull-bearing, and deformed— is not logically possible as the Self of the Universe.
For the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign self-ruler and creator of the world, is the Blessed One whose nature is *sattva*; he is worshipped in all ritual acts.
Dadhīca said: "Why do you not behold this Blessed One, the thousand-rayed one,
the sole destroyer of all worlds, the Supreme Lord whose nature is Time?"
"He whom the wise, righteous, and exponents of the Veda praise here—
He is this very one, the witness of intense radiance, whose self is Time, and whose body is that of Śaṅkara."
This is Rudra, Mahādeva, the wearer of matted hair, the compassionate Hara;
he is the blessed Āditya, Sūrya, the blue-throated one, and the deep-red one.
The thousand-rayed sun is praised by the Sāman-singers, Adhvaryus, and Hotṛs;
behold him, the Viśvakarman, the embodiment of Rudra, who consists of the three Vedas.
Dakṣa said:
These twelve Ādityas who have arrived as sharers of the sacrifice are all to be known as Sūryas; for there is no other Sun (Ravi) to be found.
When this was said, the sages who had arrived, desiring to see [him],
replied with the words "So be it," acting as his assistants.
Those whose minds are possessed by darkness do not see the bull-bannered Lord;
they are censured all the more, by the thousands and even by the hundreds.
Blaming the Vedic mantras and Hara, the Lord of all beings,
they failed to honor the words of Dakṣa, being deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu.
And all the gods, Vāsava and the others, having come for their shares,
did not see the god Īśāna, except for Nārāyaṇa Hari.
The blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha Brahmā, the best among those who know Brahman,
vanished in an instant while everyone was looking on.
When the Blessed One had vanished, Dakṣa himself went for refuge to Nārāyaṇa Hari, the god who is the protector of the worlds.
Then Dakṣa, free from fear, proceeded with that sacrifice,
for the Blessed Viṣṇu is the protector of those who have come for refuge.
Furthermore, the venerable ṛṣi Dadhīca spoke to Dakṣa,
having gazed upon all the hosts of ṛṣis and gods who were indeed haters of Brahman.
By honoring those who are unworthy of honor, and by failing to honor those who are worthy of honor, a man incurs great sin; of this there is no doubt.
Where there is the favoring of the wicked and the humiliation of the virtuous,
a terrible divine punishment falls instantly upon that place.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin-sage cursed those assembled brahmins who were enemies of Īśvara and had come to assist Dakṣa.
Because you have cast out the Vedas and reviled the Supreme Lord,
Mahādeva Śaṅkara, who is worshipped by the world.
You shall all become outsiders to the Triple Veda and haters of the Lord,
censuring the path of the Lord with minds attached to false scriptures.
Having acquired a distorted understanding of proper conduct and speaking with false knowledge,
they will indeed be afflicted by those born of the Kali age upon reaching the terrible Kali Yuga.
"Having abandoned the entirety of the power of asceticism, you shall go back to the hells;
even Hṛṣīkeśa, though he has taken refuge in us, will turn his face away."
Having spoken thus, the brahmin seer, a treasure-house of asceticism,
ceased speaking and went in his mind to Rudra, the destroyer of all sins.
In the meantime, the Goddess, perceiving her husband to be the god Maheśvara, Mahādeva, Paśupati, the all-seeing one, spoke this.
The Goddess said:
"O Śaṅkara, in a previous birth my father Dakṣa performed a sacrifice while censuring both your disposition and himself. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.14.35)
"The gods, together with the ṛṣis, were there as his helpers;
destroy that sacrifice quickly—I choose this one boon. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.14.36)
Thus addressed by the goddess, the Lord, the sovereign and best of gods,
suddenly created Rudra with the intent to destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
He has a thousand heads and feet, a thousand eyes, and mighty arms;
he has a thousand hands, is invincible, and resembles the fire at the end of an eon.
With fangs formidable and difficult to behold, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
holding a staff in his hand, possessing a great roar, wielding the Śārṅga bow, and adorned with sacred ashes.
Known as Vīrabhadra, he was endowed with the power of the God of gods;
as soon as he was born, he approached the Lord of gods with palms joined in reverence.
He said to him, "Destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice; may it be well with you.
"Having reviled me, he performs that sacrifice at Gaṅgādvāra, O Lord of the Gaṇas," [he replied]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.14.41)
Then, by a single lion employed by Bandhu,
Vīrabhadra effortlessly brought about the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
And from Wrath (Manyu), the Great Goddess Bhadrakālī was created;
together with her, the Gaṇa ascended his bull and departed.
Thousands of other Rudras were dispatched by that wise one;
they are renowned as the "Hair-born" (Romajas), acting as his assistants.
With tridents, spears, and maces in their hands, and likewise with chisels and stones in their grasp,
they resemble the Rudra of the fire of time (Kālāgnirudra) as they roar through the ten directions.
All of them, mounted upon bull-seats with their wives and appearing exceedingly terrifying,
surrounded the foremost of the Gaṇas and proceeded toward the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
Having all reached that region known as Gaṅgādvāra,
they beheld that sacrificial ground of Dakṣa, who possessed immeasurable splendor.
It was filled with thousands of celestial damsels, resounded with the songs of apsarases,
enriched by the melodies of lutes and flutes, and made resonant by the recitation of the Vedas.
Seeing Prajāpati seated together with the ṛṣis and the gods,
Vīrabhadra, as if smiling, spoke auspiciously to him along with the Rudras.
"For we are all attendants of Śarva, who possesses immeasurable splendor;
having arrived here with the desire for a share, grant us the portions we seek."
"O best of divine sages, if this command belongs to someone else—
if it is said that 'the portion must be given to you, but not to us'—
then tell us who it is that issues the command; for we shall find out from him."
Thus addressed by Gaṇeśa, the gods, led by Prajāpati, said to the Lord: "There are no mantras for our share of the sacrifice. (KūrmP 1.14.52)
The mantras said to the gods: "You are those whose minds are struck by darkness, you who do not worship Maheśvara, the king of the sacrifice."
The Lord of all beings, Hara, whose body is all beings,
is worshipped in all sacrifices as the bestower of all prosperity and success.
Though addressed in this way, their minds were deluded by Māyā;
they did not heed Īśāna, and the mantras departed from the gods and went to their own abode.
Then the blessed Lord Rudra, together with his wife and the lord of his hosts,
touched the brahmin-sage Dadhīca with both hands and spoke to the deities.
"Mantras have not been made authoritative by you who are arrogant in your strength;
therefore, because you have acted with such insolence, I shall today destroy your pride."
Having spoken thus, the leader of the Gaṇas set that sacrificial hall on fire;
and the enraged lords of the Gaṇas uprooted the sacrificial posts and hurled them away.
Together with the Prastotṛ and the Hotṛ, all those terrifying lords of the Gaṇas seized the horse and threw it into the current of the Gaṅgā.
Vīrabhadra, whose nature was blazing and whose soul was undaunted, paralyzed the upraised arm of Śakra as well as those of the other inhabitants of heaven.
Having effortlessly plucked out the eyes of Bhaga with the tips of his fingernails,
he struck Pūṣan’s teeth with his fist and thus knocked them out.
Likewise, the powerful Lord of the Gaṇas, smiling, playfully overpowered the god Candra with his big toe.
O lords of sages, having effortlessly cut off both hands of Vahni and torn out his tongue,
he struck even the sages on the head with his foot.
Likewise, the one of great strength, having paralyzed the Sudarśana discus, pierced Viṣṇu— who was approaching together with Garuḍa— with sharp arrows.
Having observed the host, the mighty-armed Garuḍa approached and suddenly struck them with his wings, roaring like the ocean.
Then Bhadra himself created thousands of Garuḍas who were even superior to Vainateya;
they all fled from Garuḍa.
Seeing them, the wise Garuḍa, possessing great speed, fled with haste, leaving Mādhava behind; that was like a marvel.
When Vainateya had vanished, the Blessed One born from the lotus arrived and restrained both Vīrabhadra and Keśava.
Out of reverence for the Supreme Lord, he propitiated him by offering hymns of praise; then the Blessed Lord Īśa himself arrived there accompanied by Ambā.
Beholding that God of gods, accompanied by Ambā and surrounded by all his attendants,
the blessed Brahmā, Dakṣa, and all the inhabitants of heaven offered praise.
Out of particular devotion, Dakṣa, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, praised the goddess Pārvatī, who shares half the body of the Lord, with various kinds of hymns.
Then the Blessed Goddess,
smiling at Maheśvara with a serene mind, Rudra, that treasure-house of compassion, spoke these words.
"You alone are the creator, the ruler, and the protector of the world;
and Dakṣa, as well as the inhabitants of heaven, are to be favored by the Blessed One."
Then, laughing, the Lord Kapardin Nīlalohita,
Hara, spoke to the prostrate gods and to the son of Pracetas.
"Go now, all you deities; I am pleased with you.
I am to be honored in all sacrifices, and especially I am not to be reviled."
And you too, O Dakṣa, listen to my words which provide protection from all [evils]:
having abandoned this desire for worldly things, become a devotee of me with diligence.
"By my grace, you shall become the Lord of the Gaṇas at the end of the kalpa;
until then, remain at your own offices, contented, by my command."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, together with his wife and his followers,
vanished from the sight of Dakṣa of immeasurable splendor.
When the great god Śaṅkara had vanished, the lotus-born Brahmā himself spoke for the welfare of the entire world to Dakṣa.
Brahmā said:
"Has your delusion departed now that the bull-bannered Lord is pleased?
Since the God himself has spoken thus, protect this world with vigilance."
This Lord dwells within the heart of all beings;
those who have become Brahman, the wise who proclaim the Vedas, behold Him.
He is the self of all beings, he is the seed, the supreme goal;
Maheśvara, the God of gods, is praised by Vedic mantras.
He who worships that Rudra, the one eternal being within his own self,
with a mind endowed with devotion, goes to the supreme state.
Therefore, having realized that the Supreme Lord is without beginning, middle, or end,
worship Him with diligence through action, mind, and speech.
One should diligently avoid disparaging this [teaching], which brings about one's own destruction;
for the actions of a disparager lead to every kind of fault.
He who is this great yogin of yours, the imperishable protector Viṣṇu—
he is undoubtedly the Lord, the God of gods, Mahādeva.
Those men who, out of delusion and due to their lack of devotion to the Vedas, believe that Viṣṇu— the source of the universe— is distinct from the Lord (Īśvara), go to hell.
Those who follow the Vedas and perceive the god Rudra as well as Nārāyaṇa as one and the same become partakers of liberation.
"He who is Viṣṇu is himself Rudra; he who is Rudra is Janārdana.
Thinking thus, one should worship the God; he goes to the supreme goal. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.14.89)
Viṣṇu creates this entire world, and the Lord (Īśvara) beholds it;
thus, this whole world originates from Rudra and Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, having abandoned the reviling of Hari, one who is composed even toward Viṣṇu should take refuge in Mahādeva, the protector of those who discourse on Brahman.
Then, having heard the words of Viriñca,
the Lord of Creatures went for refuge to the god Gopati, who is clothed in a tiger skin.
Those other great ṛṣis who were consumed by the fire of Dadhīca’s curse,
being deluded and hostile toward the God, were then reborn during the Kali ages.
Having abandoned their entire power of asceticism, those born of the lineage of Brahmins [remained] here due to the greatness of their prior impressions and by the word of Brahmā.

Then, at the end of the kalpa, all those who had been released from their curse were cast by Time into the Raurava and other hells; having reached Brahmā, the lord of the worlds, who possesses the splendor of the sun, they were granted permission by the Self-born One.
Having propitiated Īśāna, the lord of the thirty gods, through the practice of austerity and yoga,
they shall become as they were before, by the grace of Śaṅkara.
All this has been told to you concerning the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice;
now hear the lineage of all the daughters of Dakṣa.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the first part of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Formerly, Dakṣa was commanded by the Self-born One (Brahmā) to create progeny.
He created the gods, the Gandharvas, the Ṛṣis, as well as the Asuras and the Uragas.
When those creatures did not increase as he was creating them,
he then created living beings through sexual union according to the natural law.
He begot a thousand sons upon Asiknī, the daughter of the patriarch Vīraṇa, who was endowed with righteousness.
When those sons had been lost through the illusory power (*māyā*) of Nārada,
that Prajāpati Dakṣa indeed begot sixty daughters upon Vairaṇī.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Two [mantras] belong to Bahuputra, two to the wise Kṛśāśva, and likewise two to Aṅgiras; I shall now declare their successful application.
Arundhatī, Vasu, Jāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, Marutvatī,
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and the radiant Viśvā.
These ten are his lawful wives; learn now of their sons:
Viśvā gave birth to the Viśvedevas, and Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas.
The Marutvants were born of Marutvatī; the eight Vasus were the sons of Vasu;
the Bhānus were the sons of Bhānu; and the Muhūrtas were indeed the sons of Muhūrta.
From Lambā was born Ghoṣa, and Nāgavīthī was born from Jāmī.
The entire realm of the earth was born from Aruṇvatī.
From Saṃkalpā came Saṃkalpa; these are remembered as the ten sons of Dharma.
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa— these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Āpasya’s sons were Vaitaṇḍya, Śrama, Śrānta, and Dhuni;
and the son of Dhruva was the blessed Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds.
The venerable Varcas shall be the son of Soma; Draviṇa, the son of Dhara;
Purojava shall be the son of Anila; and likewise Avijñātagati.
Kumāra was indeed the commander-in-chief of Anala;
the lordly yogi Devala became the son of Pratyūṣa;
and Viśvakarman, the Prajāpati and master craftsman, was the son of Prabhāsa.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, as well as Ariṣṭā, Surasā, Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā,
Kadrū, and Muni— who was likewise a knower of dharma— learn now of their sons.
Aṃśa, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman,
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Aṃśumān, and Viṣṇu.
Formerly, during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu, they were known as the Tuṣitas;
in the interval of Vaivasvata, they are declared to be the Ādityas, the sons of Aditi.
Diti obtained two sons endowed with great strength from Kaśyapa:
Hiraṇyakaśipu as the elder, and likewise Hiraṇyākṣa as the other.

The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, possessed of great strength and prowess, propitiated the god Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, through ascetic penance; having beheld him and praised him with various hymns, he obtained divine boons. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.15.19)
Then all the gods and the celestial sages, oppressed and struck by his power, went to the Grandfather, the God of gods.
[He approached] Śambhu, the refuge, the one worthy of refuge, the god who pervades the entire world,
Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, the protector, the supreme Puruṣa,
the immutable, the sole one of the worlds, the ancient, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.15.21)
O lords of sages, having been entreated by the gods and the sages for the sake of the welfare of all the deities, that one whose seat is the lotus departed.
Being praised by the lords of sages and even by the immortals who bowed before him,
he proceeded to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, where Lord Hari resides.
Having beheld the Lord Viṣṇu, the source of the world, the teacher of the universe, and the auspicious one,
he prostrated with his head at His feet and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke.
Brahmā said:
You are the refuge of all beings, the infinite one whose self is the entirety;
you are the pervasive one, possessing the bodies of all the immortals, the eternal Great Yogin.
You are the self of all beings, the primary cause, the supreme nature;
you are devoted to dispassion and sovereignty, transcending passion, and untainted.
"You alone are the creator, the sustainer, and the slayer of the enemies of the gods;
O Infinite Lord, you ought to protect us, for the Supreme Lord is indeed the protector."
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the blessed Lord Viṣṇu,
whose eyes were like blossoming lotuses and who wore yellow garments, spoke to the enemy of the asuras.
"For what purpose have the gods, together with Prajāpati, arrived at this place despite their great heroism? Or what service may I perform for you? (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.15.29)
The gods said: "O Blessed One, the Daitya named Hiraṇyakaśipu, arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā,
oppresses all the gods along with the ṛṣis."
"O Supreme Person, you are incapable of being slain by any living beings except yourself;
you ought to slay them all, for you are the protector of the entire world."
Having heard what was said by the deities, Viṣṇu, the creator of the worlds,
himself created a being for the sake of slaying the chief of the Daityas.
To him, who was as tall as Mount Meru, of terrible form and fearsome appearance,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, the one whose banner is Garuḍa spoke.
Having slain that king of the Daityas, Hiraṇyakaśipu,
you ought to return quickly to this place through your prowess.
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu and having bowed down to Puruṣottama,
the unmanifest Great Being, he went to the great city of the Daityas.
Uttering a terrifying roar and bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
the Lord mounted Garuḍa like a second Mount Mahāmeru.
Having heard that sound, which resembled the roar of a great cloud, the foremost of the Daityas then reported it out of fear for the lord of the Daityas.
The Asuras said:
"O crusher of the immortals, some great being, impelled by the gods, is approaching while emitting a terrifying roar; we do not know him."
Then Hiraṇyakaśipu himself, accompanied by the foremost of the Asuras and his sons led by Prahlāda, all equipped with armor and weapons, set out at that time.
Having seen him seated upon Garuḍa, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
a person of mountain-like form like another Nārāyaṇa.
Some fled, while others, with eyes agitated by fear, said to one another:
"This is that very god of the gods, the protector Nārāyaṇa, who is our enemy."
"Surely our imperishable Lord, or perhaps his son, has arrived!"—
having said this, those men discharged showers of weapons at the Person;
but the God effortlessly destroyed them all without exception.
Then the four sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu, renowned for their prowess and possessing voices like the roar of clouds— Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, and Hrāda— fought against that being born from Nārāyaṇa.
Prahlāda discharged the Brahma weapon, Anuhrāda the Vaiṣṇava,
Saṃhrāda the Kaumāra, and Hrāda the Āgneya.
Having reached that man, those four weapons, including the Vaiṣṇava,
were unable to afflict him, just as they could not afflict Viṣṇu Vāsudeva.
Then that mighty-armed and immensely powerful one, seizing his four sons by their feet with his hands, hurled them down and let out a roar.
Then, once his sons were liberated, the powerful Hiraṇyakaśipu himself struck him violently in the chest with his foot.
Greatly tormented by that Garuḍa and thus swiftly pursued,
he went quickly and invisibly to where the Lord Nārāyaṇa was; having arrived, he reported everything exactly as it had occurred.
Having reflected thus in his mind, the stainless God, who consists of all-knowledge,
made half of his body human and likewise half of his body a lion.
In the form of Nṛsiṃha, the unmanifest one suddenly appeared in the city of Hiraṇyakaśipu, bewildering the foremost of the Daityas.

Fierce with tusks, his soul absorbed in yoga, resembling the fire at the end of an eon, Nārāyaṇa shines like the midday sun, having mounted his own power that effects the destruction of all things, he who is infinite.
Seeing his eldest son Prahlāda in the form of Narasiṃha,
that asura incited him to slay Narasiṃha.
"Commanded by me, destroy this one who possesses the body of a man-lion, who is far more powerful than before, together with all his younger brothers, quickly!"
Due to that association, the Asura Prahlāda fought with all his might against the imperishable Viṣṇu, but was defeated by Narasiṃha.
Then, thus urged on, the Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, the younger brother,
meditated upon the weapon of Paśupati, discharged it, and let out a roar.
The weapon did not cause any loss to that Viṣṇu, the god of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor, just as it did not affect the god who wields the trident.
Seeing his weapon repelled, Prahlāda, due to the weight of his good fortune,
recognized Vāsudeva as the eternal God who is the soul of all.
Having laid aside all weapons with a mind endowed with purity,
he bowed his head to the God who dwells in the hearts of yogis.
Having praised him with hymns to Nārāyaṇa derived from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas,
and having restrained his father and brothers, he then spoke to Hiraṇyākṣa.
This is Nārāyaṇa, the infinite, eternal, blessed, unborn Lord;
the ancient Puruṣa, the God, the great Yogin who consists of the universe.
He is the Ordainer and the Disposer, self-luminous and stainless;
he is the Primal Spirit, the ultimate principle, the root nature, and the imperishable.
The Lord is the inner controller of all beings, transcending the qualities;
go for refuge to this Viṣṇu, the unmanifest and imperishable.
When this had been said, the evil-minded Hiraṇyakaśipu himself,
utterly deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu, spoke to his son.
"This Nṛsiṃha, whose prowess is slight, must be slain with all our might;
impelled by Time, he has now arrived at our abode."
Smiling, the high-minded son spoke these words to his father:
"Do not revile this Lord of beings, the one and immutable."
How is it that the god Mahādeva, who is eternal and devoid of time,
how is Viṣṇu— who is the self of time and assumes the form of time— slain by time?
Then the evil-minded Suvarṇakaśipu, impelled by fate,
fought the imperishable Hari even though he was forbidden by his son.
With bloodshot eyes, he tore open Hiraṇyanayana’s elder brother with his claws, even as Prahlāda looked on.
When Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain, the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa,
overwhelmed by fear, fled after sending his son Prahlāda away.
Anuhrāda and the other sons, as well as hundreds of other asuras,
were sent to the abode of Yama by lions born from the body of Nṛsiṃha.
Then, having withdrawn that form, the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa returned to his own supreme form known as Nārāyaṇa.
When Nārāyaṇa had departed, Prahlāda, the best of the asuras,
joined Hiraṇyākṣa with a formal consecration.
Having propitiated Śaṅkara through austerity and obtained his great son Andhaka, he conquered even the sages in battle and oppressed the gods.
Having conquered the gods along with Indra and having bound this earth,
he took Indīvaraprabhā to the subterranean realm (rasātala) and made her his captive.
Then the gods, including Brahmā, their facial splendor withered,
went to Hari’s abode and made this representation to Viṣṇu.
Having reflected upon the means for his destruction, the imperishable Soul of the Universe assumed a radiant boar-form composed of all the gods.
Having gone and slain that Hiraṇyanayana, the Supreme Person raised up this earth with his tusk, just as at the beginning of a kalpa.
Having abandoned his form as a boar and having established the gods and the twice-born in their own states,
Viṣṇu returned to his own divine nature and the supreme abode.
When that enemy of the gods had been slain, Prahrāda, devoted to Viṣṇu,
ruled his own kingdom, having abandoned his asuric disposition.
Devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, he sacrificed to the gods according to the prescribed rites;
then, by the power of Viṣṇu, his kingdom became free from rivals.
Then, on one occasion, the asura did not honor a brahmin ascetic who had come to his house, owing to the illusion of the gods.
Having been thus insulted by that ascetic who was utterly deluded, he,
with eyes bloodshot with rage, cursed the king of the asuras.
That divine Vaiṣṇava devotion by which you rely upon strength to treat the Brāhmaṇas with contempt shall surely come to an end for you.
Having spoken thus, the twice-born departed quickly from Prahrāda’s house;
and he too, though attached to his kingdom, then fell into a state of delusion through the power of the curse.
He oppressed the foremost of the brahmins and did not recognize Janārdana;
remembering the slaughter of his father, he directed his wrath toward Hari. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.15.85)
Between those two— the god Nārāyaṇa and Prahlāda, the enemy of the gods— there occurred a most terrible battle that made the hair stand on end.
Having fought a truly great battle with that Viṣṇu, he was defeated; yet,
due to the power of his previous impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), knowledge of Hari, the Supreme Person, arose within him, and he went for refuge to Him who is the worthy protector.
From that time forward, the lord of the Daityas, bearing exclusive devotion toward Nārāyaṇa,
the Supreme Person, attained the great yoga.
While Hiraṇyakaśipu’s son had his mind absorbed in yoga, Andhaka,
the preeminent among the asuras, obtained that great kingdom.
The son of Hiraṇyanetra, born from the body of Śambhu,
desired Umā, the goddess who was the daughter of the mountain and resided on Mount Mandara.
Formerly, in the sacred Dāruvana forest, thousands of sages who were householders performed austerities for the sake of propitiating the Lord.
Then, after some time had passed, there occurred a most terrible and difficult-to-overcome drought, which was exceedingly fierce and destructive of living beings.
Having gathered together, all the sages, overcome by hunger, entreated Gautama— the treasury of asceticism— for food to sustain their lives.
The wise one gave them abundant, delicious food;
all the brahmins ate it with minds free from hesitation.
When the twelfth year had passed, a great and terrifying rain fell like at the end of a kalpa, and the world became as it was before.
Then all the best of sages, having consulted with one another,
said to the great seer Gautama, "Let us go with speed."
And he restrained them, saying, "O wise ones, having stayed in my house for some time as you please, you must certainly depart. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.15.97)
Then, having created an illusory emaciated cow, they all brought it into the presence of the high-souled Gautama.
Having observed this, he was overcome with compassion and, eager to protect her, tied her up in the cow-pen; as soon as she was touched, she died.
Tormented by grief, that great sage suddenly failed to perceive what ought and ought not to be done; the sages spoke thus to him.
"O best of the twice-born, as long as this cow intended for slaughter remains within your body, you must not eat food; let us depart from here at once."
Thereupon, being gladdened, they went to the auspicious Devadāru forest to perform penance as before, though they had been led into the power of sin.
Having learned by some means that their cow-slaughter had been produced through illusion, the sage Gautama, being exceedingly prone to anger, cursed them.
They will become excluded from the Triple Veda (trayī-bāhya) and equal to those who commit great sins (mahāpātakin);
they shall remain so through that curse as they are born again and again.
Having all approached Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, and Viṣṇu, the imperishable,
they praised them with worldly hymns, like those who have consumed leftovers, yet moving everywhere.
O gods of gods, O great gods, destroyers of the afflictions of your devotees,
you who are great yogis acting according to your will, you ought to protect us from sin.
Then, beholding Viṣṇu standing at his side, the bull-bannered god asked:
"What might be the purpose of these seekers of merit?"
Then the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the refuge of all and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees,
looked upon the great lords of brahmins as they bowed down and spoke to Gopati, O best of sages.
O Śaṅkara, O Mahādeva, not even a trace of merit can accrue to a person outside the Veda; for Dharma has emerged from the Veda alone. *Kūrma Purāṇa* 1.15.109.
Nevertheless, O Maheśvara, out of affection for your devotees,
all these who are about to go even to the hells must be protected by us.
Therefore, O Bull-bannered One, for the sake of protecting those who are outside the Vedas and for the purpose of deluding sinners, we shall compose scriptures.
Thus enlightened by Mādhava, the enemy of Mura, Rudra composed treatises on delusion; and Keśava, too, was impelled by Śiva [to do the same].
The Kāpāla, Nākula, Vāma, Bhairava, Pūrvapaścima,
Pañcarātra, and Pāśupata, as well as thousands of others.
Having created them, the two gods said: "Performing what is enjoined by the scriptures, yet falling again and again into terrible hell for many kalpas."
Then, being born in the world of men with the accumulation of your sins exhausted, go by the power of propitiating the Lord to the destination of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Abide by my grace; for otherwise, there is no atonement for you.
Thus urged by Īśvara and Viṣṇu, those great ṛṣis accepted the command of the two enemies of the asuras with their heads bowed.
Delighting in various places, they composed other treatises and,
having demonstrated results, they taught their disciples.
Having descended to the surface of the earth and deluding this world,
Śaṅkara, together with the twice-born, went about begging for their benefit.
Adorned with a garland of skulls and smeared with the ashes of a corpse,
he bewilders this world, decorated with a mass of matted hair.
Having entrusted the goddess Pārvatī to Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor, and having appointed Rudra, born from his own body, as Bhairava for the subduing of the wicked; KūrmP_1.15.120.
Having given the goddess to Nārāyaṇa, and having established Nandin, the joy of the lineage, there along with the Gaṇapa lords and the gods headed by Indra; KūrmP_1.15.121.
Then, when Mahādeva had departed, Viṣṇu himself, whose body is the universe,
assumed the form of a woman and devotedly served Maheśvarī.
Brahmā, Agni, Śakra, Yama, and other preeminent gods,
having assumed beautiful female forms, waited upon the Great Goddess.
And the blessed Nandīśvara, the supreme favorite of Śambhu and chief of the Gaṇas, stood at the gateway as he had done before.
In the meantime, a wicked-minded Daitya named Andhaka,
desiring to carry off the Daughter of the Mountain, then came to Mount Mandara.
Seeing that Andhaka had arrived, Śaṅkara,
the immeasurable soul Hara who assumes the form of Time as Kālabhairava, restrained him.
Between the two of them there occurred a most terrible battle that made the hair stand on end;
the bull-bannered god struck that Daitya in the chest with his trident.
Then he created thousands of Daityas known as Andhakas;
by these Andhaka Daityas, Nandiṣeṇa and the others were utterly defeated.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Meghanāda, Caṇḍeśa, Caṇḍatāpana,
Vināyaka, Meghavāha, Somanandī, and Vaidyuta.
Having encountered Andhaka, the foremost of the Daityas, all those endowed with great strength fought him with spears,
javelins, double-edged swords, mountain peaks, and battle-axes.
Then, having whirled them around and grasped their two feet with both hands,
they were hurled a hundred yojanas away by the exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas.
Then, released by Andhaka, they— resembling the sun at the end of time— numbering in the hundreds and thousands, rushed toward Bhairava with terrifying force.
A very great and most terrifying sound of "Hā!
Hā! arose; Rudra, assuming a fearsome form, fought while wielding a formidable trident.
Having seen the exceedingly powerful and invincible army of the Andhakas, Hara was threatened;
he went for refuge to the divine Vāsudeva, the unborn and all-pervading Lord.
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu created one hundred supreme goddesses;
the God, stationed at the side of the Goddess, was for the destruction of the enemies of the immortals.
Likewise, by the greatness of Keśava, a thousand Andhakas were led to the abode of Yama by the goddesses with ease alone upon the field of battle.
Seeing his army utterly defeated, the great asura Andhaka also fled from that battlefield with great speed, turning his back on the fight.
Then, having performed his play for twelve years, Mahādeva returned to Mount Mandara for the welfare of his devotees in the world.
Knowing that the Lord had arrived, all the lords of the Gaṇas gathered together and waited upon him, just as the twice-born wait upon the radiant sun.
Having entered the holy abode, which is difficult for the undisciplined to approach,
Śiva beheld the god Nandin, Bhairava, and Keśava.
Then the Lord Īśāna, having favored Nandin who was inclined toward prostration,
smelled the crown of Keśava’s head and embraced him.
Having seen Mahādeva, the goddess, her eyes wide with joy,
bowed her head at the feet of that Lord.
Then, having reported the victory to that Śaṅkara, Śaṅkarī stood by his side,
and Bhairava, bowing down, spoke of the greatness of Viṣṇu.
Having heard of that victory and the prowess of Keśava,
the Lord Śambhu sat together with the Goddess upon an excellent throne.
Then all the hosts of gods and the twice-born sages, headed by Marīci,
went to Mount Mandara to behold the three-eyed God of gods.
By him that excellent hundred of goddesses was formerly conquered;
now the army of the Daityas has assembled, desiring a vision of the Lord.
Seeing the moon-adorned Lord seated upon his excellent throne with the Goddess,
the goddesses bowed down with reverence and sang with great longing.
They bowed down to the goddess Girijā on the left side of the wielder of the Pināka bow,
and to the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who was seated upon his divine throne and free from all ailment.
Having seen the Lord Īśāna seated upon his throne together with the Goddess and Nārāyaṇa,
those beautiful women bowed to the God and questioned him.
The maidens said:
"Who are you who shine with such splendor? Who is this girl with the luster of the morning sun?
And who is this being of such form, with eyes as long as lotus petals?"
Having heard their words, the great yogin, the imperishable lord of beings, whose vehicle is the best of bull-elephants, spoke.
"I am Nārāyaṇa; Gaurī is the eternal Mother of the World.
Having divided himself, the Lord, the Sovereign, has remained as many through his own self."
Neither the gods nor the great seers know my supreme reality;
only this Universal Soul—Bhavānī and Viṣṇu alone—knows it.
For I am indeed actionless, peaceful, solitary, and without possessions;
they call me alone the god Keśava, as well as the goddess Ambikā.
He is the Ordainer and the Disposer, both the cause and the effect;
he is Viṣṇu, the agent and the instigator, who bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Vāsudeva, the soul of the universe and facing in all directions, is the enjoyer, the immeasurable person, the destroyer assuming the form of time, the creator, and the protector.
For Nārāyaṇa himself is the immutable, all-pervading, and immovable yogin;
he is the deliverer, the Puruṣa, the Self, the absolute, and the supreme state. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.15.157)
This very Gaurī, the power (śakti) of Maheśvara, is stainless, peaceful, true, and eternally blissful; she is the supreme state—so says the Śruti.
All this has been born from her, and into her alone it shall go to its dissolution;
she indeed is the supreme goal among all the goals of living beings.
United with that Goddess, I am the absolute, partless, supreme one;
I behold this entire universe in its entirety, and whoever knows that is liberated.
Therefore, know Viṣṇu alone—the beginningless non-dual Self, the Lord—as the one and only; through that, you shall attain liberation.
Those endowed with faith who regard Viṣṇu as the unmanifest Self,
yet worship the Lord with a divided vision, are not dear to me.
Those deluded ones who hate the source of the world are cooked in the Raurava and other hells;
they are not released even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Therefore, having correctly understood him here as the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu, the protector of all beings without exception, he should be meditated upon in every time of distress.
Having heard the words of the Blessed One, the goddesses, who were the sovereigns of all their hosts,
bowed down to the god Nārāyaṇa and to the goddess born from the snowy mountain.
They prayed for devotion to the Lord, who is dear to his devotees,
toward the pair of feet of Bhavānī and toward the lotus-feet of Nārāyaṇa.
Then the Gaṇeśas and the Mothers did not see the god Nārāyaṇa, the progenitor of the world; it was as if a miracle had occurred.
In the meantime, the great Daitya Andhaka, afflicted by the god of love and deluded,
went to the mountain to abduct the goddess Girijā.
Then the glorious and stainless yogi Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person of infinite form,
appeared right there for battle with the Daityas.
Then the Lord, having placed the Blessed One Viṣṇu at his side along with the chief gods of the Gaṇas, the son of Śilāda, and the Mothers, set out for battle.
That god, Kālarudra, approached.
Taking up a trident that resembled fire,
that God of gods went on ahead; the foremost of the lords of the Gaṇas followed him.
The thousand-armed god also departed.
The Blessed One, the color of a water-lily, shone in the midst of the gods like a cloud atop the peak of Mount Sumeru. At that time, he was mounted upon his vehicle.
The Blessed One, like the sun, is the beholder of the three worlds.
In this world, the beginningless, immeasurable Lord Hara, possessing a thousand forms and holding a trident in his hand, appeared in the sky with a resonant sound.
A rain of flowers fell upon the god.
Seeing Gaṇeśarāja arrived,
surrounded by the lords of the hosts, the enemy of the gods fought with Śakra and the Mothers.
Together with all the hosts, whose leaders were the immortals.
Having conquered all [enemies] in battle through the strength of his arms, he, whose splendor is infinite, approached Śambhu,
where that Kālarudra resided.
Having mounted the celestial chariot, his vital strength was depleted.
Seeing that Andhaka was at the end of his time, the Blessed One, whose banner is Garuḍa,
addressed Mahādeva, who is Bhairava and adorned with ashes.
"You ought to slay Andhaka, the lord of the Daityas and a thorn to the worlds;
for there is no other capable of slaying him except you, O Blessed One."
You are the destroyer of all worlds, for you are the soul of Time and the sovereign body;
you are praised with various mantras by wise scholars learned in the Vedas.
Having heard the words of Vāsudeva,
the Blessed Lord Hara looked at Viṣṇu and set his mind upon the slaying of the lord of the Daityas.
He went to the host of deities, bringing supreme joy to the attendants;
the beings moving through the atmosphere praised the god Bhairava.
Victory to you, O Infinite One, Great God, Eternal Form of Time!
You are the fire that perpetually moves within all beings.
You are the Knower of All, you are the Vaṣaṭkāra, you are the Sustainer, the golden-hued, the imperishable;
you are Brahmā, you are Mahādeva, you are the Abode, the supreme state.

O Lord of Yoga, whose form is the syllable Oṃ, whose eyes are the three Vedas, the three-eyed one, the Lord of gods possessed of great majesty; victory to you, the Sovereign of the entire world! KūrmP 1.15.183.
Then that Lord Kālāgnirudra, the refuge of the virtuous, having seized Andhaka and placed him upon the points of his trident, began to dance.
Having seen Andhaka impaled upon the trident, the hosts of gods and the Grandfather (Brahmā) bowed down to the Lord,
the divine Bhairava, the liberator from worldly existence.
The sages offered hymns of praise, the Siddhas sang, and the Gandharvas and Kinnaras chanted; in the sky, throngs of beautiful Apsarases danced.
Then Andhaka, his sins burnt away, was established upon the tip of the trident;
with all-encompassing knowledge arisen within him, he praised the Supreme Lord.
Andhaka said:
With my head bowed, I pay homage to the one Blessed One,
whom those who are concentrated know as the reality of the Lord (Īśatattva).
The ancient merit, whose form is infinite,
is Time, the seer who is the cause of union and separation.
With fangs formidable, dancing in the sky,
with a mouth of fire, having the form of a blazing sun,
and endowed with thousands of feet, eyes, and heads;
I bow down to you alone, O Rudra.
O Lord whose feet are worshipped by the gods headed by Jayā, whose nature is the stainless reality free from divisions—
you alone, the one fire, are worshipped in many forms.
O you whose entire self-nature consists of the divisions of wind and the other elements! KūrmP 1.15.190.
They call you alone the ancient Puruṣa, resplendent as the sun, beyond the darkness;
you behold this entire world and protect it eternally.
You are the Ender, attended by hosts of yogis.
The one inner self is established in manifold ways within bodies, yet is devoid of distinctions such as body and so forth;
you are the word "self," the reality of the supreme self.
Some call you Śiva alone.
You are the imperishable Brahman, the supreme purifier, whose nature is bliss and who is designated as the Praṇava;
you are the Lord established within the words of the Vedas.
He is self-luminous and devoid of all distinctions.
You are Indra in form, Varuṇa, Agni, and in form;
you are the Haṃsa, the vital breath, death, and the end; you are the sacrifice, Prajāpati, the Blessed One, and the Sole Rudra.
O Blue-necked One, you are praised by those who know the Vedas.
You are Nārāyaṇa, the primordial source of the worlds; you are the grandfather and the great-grandfather,
celebrated in the secret Upaniṣads of Vedānta.
You are Sadāśiva; you are the Supreme Lord.
Salutation to the Supreme Self, who is beyond darkness, who transcends all, who exists within the five states,
and who is stainless, beyond the three powers.
To him who is seated upon the thousandfold-power throne.
Salutation to the one who is the triple form, whose body is the state of bliss, the abode of the world, and identical with the world;
salutation to him who has fixed his eye upon his forehead.
Homage to him who dwells in the hearts of all people.
Homage be to you,
whose pair of feet is worshipped by the lords of sages and the perfected ones, who are seated upon the throne of sovereignty and dharma, and who wear the lord of serpents as a necklace.
Homage to the one who is the ultimate limit, who arises from existence.
Salutations be to you, whose eyes are like a thousand moons and suns; salutations, O Soma, to you of the slender waist;
salutations be to you, O God, whose arms are golden.
Homage to Mṛḍa, the lord of Ambikā.
Homage to the one who is exceedingly secret, who dwells within the cave of the heart, whose nature is perfectly ascertained through the wisdom of Vedānta,
and whose abode is the stainless realm devoid of the three times.
Homage to Maheśa; homage to Śiva! KūrmP 1.15.200.
As he was thus praising him, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, being pleased, lowered him from the tip of the stake and spoke, touching him with both hands.
"O Daitya, I am now entirely pleased by this hymn;
having attained the status of a leader of my attendants (gāṇapatya), dwell in my presence as an immortal."
Free from disease, with all doubts severed, and highly honored even by the gods,
he is an attendant of Nandīśvara, entirely devoid of suffering.
As soon as these words had been spoken by the God of gods,
the deities and the lords of the Gaṇas [confronted] Andhaka before Mahādeva in the presence of the gods.
Resembling a thousand suns, three-eyed, marked by the moon,
blue-throated, with matted hair upon his crown, and holding a great trident in one hand.
Having seen him, they praised the Daitya, overcome with supreme wonder;
then the Blessed Viṣṇu spoke to the God of gods, as if smiling.
It is fitting, O Mahādeva, that you, a great person, possess such power;
for one does not perceive the defects born of ignorance, and perceives even virtues.
Thus addressed by the preeminent gods, Gaṇeśa and the others, Bhairava,
together with Keśava and Andhaka, went into the presence of Śaṅkara.
Beholding the God who had arrived together with Śaṅkara, along with Andhaka,
Mādhava, and his mother, Hara attained complete peace.
Taking the son of Hiraṇyalocana by the hand,
the Lord went to where the daughter of the mountain, the beloved of the Lord, was in her celestial chariot.
Beholding that Bhava, the remover of the afflictions of worldly existence, who had arrived,
she attained a bliss profound as darkness and a serene clarity toward Andhaka.
Then Andhaka beheld Maheśvarī standing by the side of the god;
he fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff and bowed at her lotus feet.
I bow to this primordial Daughter of the Mountain, beloved of the gods,
by whom both Pradhāna and Puruṣa destroy the entire world.
I bow to that unborn one who, imperishable, shines together with Śiva upon the auspicious seat, golden and exceedingly pure.
I bow to that Umā, within whom the entire universe and all worlds go to their destruction,
and who is devoid of all Vedas.
I bow to this Umā, the daughter of the Lord of the Mountains, who is neither born nor perishes, who does not increase, and who transcends all qualities.
Forgive me, O Goddess born of the mountain; I have acted out of delusion. I bow to your lotus feet, which are worshipped by gods and asuras alike.
Thus was the blessed Gaurī praised by Pārvatī, the lord of the Daityas, who was bowed with devotion; she accepted Andhaka as her son.
Then that Bhairava, born of Rudra and the Supreme Lord, went to Pātāla together with his Mothers,
by the permission of Śambhu.
Where that tamasic form of Viṣṇu, the agent of destruction, resides,
there the unmanifest Lord Hari sits in the form of Nṛsiṃha.
Then Śambhu, of infinite form, having been well-worshipped even by Śeṣa,
the blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra, united himself with his own self.
Then, as that god was engaged in yoga, all his mothers,
being hungry, bowed down to Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident, and spoke.
The Mothers said:
"O Mahādeva, we are hungry; let permission be granted by you.
We shall devour the three worlds, for otherwise there is no satisfaction for us."
Having spoken these words, the mothers born of Viṣṇu devoured the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Then that god Bhairava meditated upon Hari in the form of Nṛsiṃha, the divine Nārāyaṇa; in an instant, Hari appeared.
And while devouring their mothers here, they addressed him, saying:
"O Blessed One, quickly restrain the three worlds from becoming yours!"
Remembered again by Viṣṇu in his form as Nṛsiṃha, the goddesses approached Mahādeva,
who was likewise in the form of Narasiṃha.
Having come into the presence of Viṣṇu, all those powers that effect destruction bestowed their energy upon Śambhu, who was in the form of Bhairava of exceeding splendor.
Then the Mothers beheld that source of the universe, the fierce Nṛsiṃha, who in an instant had attained oneness with the serpent Śeṣa.
Hṛṣīkeśa declared: "Those who are devotees of the wielder of the trident, and those who here constantly remember me, must be protected with great effort."
This incomparable form of mine, which effects the dissolution of all things,
is born from a portion of Maheśvara and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The Blessed One Ananta is Time itself; my own state is twofold:
the Tāmasī and Rājasī forms, as well as the four-faced God of gods.
Thus this god, invincible, Time who consumes the worlds,
the very self of Rudra, shall devour the entire universe at the end of the aeon.
That form of mine called Nārāyaṇa, which is delusive and abounds in the quality of goodness (sattva),
eternally sustains the entire world.
For he is Viṣṇu, the supreme Brahman, the supreme Self, the ultimate goal;
he is called the unmanifest root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) and eternal bliss.
Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, the goddesses, the mothers of the universe,
sought refuge in that very Mahādeva, Hari.
All this has been told to you by me—
the slaying of Andhaka and the majesty of Bhairava, the god of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the first division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The glorious Kūrma said: When the egg had indeed been seized by the high-souled Prahlāda, [the following occurred].
In ancient times, there was a king named Virocana who was his son.
Having conquered the gods together with Indra, the great Asura protected the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, according to righteousness for many years.
While he was living in this manner, the venerable great sage Sanatkumāra, impelled by Viṣṇu, once arrived at his city.
Seeing the son of Brahmā seated upon the lion-throne, the great Asura rose,
bowed his head with palms joined in reverence, and spoke these words:
I am blessed, I am graced; for today I have encountered my ancient Lord, the Master of Yoga, who is himself a knower of Brahman.
"For what purpose has the Lord Pitāmaha himself come, O Brahmin?
Tell me, son of Brahmā, what task shall I perform?"
The Blessed Lord said to that great asura who was endowed with righteousness:
"I have indeed come to see you; you are truly fortunate."
O best of Daityas, this policy of the Daityas is very difficult to find;
indeed, in the three worlds, there is surely no other righteous person like you.
Thus addressed, the king of the asuras spoke again to that great sage:
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, tell me the supreme dharma among all dharmas."
That blessed yogi spoke to the high-souled lord of the Daityas concerning the dharma that is the most secret of all— the unsurpassed knowledge of the Self.
Having attained supreme knowledge and having paid the teacher’s fee,
he entrusted that kingdom to his son and became devoted to the practice of yoga.
His son was the wise and great asura named Bali;
devoted to Brahmanas and exceedingly righteous, he then conquered Purandara.
Having engaged in a great battle with him, Śakra, surrounded by all the immortals,
went for refuge to the infallible god Viṣṇu, having been defeated.
In the meantime, the goddess Aditi, the mother of the gods, being deeply distressed, [prayed] herself:
"May I have a son for the sake of slaying the lords of the Daityas. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.16.14)
That mass of asceticism performed a most great and terrible supreme penance,
having sought refuge in Viṣṇu, the unmanifest Hari, the protector worthy of seeking refuge.
Having placed within the filaments of the heart-lotus the supreme state— the partless Vāsudeva, who is without beginning or end, bliss, the void, and absolute— KūrmP_1,16.16.
The blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace,
whose essence is yoga, appeared before the mother of the gods as Hari.
Seeing that Viṣṇu had arrived, Aditi, filled with devotion,
considered herself to have achieved her life's purpose and gratified Keśava.
Aditi said:
Victory to you, the sole cause for the destruction of the entire flood of suffering; victory to you, who are devoted to the yoga of infinite majesty!
Victory to you, O embodiment of primordial consciousness, without beginning, middle, or end;
victory to you, whose nature is stainless bliss beyond all conceptual constructions!
Salutations to you, Viṣṇu, who have the form of Time;
salutations to you, Nārasiṃha, who are Śeṣa;
salutations to Kālarudra, the agent of dissolution.
Homage to you, Vāsudeva; homage be to you! KūrmP_1,16.20.
Homage to you, the ordainer of the universal illusion; homage to you, the truth accessible through yoga;
homage to you, who have reached the culmination of the knowledge of phenomena.
Salutations to you, O Varāha; again, salutations to you! KūrmP_1,16.21.
Salutations to you, whose form possesses the luster of a thousand suns and moons; salutations to you, who are accessible through the Vedas, spiritual knowledge, and dharma;
salutations to the God of gods, the primordial God of gods.
O Lord, source of the universe, homage once more be to you!
Salutations to you, Śambhu, who are established in truth;
salutations to you, the cause, whose form is the universe;
salutations to you, who abide within the seat of yoga.
Salutations again to you, Śiva, who possesses a single form. KūrmP_1,16.23.
Thus the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa, who pervades the universe, being gratified by Devakī,
offered her a boon as if smiling.
Bowing her head to the ground, she chose this supreme boon:
"I choose you alone as my son for the welfare of the gods; this is my boon. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.16.25)
"So be it," said the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward those who have sought refuge;
having granted the boons, the immeasurable Lord vanished right there.
Then, after a long time had passed, the mother of the gods herself bore in her womb Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Janārdana.
When Hṛṣīkeśa had entered the womb of the goddess’s mother,
terrible portents arose in the city of Bali, the son of Virocana.
Having observed all these portents, the lord of the Daityas, overwhelmed with fear,
bowed down to his grandfather, the elder asura Prahlāda, and spoke.
Bali said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, what portents are arising in our city now? What should be done by us, and for what cause do they occur?"
Having heard his words and reflected for a long time, the great Asura paid homage to Hṛṣīkeśa and spoke these words.

Prahlāda said: That Viṣṇu who is worshipped with sacrifices, whose this entire world is, and who, for the sake of destroying the asuras, became the mother of the inhabitants of heaven—[that one she bore]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.16.32)
He who is undivided yet divides everything, and who is distinct even from the entire universe—
that Vāsudeva entered the body of the mother of the gods.
He whose true nature the gods do not know in its ultimate sense—
that Viṣṇu has today entered the body of Aditi by his own will.
He from whom all beings arise and into whom they go to their dissolution—
he is the Great Yogin descended here, the Ancient Person, Hari.
Where there exists no conceptual construction of name, genus, and so forth—
that Viṣṇu, whose nature consists of pure existence alone, is born as a partial incarnation.
He whose power is that Mother of the worlds, who upholds His attributes—
that Illustrious Māyā, Lakṣmī— He is Janārdana descended here.
He whose form is that of Tamas is Śaṅkara; his body is Rājasika;
and from him Brahmā is born, while Viṣṇu, the upholder of Sattva, arises through one portion.
Having reflected thus with a mind bowed in devotion toward Govinda, go to him alone for refuge; from that, you shall attain liberation.
Then, at the word of Prahlāda, Bali, the son of Virocana, went for refuge to Hari; he protected the entire universe according to dharma.
When the time had arrived, Aditi herself, the mother of the gods, gave birth from Kaśyapa to Mahāviṣṇu, the increaser of the joy of the deities.
Four-armed, with wide eyes, his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa,
resembling a dark blue cloud, radiant and enveloped in splendor.
All the gods, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, and the Cāraṇas waited upon Upendra;
Indra and the other deities were there, and Brahmā was surrounded by hosts of seers.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony, the Blessed Lord Hari studied the Vedas under Bharadvāja,
demonstrating proper conduct to the three worlds.
For in this way that Lord demonstrates the worldly path;
whatever standard he establishes, the world follows it.
Then, in the course of time, the wise Bali, son of Virocana,
himself worshipped Viṣṇu, the omnipresent Lord of Sacrifice, with sacrifices.
He honored the Brahmins by bestowing upon them abundant wealth;
then the brahmin-sages arrived at the sacrificial enclosure of that high-souled one.
Having understood this, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, urged by Bharadvāja,
assumed the form of a dwarf and then went to the place of sacrifice.
With his body draped in a black antelope skin and adorned with a sacred thread,
the brahmin, matted-haired and decorated with ashes, shone brilliantly with his Āṣāḍha staff as he recited the Vedas.
Having approached the presence of the king of the Asuras, Hari, appearing as a mendicant,
asked Bali for a piece of land measured by his three steps.
Having washed the feet of Viṣṇu, Bali, accompanied by Bhāsa,
offered water for rinsing the mouth and took up a golden pitcher.
"I shall give you these three steps;
may the Lord Hari, of imperishable form, be pleased.
Having reflected thus upon the sprout-like tip of the Lord's hand, he spoke.
He caused very cool water to fall down.
This primordial deity strode across this earth, as well as the intermediate space and the heavens;
he is that Lord of the Daityas, free from all passion.
Desiring to act [thus], he [protected] one who had sought refuge.
Having traversed the three worlds, the Lord’s foot went from the realm of Prajāpati to the world of Brahmā;
they bowed down before it, which was like a thousand suns.
Those perfected ones (siddhas) who dwell there in that world.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu, who is without beginning, appeared before the Grandfather (Brahmā) and gratified him;
having split the upper shell of that cosmic egg, he emerged.
He again assumed his divine coverings.
Then, from the breaking of the egg, a cool and great mass of water fell down, frequented by those who have performed meritorious deeds;
and at that time, the best of rivers also began to flow.
Addressed as "Ganga" by Brahmā, she remained stationed in the sky.
Having gone to the Great One, the primordial nature, the preeminent, the sole Brahman, the Person who is one's own seed,
he remained at that imperishable station of the Lord.
Having seen him there in various places, the gods offer praise.
Beholding that Puruṣa whose body is the universe, the great Bali, through the yoga of devotion, bowed to Viṣṇu—
the one, undecaying Nārāyaṇa.
Whom the gods pay homage with their own minds.
To him spoke the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, having become the primordial creator once more as Vāmana:
"O Lord of Daityas, this [world] now belongs to me alone."
The three worlds have been bestowed by you as a gift of existence.
Having bowed his head once more, the Daitya poured water from the tip of his hand, saying:
"I offer myself as a servant to You, whose abode is infinite."
To Trivikrama, of immeasurable prowess.
Then Śaṅkhapāṇi, the inner self of the universe, having accepted what was offered even by his own son, spoke to the Daitya, the son of Prahlāda.
"Enter the root of the netherworld once again."
Dwell there eternally, having enjoyed pleasures unattainable even by the gods;
meditate upon me constantly through the yoga of devotion.
"You shall enter me again during the conflagration at the end of the eon."
Having spoken thus to that lion among the Daityas, Viṣṇu of true prowess,
the wide-striding Viṣṇu, gave the three worlds to Purandara.
The Siddhas, celestial rishis, and Kinnaras praise this Great Yoga,
as do Brahmā, Śakra, the Blessed One, and the hosts of Rudras, Ādityas, and Maruts.
Having performed this miraculous deed, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a dwarf,
vanished right there while everyone was looking on.
That illustrious and excellent Daitya, devoted to Viṣṇu, was also sent by Prahlāda, the foremost of the Asuras, and by Viṣṇu himself, and he reached Pātāla.
He asked about the majesty of Viṣṇu and the unsurpassed yoga of devotion;
then he (Viṣṇu) spoke to Prahlāda and performed the ritual of worship for him.
Then, through the power of meditative cultivation, he went for refuge to the immeasurable Lord, who holds the discus, sword, and conch in his hands and has eyes like lotus petals.
Having resolved upon the yoga of action with a humble disposition.
O brahmins, this prowess of Vāmana has been recounted to you;
that Supreme Person always performs the works of the gods.
Thus, in the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses, in the first part, the sixteenth chapter: "Bali had a hundred sons of great strength and prowess;
among them, the foremost was the exceedingly powerful one named Bāṇa, who was radiant."
That king, being exceedingly devoted to Śaṅkara, protected his kingdom;
having brought the three worlds under his control, he oppressed Vāsava.
Then Śakra and the other gods went and said to the one clad in animal skins (Kṛttivāsas):
"The great asura named Bāṇa is indeed harassing us."
Urged by all the gods, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
playfully burnt Bāṇa’s city with a single arrow.
While that city was being consumed by fire, Bāṇa went for refuge to Rudra, the wielder of the trident, the Lord Īśāna, the Lord of cattle, who is blue-and-red in hue.
Placing that Śāmbhava liṅga upon his head, free from fear,
he departed from that city and praised the Supreme Lord.
The Lord Īśa Śaṅkara Nīlalohita, having been praised,
joined Bāṇa with devotion to the state of being a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya).
Now, there were the exceedingly terrifying sons of Danu, headed by Tārā;
namely, Tāra, Śambara, Kapila, Śaṅkara,
Svarbhānu, and Vṛṣaparvan— these are proclaimed as the principal ones.
O twice-born ones, there were a thousand serpents of Surasā,
as well as many-headed, high-souled beings who move through the sky.
Ariṣṭā gave birth to a thousand Gandharvas;
the great Nāgas beginning with Ananta are proclaimed as the offspring of Kadrū.
And Tāmrā gave birth to six daughters, O best of the twice-born:
Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvā, Gṛdhrikā, and Śuci.
In that manner, Surabhi gave birth to cows and likewise to buffalo;
Irā produced trees, creepers, climbing plants, and all varieties of grasses in every way.
O best of beings, Khasā gave birth to the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, while Muni gave birth to the Apsarases; and Krodhavaśā gave birth to the host of Rākṣasas.
Vinatā had two famous sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa;
of these two, the wise Garuḍa, having performed most difficult austerities,
by the grace of Śiva attained the state of being the vehicle of Hari himself.
Having propitiated Rudra, the Great God, with ascetic penance, Aruṇa was formerly appointed to the office of charioteer for the Sun by Śambhu, who was pleased with him.
These descendants of Kaśyapa, both stationary and moving, have been proclaimed;
indeed, in this Vaivasvata age, they destroy the sins of those who hear them.
Twenty-seven sons are proclaimed, as well as the wives of Soma who were observant of excellent vows;
and here, the offspring of the wives of Ariṣṭanemi numbered sixteen.
Just as four kinds of lightning are recorded for the learned Bahuputra,
so too are the sons of Aṅgiras, the sages honored by Brahman.
The sons of the divine seer Kuśāśva were the celestial weapons;
indeed, at the end of every thousand yugas, they are born again during the various Manvantaras, invariably with identical names and identical functions. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.17.19)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the first part of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having produced these sons for the sake of the continuation of progeny, [he said:]...
But Kaśyapa, desiring [a specific] lineage, performed very great austerity.
While he was performing intense austerities, these two sons were born to him:
Vatsara and Asita; both of them were exponents of the Veda.
