From Vatsara were born Naidhruva and the highly illustrious Raibhya;
from Raibhya were born the sons of Raibhya, the most excellent among the radiant ones.
Sumedhā, the daughter of Cyavana and wife of the high-souled Naidhruva,
gave birth to sons known as the Kuṇḍapāyins.
To Asita, by means of Ekaparṇā, was born a son most devoted to Brahman,
named Devala, a master of yoga and a man of great austerity.
The most illustrious among the Śāṇḍilyas, a wise man who knew the meaning of all principles,
attained supreme yoga through the grace of the Lord of Pārvatī.
The Śāṇḍilyas, Naidhruvas, and Ārebyas are the three branches of Kaśyapa;
these brahmins are of human nature. Now I shall describe to you the descendants of Pulastya.
O brahmins, the daughter of Tṛṇabindu was known by the name Ilavilā;
that royal sage bestowed that maiden upon Pulastya.
From that [wife] of the rishi Tvaṣṭṛ, Viśravas was born;
he had four wives who increased the lineage of Paulastya.
Puṣpotkaṭā, Rākā, Kaikasī, and Devavarṇinī were endowed with beauty and grace; now hear of their offspring.
To him, Kaikasī, possessing a divine form, gave birth to Jyeṣṭha Vaiśravaṇa;
she also bore a son, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas.
Puṣpotkaṭā gave birth to these auspicious sons of Viśravas: Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā, and likewise Vibhīṣaṇa.
O subjects, hear now concerning Mahodara, Prahasta, Mahāpārśva, Khara, as well as the daughter Kumbhīnasī, who were born on the day of Rākā.
Triśiras, Dūṣaṇa, and the mighty Vidyujjihva—
these ten Rākṣasas of the Paulastya lineage were performers of cruel deeds;
all were preeminent in the power of asceticism, devoted to Rudra, and most terrifying.
The sons of Pulaha were all deer, as well as fanged beasts of prey;
likewise, spirits, piśācas, serpents, boars, and elephants.
In that Vaivasvata interval, Kratu was remembered as being childless;
Marīci’s son Kaśyapa himself became the Prajāpati.
From Bhṛgu was born Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas, a man of great asceticism,
devoted to the yoga of Vedic study, a devotee of Hara, and possessed of great splendor.
O best of brahmins, I have heard that Atri had many sisters who were devoted wives; they became the wives of Kṛśāśva through Ghṛtācī.
He begot upon them the highly powerful Svastyātreyas,
who were devoted to the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and whose sins had been destroyed by ascetic penance.
Nārada, however, gave the lady Arundhatī to Vasiṣṭha;
for there, due to the curse of Dakṣa, the sage Nārada became one whose vital seed was drawn upward (an ascetic).
When the Haryaśvas had vanished through the illusory power of Nārada,
Dakṣa, his eyes bloodshot with rage, cursed Nārada.
"O twice-born one, because all my sons have been brought to complete destruction by your power of illusion, I shall be left without offspring."
Vasiṣṭha begot a son, Śakti, by Arundhatī;
from Śakti was born the illustrious Parāśara, the omniscient one, the best among those who practice austerity.
Having propitiated Īśāna, the Lord of the gods of gods and the destroyer of Tripura,
he obtained as his peerless son the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
From Dvaipāyana was born Śuka, who was indeed the Lord Śaṅkara himself;
having descended to earth by a portion of a portion, he attained his own supreme state.
Śuka also had five sons who were exceedingly ascetic:
Bhūriśravas, Prabhu, Śambhu, Kṛṣṇa, and Gaura as the fifth;
and there was also a daughter named Kīrtimatī, a mother of yoga who was firm in her vows.
These Brahmins, the exponents of the Veda, have been declared here as belonging to this lineage.
Hereafter, learn from me the royal succession descending from Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the first section of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Aditi gave birth to the lord Āditya as her son from Kaśyapa.
That Āditya had four wives:
the queen Saṃjñā, Prabhā, and Chāyā. Learn now of their sons.
Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, gave birth to Manu, the unsurpassed son of Sūrya,
as well as Yama, Yamunā, and the queen Raivata.
From the Sun [came] Prabhā; from Sāvarṇa, his son Chāyā;
and from Śani, Tapatī and Viṣṭi, respectively.
The first Manu had nine sons who were self-restrained:
Ikṣvāku, Nabhaga, Dhṛṣṭa, and Śaryāti.
Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Ariṣṭa, Kāruṣaka,
and the highly resplendent Pṛṣadhra— these nine were equal to Śakra.
Ilā, the eldest and most excellent, went to the abode of Budha for the sake of increasing the Lunar dynasty and united with the son of Soma.
The goddess gave birth to Purūravas, the most excellent son of Soma, who brought satisfaction to the ancestors; this we have heard from Budha. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.19.7)
Having attained pure manhood, he became renowned as Sudyumna;
Ilā obtained three sons, and then she regained her womanhood.
Utkala, Gaya, and Vinatāśva—
all of them, renowned for their incomparable splendor, took refuge in the Lotus-born One.
And from Ikṣvāku was born the heroic king named Vikukṣi; he had one hundred and fifteen sons, of whom he was the eldest. KūrmP_1.19.10.
The eldest among them was Kakutstha; for Kakutstha was Suyodhana.
From Suyodhana came the illustrious Pṛthu, and Viśvaka was the son of Pṛthu.
From Viśvaka came Ārdraka, the wise one; Yuvanāśva was his son. Having reached Gokarṇa, the powerful Yuvanāśva— ||| KūrmP_1,19.12 |||

Having seen the brahmin Gautama performing austerities with the brilliance of fire, the king, desiring a son, prostrated himself on the ground like a staff and asked: "By what action may one obtain a righteous son? (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.19.13)
Gautama said:
"By propitiating the primordial ancestor Nārāyaṇa, the faultless,
beginningless and endless God, one shall obtain a righteous son."
By worshipping Īśāna, the primordial Kṛṣṇa, one obtains a virtuous son— he whose son is Brahmā himself and whose grandson is Nīlalohita.
Having propitiated that Hṛṣīkeśa, whose true power even the Blessed Lord Brahmā does not know, one shall obtain a righteous son.
Having heard the words of Gautama, King Yuvanāśva propitiated Vāsudeva, the eternal one of great yoga.
He had a heroic son, renowned as Śrāvastī,
by whom the great city of Śrāvastī was built in the Gauḍa country.
From him was born Bṛhadaśva, and from him came Kuvalayāśvaka;
he attained the name Dhundhumāra after slaying the great asura Dhundhu.
O best of the twice-born, it is said that Dhundhumāra had three sons:
Dṛḍhāśva, Daṇḍāśva, and Kapilāśva.
Dṛḍhāśva’s son was Pramoda, and Haryaśva was his son; Nikumbha was the son of Haryaśva, and from Nikumbha came Saṃhatāśvaka.
Kṛśāśva and Raṇāśva were indeed the two sons of Saṃhatāśva;
Yuvanāśva was the son of Raṇāśva, and he possessed strength equal to Śakra in battle.
Having performed the Vāruṇī sacrifice through the grace of the sages,
he obtained an incomparable son, a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu,
the highly wise Māndhātṛ, the best among all wielders of weapons. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.19.23)
Māndhātṛ’s sons were Purukutsa and the heroic Ambarīṣa, as well as the meritorious Mucukunda; all were equal to Śakra in battle.
The heir of Ambarīṣa is remembered as the other Yuvanāśva;
Harita was the son of Yuvanāśva, and Hārīta was his son.
The highly illustrious Trasadasyu was the heir of Purukutsa;
he was born of Narmadā, and Saṃbhūti was his son.
Viṣṇuvṛddha was his son, and Anaraṇya was the next;
Bṛhadaśva was the son of Anaraṇya, and Haryaśva was his son.
That exceedingly righteous king,
through the grace of the progenitor Kardama, obtained a virtuous son who was devoted to the Sun.
Having worshipped the auspicious Sun,
King Vasumān obtained an incomparable son, Tridhanvā, the subduer of enemies.
O best of the twice-born, having conquered his enemies, he performed the horse sacrifice;
he was devoted to sacred study, charitable by nature, patient, and intent upon righteousness.
The sages,
headed by Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa, as well as the gods led by Indra, assembled at the sacrificial enclosure of the high-souled one.
Having duly completed the sacrifice, the great king, filled with humility, bowed down to those best of the twice-born, Vasiṣṭha and the others, and questioned them. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.19.32)
Vasumān said:
"O bulls among brahmins, what is most conducive to welfare in this world—is it sacrifice, austerity, or renunciation? Tell me, for you know all things."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having worshipped the Lord of Sacrifice with sacrifices, the self-possessed man should then go to the forest.
Pulastya said:
Having propitiated the Lord, the supreme ascetic, through austerity,
and having first worshipped the foremost of gods with sacrifices according to the rules, one should go forth into the life of a wandering mendicant.
Pulaha said:
By propitiating through austerity that thousand-rayed one whom they call the one ancient Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord, one shall attain liberation.
Jamadagni said:
"In the navel of the Unborn, a single seed was placed by the Lord; that deity, by whom [all things are sustained], is worshipped for the sake of austerity."
Viśvāmitra said:
That Agni who is the soul of all, infinite, self-born, and facing in every direction—he is Rudra;
he is worshipped through fierce austerity, not by other sacrifices.
Bharadvāja said:
That eternal god Jātavedas, who is worshipped with sacrifices,
whose body consists of all the deities, is honored as the Lord of austerity.
Atri said:
He from whom all this has been born, whose offspring is Prajāpati—
he, Maheśvara, having undertaken most great austerity, is worshipped.
Gautama said:
He from whom Pradhāna and Puruṣa arise, whose world consists of power—
that eternal God of gods is to be worshipped through austerity.
Kaśyapa said:
"The thousand-eyed god is indeed the witness, that Prajāpati;
the supreme Great Yogin, when honored with austerity, becomes propitious."
Kratu said:
"For one who has completed his studies and performed sacrifices, and who has obtained a son,
no dharma whatsoever is seen in the scriptures that exists apart from austerity."
Having heard this, that royal sage, his mind exceedingly delighted, bowed to them;
then, after dismissing and honoring them, he spoke to Tridhanvan.
I shall propitiate through austerity the God named the Single Syllable (Ekākṣara)—
the Great Breath, the Puruṣa who dwells within the sun.
But you, ever devoted to dharma, must protect without weariness this entire circle of the earth, comprising all four social orders.
Having spoken thus, that sinless king, having entrusted that kingdom to his own son,
went to the forest to perform unsurpassed austerity.
On a beautiful peak of the Himalayas, in the auspicious forest of Devadāru trees,
subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, he worshipped the gods with the food of sages.
For more than a hundred years, having shaken off his impurities through austerity,
he mentally recited the goddess Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas.
As he was thus reciting, the self-existent god, the Supreme Lord,
Hiraṇyagarbha, the Soul of the Universe, came to that place himself.
Seeing the god Brahmā, who faces all directions, approaching,
he bowed his head at his feet while proclaiming his name.
Homage to you, the god beyond gods, to Brahmā, the Supreme Self;
to you, the golden-formed, the thousand-eyed, the Creator.
Salutations to the Creator and the Ordainer; salutations to you whose form is the soul of the Vedas;
salutations to you who are attainable through Sāṃkhya and Yoga; salutations to you whose form is knowledge.
Salutations to you, the threefold-formed creator who knows all things;
salutations to the ancient Puruṣa, the teacher of yogins.
Then the blessed Lord Viriñca, the creator of the universe, being pleased, spoke:
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you; I am the giver of boons."
The king said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, may I chant the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, for more than a hundred years; let my lifespan be that long."
"So be it," said the Soul of the Universe, gazing upon the lord of men;
and having touched him with both hands, being well-pleased, he vanished right there.
Having obtained the boon, that illustrious one, with a mind exceedingly serene,
remained peaceful, bathing at the three periods of the day and subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits, as he recited his prayers.
When a full hundred years had passed for him, the Lord Ugradīdhiti,
the great yogi, appeared from the center of the solar orb.
Seeing that eternal Brahmā, the knower of the Vedas, seated in the circle, self-existent and without beginning or end, he was filled with wonder.
He praised him with Vedic mantras, and especially with those dedicated to Sāvitrī;
in an instant, he beheld that very person, the Supreme Lord.
Hara has four faces, a crown of matted locks, eight hands, and three eyes;
he is marked by the digits of the moon and possesses the bodies of both man and woman.
Illuminating the entire world with his own rays, he is blue-throated,
wearing red garments, and is red-hued, adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Perceiving Rudra through his supreme true being, being himself permeated by that very state of being,
he indeed bowed his head to him with this *Sāvitrī* verse.
Salutations to you, O blue-throated one, the radiant, the supreme dweller,
Rudra who consists of the three Vedas, whose form is Time, and who is the primal cause.
Then Mahādeva, with a joyful mind, said to the king:
"O sinless one, listen to these secret names of mine. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.19.66)
O King, being pure, always pay homage to me with these songs from all the Vedas, which bring peace to the cycle of worldly existence.
O King, recite with an undistracted mind and a heart attached to me this chapter of the Śatarudrīya, which is extracted as the very essence of the Yajurveda. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.19.68)
A celibate practitioner, moderate in diet, established in ashes, and composed in mind,
who recites the Rudra-mantra until death, attains the supreme state.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra, out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotee,
granted the king an additional lifespan of one hundred years.
Having bestowed that supreme knowledge and dispassion upon him, the Supreme Lord Rudra vanished in an instant; it was like a marvel.
The king also, with a single-minded focus, recited the mantra of Rudra through ascetic penance;
covered in ashes, bathing at the three periods of the day, he remained peaceful and concentrated.
As that king continued his recitation, when another hundred years were complete,
there arose in him the engagement with yoga— the supreme state which is time itself beyond time.
By means of his Vedic knowledge, he entered that auspicious orb of the Sun, the abode of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), which is the essence of the Vedas; from there, he went to Maheśvara.
Whoever should read or even hear this supreme account of the king,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the first section of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Now, King Tridhanvan, protecting the earth in accordance with righteousness, [ruled].
He had a learned son known as Trayyāruṇa.
He had a son named Satyavrata, who was possessed of great strength;
his wife, named Satyadhanā, gave birth to Hariścandra.
Hariścandra had a powerful son named Rohita;
Harita was the son of Rohita, and Dhundhu was his son.
Vijaya and Sudeva were the two sons of Dhundhu;
Vijaya had a son named Kāruka, who was full of valor.
Vṛka was the son of Kāruka; from him Bāhu was born.
Sagara became his son, a king who was supremely righteous.
Sagara also had two wives, Prabhā and Bhānumatī;
propitiated by them, Aurva Agni granted them an excellent boon.
Bhānumatī took one son, Asamañjas,
while the auspicious Prabhā took sixty thousand sons.
The son of Asamañjas was the king named Aṃśumān;
his son was Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa came Bhagīratha.
By whom the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā was brought down after performing austerities,
through the grace of Mahādeva, the wise God of gods.
Pleased by the ascetic penance of Bhagīratha, the Lord Hara,
whose ornament is the moon, bore Gaṅgā upon his head at the conclusion of the Soma sacrifice.
The son of Bhagīratha was indeed Śruta by name;
his heir was Nābhāga, and from him Sindhudvīpa was born.
Ayutāyu was his son, and Ṛtuparṇa was his son;
Ṛtuparṇa’s son was the righteous one named Sudāsa.
His son was the famous Saudāsa, known as Kalmāṣapāda.
But the highly resplendent Vasiṣṭha begat Aśmaka upon the wife of Kalmāṣapāda; he was the banner of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
In Utkalā, however, was the king named Nakula, the son of Aśmaka;
for that king, out of fear of Rāma, went to the forest deeply distressed.
Wearing the armor of a woman, he became Śataratha from him;
from him came the illustrious Bilibili, and Vṛddhaśarman was his son.
From that Viśvasaha was born he who is renowned as Khaṭvāṅga;
his son was Dīrghabāhu, and from him Raghu was born.
From Raghu was born King Daśaratha;
from him came the heroic Rāma, son of Daśaratha, who knew the Dharma and was world-renowned.
Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and the mighty Śatrughna—
all equal to Śakra in battle and endowed with the power of Viṣṇu—
were born as portions of Viṣṇu, the creator of the universe, for the sake of destroying Rāvaṇa.
Rāma’s fortunate wife was the auspicious daughter of Janaka,
Sītā, renowned throughout the three worlds and endowed with the virtues of character and nobility.
The Goddess, daughter of the Lord of Mountains, being gratified by Janaka’s asceticism,
bestowed upon him Jānakī Sītā as a wife who was devoted solely to Rāma.
And the blessed Lord Īśa, the trident-bearer Nīlalohita, being pleased,
gave to Janaka a wondrous bow for the purpose of destroying his enemies.
O best of the twice-born, that wise King Janaka, the slayer of his enemies, desiring to give away this daughter of his, issued a proclamation throughout this world.
"Whoever in the three worlds is able to take up this bow—
whether a god or even a dānava— he shall be worthy to win Sītā."
Having recognized [the situation], the powerful Lord Rāma went to the house of Janaka and,
taking hold of it, broke it with ease as if in play.
And the supremely righteous Rāma married that maiden, just as Śaṅkara wedded Pārvatī, or as Ṣaṇmukha wedded his army.
Then, after a long time had passed, King Daśaratha himself began to appoint his eldest son, the heroic Rāma, as king.

"You ought to make my heroic son Bharata the king,
since a boon was previously granted to me by you for that very reason."
Having heard her words, the king, his mind filled with sorrow, replied with the words, "So be it"; and Rāma, likewise, who knew the dharma, spoke the same.
Then, having prostrated at his father's feet together with Lakṣmaṇa,
the self-possessed Acyuta, having made a solemn agreement, departed for the forest accompanied by his wife.
The wise and powerful lord dwelt there for fourteen years together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Once, while he was dwelling in the forest, a rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa,
having abducted Sītā in the guise of a wandering mendicant, went to his city.
Not seeing Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa and Rāma, those subduers of enemies, became agitated in their senses and were consumed by pain and grief.
Then once, O best of the twice-born, a friendship arose between the monkey Sugrīva and Rāma, whose deeds are effortless, among the monkeys.
The heroic monkey named Hanumān was a follower of Sugrīva;
the son of Vāyu and possessed of great splendor, he was always dear to Rāma.
Having summoned the utmost fortitude and made his resolve regarding Rāma,
he wandered about, saying, "I shall bring back that Sītā."
Intent on finding Sītā, he traversed the earth bounded by the ocean and reached Laṅkā, the city of Rāvaṇa situated upon the sea.
Then, in that desolate place at the foot of a tree, he beheld the pure Sītā of radiant smiles, surrounded by ogresses.
With eyes filled with tears, she remembered her beloved and blameless [husband],
Rāma, who was dark as a blue lotus, and Lakṣmaṇa, who remained ever present within her own being.
Having personally introduced himself to Sītā in private,
he gave her Rāma’s ring so that she might have no doubt.
Seeing her husband’s most beautiful ring, Sītā,
her eyes wide with joy, believed that Rāma had returned.
Having then comforted Sītā and said,
"I shall lead you into the presence of Rāma," the mighty-armed one departed once more toward Rāma.
Having reported the sight of Sītā to Rāma,
the self-possessed one stood before him, honored by both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Then the powerful Rāma himself, together with Hanumān and Lakṣmaṇa, set his mind upon fighting the Rākṣasas.
Then, having constructed a bridge across the great ocean with hundreds of monkeys,
the Lord, whose soul is supremely righteous, slew Rāvaṇa.
Accompanied by the son of the Wind-god, the subduer of enemies brought back that Sītā along with her husband, her sons, and her brothers.
In the middle of the bridge, Rāghava installed Mahādeva Īśāna, clad in animal skins, established within a liṅga, and worshipped him.
To him, the Lord Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, together with Pārvatī,
appeared in person and granted an excellent boon.
"Whatever twice-born men here behold the linga established by you,
may their sin, even if joined with great transgressions, be destroyed."
Furthermore, whatever other sins exist, they go to destruction merely by the sight of these lingas after one has bathed here in the great ocean; of this there is no doubt.
As long as the mountains shall endure, as long as this earth shall remain,
and as long as the bridge shall stand, so long shall I remain here, hidden from view.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and ancestral rites—whatever has been done will become inexhaustible;
by the mere remembrance of the Liṅga, the sin of the day is destroyed.
Having spoken thus and embraced Rāghava, the Blessed Lord Śambhu,
Rudra, together with Nandin and his attendants, vanished right there.
Rāma, of great splendor and immense strength, being consecrated by Bharata, protected the kingdom, devoted as he was to righteousness.
Having honored all the Brahmins with special distinction, we shall worship the Lord Śaṅkara,
the destroyer of sacrifice, with the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
To Rāma was born a son, widely renowned as Kuśa;
and Lava, who was highly distinguished, wise, and a knower of the true meaning of all principles.
Atithi was born from Kuśa, and Niṣadha became his son;
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, and Nabhas was born from him.
From Nabhas was born the one named Puṇḍarīka, and his son was Kṣemadhanvan;
his son was the heroic and powerful Devānīka.
The son of Ahīnaguṣṭha was Sahasvān;
his son was Candrāvaloka, and Tārāpīḍa was his son.
From Tārāpīḍa came Candragiri, and from him Bhānuvitta was born;
from him Śrutāyu arose. These, O best of the twice-born, are all born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, described here in brief according to their primary importance.
Whoever should constantly hear this supreme lineage of Ikṣvāku,
being liberated from all sins, is honored in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the first part of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Romaharṣaṇa said:
Now, King Aila Purūravas protected the kingdom.
He indeed had six sons, whose splendor was equal to that of Indra.
Āyu, Māyu, Amāyu, Viśvāyu,
the heroic Śatāyu, and Śrutāyu were the sons of Urvaśī born of the gods.
We have heard that Āyuṣ had five heroic sons of great majesty, born of Prabhā, the daughter of Svarbhānu.
Nahuṣa was the first among them, a knower of dharma renowned throughout the world.
Nahuṣa’s heirs were six in number, possessing splendor equal to that of Indra.
These mighty ones were born of Virajā, the daughter of the Pitṛs:
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, Pañcaka, and Aśvaka.
Among those five sons, Yayāti, possessed of great strength and prowess,
obtained Devayānī as his wife—
the daughter [of Śukra] who was devoted to him— and also Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of the Asura Vṛṣaparvan.
Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu;
Śarmiṣṭhā also gave birth to Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru.
Passing over his blameless elder son Yadu,
he consecrated Puru, the younger, who was obedient to his father’s word.
In the south-eastern direction he assigned his son Turvasu;
in the south-west, he appointed his eldest son Yadu as king;
and in the west and north, he established Druhyu.
By them this entire earth was protected in accordance with righteousness;
and the king, together with his wife, attained great fame anew.
Then, five sons were born to Yadu, resembling the sons of gods:
Sahasrajit was the eldest, as well as Kroṣṭu, Nala, Ajita, and Raghu.
Likewise, the son of Sahasrajit was the king named Śatajit;
Śatajit also had three sons who were supremely righteous.
Haihaya, Haya, and the king Veṇuhaya were the others;
Haihaya’s son was the one renowned as Dharma.
O brahmins, his son was the powerful Dharmanetra;
Dharmanetra’s son was Kīrti, and Saṃjita was his son.
Mahiṣmān was the son of Saṃjita, and Bhadraśreṇya was his successor;
the heir of Bhadraśreṇya was the king named Durdama.
The wise and heroic son of Durdama was named Dhanaka;
and Dhanaka had four heirs who were esteemed by the world.
Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtāgni, and likewise Kṛtavarmā, and Kṛtaujas was the fourth; [the son] of Kṛtavīrya became Arjuna.
The radiant Sahasrabāhu, the best among those skilled in the science of archery,
had as his death Rāma Jāmadagnya, O Janārdana.
He had five hundred sons there, all of whom were great chariot-warriors (mahāratha), skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous, and devoted to the gods.
Śūra, Śūrasena, Dhṛṣṇu, and likewise Kṛṣṇa;
and the powerful Jayadhvaja, the king devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Śūrasena and all the others—these four of renowned prowess, high-souled devotees of Rudra—worshipped Śaṅkara. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.21.21)
But the wise Jayadhvaja, devoted to dharma, went for refuge to the god Nārāyaṇa Hari, to Viṣṇu, the supreme deity.
The other sons said to him: "O sinless one, this is not dharma for you;
our father was always devoted to the propitiation of the Lord."
The one of great splendor said to them: "This is my supreme law:
that kings on the surface of the earth are born from a portion of Viṣṇu."
While protecting the kingdom, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, must certainly be worshipped; for Viṣṇu, Hari, is the protector of the world.
The three forms of the Self-born One— sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa—
are declared to be the causes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
The Blessed Viṣṇu, whose essence is sattva, always sustains [the world];
Brahmā, whose form is rajas, creates; and Hara, whose nature is tamas, destroys.
Therefore, for those lords of the earth who protect their kingdom,
this Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, is to be propitiated.
Having heard his words, the other wise brothers said:
"Rudra, the agent of dissolution, is to be worshipped by those seeking liberation."
For this Lord Rudra is Śiva, the entirety of this world;
resorting to the quality of darkness (tamas), the Master shall withdraw it all at the end of the kalpa.
With that supreme, most terrible form consisting of splendor,
the wielder of the trident shall withdraw the entire cycle of existence by means of knowledge.
Then King Jayadhvaja, having reflected, said to them:
"A living being is liberated through *sattva*; the Blessed Lord Hari is the very soul of *sattva*."

His brothers said to him: "Rudra is worshipped by people endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva); being possessed of that same goodness, he shall grant liberation. Therefore, worship Hara, the Lord. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.21.33)
Then the prince Jayadhvaja, smiling, said:
"One's own duty is the path to liberation; no other is sought even by the sages."
And so, the Vaiṣṇava power is always the presiding deity of kings;
the supreme duty is the worship of Purāri, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
To him spoke the prince Kṛṣṇa, the best among the wise: "In that Arjuna, our father, has performed his own duty."
When the dispute had thus unfolded, Śūrasena spoke these words:
"The sages are indeed the authority in this matter; whatever they say shall be exactly so."
Then all those tigers among kings, having gone with great agitation to the hermitage of the Seven Sages, questioned those exponents of the Veda.
Those sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, spoke to them according to the truth:
"For whatever deity is favored by a man, she alone is his deity."
However, O kings, when worshipped on specific occasions, they grant the desires of men; indeed, this rule does not apply at all times, for otherwise it would not be so.
For kings, Viṣṇu and likewise Purandara are the deities;
for Brahmins, Agni, Āditya, Brahmā, and the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva) are the deities.
Viṣṇu is the deity of the gods, the wielder of the trident (Śiva) of the Dānavas,
Soma likewise of the Gandharvas, and he is also said to be [the lord] of the Yakṣas.
Vāgdevī is the deity of the Vidyādharas; the Lord Ravi is the deity of the Sādhyas;
Śaṅkara Rudra is the deity of the Rakṣasas; and Pārvatī is the deity of the Kiṃnaras.
Among the sages, the deity is Brahmā and Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident;
among the Manus, the goddess Umā, as well as Viṣṇu together with Bhāskara (the Sun).
For householders, all [the gods] are [deities]; for those practicing celibacy, it is indeed Brahmā;
for the forest-dwellers, it is Arka (the Sun); and for ascetics, it is Maheśvara.
The Blessed Lord Rudra is the master of the bhūtas; Vināyaka is the master of the kūṣmāṇḍas; and the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the god of gods and lord of creatures, is the master of all.
Thus spoke the Lord Brahmā himself;
therefore, Jayadhvaja certainly deserves to propitiate Viṣṇu.
Having bowed down to them, they then went to that most beautiful city;
having conquered all their enemies in battle, they protected the earth.
Then once, O best of Brahmins, a Danava named Videha,
who was terrifying to all living beings, approached their city.
Terrifying with his fangs, blazing in nature like the fire at the end of an eon,
he took up a trident radiant as the sun and made the ten directions resound.
Upon hearing that roar, the mortals dwelling there either gave up their lives or fled, overwhelmed by fear.
Then all the sons of Kārtavīrya, being well-prepared,
fought the Dānava with spears, mountain peaks, swords, and mallets.
O brahmins, that Dānava of terrible nature, as if laughing, warded off all of them with his trident,
like Bhairava at the end of a kalpa.
The five kings, Śūrasena and the others, who were possessed of great strength and were filled with fury for battle, rushed against Videha.
Śūra discharged the Raudra weapon, while Śūrasena discharged the Vāruṇa;
likewise, Kṛṣṇa discharged the Prājāpatya, and Dhṛṣṇu the Vāyavya.
And that Dānava Jayadhvaja shattered those weapons— the Kaubera, Aindra, and Āgneya— with his trident.
Then Kṛṣṇa, of great heroism, taking up his formidable mace and touching it with a mantra, swiftly hurled it and did not roar.
Having reached the chest of Gādhi’s son,
which was like a rock and resembled the Destroyer himself, she was unable to move that Dānava.
Seeing his extraordinary prowess, they fled, seized by fear;
but the wise Jayadhvaja called to mind the Lord of the World.
[He saw] Viṣṇu, the devourer, the source of the worlds, the immeasurable, the healthy,
the protector, the primordial Puruṣa, the Lord of Śrī, clad in yellow garments.
Then, at the command of Vāsudeva and for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees, a discus appeared, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
Remembering Nārāyaṇa, the king seized the source of the worlds and dispatched it to Videha,
just as Hari did for the sake of the Dānavas.
Having reached the shoulder of that terrible one, Sudarśana struck down his head,
which was shaped like a mountain peak, onto the earth.
When that enemy of the gods had been slain, the royal brothers Śīra and the others returned to the beautiful city and honored their brother.
Having heard this, the venerable great sage Viśvāmitra came to see the son of Kārtavīrya, Jayadhvaja, whose prowess was renowned.
Then, seeing him arrived, the king, with a mind full of agitation,
seated him on a beautiful throne and honored him with sincere devotion.
The formidable Lord said: "O Asura, by your grace, that lord of the Dānavas, Videha, has been struck down by me in battle."
With my doubts severed by your words, I have sought refuge in Viṣṇu, whose prowess is truth; by him, a gracious favor has been bestowed upon me.
"I shall worship Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, whose eyes are like lotus petals; by what means and according to what ritual procedure is Hari, the Sovereign, to be fully honored?"
"Who is this god Nārāyaṇa, and what is his power, O observer of noble vows?
Tell me all of this, for my curiosity is indeed great."
Viśvāmitra said:
He from whom the activity of all beings proceeds, in whom this entire world resides—he is Viṣṇu, the self of all beings; by taking refuge in him, one is liberated.
This Supreme Person is to be worshipped through the dharma of one's own caste and stage of life;
He is to be propitiated with a state of mind free from desire, and not otherwise.
Having spoken thus, O brahmins, the blessed great sage Viśvāmitra, honored by Śūra and the others, then departed for his own abode.
Then Śūra and the others worshipped the god Maheśvara with a sacrifice—
that immutable Rudra, who is attainable through sacrifice and is free from desire.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha, the omniscient one,
as well as Gautama, Atri, and Agastya— all of whom were devoted to Rudra— performed the sacrifice for them.
The venerable Viśvāmitra, however, caused Janārdana— the origin of all beings, the primordial god, and the subduer of enemies— to perform the sacrifice for Jayadhvaja.
At his sacrifice, the great yogi, the Lord Hari himself, appeared visibly;
that Blessed One manifested, and it was like a marvel.
Whoever should constantly hear this account of the prowess of Jayadhvaja,
being liberated from all evil, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Jayadhvaja had a son known as Tālajaṅgha.
He had one hundred sons who were celebrated as the Tālajaṅghas.
Among them, the eldest was the king Vītihotra, who possessed great heroism;
the others were the Yādavas, such as Vṛṣa and the rest, all performers of meritorious deeds.
Vṛṣa was the founder of their lineage; his son was Madhu.
Madhu had a hundred sons, and Vṛṣaṇa was the one who continued his line.
The son of Vītihotra was the renowned Ananta,
and his son was Durjaya, who was proficient in all the scriptures.
His wife was beautiful and adorned with all virtues;
she was devoted to her husband and protected her own duty as a wife.
Once that illustrious one beheld the goddess Urvaśī standing on the bank of the Kālindī, singing with a sweet voice.
Then, his mind struck by desire, he approached her and said: "O Goddess, you ought to sport with me for a very long time."
Having seen the king endowed with beauty and charm, that queen took delight with him for a long time, as if with another god of love.
Awakened at the proper time, the king spoke to that beautiful Urvaśī;
"I shall go to my lovely city. She, smiling, spoke these words: KūrmP_1.22.9.
"O King Sundara, no pleasure arises in me from this enjoyment of yours; you must remain [here] for another year."
Having gone to the city very quickly, that wise one said to her:
"I shall come here again; you ought to grant me permission for this."
That fortunate woman said to him, "O lord of the people, act accordingly;
you must not dally with another apsaras for the time being."
Having said "Om," he quickly went to that most beautiful city;
having arrived and seen his devoted wife, the king became terrified.
Beholding her husband thus terrified, his virtuous and devoted wife, who possessed full breasts, spoke to him with a gracious voice.
"O Lord, what fear arises within you today?
Tell me that according to the truth; however, I shall not proclaim this to the kings."
Having heard her words, the king, his mind bowed down with shame, said nothing; she, however, understood this through her vision of knowledge.
"You must not fear, O Lord; you must perform the purification of your sin.
For if you are afraid, O Great King, your kingdom will go to ruin."
Then that radiant king, having departed from that city and gone to the holy hermitage of Kaṇva, beheld the great sage there.
Having heard from the mouth of Kaṇva the auspicious procedure for expiation,
the mighty one set out toward the ridge of the Himalayas.
On the road, that lord of kings beheld an excellent Gandharva shining with splendor in the sky, adorned with a divine garland.
Beholding that garland, the slayer of enemies recalled Urvaśī, the most excellent of the Apsarases;
he set his mind upon her alone, thinking, "She alone is worthy of this."
Then that king, being exceedingly lustful, engaged in a very great battle with that Gandharva, intent on seizing the garland.
O twice-born ones, having conquered in battle and taken the garland,
the invincible one went with reverence to see that Apsaras, Kālindī.
Not seeing the Apsaras there, and tormented by the arrows of desire,
he wandered over the entire earth, including its seven continents.
Having reached the side of the Himavat, eager for a sight of Urvaśī,
he went to that preeminent mountain known as Hemakūṭa.
Seeing him there in every place, possessing the prowess of a lion and adorned with a variegated garland, the excellent apsarases conceived a terrible passion for him.
Recalling the words of Urvaśī, his mind entirely absorbed in her,
he did not perceive all those mountain peaks as he was traveling along.
Even there, not seeing any divine apsarases, he, afflicted by desire and possessing the prowess of a god,
went to Devaloka on Mount Mahāmeru.
Having traversed the mountain peaks, he, empowered by the strength of his own arms, reached the lake there known as Mānasa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
On its bank he saw a woman of faultless limbs moving about, beautiful and full of longing; he gave her the garland once again.
Then, beholding the goddess adorned with that garland, he was infatuated;
knowing himself to have achieved his purpose, he dallied with her for a very long time.
Then, at the conclusion of their dalliance, Urvaśī spoke these words to the best of kings:
"O King, what was done by you previously upon entering the city? It was in vain."
He related everything to his wife that had been uttered [by the sage],
including the vision of Kaṇva and likewise the taking away of the garland.
Having heard what he had said, she who desired his welfare told him, "Go; Kaṇva will cast a curse upon you, and I shall become dear to you. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.22.34)
Although he was repeatedly addressed by her, O Great King, the king, deluded by intoxication,
did not leave her side, his mind being entirely fixed upon her.
Then Urvaśī, who could assume any form at will, constantly showed the king her own true form— covered in thick hair and with tawny eyes.
With his mind detached from her, and remembering what Kaṇva had spoken, he resolved, "Fie on me! and began to perform austerities.
For twelve years the king subsisted on bulbs, roots, and fruits;
furthermore, for another twelve years, he lived on air alone.
Having gone to Kaṇva’s hermitage out of fear, he reported everything to him:
his dwelling with the Apsarases and his unsurpassed application to asceticism.
Beholding that tiger among kings, the blessed sage was pleased;
desiring to render his sin seedless, he spoke as follows.
Go to the divine city of Vārāṇasī, inhabited by the Lord;
there dwells the god Maheśvara to liberate the world.
Having bathed and duly offered libations to the gods and ancestors in the Gaṅgā,
and having beheld the Viśveśvara Liṅga, you shall be liberated from all sin.
Having bowed his head and received permission from Kaṇva, Durjaya went to Vārāṇasī; there, upon seeing Hara, he was liberated from sin.
He went to his own bright city and protected the earth;
the sage Kaṇva, being entreated out of compassion, performed a sacrifice for him.
Then his son, the wise one known as Supratīka, was born;
as soon as he was born, they attended upon him as king.
And from Urvaśī, O twice-born ones, seven sons of great heroism, resembling the sons of gods, were born;
all these maidens were wedded by the Gandharvas.
This supreme lineage of Sahasrajit, which destroys the sins of men, has been correctly recounted to you; now learn also that of Kroṣṭu.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the first part of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
"It is heard in the sacred tradition that Kroṣṭu had one son named Vṛjinīvān."
His son was the great Svāti; Uśadgu was born as his son.
The son of Uśadgu was the powerful Citraratha by name;
he is remembered in the world as Śaśabindu, the son of Citraratha.
His son was King Pṛthuyaśas, who was devoted to righteousness;
his son was Pṛthukarman, and from him was born Pṛthujaya.
From him was born Pṛthukīrti; from him came Pṛthudāna;
his son was Pṛthuśravas, and his son was Pṛthusattama.
Uśanas was his son; Siteṣu was his son; his son was Rukmakavaca; and Parāvṛt was the son of that best of men, O sages.
From Parāvṛta was born a son, Jyāmagha, renowned throughout the world;
from him Vidarbha was born, and from Vidarbha came Kratha and Kaiśika.
Romapāda was the third; his son was King Babhru;
Dhṛti was his son, and Saṃsta was his son as well.
Saṃta’s son was the powerful Viśvasaha;
his son was the highly heroic Prajāvān; from him came Kauśika;
his son was the wise Sumantu, and his son was Anala.
Kaiśika’s son was Cedi, and the Caidyas were his sons;
among them, Jyotiṣmān was the preeminent one, and Vapuṣmān was his son.
Vapuṣmat’s son was Bṛhanmedha, whose son was Śrīdeva;
his son, O brahmins, was the mighty Vītaratha, a devotee of Rudra.
Kuntī was also the daughter of Kratha; Vṛṣṇi was his son.
From Vṛṣṇi, Nivṛtti was born, and from him, O twice-born ones, Daśārha was born.
The son of Daśārha was Āroha, and his son was Jīmūta;
from him was born the heroic Jaimūti, Vikṛti, the slayer of enemy heroes.
His son was Bhīmaratha; from him Navaratha was born, who was constantly devoted to the duty of giving and eternally dedicated to perfect moral conduct.
Once, O best of sages, having gone out on a hunt and seeing a powerful Rākṣasa, he fled through the great forest out of fear.
Enraged, that mighty Rākṣasa Duryodhana, who resembled fire and held a great spear in his hand, pursued him.
Out of fear, King Navaratha beheld from no great distance the unsurpassed, supreme abode of Sarasvatī, which was well-guarded.
Having reached that place with great speed, the wise king beheld the goddess Sarasvatī in person and paid homage to her with his head bowed low.
The conqueror of enemies, with palms joined in reverence, praised you with pleasing words;
he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, saying, "I have come to you for refuge."
I pay homage to the Great Goddess, the manifest Goddess Sarasvatī herself—
the goddess of speech, who is without beginning or end, the sovereign mistress, and the observer of the vow of celibacy.
I pay homage to the source of the worlds, the supreme Yoginī, the subtle digit,
the consort of Hiraṇyagarbha, the three-eyed one who bears the moon upon her crest.
I pay homage to the digit of consciousness (citkalā) in the form of Brahman, which is supreme bliss;
protect me, O Supreme Goddess, who am terrified and have come for refuge. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.23.21)
In the meantime, the enraged lord of the Rākṣasas arrived at the place where the goddess Sarasvatī was, in order to slay the king.
Then, arrogant in his strength, he raised his trident and strove to enter that abode of the Mother of the Three Worlds, which was as radiant as the moon and the sun.
In that interval, a great being, resembling the sun at the end of an eon,
pierced him in the chest with a trident and cast him down to the earth.
"Go," said the Great King; "you must not stay here again.
Now, being free from fear, depart quickly; the Rākṣasa has been slain in this place."
Then, O best of Brahmins, King Navaratha, his soul filled with joy,
bowed down and departed for the supreme city, which resembled the city of Purandara.
Filled with devotion, he established the Goddess of the gods there and worshipped the goddess Sarasvatī with various golden sacrifices.
His son was Daśaratha, who was supremely righteous;
his son was the highly effulgent Śakuni, who was devoted to the Goddess.
From him was born Karambha, and from him Devarāta arose;
he performed the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), as did his son Devakṣatra.
Madhu was his heir, and from him Kuruvaṃśa arose;
he had two sons, Sutrāman and Anu.
Anostu was Purukutsa’s son, and Aṃśu was his heir.
Now, from Aṃśu was born the powerful Sattvata, a devotee of Viṣṇu,
a high-souled man devoted to charity, and the best among those skilled in the science of archery.
At the word of Nārada, he promulgated that scripture concerning the worship of Vāsudeva,
which had been heard from the Kuṇḍas, Golakas, and others.
In his name, moreover, the beautiful and great scripture known as the Sāttvata shall circulate, bringing benefit to Kuṇḍa and the others.
His son was Sāttvata, who was learned in all the scriptures;
that great king, Puṇyaśloka, indeed established that [system].
Sāttvata, endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva), begot sons upon Kauśalyā:
Andhaka, Mahābhoja, Vṛṣṇi, King Devāvṛdha,
and his eldest son named Bhajamāna, the foremost among those skilled in the science of archery.
Among them, King Devāvṛdha, the lord, performed supreme austerity, thinking:
"May I have a son endowed with all virtues."
His son was the king known as Babhru, a man of virtuous fame,
righteous, endowed with beauty, and always devoted to the knowledge of reality.
From Bhajamāna, by his wife Sṛñjayī, were born the Bhajamānas;
among them, two were preeminent and renowned: Nimi and Kṛkaṇa.
Born in the great Bhoja lineage were the Bhojas and the Vaimārtikas;
likewise, from Vṛṣṇi came the powerful Sumitra, Anamitra, and Śini.
From Anamitra was born Nighna; Nighna had two sons:
the highly fortunate Prasenajit and the excellent one named Satrājit.
From Anamitra, the youngest son of Vṛṣṇi, Śini was born;
Satyavān, who was endowed with truthfulness, was his son, and Satyaka was his son.
Yuyudhāna’s son was Sātyaki, whose son was Asaṅga;
his son was the wise Kuṇi, and his son was Yugandhara.
From Mādrī was born the son of Vṛṣṇi, Pṛśni, the joy of the Yadus;
and two sons were born to Pṛśni, namely Śvaphalka and Citraka.
Śvaphalka took as his wife the daughter of the King of Kāśī;
upon her he begot a righteous son named Akrūra,
as well as Upamaṅgu, Maṅgu, and many other sons.
The son of Akrūra is remembered as the renowned Devavān; Upadeva was his [other] son, a virtuous soul, and from those two were born Viśva and Pramāthin.
Citraka had sons named Pṛthu and Vipṛthu,
as well as Aśvagrīva, Subāhu, Supārśvaka, and Gaveṣaṇa.
And from Andhaka, the daughter of Kaśya obtained four sons:
Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śuci, and Kambalabarhiṣa.
Kukura’s son was Vṛṣṇi, and Vṛṣṇi’s son was born as Kapotaroman; Vipula was his son, and Vilomaka was his son.
He had a learned son named Nala, who was indeed a friend of Tumburu; his son is renowned by the name Ānakadundubhi, which follows from the name of his father.
Having reached Govardhana, he performed extensive austerities;
the god Brahmā, the great lord of the worlds, granted him a boon.
O Brahmins, [he shall obtain] imperishable fame for his lineage, the unsurpassed yoga of song, a power greater than that of his preceptor, and the ability to assume any form at will.
Having obtained that most excellent boon from the bull-vehicled Lord, he, remaining unperturbed,
worshipped Sthāṇu, who is honored by the thirty gods, with song.
Then, to him who was devoted to singing, the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Ambikā,
gave a jewel of a daughter, difficult even for the gods to obtain.
United with her, that king, the slayer of enemies, taught his beloved, whose eyes were rolling with passion, the unsurpassed art of singing.
In her, he begot a beautiful daughter named Subhujā,
who was endowed with form and loveliness and possessed a sense of modesty.
Then his mother duly instructed that handsome son, while he was still in his childhood, in the science of singing and in the arts of a maiden.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony and having studied the Vedas according to the rules from his preceptor,
he married a maiden who was the mind-born daughter of the Gandharvas.
In her, he begot five unsurpassed sons who were experts in the true principles of playing the lute and proficient in the science of singing.
Accompanied by his sons, grandsons, and wives, the king, who was skilled in song,
honored the god who destroyed Tripura with his singing.
And the maiden named Hrīmatī, long-eyed like Śrī herself,
was taken by the Gandharva named Subāhu and departed for his city.
To that Gandharva Sutejas were born sons:
Suṣeṇa, Vīra, Sugrīva, Subhoja, and Naravāhana.
Then Abhijit was the heroic son of Ānakadundubhi;
and from Abhijit was born Punarvasu, whose son was Āhuka.
O best of the twice-born, Ugrasena and Devaka were the sons of Āhuka;
and from Devaka were born heroic sons who resembled the gods.
Devavān, Anupadeva, Sudeva, and Devarakṣita—
they had seven sisters, and he gave them all to Vasudeva.
Vṛkadevā, Upadevā, as well as another, Devarakṣitā, Śrīdevā, Śāntidevā, Sahadevā, Sahadevā the virtuous,
and Devakī— of them all, the slender-waisted Devakī was the most excellent.
Agrasena’s sons were Nyagrodha, Kaṃsa,
Subhūmi, Rāṣṭrapāla, Tuṣṭimat, and Śaṅku.
From Bhajamāna was born a son, the renowned Vidūratha;
from him came Śūra, from him Śami, and from him Pratīkṣatra was born.
From him was born Svayaṃbhōja; from him came Hṛdika, the scorcher of enemies.
Then his son was Kṛtavarman, and Devara is known as his son.
Śūra was his son, and the wise Vasudeva was then his son.
Then, at the request of the gods, the mighty-armed Vāsudeva, the preceptor of the world and Hari, became the son of Devakī, born from Vasudeva.
And Rohiṇī, the highly fortunate and beautiful wife of Vasudeva,
gave birth to Saṃkarṣaṇa Rāma, the eldest, who wields the plow.
He alone is that Supreme Self, Vāsudeva, who consists of the universe;
he is Halāyudha himself in person, the Lord Śeṣa Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Under the very pretext of Bhrigu’s curse, honoring his human form,
Mādhava was born of her— Devakī— and also of Rohiṇī.
Born from the body of Umā, Yoganidrā became Kauśikī; by the command of Vāsudeva, she indeed became the daughter of Yaśodā.
O best of sages, Kaṃsa had already slain all those other sons of Vasudeva who were born before Vāsudeva.
Suṣeṇa, as well as Udāyī, the mighty Bhadrasena,
Ṛjudāsa, Bhadradāsa, and the illustrious Pūrvaja.
When all these [enemies] had been slain, Rohiṇī bore to Vasudeva Rāma, the lord of the world, Balabhadra, whose weapon is the plow.
Then, after Rāma had been born, Devakī gave birth to Kṛṣṇa— the primordial, imperishable Self of the gods— whose chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa.
Rāma had a wife named Revatī, who was endowed with excellent virtues;
through her he begot two sons, Niśaṭha and Ulmuka.
Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, had sixteen thousand wives;
from them were born sons by the hundreds and thousands.
Cārudeṣṇa, Sucāru, Cāruveṣa, Yaśodhara,
Cāruśravas, Cāruyaśas, Pradyumna, and Śaṅkha.
To Rukmiṇī, the wife of Vāsudeva, were born these sons, endowed with great strength and prowess, who excelled among all his other sons.
Seeing those heroic sons of Rukmiṇī,
Jāmbavatī, his wife of pure smiles, spoke to Añjanārdana Kṛṣṇa.
O lotus-eyed one, O slayer of the Dānavas, grant me a son who is distinguished, most virtuous, and equal to the Lord of the Gods.
Having heard the words of Jāmbavatī, Hari himself, the Lord of the World,
a treasure-house of austerity and subduer of enemies, began to perform penance.
Listen to that, O best of sages, how that son of Devakī,
having performed intense and great penance, beheld Rudra and obtained a son.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Now, the Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person—
For the sake of a son, he performed a terrible penance, a vow of austerity within austerity.
Although he had descended by his own will and had already accomplished all that was to be done, the Sustainer of the Universe moved about,
awakening the divine nature within his own self.
He went to the hermitage of the high-souled lord of sages, Upamanyu, which was frequented by yogis and filled with various birds.
Mounted upon the exceedingly radiant Garuḍa, the scorcher of the three worlds,
he held a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and was marked with the Śrīvatsa sign.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, adorned with diverse flowers,
frequented by the hermitages of sages, and resounded with the chanting of the Vedas.
It was crowded with lions, rhinoceroses, and śarabhas, and filled with tigers and elephants;
it was adorned with lakes containing pure and sweet drinking water.
It was graced with various pleasure groves and auspicious temples of the deities,
as well as by ṛṣikas, sons of ṛṣis, and hosts of great sages.
It was frequented by those perfected in the study of the Vedas, by performers of the agnihotra sacrifice,
and by yogis devoted to meditation with their eyes fixed on the tip of the nose.
It was endowed on all sides with merit by those possessed of knowledge who perceive reality;
it was graced on every side by rivers and by reciters of prayers who discourse upon Brahman.
It was frequented by meritorious ascetics devoted to the worship of Īśa—
men who were tranquil, whose resolves were true, and who were free from sorrow and affliction.

It was constantly frequented by ascetics and celibate students who were knowers of reality, whose entire bodies were white with ashes, who were devoted to the recitation of the Rudra-hymns, some shaven-headed, some with matted hair, some pure, and others with tufts of hair on their heads.
There, in that most excellent and delightful hermitage adorned by Siddhāśrama,
the blessed Gaṅgā, the destroyer of sins, flows eternally.
Having sought out those ascetics who were free from all taint,
Mādhava, the soul of the universe, then honored them with a prostration and with words.
Having seen him— the source of the universe, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace— they bowed down,
filled with devotion, to the supreme teacher of yogins.
Having placed the Eternal One in their hearts, they praised him with Vedic mantras;
they spoke to one another concerning the Unmanifest, the Primordial God, the Great Sage.
"This is that one Blessed One, the supreme Nārāyaṇa in person;
now the God, the Ancient Puruṣa himself, is approaching."
He alone is the imperishable creator, the destroyer, and the protector;
having become embodied though being formless, he has come here to behold the sages.
This all-pervading one, the Ordainer and the Disposer, arrives;
he is without beginning, imperishable, infinite, the great element, the Great Lord.
Having heard those words of theirs again and again, Govinda, who transcends all speech,
went swiftly to the abode of that great-souled one.
Then, having touched the water with devotion at each sacred ford, that Yādava,
the son of Devakī, performed the libations for the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors.
He worshipped the Liṅgas of Śambhu, who possesses immeasurable splendor, which had been established by the lords of sages on the banks of rivers.
Wherever they saw Janārdana approaching,
the inhabitants there worshipped him with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having beheld that Vāsudeva, who bears the Śārṅga bow, the conch, and the sword,
all those inhabitants stood motionless, their limbs radiant with auspiciousness.
When those who desired to ascend there beheld Janārdana, their minds, which had previously been departing, became fixed upon him.
Then, having plunged into the Gaṅgā and performed the libations for the gods and others,
he took excellent flowers and entered the house of the lord of sages.
Having seen that best of yogis, whose body was smeared with ashes,
who wore matted hair and bark garments, and who was peaceful, he bowed his head to the sage.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa approaching, the knower of reality honored him and seated him upon a throne as the foremost guest of the yogins.
He spoke: "We recognize Viṣṇu, the source of all speech, the supreme state, whose abode is unmanifest, who stands here in the manner of a disciple. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.24.28)
Welcome to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa! Our ascetic penances have borne fruit, since Viṣṇu, the Soul of the Universe, has come to my home in person.
Even sages who strive as yogis do not perceive you;
what, then, is the reason for your coming here, O such as you?
Having heard those words of Upamanyu, the Blessed One, the crusher of Keśin and great yogi, prostrated before him and spoke these words.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to see Girīśa, who is clothed in an elephant hide;
having arrived at your abode, I am eager for a vision of the Blessed One."
How may that Blessed Lord, the Sovereign and best among those who know yoga, be seen by me?
Where shall I behold that Lord of Umā before long?
Thus spoke the Blessed One: "The Supreme Lord is seen through devotion and through fierce austerity; therefore, perform this here with diligence."
The lords of sages who discourse on Brahman,
as well as those reciters and ascetics, dwell here meditating upon the Lord, the God of gods.
Here, the divine Lord whose banner is the bull sports together with his consort, surrounded by various beings and yogis.
In this hermitage, in former times, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, having performed most rigorous austerity before Rudra,
obtained Yoga from Maheśvara.
Right here, the venerable Lord Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana,
having beheld that supreme knowledge, obtained the Lord of lords.
Having performed austerities here in this beautiful, excellent hermitage for the matted-haired Lord,
Surabhi, endowed with devotion, obtained sons from Rudra.
In this very place, the deities, previously terrified by Time (Kāla), beheld Maheśvara, Hara; and being glorious, they became fearless and attained peace.
Having propitiated Mahādeva here, Sāvarṇi, the best among those who practice austerity,
obtained supreme yoga and the highest status as an author of scriptures.
Having composed the auspicious collection concerning the Purāṇas, which contains highly meritorious meanings, the twice-born sage set it forth among his excellent brahmin disciples.
"O Puruṣottama, having seen this very Saṃhitā here, Kāpeya Śāṃśapāyana composed this ancient [work] concerning Mahādeva by his command, consisting of exactly twelve thousand verses."
Herein has been set forth this meritorious Purāṇa named Vāyavīyottara, consisting of eighteen thousand verses, equal to the Vedas;
it was proclaimed here by the disciples as spoken by Śāṃśapāyana.
The great yogi Yājñavalkya, having seen Hara here through his ascetic penance,
composed at his command this unsurpassed treatise on yoga.
In this very place, having previously performed supreme austerity, Bhṛgu obtained as a son from Maheśvara Śukra, the best among those who know yoga.
Therefore, right here, having performed austerities, you ought to behold the Lord of Gods, Maheśvara—
the fierce, formidable Viśveśa with matted hair.
Having spoken thus, the great sage Upamanyu bestowed upon Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, the knowledge of the Pāśupata vow and yoga.
Thus addressed by that best of sages, the Lord Madhusūdana remained right there and propitiated the god Rudra through ascetic penance.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, shaven-headed, and clad in bark garments,
he incessantly recited the Rudra-mantra, his mind fixed solely on Śiva.
Then, after a long time had passed, the great god Maheśvara, Soma, whose ornament is the crescent moon, appeared in the sky before the Goddess.
The god of gods, wearing a crown, bearing a mace, adorned with a variegated garland, holding the Pināka bow and a trident,
his body clothed in a tiger-skin garment.
He beheld Mahādeva with the Goddess.
With an axe held in his hand, three-eyed,
his entire body covered by the skin of a man-lion,
emitting the great *praṇava*.
He beheld him resembling a thousand suns.
To the ancient Lord, the primordial Person, the eternal one standing before all, the yogi, the sovereign ruler,
subtler than the subtlest, and possessed of infinite power.
He beheld Śambhu, the Lord of Prāṇa.
Even the gods, nor even the Grandfather, nor Indra, nor Agni, nor Varuṇa, nor Death,
do not yet speak of Rudra’s power.
He beheld that primordial deity before him.
Then he beheld himself on the left side of Giriśa, unmanifest and of infinite form,
praising the Lord with many words.
The first [form] has its hands placed upon a conch, a sword, and a discus.
To the right, he saw the Lord of the Gods, a person mounted upon a swan, with palms joined in reverence,
praising the supreme power of the Lord.
The Grandfather, the teacher of the world, situated in heaven.
He beheld before the Lord of the Three Worlds the lords of the Gaṇas, such as Nandīśvara and others of immeasurable power, who were like thousands of suns.
The youth, who is like the lord of fire, together with his branch.
Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Pracetas, Dakṣa, and Kaṇva;
after him, Parāśara, and then Vasiṣṭha.
And he also beheld Svāyambhuva Manu.

Having prostrated with devotion before the Lord of the Mountain together with the Goddess, Viṣṇu, of noble intellect, praised the foremost of the immortals with mantras while joining his palms in reverence.
Then, having contemplated the Self within his own self...
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Obeisance be unto you, the eternal one, the source of all!
The sages declare you to be the sovereign of Brahmā."
The virtuous declare that austerity, goodness, passion, and darkness— all these are you alone.
You are Brahmā, you are Hari, the source of the universe, and Agni; you are the destroyer residing within the orb of the sun;
you are the vital breath (prāṇa), and the distinctions of Hutavaha, Vāsava, and the others [are you].
I go for refuge to that one being, the divine Lord.
The Sāṃkhyas call you devoid of qualities and of a single form;
the Yogins constantly worship you as abiding in the heart;
and the Vedas here declare you to be Rudra-Agni.
I go to you alone for refuge, the divine Lord.
By placing even a single flower or leaf at his feet, one becomes liberated from all worldly bonds; this practice,
frequented by perfected yogis, dispels every evil.
Having remembered Your pair of feet, by Your grace...
They declare that Reality to be free from all divisions, stainless, situated within the heart,
an infinite light, one, immovable, true, supreme, and all-pervading;
it is the state without beginning, middle, or end, from which this world is born.
I constantly approach you, the Lord of All, the auspicious one, whose power is truth.
Oṃ, salutations to the blue-throated one, to the three-eyed, and to the impetuous;
constant salutations, salutations to you, Mahādeva, the Sovereign Lord.
Salutations to you, the wielder of the Pināka bow; salutations to the shaven-headed one who carries a staff;
salutations to you, the thunderbolt-handed one, clothed in the directions, with matted hair.
Homage to Bhairavanāda, who has the form of Time, the fanged one, whose sacred thread is a serpent; homage to you, whose seed is fire! KūrmP_1,24.68.
Homage be to you, O Lord of the Mountains; homage to you who are the utterance of Svāhā.
Homage to you whose loud laughter is like a pearl; and again and again, homage to the Terrifying One.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of desires; salutations to the one who crushes time;
salutations to the one in the guise of Bhairava, to Hara, and to the one who carries a quiver.
Homage be to you, the three-eyed one; homage to you, the one clothed in a hide!
Homage to the lord of Ambikā; homage to the lord of creatures!
Salutations to you whose form is space, salutations to the Lord of Space;
salutations to him who possesses the bodies of both man and woman, and who is the originator of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Homage to you, the lord of the gods, whose emblem is followed by the deities;
homage to you, the teacher of Kumāra, the god of gods.
Salutation to Tamas, the Lord of Sacrifice; salutation to you, the observer of celibacy;
salutation to the Great Deer-Hunter, the Sovereign of Brahman.
Homage to the Swan, to the Universal One; homage again and again to the Enchanter. Homage to You, the Yogi, who is attainable through yoga, and whose nature is the power of yoga (yogamāyā).
Salutations to you, the protector of life, who delights in the sound of the bell;
salutations to you, the skull-bearer, and salutations to the lord of the luminaries.
Homage, homage, homage be to you; again and yet again, homage and homage!
O Supreme Lord, grant me all my desires with your whole self.
Having thus praised the Lord of Gods with devotion, that Mādhava,
O brahmins, prostrated himself like a staff at the feet of the God and the Goddess.
Having raised up Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Keśin, the Blessed Lord Soma spoke these sweet words in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
For what purpose, O lotus-eyed one, was austerity performed by you, O imperishable one?
For you alone are the giver of all desires here for those who long for them.
For you indeed are that supreme form of mine called Nārāyaṇa;
O dear one, O Puruṣottama, there exists nothing unattained by you.
O Keśava, by means of your own yoga, do you know the infinite Nārāyaṇa, the Self, the Supreme Lord, Mahādeva, and the Great Yoga?
Having heard those words, Kṛṣṇa, smiling,
spoke to the bull-bannered god while looking at the Lord of the Universe and the goddess born of the snowy mountain.
"O Śaṅkara, everything has indeed been known by you through your own yoga;
I desire a son equal to myself who is devoted to you—grant him to me, O Śaṅkara. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.24.84)
"So be it," said Hara, the soul of the universe, with a delighted mind;
looking toward the goddess Girijā, he embraced Keśava.
Then that goddess, the mother of the worlds, who forms half the body of Śaṅkara and is born of the lord of the snowy mountains,
addressed Hṛṣīkeśa.
"O child Acyuta, I know your infinite, unwavering, and eternal devotion to the Lord, as well as your devotion to me, O Keśava, which is directed toward no other."
For you are indeed Nārāyaṇa in person, the Self of all, the Supreme Person;
having been entreated by the gods in the past, you were born as the son of Devakī.
Behold the Self by means of the self, your own stainless state;
no difference exists between us—thus do the wise perceive.
"O Keśava, accept from me these desired boons:
omniscience as well as sovereignty, that supreme knowledge of the Lord, unwavering devotion to the Lord, and supreme strength within yourself. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.24.90)
Thus addressed by that great goddess, Janārdana,
the god Maheśvara, accepted her blessing with his head and spoke.
Then the Lord Īśa, the God of gods, taking Kṛṣṇa by the hand together with the Goddess,
was being honored by the sages and the lords of the gods.
The Lord of the Mountains went to Mount Kailāsa.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Purvavibhaga of the Shat-sahasri Samhita of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
Having entered Mount Meru’s peak, [he beheld] Kailāsa, which possesses the luster of gold.
The blessed Soma, the great lord, took his pleasure with Keśava.
The inhabitants of Mount Kailāsa beheld that high-souled one;
they then worshipped Kṛṣṇa, the god of gods, the infallible Acyuta.
He has four arms and noble limbs, with a luster like a dark cloud;
he wears a crown, holds the Śārṅga bow in his hand, and his chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa.
Long-armed, large-eyed, clad in yellow garments,
and infallible, he wore upon his chest the unsurpassed Vaijayantī garland.
Radiant with divine splendor, youthful and exceedingly tender,
with lotus-like feet and eyes, beautiful, smiling, and the bestower of the happy realms.
Once, for the sake of sport, Kṛṣṇa, the increaser of Devakī’s joy, radiant with splendor, wandered through a mountain cave.
The foremost of the Gandharvas and Apsarases, all the daughters of the Nāgas,
as well as the Siddhas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas, were present here and there, consisting of the universe.
Having beheld this marvel and attained supreme joy, their eyes wide with delight,
they released showers of flowers upon the head of that Great-Souled One.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa, the divine daughters of the Gandharvas and the most excellent of the Apsarases likewise desired him, their garments and ornaments falling away.
Some beautiful women, experts in song and deluded by desire, beheld the son of Devakī and sang various melodies.
Some, full of graceful charms, danced before him;
others, standing by and gazing intently, drank the nectar of his face.
Some loving women respectfully took excellent ornaments from their own bodies and adorned Kṛṣṇa, the ornament of the world.
Some, taking excellent ornaments from his body, adorned themselves with them,
while others adorned Mādhava with ornaments from their own bodies.
Some, having approached Kṛṣṇa, deluded by desire,
those gazelle-eyed women kissed the lotus-face of Hari.
Some, having seized Govinda by the hand, brought him to their own home,
being deluded by his illusory power (māyā), even though he was the origin of the worlds.
Having assumed many forms by his divine play, the lotus-eyed Lord Kṛṣṇa fulfilled their desires.
Thus, for a very long time, the glorious Nārāyaṇa, Hari, took delight in the city of the God of gods, deluding the world with his Māyā.
After a long time had passed, the people residing in Dvāravatī became overwhelmed with distress and afraid due to their separation from Govinda.
Then the powerful Suparṇa, having been dispatched earlier by Kṛṣṇa while searching for him, went to that Himavat mountain.
Not seeing Govinda there, he bowed his head to the sage Upamanyu and returned again to that city, Dvāravatī.
In the meantime, thousands of most terrifying great daityas and rākṣasas arrived at the radiant city of Dvārakā, striking fear into all.
That powerful Suparṇa, whose prowess was equal to that of Kṛṣṇa,
having slain them in a great battle, protected the auspicious city.
At that very time, however, the venerable sage Nārada,
having seen Kṛṣṇa on the peak of Kailāsa, went to Dvāravatī.
Seeing the sage Nārada there, all the inhabitants said,
"Where is the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the blessed Hari?"
On the peak of Kailāsa, the Blessed One Hari said to them:
"The great yogin is sporting today; having seen him, I have come here."
O brahmins, having heard his words, Suparṇa, the best of birds and traveler of the sky, went to the supreme mountain Kailāsa.
He beheld Hari, the son of Devakī, seated upon an excellent throne in a palace adorned with jewels, in the presence of the God of gods, Govinda.
He was being worshipped on all sides by immortals and celestial women,
and was surrounded by the great hosts of Mahādeva, as well as by Siddhas and yogins.
Having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before Śaṅkara Śiva, Suparṇa reported the news concerning Hari in the city of Dvārakā.
Then, having bowed his head to Śaṅkara Nīlalohita and being granted permission by Hara, Kṛṣṇa returned to the city.
Having mounted the son of Kaśyapa, Madhusūdana was honored by the throngs of women with words that tasted like nectar.
Beholding the slayer of enemies, the possessor of great yoga, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, as he departed, the foremost of the Gandharvas and Apsarases followed after him.
Having dismissed all those women, Hari, the soul of the universe,
Govinda, went swiftly to the divine city of Dvāravatī.
O best of sages, when Murāri had departed, the amorous women did not shine at all without him,
like a night devoid of the moon.
Having heard of the excellent arrival of Kṛṣṇa, the citizens quickly adorned the divine and auspicious city of Dvāravatī.
Then they adorned the beautiful city with vast banners, with flags decorated with jewels, and with parched grain and other offerings.
They played various musical instruments with sweet sounds;
they blew thousands of conch shells and stretched out the lutes.
As soon as Govinda had entered the auspicious city of Dvāravatī,
women endowed with youth sang sweet songs.
Having seen the Lord, those stationed on the tops of the palaces danced and released showers of flowers upon the son of Vasudeva.
Having entered the palace, Kṛṣṇa, the great yogin, was honored with blessings; accompanied by the goddesses, he shone upon his excellent throne.
In a beautiful and bright pavilion, surrounded by conchs and other instruments,
he was encompassed on all sides by his chief sons and thousands of women.
There, upon that beautiful and excellent seat, Acyuta shone together with Jāmbavatī, like a god accompanied by his goddess and adorned with a garland.
The gods and Gandharvas arrived to behold the immutable source of the worlds,
as did the great seers born in former times, such as the twice-born Mārkaṇḍeya and others.
Then the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, Hari, rose and saluted Mārkaṇḍeya with his head as he approached, and offered him his own seat.
Having honored those hosts of sages with a prostration, the mighty-armed Hari dismissed them after granting them their desired boons.
Then, at the time of midday, Hari himself, the god of gods,
having bathed and wearing white garments, stands before the sun with palms joined in reverence.
Beholding the sun, the Lord of Gods recited his prayers according to the prescribed rite;
he offered libations to the gods, the hosts of sages, and the ancestors.
Having entered the abode of the gods together with Mārkaṇḍeya,
he indeed worshipped the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa), who resides in the Liṅga and is adorned with ashes.
Having completed all the observances himself, that controller of men fed the best of sages and honored the brahmins.
O best of Brahmins, having established his spiritual connection with Mārkaṇḍeya, the Infallible One (Acyuta),
surrounded by his sons and others, recounted the meritorious stories of the Purāṇas.
Then, having seen all this entire deed, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, smiling, spoke these sweet words to Kṛṣṇa.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Which deity is being propitiated by you through these auspicious deeds? Tell me, who is the one worthy of worship through rites and the very object of meditation for yogins? (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.25.52)
For you, O Lord, are that supreme Brahman, the stainless state of Nirvana;
you were born in the Vṛṣṇi clan for the purpose of removing the world's burden.
To him spoke the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, the best among the knowers of Brahman, as if laughing while all his sons were listening. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.25.54)
The Blessed Lord said: "Everything you have said is indeed true; there is no doubt.
Nevertheless, I worship the eternal God, the Lord."
O Brahmins, there is nothing for me to do, nor is there anything whatsoever that remains unattained;
nevertheless, knowing this to be the supreme Śiva, I worship the Lord.
"Indeed, people deluded by illusion do not see that God;
therefore, making known the root of my own self, I worship Him. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.25.57)
In this world, there is no merit greater than the worship of the Liṅga, nor is there anything that so destroys fear;
therefore, for the welfare of these worlds, one should worship Śiva in the Liṅga.
"I am that which those who know the Vedic doctrines call the *liṅga*;
therefore, I worship the Lord Ātman by means of the Ātman itself. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.25.59)
That very one is my supreme form; I am identical with him, there is no doubt. There is no difference between us two; such is the certainty established in the Vedas.
This god, Mahādeva, the Great Lord, is always to be meditated upon, worshipped, saluted, and known within the *liṅga* by those who are perpetually afraid of *saṃsāra*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O best of gods, what is that liṅga, and who is worshipped within the liṅga?
Tell me, O large-eyed Kṛṣṇa, for this is a most profound and supreme mystery."
They call the unmanifest the *liṅga*, the bliss, the light, and the imperishable;
the Vedas call the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the god, the possessor of the *liṅga* (*liṅgin*), and the immutable.
And in the past, when the terrible single ocean had arisen and all things mobile and immobile had perished,
Śiva himself appeared for the sake of awakening me, Brahmā.
From that time onwards, both Brahmā and I have always worshipped Mahādeva with the desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Kṛṣṇa, you yourself ought to explain now how the supreme abode of the Lord first became a *liṅga*, for the sake of our enlightenment.
The Blessed One said:
There was a terrible, undifferentiated ocean of darkness consisting of pure gloom;
and in the midst of that single ocean, there was [the Lord] bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Having become thousand-headed, thousand-eyed,
thousand-footed, and thousand-armed, I, the eternal one, lie down with my self-yoked.
In the meantime, from afar I beheld one of immeasurable radiance,
resembling ten million suns, blazing and enveloped in glory.
The great yogin with four excellent faces, the Person (Puruṣa) with the luster of gold,
the god clad in black antelope skin, praised by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, that best of those who know yoga reached me;
the immensely radiant Brahmā himself, smiling, spoke.
"Who are you, from where have you come, and why do you stand here? Tell me, O Lord!
For I am the creator of the worlds, the self-existent Great-Grandfather."
Having been addressed thus by Brahmā at that time, I spoke:
"I am the creator of the worlds and their destroyer again and again."
Thus, while the dispute was unfolding through the illusion of the Supreme Lord,
the supreme Liṅga, whose nature is Śiva, manifested for the sake of awakening them.
Resembling the fire of universal destruction, filled with garlands of flames,
it is free from decay and growth, and devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
Then the Blessed One said to me: "Go down quickly;
let us find the end of this [world]. I, the Unborn, shall go upward. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.25.76)
Then, having quickly made an agreement, the two of us went upwards and downwards;
even though we were the Grandfather and I, we did not know the end after a hundred years.
Then, filled with wonder and struck with fear of the trident-bearing God,
they were deluded by his illusory power as they meditated upon the Lord of the Universe.
Uttering the great roar of the syllable Om, the supreme state,
they praised Śambhu, the Supreme, with their hands joined in humble reverence.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu said:
"Salutation to Śambhu, the physician for the disease of beginningless impure saṃsāra;
salutation to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman, whose form is the Liṅga."
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, to Brahman whose form is the *liṅga*, who abides in the ocean of dissolution and is the cause of the emergence from dissolution. KūrmP 1.25.81.
