Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the Brahman whose form is the *liṅga*, whose limbs are encircled by garlands of flames, and who has the appearance of a pillar of fire. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.25.82)
Homage to Śiva, the peaceful one, to Brahman whose form is the *liṅga*, who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and who shines with the purity of his own nature.
Salutation to Mahādeva, the great light, of infinite splendor;
salutation to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman whose form is the *liṅga*.
Salutation to the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, whose form is space, the Creator;
salutation to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman, who has the Liṅga as his manifest form.
Salutation to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman whose form is the *liṅga*, who is changeless, true, eternal, and of stainless splendor. KūrmP 1.25.86.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, to Brahman in the form of the Liṅga, who is the essence of the Vedānta, who is the form of Time, and who is possessed of wisdom. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.25.87)
Being thus praised, Maheśvara became manifest;
the god, the great yogin, shone with a splendor equal to ten million suns.
With thousands of millions of mouths, as if swallowing the sky,
he has a thousand hands and feet, and the sun, moon, and fire for his eyes.
The Blessed One, Pinākapāṇi, clad in animal skins, bearer of the trident,
with a serpent as his sacred thread, and possessing a voice like the thunder of clouds.
Then Mahādeva said: "I am pleased, O best of gods;
behold me, Mahādeva, and let all fear be cast off."
"You two were born from my limbs in the past, eternal ones.
Here on my right side is Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds;
on my left side is Viṣṇu, the protector; and in my heart is Hara."
"I am pleased with both of you; I grant you a boon according to your desire.
Having spoken thus to me, the god Mahādeva Śiva himself embraced the god Brahmā and became inclined toward showing his favor.
Then, with delighted minds, Nārāyaṇa and Pitāmaha, having prostrated before Maheśvara and gazed upon his face, spoke.
If affection has arisen [in you], and if a boon is to be granted to us two,
O God Maheśvara, may we have eternal devotion toward you.
Then the Blessed Lord Īśa, the Supreme Sovereign Mahādeva, smiling with a joyful heart, spoke to me in his pleasure.
The God said:
"O Lord of the Earth, you are the creator of dissolution, maintenance, and creation.
My child, my child, O Hari, protect this entire universe, both moving and unmoving."
O Viṣṇu, though I am stainless and devoid of qualities, I am divided threefold under the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, by means of the qualities of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
"O Viṣṇu, abandon your delusion; protect this Grandfather.
He shall become your eternal son, O Blessed One."
And at the beginning of the kalpa, from your mouth, I shall become Śūlapāṇi, assuming a terrible form, born of your wrath as your son.
Having spoken thus to Brahmā, O best of sages, and having shown me favor, the god Mahādeva vanished right there.

From that time forward, O Brahmin, the worship of the *liṅga* became firmly established in the worlds; for that *liṅga*, due to its being the locus of absorption (*layana*), is the supreme form of Brahmā.
O sinless one, this majesty of the Liṅga has been described to you by me;
those who know Yoga understand this, neither the gods nor the Dānavas.
For this indeed is the supreme knowledge, unmanifest and designated as Śiva,
by which those with the eye of wisdom behold that which is subtle and inconceivable.
To that Blessed One we perpetually offer our salutation—
to Mahādeva, to Rudra, to the God of gods, who possesses the *liṅga*.
Salutation to the secret essence of the Vedas, salutation indeed to Nīlakaṇṭha;
salutation to Vibhīṣaṇa, to Śānta, to Sthāṇu, and to Hetu.
To Brahmā, to Vāmadeva, to the three-eyed one, to the most exalted;
to Śaṅkara, to Maheśa, to Girīśa, and to Śiva.
Pay homage constantly and meditate upon Hara with your mind;
you shall soon cross over this ocean of saṃsāra.
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva,
that bull among sages went in his mind to the Lord Īśāna, whose face is turned in every direction.
Having bowed his head to Kṛṣṇa and received his permission, the great sage departed for the desired region of the trident-bearing God of gods.
Whoever would constantly cause this unsurpassed Liṅgādhyāya to be heard,
or who would listen to it, or even read it, is liberated from all sins.
O best of Brahmins, by hearing even once this supreme account of Vāsudeva’s ascetic practice, a human being is released from sin.
"Or one who recites it daily, morning and evening, is honored in the world of Brahmā;
thus spoke the great yogi, the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana."
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the first section of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Then, having obtained boons from Maheśvara through Jāmbavatī, Kṛṣṇa—
She gave birth to the high-souled Sāmba, her most excellent son.
Pradyumna also had a son named Aniruddha, who was possessed of great strength;
both of them were endowed with excellent qualities and were like other bodies of Kṛṣṇa himself.
Having slain Kaṃsa, Naraka, and hundreds of other asuras, and having effortlessly conquered Śakra and the great asura Bāṇa; KūrmP_1,26.3 //
Having established the entire world and the eternal laws within it,
Nārāyaṇa formed the supreme resolve to go to his own abode.
In the meantime, O brahmins, Bhṛgu and the other sages arrived at Dvārakā to see the eternal Lord Kṛṣṇa, who had accomplished his task.
Having prostrated and honored them, that Soul of the Universe spoke to them as they were seated upon their thrones together with the wise Rāma.
"I shall go to that supreme abode of my own, known as Viṣṇu;
all tasks have been accomplished, so be gracious, O lords of sages."
This terrible and inauspicious Kali age has now arrived;
indeed, all people in this age will follow after sin.
Cause my knowledge, which brings benefit to the brahmins, to be set forth,
so that these best of the twice-born may indeed be liberated from the sins born of the Kali age.
"May that sin of those devotees perish who remember me, the Lord, even once during the Kali age—those who are devoted to Puruṣottama. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.26.10)
O twice-born ones, those who shall always worship this [deity] with devotion according to the rite seen in the Vedas during the Kali Yuga will go to that supreme state.
Those brahmins who are born of your lineage by the thousands will indeed possess devotion to Nārāyaṇa in the Kali age.
Those who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa go to that which is higher than the highest;
those who hate Maheśvara shall not go there.
Meditation, fire-offerings, ascetic penance, knowledge, and rituals such as sacrifices—
all these perish quickly for those who revile the wielder of the Pināka bow.
He who would constantly take refuge in me, relying on a single-minded devotion while reviling the Lord God, goes to ten thousand hells.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, that censure of Paśupati must be avoided with effort,
whether by deed, thought, or speech, as well as among his devotees.
But those best of the twice-born who were cursed by Dadhīci at the sacrifice of Dakṣa shall appear in the Kali age; they must be avoided with great effort by devotees.
Those born in your lineage who hate the Lord God and have been cursed by Gautama shall not be spoken to on earth by the best of the twice-born.
Having been addressed thus by Kṛṣṇa, all those excellent great sages said,
"So be it," and quickly departed for their own abodes.
Then Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, who is identical with the universe,
having effortlessly withdrawn his entire family, departed for that supreme abode.
Thus has this lineage of kings been recounted to you in brief;
it is not possible to describe it in detail. What more do you wish to hear?
Whoever should read or even hear this auspicious narration of the lineages,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The sages said:
"The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—these constitute the four ages."
O Sūta, tell us today in brief the essential nature of these [beings].
Sūta said:
When Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa had departed for his own supreme abode,
Pārtha, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose soul was devoted to the highest dharma and who scorched his enemies, [remained].
Having performed the subsequent rites, he was overwhelmed by great grief;
then, as he was traveling along the road, he beheld the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
Then Arjuna, casting off his grief, fell like a staff upon the ground before the teacher who was surrounded on all sides by disciples and grand-disciples as he discoursed on the Brahman.
Being supremely pleased, he said: "O great sage, from which country do you come now?
O Lord, to which country are you going so quickly?"
"Indeed, upon seeing you, my vast sorrow has vanished.
Now, O lotus-petal-eyed one, tell me what task I must perform."
The great yogi Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself,
the sage surrounded by his disciples, sat down on the riverbank and spoke to him.
"O son of Pāṇḍu, this terrible Kali age has arrived;
therefore, I shall go to the great city of Vārāṇasī, belonging to the Lord."
In this terrible Kali age, people will follow after sin;
they will become great evildoers, devoid of the system of social classes and stages of life.
I see no other atonement for living beings in the Kali age that pacifies all sins except for the city of Vārāṇasī. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.27.10)
In all these ages— the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara—
men will indeed be high-souled, righteous, and speakers of truth.
For you are renowned throughout the worlds as steadfast and kind to your people; protect now the supreme dharma of your own station, and you shall be released from fear.
O best of the twice-born, having been thus addressed by the Blessed One, Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities, prostrated himself and inquired about the duties of the Yuga.
To him, the sage who was the son of Satyavatī, having bowed to the Lord Īśāna, explained in its entirety the eternal duties of the ages.
I shall describe to you in brief, O lord of men, the characteristics of the ages;
it is not possible for me, O Pārtha, to speak of them in detail.
The first is declared by the wise to be the Kṛta Yuga; then follows the Tretā Yuga;
the third, O Pārtha, is Dvāpara; and the fourth is called Kali.
In the Kṛta age, meditation is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity alone.
In the Kṛta age, the god Brahmā is the deity; in the Tretā age, the blessed Sun;
in the Dvāpara age, Viṣṇu is the deity; and in the Kali age, Rudra Maheśvara.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Sūrya—all are worshipped even during the Kali ages; yet the Lord Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, is worshipped in all four ages alike.
In the first age, the Kṛta Yuga, the eternal Dharma stands on four feet;
in the Tretā Yuga, it has three feet; in the Dvāpara, it remains with two feet;
but in the Tiṣya (Kali) age, deprived of three feet, it persists merely in its essence.
In the Kṛta age, however, the means of subsistence was the direct production of couples, overflowing with the essence of rasa;
all subjects were always satisfied, eternally blissful, and full of enjoyment.
O Purañjaya, there is no distinction of inferiority or superiority among them;
in that Kṛta Yuga, their lifespan, happiness, and form were equal.
Free from sorrow, abounding in goodness, and likewise devoted to solitude;
established in meditation, established in austerity, they have Mahādeva as their supreme goal.
O scorcher of foes, they indeed wander free from desire, always joyful in mind, dwelling upon mountains and by the oceans, without a fixed abode.
Then, due to the conjunction of time, the *rasollāsa* perished during the age known as Tretā;
when that accomplishment had been lost, another accomplishment came into being.
When the subtlety of the waters was obstructed, they then took the form of clouds;
from those thundering clouds, the emission of rain proceeded.
When the surface of the earth was once joined with that rain,
trees known as "houses" then appeared for them.
From them, all practical applications for those [beings] arose;
at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, the people maintained themselves by means of them.
Then, after a long time, due to a reversal of those very [qualities],
a state consisting of passion and greed suddenly arose among them.
By the reversal of those [qualities] through that which arises at that time,
all those trees designated as houses then perish.
Then, when those [means] had perished, those born of sexual union became bewildered;
yet, being intent upon truth, they then meditated upon that perfection.
Then those trees, known as houses, appeared for them;
they produced garments, fruits, and ornaments.
In those very [trees], there arises in every leaf-cup a honey that is free from bees, endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor, and possessed of great potency.
By that means, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, those beings sustained themselves;
through that accomplishment, they were all indeed joyful, well-nourished, and free from affliction.
Then, after some time, being once again overcome by greed,
they forcibly seized those trees and the honey produced by bees.
Due to that misconduct of theirs, indeed brought about by greed,
the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) have now perished in various places.
Then, greatly distressed by intense cold, rain, and heat,
and being tormented by these pairs of opposites, they constructed shelters.
Having engaged in mutual conflicts and ceased to consider the means of livelihood,
the *kalpavṛkṣa* trees then vanished along with the honey.
Then, in the Tretā Yuga, their perfection (siddhi) appeared once more;
for there was another [perfection] that furthered their livelihood, as rain fell for them according to their desire.
The waters of those rains which flowed here through low-lying places became rivers that carried away the sites of streams by means of a continuous downpour.
Furthermore, those drops of water that had fallen upon the surface of the earth became medicinal herbs at that time through the union of the waters and the earth.
Fourteen kinds of plants, both cultivated and wild, grew without being ploughed or sown; likewise, trees and shrubs appeared with flowers and fruits according to the seasons.
Then, passion and greed arose among them in every way;
this was due to the inevitable occurrence of that matter, and not by the power of the Tretā Yuga.
Then they seized the rivers, fields, and mountains,
as well as the trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, by force according to their respective strength.
By the contrary process, those medicinal herbs entered the earth;
by the command of the Grandfather, Pṛthu milked the earth.
Then, all of them, overcome with mutual rage, seized by the force of Time, took away the wealth, wives, riches, and other possessions by means of violence.
Knowing this for the sake of establishing the boundaries of social order, the unborn Lord Brahmā created the Kṣatriyas for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas.
And in the Tretā age, the Lord established the system of the social classes and stages of life,
as well as the performance of sacrifice devoid of injury to animals.
Furthermore, in the Dvāpara ages, there always exist differences of opinion among men;
there is passion, greed, as well as strife, and a lack of certainty regarding the principles of reality.
In the Tretā ages, the single Veda is prescribed here as having four quarters;
however, during the Dvāpara and subsequent ages, it is divided into four by the Vedavyāsas.
Furthermore, through the sons of the sages, [the Vedas] are divided by various schisms and delusions of view,
by the arrangement of mantras and brāhmaṇas, and by the inversion of vowels and consonants.
The *saṃhitās* of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas were compiled by the seers who heard them,
through similarities, modifications, and various differences in vision here and there.
O observer of noble vows, [he taught] the Brāhmaṇas, the Kalpasūtras, the collections of Mantras,
the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras.
Drought, death, and likewise afflictions caused by wind,
as well as sufferings born of speech, mind, and body, give rise to despondency among men.
From world-weariness arises in them the contemplation of liberation from suffering;
from contemplation comes dispassion, and from dispassion comes the perception of defects.
And because of the perception of defects, the arising of knowledge occurs in the Dvāpara age;
this activity, indeed, is remembered as being joined with rajas and tamas in the Dvāpara age.
When the Kṛta age has passed, Dharma exists; it prevails in the Tretā age;
having become disordered in the Dvāpara age, it perishes in the Kali Yuga.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Pūrva-vibhāga of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
"In the Tiṣya age, there will be illusion, malice, and even the slaughter of ascetics."
Men, perpetually agitated by darkness, strive for that [world].
In the Kali age, there will be disease that destroys, constant hunger, fear likewise,
the terrible fear of drought, and the ruin of countries.
Unrighteous, lacking proper conduct, highly irascible, and small-minded,
those greedy and evil-born people speak falsehoods when born in the Tiṣya age.
Through ill-performed sacrifices, poorly studied texts, misconduct, false traditions, and the ritual defects of Brahmins, fear arises among the subjects.
In the Kali age, the twice-born do not study the Vedas nor do they perform sacrifices;
they sacrifice in an unrighteous manner, and those of small intellect merely recite the Vedas.
In that Kali age, there will be a connection between Śūdras and Brāhmaṇas through mantras, marriage, and even by means of sharing beds, seats, and meals.
O Lord of Men, kings will consist mostly of Śūdras and will oppress the Brāhmaṇas;
the killing of embryos and the killing of heroes will become prevalent.
The twice-born do not perform bathing, fire-offerings, recitation, giving, the worship of deities, nor indeed any other ritual acts.
In the Kali age, they revile Mahādeva, the Brāhmaṇas, the Supreme Person, the Vedic scriptures, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Purāṇas.
They perform various kinds of actions not seen in the Vedas;
indeed, no delight in their own duty arises among the Brāhmaṇas.
The world will be filled with those of immoral conduct and heretics of false appearance; people will be constantly begging from one another.
In the Kali age, the countryside will have its pillars of justice in ruins, crossroads will be infested with jackals, and women will have their hair disheveled.
When the end of the Yuga has arrived, Śūdras will practice the dharma while wearing white garments and deer skins, having shaven heads and clad in saffron robes.
There will be thieves of grain, as well as those who violate the modesty of women;
there will be thieves who steal from a thief, and yet another who steals from that thief.
Abundance of suffering, short lifespan, emaciation of the body, and being afflicted by disease—
due to an adherence to unrighteousness, the conduct of darkness (tamas) is said to prevail in the Kali age.
Then there were those wearing saffron robes, the Nirgranthas, as well as the Kāpālikas;
others were sellers of the Vedas, and still others were sellers of sacred fords.
Seeing the twice-born seated on their thrones, those of small intellect do not move;
moreover, Śūdras who subsist upon the king strike down the foremost of the twice-born.
O scorcher of foes, in the Kali age, by the power of time, the king does not harm Śūdras who sit on high seats among the twice-born, even though he knows it.
O twice-born ones, those endowed with little learning, meager fortune, and scant strength worship Śūdras with flowers, laughter, and other auspicious offerings.
O King, even when honored, Śūdras do not look upon the best of the twice-born;
and the twice-born stand at the door, waiting for an opportunity to serve.
In the Kali age, Brahmins surround Shudras and those who live off Shudras as they stand upon their vehicles; there they serve them and praise them with hymns of praise.
Those who subsist on Śūdras will indeed teach the Vedas to Śūdras;
they will recite Vedic mantras while having resorted to terrible nihilism.
The best of the twice-born will become sellers of the fruits of penance and sacrifice,
and ascetics will appear by the hundreds and thousands.
For they destroy what they have studied and do not attain understanding, O sinless one;
they sing secular songs to the deities, O lord of men. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.28.24)
In that Kali age, Brāhmaṇas as well as Kṣatriyas will follow the practices of the left-hand Pāśupatas and likewise those of the Pañcarātra.
When knowledge and ritual action have ceased and the world has become inactive,
insects, mice, and snakes will prey upon human beings.
Indeed, they take incarnations within the families of Brahmins;
for in ancient times, at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, those twice-born ones were consumed by the curse of Dadhīca.
With their minds possessed by darkness, they will revile Mahādeva;
in that Kali age at the end of the yuga, they will practice dharma in vain.
And all others who have been consumed by the curse of the high-souled Gautama shall all return to their own castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
Those of wicked conduct and futile exertion, who follow vows and practices outside the Veda, revile Hṛṣīkeśa and the Brahmins who discourse upon the Brahman. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.28.30)
Having displayed fruits [of their practice], those lowest of people who follow the "cat-like" way of life delude all persons, for their minds are possessed by darkness.
In the Kali age, Rudra Mahādeva, the supreme Lord of the worlds,
shall not be a deity for men, nor shall he be the deity of the deities.
Śaṅkara Nīlalohita will manifest incarnations for the sake of establishing the Śrauta and Smārta traditions, out of a desire for the welfare of his devotees.
He will teach that knowledge called Brahman to his disciples—
the essence of all Vedānta, indeed the duties revealed by the Vedas.
Those wise ones who serve him by whatever means possible,
having conquered the defects born of the Kali age, go to the supreme state.
A person obtains very great merit without effort;
this is the great virtue of the Kali age, which is otherwise corrupted by many defects.
Therefore, having attained this age of Maheśvara with every effort,
a Brāhmaṇa, in particular, should go for refuge to Rudra, the Lord.
Those who bow to Virūpākṣa, the Lord clad in animal skins,
with serene minds, go to the supreme state of Rudra.
Just as the salutation to Rudra certainly yields the fruit of all actions,
one would not obtain that same fruit from saluting other deities.
In such an age as this Kali Yuga, the singular purification of all defects is the salutation to Mahādeva, meditation, and charity; so says the sacred tradition.
Therefore, having abandoned other gods who are not the Supreme Lord, one should take refuge in the god Maheśvara,
the three-eyed Virūpākṣa, if one desires the supreme state.
Those who do not worship Rudra Śiva, who is honored by the thirty gods, their charity, austerity, sacrifice, and even their very life are in vain. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.28.42)
Homage to Rudra, the Great One, the God of gods, the wielder of the trident; homage to the three-eyed Tryambaka, the teacher of yogins. KūrmP 1.28.43.
Homage be to Vāmadeva, to Mahādeva, the creator;
to Śambhu, to Sthāṇu, to Śiva, the eternal supreme lord.
Homage to Śarva, to Rudra, to the Great Devourer, the cause.
I take refuge in Virūpākṣa, the worthy protector, the celibate student,
Mahādeva, the great yogin, Īśāna, and the husband of Ambikā.
To the bestower of yoga upon yogins, who is veiled by yogic illusion;
to the teacher of the Kurus among yogins, who is accessible only to yogins—the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Rudra, the deliverer from saṃsāra, the creator Brahmā, the sovereign of Brahmā,
the eternal, the all-pervading, the one devoted to Brahman, and the beloved of the Brāhmaṇas.
The matted-haired one, the embodiment of Time, the formless Supreme Lord;
the single-formed, the great-formed, the one to be known through the Vedas, the Lord of Heaven.

He who has a blue throat, whose form is the universe, who is all-pervading, the seed of the universe, the fire of time, the burner of time, the granter of desires, and the destroyer of desire. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.28.49)
I pay homage to the god Giriśa, who is adorned with a portion of the moon;
to the deep-red one, the licking one, the solar one, and the supreme lord; to the fierce Paśupati, the formidable one, the maker of light, who is beyond darkness.
Thus has the characteristic of the ages been declared in brief,
both of those past and those yet to come, until the end of the manvantara.
By means of a single Manvantara, all intermediate periods (antarāṇi) are indeed explained; there is no doubt that a Kalpa is likewise explained by a Kalpa.
Indeed, in all the past and future Manvantaras,
all beings possess an identical sense of self-conceit (abhimāna) according to their respective names and forms.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Kirīṭin, the rider of white horses,
conceived the highest, unwavering devotion toward Īśāna.
He paid homage to that lordly sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana,
who is omniscient, the creator of all, and who exists as Viṣṇu himself.
The sage Vyāsa spoke again to Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities,
as he bowed down, touching him with his two very beautiful hands.
"You are blessed and favored; indeed, there is no other like you found in the three worlds who is a devotee of Śaṅkara, O conqueror of enemy cities."
You have seen that God, whose eyes are everywhere and whose faces are on all sides—
the Lord of All, Rudra, the teacher of the entire world, in person.
That divine, sovereign knowledge has been understood by you exactly as it is;
Hṛṣīkeśa himself, the eternal one, spoke it out of affection.
Go, go to your own place; you ought not to grieve.
Go with supreme devotion to Śiva, the refuge and the protector.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the Master, having favored Arjuna,
departed for the city of Śaṅkara in order to propitiate Bhava.
Having obtained that auspicious refuge through those words, the son of Pāṇḍu abandoned all activities and became supremely devoted to him.
In devotion to Śambhu, there has never been nor will there ever be anyone equal to Arjuna,
except for the son of Satyavatī (Vyāsa) or Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī.
Salutations eternally to that Blessed One, the Truth, the Wise One,
the Sage Pārāśarya Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor.
Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana is indeed the eternal Viṣṇu himself;
for who else truly knows Rudra as that Supreme Lord? (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.28.65)
Pay homage to that sage Kṛṣṇa, the son of Satyavatī,
the high-souled son of Parāśara, the yogin, the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Thus addressed, all those sages, their desires fulfilled,
bowed down to that great-souled Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Pūrva-vibhāga of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of sixty thousand verses.
The sages said:
"Having reached the divine Vārāṇasī, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana—"
What did that one of great intelligence do? For we have a great curiosity to hear it.
Sūta said: Having reached the divine Vārāṇasī and performed his ablutions, the great sage worshipped the Lord Śiva, the Sovereign of the Universe, at the Jāhnavī.
Seeing that venerable one arrived there, the sages dwelling in that place honored Vyāsa, the bull among sages.
Having prostrated themselves, they all asked about meritorious stories centered on Mahādeva, which destroy sin and concern the eternal dharma of liberation.
And that omniscient Blessed One, the Rishi,
also recounted the majesty of the God of Gods and the dharmas revealed through the Vedas.
Among those lords of sages, the great sage Jaimini, a disciple of Vyāsa,
questioned Vyāsa regarding a profound and eternal matter.
Jaimini said:
"O Blessed One, you ought to resolve for me this one doubt according to the truth;
for indeed, nothing remains unknown to you, O Supreme Sage."
Some praise meditative absorption, while other people praise the Dharma alone; others likewise praise Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and other great seers praise asceticism.
Other great sages have declared that celibacy and silence are [the means];
others know non-violence and truth; and still others understand renunciation to be so.
Some praise compassion, as well as charity and study; some praise pilgrimage to sacred fords, while others praise the restraint of the senses.
O bull among sages, tell me which of these would be superior;
or if there exists something else that is secret, you should speak of that as well.
Having heard the words of Jaimini, the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana bowed to the bull-bannered god and spoke with a profound voice.
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate sage! That which has been asked by you, I shall declare—the secret of secrets. Let the other great ṛṣis listen."
This eternal knowledge was proclaimed by Īśvara in ancient times;
it is hidden, disliked by those lacking wisdom, and practiced by those who perceive the subtle.

This supreme knowledge of the knowers of knowledge should not be given to one who lacks faith, nor to one who is not devoted to the Supreme Lord, nor to those who hate the Vedas. Kūrma Purāṇa 1.29.15.
In ancient times, on the peak of Mount Meru, the Goddess, seated upon her divine throne, questioned the Great God, the Lord Īśāna, the enemy of Tripura.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O destroyer of the afflictions of devotees!
How does a person behold you, the Lord, in such a short time?
Sāṃkhya-yoga, as well as meditation, Vedic karma-yoga, and whatever other practices there are in this world that involve great exertion, O Śaṅkara— KūrmP_1,29.18.
By means of this, the subtle Blessed One indeed becomes visible to all embodied beings— both to yogins whose minds are distracted and even to those engaged in ritual action.
O destroyer of the body of Kāma, speak this most secret knowledge, hidden and practiced by Brahmā and the other gods, for the benefit of all devotees.
Īśvara said:
This realization is unspeakable; it is a knowledge excluded by the ignorant.
I shall declare to you its true nature as it was spoken by the supreme ṛṣis.
My city of Vārāṇasī is the most supreme and secret field;
it carries all living beings across the ocean of saṃsāra.
There, O Great Goddess, my devotees dwell— high-souled ones who have undertaken my vow and are established in supreme discipline.
It is the best of all sacred fords (tīrthas) and the best of all places;
it is the highest knowledge among all forms of knowledge—my supreme Avimukta.
Other sacred places, holy fords, and shrines—
whether situated in cremation grounds or located in divine lands— are likewise [sacred].
My abode is not attached to the earthly realm (bhūrloka), but resides in the intermediate space (antarikṣa);
those who are undisciplined do not see it, but those who are disciplined perceive it with their mind.
"This is the famous cremation ground known as Avimukta;
having become Time (Kāla), O beautiful one, I withdraw this entire world here."
O Goddess, this place is the most beloved of all secret places to me;
my devotees go there and enter into me alone.
Whatever has been given, recited, offered in sacrifice, performed as ritual action, or practiced as austerity;
whatever meditation, study, or knowledge has been cultivated—all that shall become inexhaustible therein.
Whatever sin has been accumulated in previous thousands of births,
all of it goes to destruction for one who has entered Avimukta.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, those of mixed castes,
women, Mlecchas, and others who are of mixed origin and born of sinful wombs— [all these attain liberation].
O fair-faced one, even moths, ants, and whatever other beasts and birds there may be,
all meet their death in time at Avimukta.
O Goddess, those men who are born there in my city, O Śivā, become three-eyed, with the crescent moon upon their crests, and have the great bull as their vehicle.
No sinner who dies in Avimukta goes to hell;
for all those favored by the Lord attain the supreme goal.
Considering liberation to be extremely difficult to attain and worldly existence to be most terrifying,
a man should dwell in Vārāṇasī, even if he must strike his feet with a stone.
O Supreme Goddess, even for one purified by austerity, such a goal—liberation from saṃsāra—is difficult to attain if one perishes here or there [without reaching it]. KūrmP_1,29.36.
For this arises from grace, O daughter of the Lord of Mountains;
those who are unawakened do not see it, being deluded by my māyā.
Those fools who, shrouded in darkness, do not resort to Avimukta,
dwell again and again in the midst of feces, urine, and semen.
Even when being struck by hundreds of obstacles, the wise man who continues to dwell [in his practice] goes to the supreme abode, having reached which he does not grieve.
Freed from birth, death, and old age, one goes to the supreme abode of Śiva;
for that is the goal of those who desire liberation and do not die again,
attaining which the wise consider their purpose fulfilled.
Neither by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices,
nor even by knowledge is that supreme state attained which is obtained in Avimukta.
Those of various complexions and discolored, such as the Caṇḍālas and others who are loathsome,
whose bodies are filled with sins and likewise with distinguished transgressions—
the wise know that Avimukta is the supreme medicine for them.
Avimukta is supreme knowledge; Avimukta is the supreme state;
Avimukta is the supreme reality; Avimukta is supreme auspiciousness.
To those who, having undertaken the lifelong vow of initiation, dwell in Avimukta,
I grant that supreme knowledge at the end [of their lives], the highest state.
Prayāga, the meritorious Naimiṣa, Śrīśaila, and Mahālaya;
Kedāra, Bhadrakarṇa, Gayā, and Puṣkara as well.
Kurukṣetra, Rudrakoṭi, Narmadā, Āmrātakeśvara,
Śāligrāma, Kubjāmra, the unsurpassed Kokāmukha,
Prabhāsa, Vijayeśāna, Gokarṇa, and Bhadrakarṇaka.
These places of merit are indeed renowned throughout the three worlds;
yet they do not lead to supreme liberation as does death in Vārāṇasī.
Especially at Vārāṇasī, the Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths,
destroys the sin committed over hundreds of previous births once she has entered [the city].
Elsewhere, the Gaṅgā is easily accessible for performing ancestral rites, giving gifts, penance, recitation, and all such vows; however, all of this is very difficult to obtain in Vārāṇasī.
A man who dwells in Vārāṇasī should constantly sacrifice, offer oblations, give gifts, and worship the immortals, while subsisting perpetually on air alone.
Whether a man be sinful, deceitful, or unrighteous,
upon reaching Vārāṇasī, he purifies his entire being.
Those who indeed worship and praise Mahādeva in Vārāṇasī should be known as lords of the Gaṇas, completely liberated from all sins.
Except through the knowledge of yoga, renunciation, or some other means,
that supreme state is attained only after a thousand births.
Those devotees who indeed dwell in Vārāṇasī, the sovereign of the gods of gods,
attain supreme liberation in that very same birth.
Where there is yoga and likewise knowledge, liberation occurs in a single birth;
having reached Avimukta, one need not go to any other penance grove.
Because it was not released by me, it is therefore known as "Unreleased" (Avimukta). Having understood that this very [place] is the secret among secrets, one is liberated.
O fair-browed one, the destination ordained for those who are devoted to knowledge or ignorance and who desire supreme bliss is indeed attained by one who dies at Avimukta.
And compared to all those places that have been described in their entirety as being within the body of one who is not yet liberated,
the city of Vārāṇasī is indeed more auspicious than them.
For it is there at Avimukta that Mahādeva himself, the Lord, at the end of one's life, directly reveals the liberating Brahman.
O Goddess, that supreme reality which is heard of as Avimukta can be attained in a single lifetime by residing in Vārāṇasī.
It is established between the eyebrows, in the center of the navel, in the heart, and in the head,
just as the sun is situated in Vārāṇasī when it has risen.
Likewise, between the Varaṇā and this [Asi], lies the city of Vārāṇasī;
it is there that the reality known as the Ever-Unforsaken (Avimuktaka) is eternally established.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a place superior to Vārāṇasī,
where the god Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, the lord of heaven, resides.
There, the gods, along with the gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
constantly attend upon me, the Grandfather, the God of gods.
Those who are guilty of the great sins and those who are the worst evildoers among them,
upon reaching Vārāṇasī, attain the supreme goal.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should dwell with self-restraint in Vārāṇasī until death; having obtained knowledge from Mahādeva, he is liberated.
However, obstacles will arise for one whose mind is afflicted by sin;
therefore, one should never commit evil through body, mind, or speech.
O you of excellent vows, no one knows in truth this secret of the Vedas and the Purāṇas— the knowledge that has its locus in Avimukta.
While the gods, the sages, and the supreme beings were listening,
the God spoke to the Goddess this [teaching] which destroys all sins.
Just as Nārāyaṇa is the best among the gods, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
and just as Giriśa is the lord among lords, so too is this [place] the most excellent among all sacred sites.
Those by whom Rudra was propitiated in a previous birth alone attain the supreme field, Avimukta, the abode of Śiva.
For those whose intellect has been impaired by the defilements born of the Kali age,
it is impossible to know that abode of the Supreme Lord.
Those who always remember this city and find it,
their sins perish quickly both in this world and the next.
And whatever sins those who have made their home here commit,
may the divine Śiva, whose body is Time, destroy them all.
"Let those who desire liberation come to dwell in this place,
so that once dead, they shall not be born again in the ocean of existence."
Therefore, with every effort, a person should dwell in Vārāṇasī—
whether he be a yogi or a non-yogi, a sinner or the most virtuous of men.
One's mind should not be diverted from the path to Avimukta, neither by the words of the Vedas nor by the instructions of one's father or teacher.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Vyāsa, the best among those who know the Vedas,
wandered about in Vārāṇasī together with his most eminent disciples.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the first part of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, a compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Surrounded by his disciples, the wise sage Dvaipāyana, the preceptor, [proceeded].
He went to the vast Linga, Oṃkāra, the bestower of liberation.
Having worshipped Mahādeva there together with his disciples,
the great sage spoke of His majesty to the sages of purified souls.
This is that stainless, beautiful *liṅga* named Oṃkāra;
by the mere remembrance of it, one is liberated from all sins.
This is the supreme knowledge, the highest among the five seats;
it is constantly resorted to by the wise in Vārāṇasī as the bestower of liberation.
Here the Lord Rudra, Mahādeva himself, whose form consists of the five abodes, sports, bestowing liberation upon living beings.
That Pāśupata knowledge which is designated as the "Fivefold Object" (pañcārtha)—
this very same stainless Liṅga is established within the syllable Om.
Śāntyatītā, Śānti, Vidyā, the supreme Kalā,
Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti— these are the fivefold purpose of the Īśvara-liṅga.
The Liṅga that is the eternal refuge for the five deities beginning with Brahmā,
and which makes manifest the syllable Oṃ, is called Pañcāyatana.
One should meditate upon the divine Liṅga, the imperishable abode of the five;
at the end of the body, the wise one enters that supreme light of bliss.
In this place, the celestial seers (devarṣis), the perfected ones (siddhas), and likewise the brahminical seers (brahmarṣis) formerly worshipped the Lord Īśāna and attained the supreme state.
O best of Brahmins, on the bank of the Matsyodarī is a meritorious, most secret, and auspicious place,
the supreme Oṃkāreśvara, which is the size of a cow-hide.
The Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga, the excellent Madhyameśvara, Viśveśvara, likewise Oṃkāra, and Kapardeśvara as well. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.30.12)
O best of the twice-born, no one here knows these secret lingas in Vārāṇasī except by the grace of Śambhu.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa and the great sage Pārāśarya departed to behold the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga of the trident-bearing Lord.
Having been thus honored by his disciples, the Blessed One, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, recounted the majesty of the Skirt-clad Lord (Kṛttivāsas) to his disciples.
In ancient times, at this place, a Daitya, having become an elephant,
came into your presence in order to kill the Brahmins who were constantly performing worship here.
O best of the twice-born, from their sacrificial signs Mahādeva, the three-eyed one who is affectionate toward his devotees, manifested for the sake of protecting them.
Having slain the Daitya who was in the form of an elephant with his trident as if in sport, Hara made his skin his garment;
therefore he is known as Kṛttivāseśvara.
In this place, sages and preeminent among ascetics attained supreme perfection;
indeed, with those very bodies, they reached that highest state.
The Vidyās, the Vidyēśvaras, and the Rudras are proclaimed as being for the sake of Śiva;
they remain eternally surrounding the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga.
Having recognized the Kali age to be terrible and abounding in unrighteousness, those people who do not abandon Kṛttivāsa have achieved their purpose; of this there is no doubt.
Liberation may or may not be attained elsewhere even after a thousand lifetimes;
however, liberation is obtained at Kṛttivāsa in a single lifetime.
For they say this place is the abode of all perfected beings (siddhas),
hidden by the God of gods, the Great God Śambhu.
For in every age, self-controlled Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas worship Mahādeva here and recite the Śatarudriya.
They constantly praise the god Tryambaka, who is clothed in animal skins;
they meditate in their hearts upon the god Sthāṇu, the auspicious one who dwells within all.
The Siddhas indeed sing these songs:
"For those Brahmins who dwell in Vārāṇasī, liberation shall come through a single birth."
Those who have sought refuge in the one clothed in an elephant hide.
Having attained in this world birth in brahmin families— which is the desire of all beings and exceedingly difficult to find—
they fix their minds in meditation and chant the Rudra-mantra.
Ascetics meditate upon Maheśa within their minds.
The lords of sages, dwelling within Vārāṇasī, propitiate the Lord, the Sovereign;
free from all ulterior motives, they offer sacrifices with sacrificial rites.
They praise Rudra and bow down to Śambhu.
Homage to Bhava, the abode of the stainless yoga; I take refuge in Sthāṇu, the ancient Giriśa;
I remember Rudra seated within my heart.
Know Mahādeva to be of manifold forms.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Pūrvavibhāga of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Having addressed the sages, the wise one [spoke] concerning the trident-bearing God of gods.
He went to see that imperishable Liṅga, Kapardīśvara.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and having offered libations to the ancestors,
the twice-born ones worshipped the wielder of the trident at the Piśācamocana tīrtha.
Beholding that wonder there together with their preceptor, those sages recognized the greatness of the sacred field and bowed down to Hara, the Lord of the Mountain.
A certain tiger of terrible appearance approached this supreme Kapardeshvara in order to devour a single doe.
There, her heart filled with fear, she circumambulated him again and again;
running away in great agitation, she fell into the power of the tiger.
Having torn her apart with his sharp claws, the exceedingly powerful tiger went to another desolate region upon seeing the lords of sages.
And as soon as that young doe died,
she was seen before Kapardin as a great flame in the sky, possessing a radiance equal to the sun.
She has three eyes, a blue throat, and hair adorned with the crescent moon;
she is mounted upon a bull and surrounded by men of a similar appearance.
The sky-dwellers released a rain of flowers upon his head,
and at that very moment, he himself became the Lord of the Gaṇas and was no longer seen.
Having beheld this most excellent wonder, the brahmins headed by Jaimini questioned their infallible teacher regarding the majesty of Kapardīśvara.
Having prostrated before the bull-bannered Lord, the Blessed One sat down in the presence of the gods and spoke to them concerning the majesty of Kapardīśa.
This is that supreme Liṅga of the Lord, Kapardīśvara;
by merely remembering it, one quickly casts off the entire flood of all sins.
For those residing in Vārāṇasī, all defects such as desire, anger, and the like,
as well as all obstacles, perish through the worship of Kapardīśvara.
Therefore, one should always behold the supreme Kapardīśvara;
he should be worshipped with diligence and praised with Vedic hymns.
For yogins of tranquil mind who meditate here with constancy, the perfection of yoga arises within six months; of this there is no doubt.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin perish for one who bathes here in the vicinity of the Piśācamocana pool after worshipping [the deity].
Long ago in this field, O Brahmins, an ascetic of celebrated vows known as Śaṅkukarṇa worshipped Śaṅkara;
he incessantly chanted the Rudra-mantra and the Praṇava, which is the very form of Brahman.
Having performed the definitive initiation (naiṣṭhikī-dīkṣā), that soul of yoga dwelt there, offering flowers, incense, and the like, along with hymns of praise, prostrations, and circumambulations.
Once, he saw a hungry preta who had arrived;
its limbs were bound together by skin and bone, and it was sighing again and again.
Seeing him, that best of sages, filled with supreme compassion, said: "Who are you, and from what country have you come to this land?"

To him, the Piśāca, tormented by hunger, spoke these words: "In a previous birth, I was a Brahmin endowed with wealth and grain; possessed of sons, grandsons, and others, I was intent on maintaining my family. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.31.21)
I have not worshipped the gods, nor cows, nor guests;
never have I performed merit, whether it be small or even very slight.
Once, the Blessed Lord, the god whose vehicle is the lordly bull, the Sovereign of the Universe, was seen in Vārāṇasī; he was touched and saluted.
Then, after a short time, I met my death;
yet, O Sage, I did not behold the terrible face of Yama.
Having entered such a Piśāca womb,
possessed by hunger and now overcome by thirst, I do not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful.
O Lord, if you perceive any means to deliver someone, please employ it;
salutations to you, for I have come to you for refuge.
Thus addressed, Śaṅkukarṇa then said this to the Piśāca:
"Indeed, there is no one in this world who is a greater performer of meritorious deeds than you."
Since the Blessed Lord Śiva, the Sovereign of the Universe, was previously seen,
touched, and repeatedly saluted by you— who else on earth is equal to you?
"By the ripening of that karma, you have arrived at this place. Perform your bath quickly with a concentrated mind in this pool,
by which you shall swiftly abandon this contemptible womb."
Thus addressed by the compassionate sage, the piśāca called to mind the three-eyed lord of gods,
the sovereign Kapardīśvara.
Having fixed my mind in concentration, I entered into deep contemplation.
Then, having plunged into the presence of the Sage, he died, endowed with divine ornaments,
and was seen in a celestial chariot resembling the sun.
His beautiful head is marked with the sign of the moon.
This god shines forth, surrounded on all sides by the Rudras stationed in heaven, encompassed by immeasurable yogins and bhairas, along with the Bālakhilyas and others.
Just as the sun, the lord of all gods, rises.
The hosts of gods in heaven praise him;
the delightful celestial nymphs dance;
they release a rain mixed with flowers and water.
Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Kiṃnaras, and others.
Then, being praised by the hosts of lords of sages and having attained awakening through the grace of the Blessed One,
he entered this supreme maṇḍala.
Wherein Rudra shines forth, consisting of the three Vedas.
Seeing that he had been liberated from his state as a piśāca,
the sage was delighted in his mind; reflecting upon Maheśa, Rudra, the solitary seer, and Agni.
Having prostrated, he praised that Kapardin.
Śaṅkukarṇa said: I bow to you, the one with matted hair, who is beyond the beyond, the sole protector, the ancient Puruṣa.
I go to the Lord of Yoga, the Sovereign,
who is Āditya, Agni, and mounted upon Kapila.
I go for refuge to you, Rudra, who are the further shore of Brahman, seated within the heart, golden-hued, the primordial yogi, and dwelling in the heavens.
The great sage, composed of Brahman, the pure.
I bow to you, Śambhu, the boundless Brahman, who possesses a thousand feet, eyes, heads, and a thousand arms, and who transcends the sky.
The three-eyed lord of Hiraṇyagarbha.
From whom the origin of the world proceeds,
and by whom— by Śiva— all this is pervaded;
to that Blessed Lord, the Supreme Brahman, the Master...
Having bowed down perpetually, I take refuge [in him].
I bow to you, the Supreme Lord, who is beyond the reach of the Vedas, whose form is devoid of light, who is self-luminous, the Lord of Consciousness, the one Rudra, and the further shore of Brahman.
I shall pay homage to him, for there is nothing else beyond him.
I bow eternally to that God whom yogins— who have abandoned yoga with seed and attained the samādhi that is the ultimate reality— behold.
That is your own nature, the further shore of Brahman.

I bow eternally to that which transcends Brahman, whose own nature does not abide within the range of perception and wherein there is no conceptual construction of distinctions such as name and so forth.
I take refuge in you, the Self-Existent One.
Those who delight in the declarations of the Vedas behold Your single, undivided nature— which is non-dual and identical with the realization of Brahman— as manifold, even though You are one.
I am eternally bowed down before that which has Brahmā as its further shore.
I bow to that ancient Puruṣa from whom Pradhāna evolves, whom the gods revere,
and who is established within the light.
The vast Time is your true form.
I go for refuge eternally to the Lord of Guha; I take shelter of Sthāṇu, the Mountain-Dweller, the Foe of Tripura;
I take shelter of Śiva, Hara, the Moon-crested One.
I go to you, the wielder of the Pināka bow, for refuge.
Having thus praised the Lord with matted hair, Śaṅkukarṇa fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff, uttering the supreme syllable Om.
At that very moment, the supreme *liṅga*, whose nature is Śiva—
consisting of knowledge, bliss, and non-duality, and resembling ten million fires of cosmic dissolution— manifested.
Then Śaṅkukarṇa, having liberated his self, became that very self—omnipresent and stainless—and merged into the pure *liṅga*; it was like a miracle.
This secret majesty of Kapardin has been declared to you;
no one knows it because of darkness, for even a learned man is deluded in this matter.
Whoever should constantly listen to this discourse that destroys sin,
being devoted, with a soul purified of sin, shall attain proximity to Rudra.
And being pure, one should constantly recite this great hymn that reaches the further shore of Brahman;
at the times of dawn and midday, he shall attain the supreme Yoga.
"Right here we shall dwell eternally; we shall constantly behold the god Kapardin, the God of gods, and we shall worship the wielder of the trident."
Having spoken thus, the blessed Vyāsa, the great sage, dwelt there with his disciples,
his mind disciplined, worshipping indeed Kapardin.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the first part of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Having dwelt there once more near Kapardīśa, the Blessed One...
The Lord went to see Madhyameśa after many groups of years had passed.
There, having seen the auspicious Mandākinī river, frequented by hosts of sages and possessing pure water, the sage was filled with joy.
Having observed her, the lord Dvaipāyana, who was pure in heart and knowledgeable in the rules of ritual bathing, performed his ablutions together with the sages.
Having duly gratified the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors,
he worshipped Bhava, the origin of the worlds, with various kinds of flowers.
Having entered together with his most eminent disciples, the son of Satyavatī worshipped the trident-bearing Lord Īśāna at Madhyameśvara.
Then the peaceful Pāśupatas, their bodies smeared with ashes,
assembled to behold Rudra, the Lord of Madhyameśvara.
With their minds fixed on the syllable *oṃ*, they were devoted to the study of the Vedas;
some had matted hair and others were shaven-headed, all wearing white sacred threads.
Some were clothed only in loincloths, while others were even naked;
they were devoted to celibacy, tranquil, and intent upon the knowledge of the Vedānta.
Having seen the sage Dvaipāyana surrounded by his disciples, the brahmins honored him according to tradition and spoke these words.
"Who are you, O great sage, and from where have you come with your disciples?
Thus did the disciples Paila and the others speak to those sages who were absorbed in Brahman.
This sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
is Hṛṣīkeśa himself, by whom the Vedas were divided.
To him, the Lord Mahādeva himself, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
became a son by means of a portion of his own portion, the powerful one known by the name Śuka.
He who has taken refuge in Mahādeva Śaṅkara himself with his whole being through supreme devotion— he possesses that divine knowledge.
Then all the Pāśupatas, their hair standing on end with joy and their minds undisturbed, bowed down and spoke to the son of Satyavatī.
O Blessed One, you have known that supreme consciousness of Parameṣṭhin, which,
through the grace of the God of gods, is that highest state belonging to Maheśvara.
In the same way, may we quickly behold that God— the unmanifest, secret, and most excellent mystery— having heard it from the mouth of the Blessed One.
Then, having dismissed those disciples headed by Sumantu,
that best of knowers of yoga spoke of that supreme knowledge to the yogis.
At that very moment, a pure and supreme light arose;
those brahmins dissolved right there and vanished in an instant.
Then the Blessed One, the supreme knower of Brahman, having summoned his disciples headed by Paila, spoke of the majesty of Madhyameśa.
In this place, the Lord Maheśvara himself,
together with the Goddess and surrounded by the Rudras, sports eternally, O Blessed One.
In this place, Hṛṣīkeśa, the son of Devakī and the soul of the universe, formerly dwelt for one year as Kṛṣṇa, always surrounded by the Pāśupatas.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes and devoted to the recitation of the Rudra-hymns,
Hari propitiated Śambhu by undertaking the Pāśupata vow.
He had many disciples devoted to the life of celibacy;
having obtained knowledge through his words, they beheld Maheśvara.
To that Kṛṣṇa, the Lord Mahādeva Nīlalohita appeared in person and, as the granter of boons, bestowed upon him the highest boon.
My devotees who shall worship Govinda according to the prescribed rites,
O you who pervade the world, in them there will arise that divine knowledge.
"You shall be one to be saluted, worshipped, and meditated upon by people devoted to me, as well as by the twice-born; of this there is no doubt, through my grace. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.32.26)
Those who, having bathed here, shall behold the Lord of Gods, Rudra the wielder of the Pināka bow,
their sin— including the murder of a Brahmin— is swiftly destroyed.
Those mortals who cast off their lives, even if they were devoted to sinful deeds, go to that supreme abode; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Blessed indeed are those brahmins who, having offered water oblations in the Mandākinī,
worship the Lord Mahādeva as Madhyameśvara.

O Brahmins, bathing, giving gifts, performing austerities, offering the Śrāddha rite, and the presentation of the funeral cake (piṇḍa)— each of these performed here purifies the family up to the seventh generation.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains by touching the waters at Saṃnihatyā when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, ten times that fruit is obtained here.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Mahāyogin dwelt for a very long time at Madhyameśāntika, indeed worshipping Maheśvara.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the first section of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said: Then [he described] all the secret holy places (tīrthas) and sanctuaries.
The Blessed Vyāsa departed, surrounded by those headed by Jaimini.
Prayāga is the supreme sacred ford, more auspicious than Prayāga itself;
likewise is the Viśvarūpa ford, as well as the unsurpassed Tāla-tīrtha.
The great pilgrimage site named Ākāśa, the supreme pilgrimage site of Arṣabha,
the great pilgrimage site Svarṇola, and the unsurpassed Gaurītīrtha.
Likewise, there is the Prājāpatya tīrtha, as well as Svargadvāra;
and what is called Jambukeśvara, the supreme tīrtha known as Dharmākhya.
Gayātīrtha is a great sacred site, as is the Mahānadī river;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme sacred site, and Vāyutīrtha is unsurpassed.
The supreme secret Jñānatīrtha, the excellent Vārāha-tīrtha,
the highly meritorious Yamatīrtha, and the auspicious Saṃvartaka-tīrtha.
O best of the twice-born, there is Agnitīrtha, the excellent Kalaśeśvara,
as well as Nāgatīrtha, Somatīrtha, and likewise Sūryatīrtha.
The great secret called Parvata, the unsurpassed Maṇikarṇa,
the excellent tīrtha Ghaṭotkaca, and the Śrītīrtha of Pitāmaha.
Gaṅgātīrtha, Deveśa, the excellent tīrtha of Yayāti,
Kāpila, Someśa, and the unsurpassed Brahmatīrtha.
When Brahmā went there in former times to bathe,
Viṣṇu then established that divine Liṅga.
Then, having bathed and returned, Brahmā said to that Hari:
"Why have you installed this linga which was brought by me?"
Viṣṇu said to him: "My devotion to Rudra is even firmer than yours;
therefore, the installed liṅga shall be known by your name. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.33.12)
Likewise, there is the Bhūteśvara Tīrtha, the Dharmasamudbhava Tīrtha,
the supreme Gandharva Tīrtha, and the excellent Vāhneya Tīrtha.
O best of the twice-born, there are Daurvāsika, Vyomatīrtha, Candratīrtha,
the meritorious Citrāṅgadeśvara, and the meritorious Vidyādhareśvara.
The sacred ford (tīrtha) called Kedāra, the formidable Ugrākhya, the unsurpassed Kālañjara,
Sārasvata, Prabhāsa, and the auspicious lake Bhadrakarṇa.
The great holy site called Laukika, the holy site of Vṛṣadhvaja,
Hiraṇyagarbha, Goprekṣya, and the holy site of Vṛṣadhvaja.
Upaśānta, Śiva, and the unsurpassed Vyāghreśvara;
the great tīrtha Trilocana, and Lolārka, known as Uttarā.
The Kapālamocana tīrtha, which destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin;
the highly meritorious Śukreśvara; and the supreme Ānandapura.
These sacred fords have been described according to their preeminence;
however, O best of the twice-born, it is not possible to state the number of sacred fords in detail.
Having bathed in all those sacred fords and having worshipped the wielder of the Pināka bow,
that great sage, the son of Parāśara, fasted at each of them.
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods and having performed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍapradāna),
he went once again to where Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, resides.
Having bathed and worshipped the supreme Liṅga together with his disciples, the righteous great sage said to his disciples, "You ought to go to your own countries."
Having paid homage to that Great-Souled One, the twice-born Paila and the others departed;
he, however, remained disciplined and took up residence there in Vārāṇasī.
Peaceful and self-controlled, having bathed at the three periods of the day and worshipped the wielder of the Pināka bow,
he should subsist on alms, be pure in soul, and be devoted to the life of celibacy.
O best of the twice-born, while Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor was once dwelling there, wandering about, he did not obtain any alms at all.
Then, my body enveloped in wrath, I shall create obstacles for all the people dwelling here, by which their spiritual success (siddhi) is lost.
At that very moment, that Great Goddess, who shares half the body with Śaṅkara,
appeared in person out of affection, having assumed a human form.
"O Vyāsa of great intellect, you must certainly not be cursed by me;
accept alms from me. Having spoken thus, Śivā gave them to him.
And the Great Goddess said: "Since you are prone to anger, you must not dwell here in this sacred field; you are ever ungrateful."
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, having known through meditation that [the goddess] was supremely auspicious,
spoke after bowing down and praising her with excellent hymns.
"O Śāṅkarī, grant me entrance on the fourteenth and the eighth [lunar days].
Having granted permission with the words "So be it," the Goddess vanished.
Thus the Blessed One Vyāsa, the ancient great yogi,
having understood all the qualities of that sacred field, remained by its side.
Knowing that the field is thus situated as an expanse, the wise resort to it;
therefore, a person should dwell in Vārāṇasī with every effort.
Sūta said:
He who recites the majesty of Avimukta, or even listens to it,
or causes peaceful twice-born men to hear it, shall also attain the supreme goal.
O twice-born ones, whether at a rite for the ancestors (śrāddha) or a rite for the gods (daivika), by day or by night,
on the banks of rivers or in temples of the deities— Kūrma Purāṇa 1.33.35.
Having bathed with a concentrated mind, free from hypocrisy and envy,
and having paid homage to the Lord, he who recites [the mantra] attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The sages said:
"The majesty of Avimukta has been described by you exactly as it is."
But now, O observer of noble vows, tell me of the majesty of Prayāga.
O Sūta, you who know the meaning of all things, tell us now of those great and renowned sacred fords (tīrthas) located right there.
Sūta said:
Listen, all you ṛṣis; I shall describe to you in detail the majesty of Prayāga, where the divine Grandfather resides.
Just as this was told by Mārkaṇḍeya to the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, so shall I relate it to you.
Having slain all the Kauravas along with his brothers,
King Yudhiṣṭhira was overcome by great grief and fell into a swoon.
Then, after a short time, Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism arrived at Hastināpura and stood at the king’s gate.
The gatekeeper, having seen him, quickly informed the king:
"This sage Mārkaṇḍeya stands at the door, desiring to see you."
Then the Son of Dharma, hastening, approached the gate and spoke these supreme words:
"Welcome to you, O one of great wisdom; welcome to you, O great sage!"
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my lineage has been saved;
today my ancestors are satisfied, O Great Sage, since you are satisfied.
Having provided a lion-throne and performed services such as washing his feet and offering worship,
the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira honored that sage.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya, being pleased, said to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O learned one, why do you despair? Knowing everything, I have come here."
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, having bowed down, said to the great sage:
"Tell me in brief that by which one may be liberated from sins."
"O bull among sages, many innocent men have been slain by us in battle along with the Kauravas through the force of circumstances."
You ought to tell me that by which one is liberated from this sin arising from violence, even if it was committed in another lifetime.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O fortunate King, descendant of Bharata, to that which you ask me concerning the journey to Prayāga— the most excellent [act] for men, which destroys all sin.
There sat the god Mahādeva, Rudra, the lord of all the immortals,
as well as the blessed Lord Brahmā, the self-born, together with the gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the fruit of going to Prayāga;
what is the destination for those who die there, and what is the fruit for those who bathe there?"
Tell me, what is the fruit for those who dwell at Prayāga? For this is known to you; tell it to me, salutations be unto you! (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.34.18)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O child, I shall tell you what the practice is and what its fruit is—
exactly as it was heard by me in the past when it was being fully narrated by the great seers."
This is the field of Prajāpati, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed here, those who die go to heaven and are not born again.
There, the gods beginning with Brahmā, having assembled together, provide protection;
there are also many other sacred fords (tīrthas) that remove all sins.
I am not able to describe it here even in many hundreds of years;
I shall, however, proclaim the glorification of Prayāga here in brief.
Sixty thousand *dhanus* protect the Jāhnavī;
the Sun, whose vehicle has seven horses, always protects the Yamunā.
At Prayāga, however, Vāsava himself dwells especially;
Hari protects the region together with all the gods.
Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, constantly protects the Nyagrodha tree;
indeed, the gods protect this auspicious place which removes all sins.
Enshrouded by their own karma, people do not reach that state; however,
O Lord of Men, when even a very small or minute sin belongs to one who remembers Prayāga, it all goes to total destruction.
By seeing that sacred ford (tīrtha), by even chanting its name,
or by touching it, a person is liberated from sin.
O Indra among kings, there are five pools into which the Jāhnavī enters at Prayāga; for a man who bathes there, his sin is destroyed at that very moment.
Even a man who has performed evil deeds, if he remembers the Gaṅgā at a distance of thousands of yojanas, attains the supreme goal.
By chanting [the name], one is released from sin; by seeing [it], one beholds auspicious things;
likewise, O Indra among kings, by touching [it] with water, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Whether a man be afflicted by disease, or miserable, or even enraged,
he should reach the Gaṅgā and Yamunā and strive diligently to give up his life there.
The preeminent sages declare that one obtains all desired objects through celestial chariots that possess the luster of blazing gold and the brilliance of the sun.
Endowed with auspicious marks, he rejoices amidst divine palaces made of every kind of jewel, crowded with various banners and filled with excellent women.
Awakened by the sounds of singing and instrumental music,
he remains honored in heaven as long as he does not remember his former birth.
Therefore, O best of men, having fallen from that heaven when his karma is exhausted,
he is born into a prosperous family filled with gold and jewels.
One remembers that very sacred site (tīrtha); by remembering it, one goes there, whether staying in one's own country, in the forest, in a foreign land, or at home.
The eminent sages declare that whoever, while recollecting Prayāga, should give up their life-breaths, attains the world of Brahmā.
In that world where the earth is made of gold and the trees bear the fruit of all desires,
he goes to that realm where seers, sages, and perfected beings dwell.
In that beautiful and auspicious place on the bank of the Mandākinī, crowded with thousands of women,
he rejoices together with sages through the fruit of his own deeds performed in this world.
He is worshipped in heaven by the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and the gods;
then, having fallen from that heaven, he becomes the lord of Jambudvīpa.
Then, by repeatedly reflecting upon auspicious deeds,
one becomes virtuous and endowed with wealth in this world; of this there is no doubt—
for one who is established in truth and righteousness through action, mind, and speech.
He who accepts a village between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā,
or gold, or pearls, or likewise other gifts—
Whether for one's own purpose, for the ancestral rites, or even for the worship of the deities,
that pilgrimage site is fruitless for him as long as he enjoys the fruits thereof.
Therefore, a twice-born man, remaining vigilant, should not accept gifts at sacred fords, in holy shrines, or on any such auspicious occasions.
He who bestows a milch cow that is tawny or pale-red in color, with horns tipped in gold, hooves in silver, a cloth around her neck, and full of milk; ||| KūrmP_1,34.45 |||
O best of beings, for as many thousands of years as there are hairs upon her limbs, she is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the first part of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O child, I shall describe to you the sequential procedure for the pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*)."
But according to the rishi-ordained procedure, as it has been seen and as it has been heard.
Listen also to the fruit obtained by that man who, for the purpose of a pilgrimage to Prayāga, travels somewhere while mounted upon a bull. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.35.2)
He dwells in a terrible hell for ten million times a hundred kalpas;
thereafter, that fierce and dreadful anger toward cows departs from him,
yet the ancestors of that embodied being do not accept his water offerings.
But he who bathes his sons and young children, and likewise causes them all to drink [the water],
should cause gifts to be given to Brahmins just as he would for himself.
If a man should go by vehicle out of pride in his power or out of greed and delusion, that sacred ford (tīrtha) becomes fruitless for him; therefore, he should avoid using a vehicle.
He who gives away his daughter in the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā by means of the Ārṣa marriage rite, according to the full extent of his wealth— Kūrma Purāṇa 1.35.6.
He does not see that terrible hell on account of that deed;
having gone to the Northern Kurus, he rejoices for an imperishable time.
Whoever should cast off their life-breaths taking refuge at the foot of a banyan tree transcends all worlds and goes to the world of Rudra.
Therein were the gods beginning with Brahmā, the quarters along with their presiding deities,
the world-protectors, the Siddhas, and the ancestors esteemed by the world.
Likewise, other brahminical seers headed by Sanatkumāra,
as well as nāgas, suparṇas, and siddhas, always sit together there;
and the blessed Lord Hari also resides there, preceded by Prajāpati.
O tiger among kings, Prayāga, renowned throughout the three worlds, is considered the hips of the earth situated between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Whoever, firm in his vows, performs an ablution there at the confluence,
obtains a fruit equal to that of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
O dear one, your mind must not be turned away from going to Prayāga, neither by the word of your mother nor even by the word of the world.
Ten thousand holy sites and sixty crores of others—
their presence is found right here at these sacred fords, O joy of the Kurus.
Whatever destination belongs to the wise man who is established in purity and disciplined in yoga,
that same destination belongs to one who gives up their life at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira,
those who have not reached Prayāga, which is renowned throughout the three worlds, do not truly live in this world, wherever they may be.
Having thus beheld that sacred ford, Prayāga, the supreme station,
one is liberated from all sins, just as the moon is freed from Rāhu.
The two nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara are on the southern bank of the Yamunā;
having bathed and drunk there, one is liberated from all sins.
Having gone there to the place of the wise Mahādeva,
a man shall first deliver himself, as well as ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Having performed the consecration, that man shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
he attains the heavenly world for as long as the dissolution of all beings at the end of the aeon.
O King, on the eastern bank of the Gaṅgā are Avacaḥ, Sarvasāmudra, and the renowned Pratiṣṭhāna, which have attained fame throughout the three worlds.
If one who observes celibacy and has conquered anger remains [there] for three nights,
his soul purified of all sins, he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
To the north of Pratiṣṭhāna and to the left of the Bhāgīrathī is the sacred ford named Haṃsaprapatana, renowned throughout the three worlds.
The fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice arises there from the mere recollection [of it];
for as long as the moon and the sun endure, one is honored in heaven.
Listen also to the fruit obtained by one who gives up their life on the beautiful, vast, and swan-white sandy bank of the Urvashī.
O lord of men, he dwells in the heavenly world together with his ancestors for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years.
Then, at the delightful Sandhyāvatī, a pure man who is a celibate student with his senses conquered should perform worship; he shall attain the world of Brahmā.
Whoever, having resorted to Koṭitīrtha, should give up their life,
is honored in the heavenly world for thousands of millions of years.

Where the highly blessed Gaṅgā flows, abounding in sacred fords and groves of ascetics—that indeed should be known as a field of spiritual perfection; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
She delivers mortals on earth, she delivers even the nāgas below, and she delivers the gods in heaven; for that reason, she is known as the "Three-Pathed" river (Tripathagā).
As long as a man's bones remain in the Ganges,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world.
She is the supreme sacred ford among all sacred fords, the supreme river among all rivers,
the bestower of liberation upon all beings, even those who have committed the greatest sins.
The Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere, yet she is difficult to find in three places:
at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
For all beings whose minds are afflicted by evil and who are seeking a refuge,
there is no destination equal to the Gaṅgā.
The purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of auspicious things,
it is the beautiful remover of all sins, fallen from Maheśvara.
In the Kṛta age, the sacred fords (tīrthas) are supreme; in the Tretā age, Puṣkara is supreme;
in the Dvāpara age, Kurukṣetra; but in the Kali age, the Gaṅgā is distinguished as the best.
One should resort specifically to the Gaṅgā at Prayāga;
there is nothing else that can destroy the impurity and evil deeds born of the Kali age.
Whether free from desire or possessed by desire, whoever perishes in the Gaṅgā,
upon dying he is born in heaven and does not see hell.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
There are sixty thousand and sixty hundred sacred fords (tīrthas).
In the month of Māgha, they shall go to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Whatever fruit is obtained from the proper gift of a hundred thousand cows,
that same fruit is gained by one who bathes for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
He who would accomplish a *kārṣāpaṇa* sacrifice between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā becomes free from physical defects,
free from disease, and endowed with all five sense faculties.
O giver of honor, for as many thousands of years as there are hair-pores on his body, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he becomes the lord of Jambūdvīpa;
after enjoying vast pleasures, he resorts once again to that sacred ford.
He who should enter the water at the world-renowned confluence shall be liberated from all sins, like the moon when it is released from being seized by Rāhu.
He attains the world of Soma and rejoices together with Soma for sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years.
Having gone from heaven to the world of Śakra, he is served by sages and gandharvas;
then, O Indra among kings, when he falls from there, he is born into a prosperous family.
If a man drinks the stream of blood with his head downward and his feet upward,
he is honored in the heavenly world for a hundred thousand years.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, a man who has fallen from that state should become an Agnihotrin;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, he resorts to that sacred ford once again.
Listen now to the fruit that belongs even to one who cuts up his own body or gives it to birds, and is thus consumed by those winged creatures.
He is honored in the world of Soma for a hundred thousand years;
then, having descended from there, he becomes a righteous king.
Endowed with virtues, perfect in form, learned, and speaking very pleasant words,
he enjoys vast pleasures and then resorts once more to that sacred ford.
On the northern bank of the Yamunā, to the south of Prayāga,
there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Ṛṇapramocana, which is remembered as supreme.
Having stayed for one night and bathed there, one is liberated from debts;
one attains the world of the Sun and shall forever be free from debt.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The goddess who is the daughter of Tapaṇa is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Where the illustrious river Yamunā has come together [with the Gaṅgā].
The Yamunā flows by the very same path through which the Gaṅgā has issued forth;
by reciting [her name], she destroys sin even at a distance of thousands of yojanas.
Having bathed and drunk there at the Yamunā, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
one is liberated from all sins and purifies his lineage unto the seventh generation;
he who gives up his life there goes to the supreme goal.
The place known as Agnitīrtha is on the southern bank of the Yamunā;
to the west of Dharmarāja is the tīrtha remembered as Anaraka.
Having bathed there, they go to heaven, and those who die there are not subject to rebirth.
Having bathed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one who is pure should offer libations to Dharmarāja; he is liberated from great sins—of this there is no doubt.
Ten thousand holy fords (*tīrtha*), as well as another thirty crores, are situated at Prayāga; so say the wise.
Vāyu declared that there are three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrtha) in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space; all of those are considered to be the Jāhnavī.
