Wherever the highly blessed Gaṅgā flows, that region is a forest for asceticism;
it should be known as a field of spiritual accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) situated along the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Where the god Mahādeva, the Great Lord Maheśvara, dwells eternally together with the Goddess at Vaṭeśvara— that is the sacred ford, that is the grove of asceticism.
This truth should be whispered into the ear of the twice-born, of the virtuous, of one's own son, of friends, and of a devoted disciple.
This is auspicious, this leads to heaven, this is pure, this is bliss;
this is meritorious, this is delightful, this is purifying, righteous, and supreme.
This secret of the great seers grants liberation from all sins;
by studying this chapter here, a twice-born man shall attain purity.
Whoever should constantly hear this sacred and meritorious site, being ever pure,
attains the memory of past births and rejoices in the vault of heaven.
Those sacred fords are reached by the virtuous who follow the example of the wise;
bathe in those sacred fords, O Kauravya, and do not be crooked-minded.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya,
recounted whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist upon the earth.

Having been questioned regarding the configuration of the earth, oceans, and so forth, as well as the established measurements of the celestial bodies, the sage explained everything and then departed.
Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites this or hears it,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the Purva-vibhaga of the Shri Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Śrī Kūrma said:
Having been addressed in this manner, the sages of Naimiṣa [spoke] to the high-minded one.
They questioned Sūta for an answer concerning the determination of the earth and the other elements.
The sages said: O Sūta, you have described to us the auspicious creation of the Self-born;
now we wish to hear about the mandala of these three worlds.
As many as there are oceans, islands, as well as regions, mountains,
forests, rivers, and even the positions of the sun and the planets.
O Sūta, you ought to tell me here in brief about those kings upon whom this entire earth was formerly supported.
Sūta said: Having paid homage to Viṣṇu, the god of gods, the sovereign lord, and the immeasurable one, I shall declare that which was spoken by that wise one.
Of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, there was a son named Priyavrata as previously mentioned;
he had ten sons who were equal to the Prajāpatis.
Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Vapuṣmān, and Dyutimān;
as well as Medhā, Medhātithi, Havya, Savana, and Putra.
The tenth among them was Jyotiṣmān, possessed of great strength and prowess;
he was righteous, devoted to giving, and compassionate toward all living beings.
Medhāgni, Bāhu, and Putra—these three were devoted to yoga;
being highly fortunate and possessing the memory of their former births, they set their minds upon sovereignty.
Priyavrata indeed consecrated those seven sons over the seven continents;
the king made his son Agnīdhra the lord of Jambudvīpa.
He made Medhātithi the lord of Plakṣadvīpa,
and he consecrated Vapuṣmat as the king of Śālmala.
The Lord made Jyotiṣmat the king in Kuśadvīpa,
and he appointed Dyutimat as the king in Krauñcadvīpa.
Priyavrata also made Havya the lord of Śākadvīpa,
and the patriarch Savana he made the sovereign of Puṣkara.
Puṣkara also had a son named Savana, and Mahāvīta was born as his son; Dhātaki and [Savana] were these two sons, the best among those who possess sons.
The region known as Mahāvīta was named after that great-souled one;
and because of the name Dhātaki, it is also called Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
Now, Havya, the lord of Śākadvīpa, also had sons:
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Maṇīcaka,
Kusumottara, Modāki, and the seventh was Mahādruma.
The first [period] of a cloud is called *jalada*; the second is *varṣa*;
and the third, that of a youth, is *kaumāra*, while the fourth is *sukumāraka*.
The fourth is Maṇīcaka, the fifth is Kusumottara,
the sixth is said to be Modāka, and the seventh is Mahādruma.
The son of Dyutimat, the lord of Krauñcadvīpa, also had sons;
of them, Kuśala was the first, and the second was Manohara.
The third is declared to be Uṣṇa, and the fourth is remembered as Pravara;
Andhakāra, Muni, and Dundubhi is the seventh.
The auspicious regions based in Krauñcadvīpa are named after them.
In Kuśadvīpa, there were seven sons of Jyotiṣmat who possessed great majesty:
Udbheda, Veṇumān, Aśvaratha, Lambana, Dhṛti as the sixth, Prabhākāra, and Kapila is recorded as the seventh.
O you of virtuous vows, the seven regions (varṣas) therein should be known as marked by their own names; they are situated within these very islands in this manner, as is traditionally held.
The sons of Vapuṣmat, the lord of Śālmaladvīpa,
were Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita,
Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and the seventh was considered to be Suprabha.
Medhātithi, the lord of Plakṣadvīpa, also had seven sons:
Śāntabhaya was the eldest among them, followed by Śiśira, Sukhodaya,
Ānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka, and Dhruva.
O twice-born ones, it should be known that in the islands beginning with Plakṣa and ending with Śāka,
one’s own duty (svadharma), according to the divisions of caste and stage of life, leads to liberation.
O best of the twice-born, the sons of Agnīdhra, the lord of Jambūdvīpa, were also possessed of great strength; learn their names.
Nābhi, Kiṃpuruṣa, as well as Harivarṣa and Ilāvṛta;
Ramya, Hiraṇvān, Kuru, Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and Bhārata.
The king who was the lord of Jambudvīpa, that wise Agnīdhra,
having divided [the land] into nine parts, gave them back to them according to what was right.
He then gave the region to the south of Nābhi, called Himavat;
thereafter, he gave the region of Hemakūṭa to Kiṃpuruṣa.
The father gave the third region, Naiṣadha, to Hari;
he bestowed Ilāvṛta, situated in the middle of Meru, upon Ilāvṛta.
The father gave the region situated on the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala) to Ramya;
the white region to the north was given by the father to Hiraṇvat.
He gave the region north of Śṛṅgavat to Kuru;
the region to the east of Meru he assigned to Bhadrāśva;
and he gave the region of Gandhamādana to Ketumāla.
Having consecrated those sons in these years, the lord of men,
realizing the suffering inherent in worldly existence, went to the forest and practiced asceticism.
From that high-souled one whose name was Himāhvaya,
there was born a son of great splendor named Ṛṣabha by Marudevī.
From Ṛṣabha was born the heroic Bharata, the eldest of a hundred sons.
Having consecrated his son Bharata as lord of the earth,
that king Ṛṣabha retired to the forest-dwelling stage of life (vānaprasthāśrama) and practiced austerities according to the prescribed rule.
Exhausted by asceticism, exceedingly emaciated, and covered with visible veins,
he became devoted to the yoga of knowledge and attained the status of a Mahāpāśupata.
Sumati was the son of Bharata, supremely righteous;
from Sumati was born Taijasa, and from him Indradyumna was born.
Parameṣṭhin was born from him; his lineage was Pratīhāra, who became renowned as Pratiharta, and from him a son was born.
From him was born Bhava, and from him came Udgītha; Prastāva was his son, and from him Pṛthu; from him came Rakta, and Gaya was the son of Rakta.
Nara was the son of Gaya; his son was Virāj;
from him was born the wise Mahāvīrya, who possessed great heroism.
From him was born Mahān, and his son was Bhauvana;
Tvaṣṭṛ was the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viraja was the son of Rajas.
O twice-born ones, Śatajit begot a hundred sons from that Rajas;
among them, the eldest was known as the powerful Viśvajyotis.
Having propitiated the god Brahmā, [he begot] a son named Kṣemaka, a king who was a knower of dharma, mighty-armed, and a subduer of enemies.
These kings of old were great beings of immense power;
by those born of their lineage, this earth was enjoyed in former times.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the first part of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, hereafter I shall proclaim [the account] in brief.
But it is not possible for you to describe the measurement of these three worlds in detail.
The world of the earth (bhūrloka), then the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), the heavenly world (svarloka), and then the great world (maharloka);
the world of living beings (janaloka), the world of austerity (tapoloka), and the world of truth (satyaloka)—these worlds are considered to have originated from the cosmic egg.
O best of the twice-born, as far as the earth is illuminated by the rays of the sun and the moon, so far is it declared to be the *bhūrloka* in the Purāṇa.
To whatever extent the terrestrial world (bhūrloka) extends in width and circumference,
the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka) shall be of the same extent as the orb of the sun.
That which extends upward from the Maṇḍala as far as the Pole Star (Dhruva) in the sky is declared to be Svarloka; there, indeed, are the rims of the winds.
Āvaha, Pravaha, and likewise Anuvaha as the next;
then Saṃvaha, Vivaha, and above those shall be Parāvaha.
Likewise, the Parivaha wind is above; indeed, there are seven rims of wind.
At a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas from the earth, the orb of the sun is situated.
At a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas] from the sun, the orb of the moon is said to be located;
at that same distance of one hundred thousand, the entire circle of the constellations shines forth.
O brahmins, two hundred thousand yojanas above the sphere of the stars is Mercury;
at that same distance from Mercury, Venus is situated.
Aṅgāraka is also situated at that same distance from Śukra;
the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati) is situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] from Bhauma.
The orb of the planets, including Saturn and Jupiter, extends for two hundred thousand [yojanas];
beyond that, the orb of the Seven Sages shines at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas].
Situated at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas] above the circle of the sages (ṛṣis) is Dhruva;
indeed, Dhruva serves as the central pivot for the entire wheel of luminaries (jyotiścakra).
Therein resides the Blessed One, Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, who is Dharma itself.
The diameter of the sun is recorded as nine thousand yojanas;
its circumference, according to measurement, is three times that.
The diameter of the moon is recorded as being twice its [the sun's] width;
Svarbhānu, becoming equal in size to those two, moves below them.
Having cast aside the shadow of the earth, it was fashioned in the form of a circle;
that vast, third abode of Svarbhānu consists entirely of darkness.
The portion of Bhārgava is prescribed as one-sixteenth of that of Candra;
indeed, Bṛhaspati is to be known as being one-quarter less than Bhārgava.
Both Venus and Saturn are recorded as being one-quarter less than Bṛhaspati;
Mercury is one-quarter less than both of them in terms of both width and orb.
Those forms of the stars and constellations that indeed possess bodies here are equal to Budha in both extent and in the size of their orbs.
The forms of the stars and constellations are smaller than one another by five hundred,
four hundred, three hundred, and two hundred yojanas respectively.
The smallest circles of stars, however, are half a *yojana* in size; nothing smaller than these exists.
Above them are those three planets which travel far;
they are to be known as the son of the Sun (Saturn), Aṅgiras (Jupiter), and Vakra (Mars), who move slowly.
And below them are four other great planets, moving swiftly: Sūrya, Sauma, Budha, and Bhārgava.
When the sun, possessing rays, moves while situated on the path of the southern solstice,
then he, the sun, glides beneath all the planets.
Having formed a vast mandala, the moon moves above it;
the entire circle of constellations glides above the moon.
Above the lunar mansions is Mercury; above Mercury is Venus;
above Venus is Mars; and above Mars is Jupiter.
Above that is Śanaiścara (Saturn), above that is the circle of the Seven Sages,
and above the Seven Sages, Dhruva is situated.
O best of the twice-born, the chariot of the Sun consists of nine thousand yojanas;
its pole-shaft is likewise double that length.
Its axle is one and a half crores and seven additional hundred thousand yojanas long; upon it the wheel is established.
The entire wheel of time (kālacakra) is established upon the year, which possesses three naves, five spokes, six rims, and is imperishable by nature. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.39.29)
O best of the twice-born, the second axle of Vivasvat’s chariot is forty-two thousand [yojanas] long, while the other five parts of the chariot are each one thousand five hundred.
The axle is the measure for both of those half-yokes;
the axle is short by the length of that half-yoke when fixed upon the chariot's support.
But on the second axle, that wheel is situated upon Mount Mānasa;
the seven horses are the Vedic meters—learn their names. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.39.32)
The Gāyatrī, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇih, Jagatī, Paṅkti, Anuṣṭubh, and Triṣṭubh—
these are said to be the meters (chandas) that serve as the bay horses of Hari.
Above Mānasa is the great city of Mahendra in the eastern direction;
to the south is that of Yama, and to the west is that of Varuṇa.
Now learn of the names of those [cities] to the north of Soma:
Amarāvatī, Saṃyamanī, Sukhā, and Vibhā, in order.
Having reached the southern limit,
the God of gods, Prajāpati, glides along like an arrow shot [from a bow], taking with him the wheel of the luminaries.
O best of Brahmins, the sun remains at the center of the day at all times,
facing the middle of the night across the seven continents.
At both sunrise and sunset, at all times indeed,
facing [him] directly in all directions as well as in the intermediate directions.
O twice-born ones, just as this Lord, revolving like a potter’s wheel,
creates the day, so too does He release the night over the earth.
O best of sages, this triple world is filled with the rays of the sun;
it is called "the three worlds" (trailokya) by the virtuous for the sake of the people.
The entire three worlds have the Sun as their root; of this there is no doubt.
From him arises the whole universe, including gods, asuras, and humans. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.39.41)
The splendor of Rudra, Indra, Upendra, and Candra; the splendor of the foremost of Brahmins and the inhabitants of heaven;
the entire radiance of all that is luminous throughout the whole world—[all this is yours].
The soul of all, the lord of all worlds, Mahādeva, the progenitor—
Sūrya alone is the root of the three worlds and the supreme deity.
Likewise, there are twelve other Ādityas who are the presiding deities;
they carry out his office as partial incarnations of Viṣṇu.
All beings— the Gandharvas, gods, serpents, Kinnaras, humans, and others— bow down to the Thousand-rayed One;
and the foremost of the twice-born worship him with various sacrifices.
Consisting of the Vedas, consisting of Brahman, and ancient.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the first part of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
That chariot was occupied by the gods, namely the Ādityas and the Vasus.
By the Gandharvas and Apsarases, by the Grāmaṇīs, Sarpas, and Rākṣasas.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Śakra;
Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Parjanya, and Aṃśu.
Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu— these twelve are the suns who indeed nourish the Sun-god in succession during the seasons beginning with spring.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu,
Bharadvāja, Gautama, Kaśyapa, and Kratu.
Jamadagni and Kauśika, sages who discourse on Brahman,
praise the God with various meters in their proper order.
Rathakṛt, Rathaujas, Rathacitra, Subāhuka,
Rathasvana, Varuṇa, Suṣeṇa, and Senajit.
Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, Rathajit, and Satyajit likewise—
these leaders of the hosts perform the task of holding the reins for the God of gods.
Then there are Heti and Praheti, as well as man-made slaughter;
likewise the serpent, the tiger, water, wind, lightning, and the sun.
O best of Brahmins, those endowed with the Veda and likewise those endowed with sacrifice—
these foremost of Rākṣasas indeed proceed one after another in front.
Vāsuki, Kaṅkanīra, Takṣaka the foremost of serpents,
Elāpatra, Śaṅkhapāla, and likewise the one known as Airāvata.
O twice-born ones, Dhanañjaya, Mahāpadma, Karkoṭaka,
and Kambalāśvatara carry him in their respective order.
Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, Hūhū, Viśvāvasu, as well as Ugrasena, Vasuruci, and another, Arvāvasu.
Citrasena, Urṇāyu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Sūryavarcas— O best of the twice-born, these twelve Gandharvas, the foremost of singers,
sing to the Sun with various melodies in the sequence of the notes beginning with Ṣaḍja.
O best of the twice-born, [there were] Kratusthalā, the excellent Apsaras Puñjikasthalā,
as well as Menakā, Sahajanyā, and Pramlocā.
Anumlocā, Ghṛtīcī, Viśvācī, and Urvaśī;
likewise there was Pūrvacitti, and another was Tilottamā.
With various kinds of tāṇḍava dances, they please Mahādeva— the sun, the imperishable Self— in due order during the seasons beginning with spring.
In this manner, the gods dwell in the sun for two months each in succession;
they nourish the sun, the treasury of splendors, with their own radiance.
The sages praise the Sun with their own composed words,
while the Gandharvas and Apsarases attend upon him with dance and song.
The village chiefs and yakṣas hold the reins;
serpents carry the Lord of Gods, and the yātudhānas go before him.
Surrounding the sun from its rising until it sets, the Bālakhilyas lead it;
these ones heat, rain, shine, blow, and create,
and they are celebrated here as those who dispel the inauspicious karma of living beings.
These, together with their followers, revolve in the sky along with the sun;
he dwells eternally in a celestial chariot that moves at will and possesses the speed of the wind.
Raining down, heating, and indeed gladdening all creatures,
they protect all beings here until the end of the eon.
According to the prowess, the austerity, the fitness, and the disposition of these very gods,
this Lord shines forth.
That Prajāpati, the Sun, is the cause of the regulation of day and night;
he constantly nourishes the ancestors, gods, humans, and others.
There the god Mahādeva, the radiant Maheśvara himself,
the eternal blue-throated one, shines before those who know the Vedas.
This very god is the Blessed One, Parameṣṭhin, Prajāpati;
those who know the Vedas recognize that station as the Sun, the embodiment of the Vedas.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the first part of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
"In this manner, this Mahādeva is the God of gods and the Grandfather."
For the divine body, whose nature is Time, certainly effects the fixed time.
Of those rays of his which are the sages and illuminators of all worlds,
there are seven further rays that are preeminent and serve as the source of the planets.
Suṣumna and Harikeśa, as well as Viśvakarmā;
then another is Viśvavyacāḥ, and beyond that is Saṃyadvasu.
The one known as Arvāvasu is proclaimed as another [form] of Svarāṭ;
Supuṣṇa, who possesses the rays of the sun, nourishes the moon.
This Suṣumṇa is recited as moving horizontally and upwards;
that which is called Harikeśa is the ray that nourishes the constellations.
Likewise, the ray Viśvakarman always nourishes Budha;
and the ray Viśvavyacas constantly nourishes Śukra.
Known as Saṃyadvasu, he nourishes Lohita;
the ray Arvāvasu nourishes Bṛhaspati, O Lord;
and likewise, the seventh, Surāṭ, nourishes Śanaiścara.
Thus, by the power of the sun, all the lunar mansions and stars increase;
once increased, they constantly grow and constantly provide nourishment.
Because he constantly takes up all divine, terrestrial, and nocturnal lights from every side, the Sun is the lord of both splendors and darkness.
With his thousand eyes, he draws from all sides through his thousand channels the waters of rivers, the oceans, and wells,
as well as the water of stationary and moving sources, and that which comes from irrigation canals and the like.
He possesses a thousand rays that discharge cool, rain, and heat;
four hundred of those channels, possessing diverse forms, pour down rain.
The rays named Vandanās, Yājyās, Ketanās, Bhūtanās,
and Amṛtās are all the ones that release rain.
Those channels are the carriers of frost; furthermore, there are three hundred rays.
These rays—namely the Meṣyas, the Pauṣyas, the Hlādinyas, and the Himasarjanās—are all known by the name Candras; they are yellowish in luster and possess radiant beams.
The Śukras, the Kakubhas, and likewise the Viśvabhr̥ts—these are all known by name as the Śukras; they are of three kinds and are the emitters of the *gharma*.
He sustains equally with these [three] the humans, the ancestors, and the gods;
here on earth, he satisfies humans with herbs, the ancestors with *svadhā*,
and all the gods with nectar— thus he gratifies the three worlds with the three.
In spring and summer, he heats [the world] with three hundred rays;
in autumn and the rainy season, he pours down rain with four hundred;
and in winter and the cool season, he emits frost with three hundred.
In the month of Māgha, Varuṇa is the sun; in Phālguna, Pūṣan;
in the month of Caitra, he becomes Aṃśa; and in Vaiśākha, Dhātṛ is the one who heats [the world].
In Jyeṣṭhāmūla, Indra is the sun; in Āṣāḍha, the sun is Savitṛ;
in the month of Śrāvaṇa, he is Vivasvat; and in Prauṣṭhapada, he is traditionally held to be Bhaga.
Parjanya is [the presiding deity] in the month of Āśvayuja, Tvaṣṭṛ in the month of Kārtika, Bhāskara in Mārgaśīrṣa,
Mitra in Pauṣa, and the eternal Viṣṇu [is the deity] in [Māgha].
In the solar rite of Varuṇa, there are five thousand rays;
Pūṣan, however, has six thousand, and the god Aṃśa likewise has seven.
Dhātṛ protects with eight thousand, Śatakratu with nine;
Vivasvat guards with ten, and Bhaga protects with eleven.
Mitra heats with seven rays, and Tvaṣṭṛ likewise heats with eight;
Aryaman protects with ten, and Parjanya heats with nine.
Viṣṇu, the creator of the universe, heats with six thousand rays.
In spring the sun is tawny; in summer it has the luster of gold;
in the rainy season it is white in color; in autumn the Lord is pale-white;
in winter he becomes copper-colored, and in the cool season the sun is red.
The Sun bestows strength upon the herbs, his own inherent power (*svadhā*) upon the ancestors, and immortality upon the nectar; thus he ordains these three things among these three.
O twice-born ones, eight other planets are to be known as presided over by the Sun:
the Moon, the son of Soma, Śukra, Bṛhaspati,
Bhauma, Mandi, Rāhu, and Ketu as the eighth.
All those planets are indeed fixed to the Pole Star by cords of wind;
being whirled about as appropriate, they revolve following the sun.
The birds fly like a whirling firebrand, driven by the wind-circles;
because the wind carries them, it is therefore known as the Pravaha.
The chariot of Soma has three wheels; its horses, white as jasmine, are yoked ten on the left and ten on the right, and by them the Maker of Night is drawn.
O best of Brahmins, just as the sun moves through the constellations that rest upon the celestial path,
so too do their waning and waxing always have Dhruva as their support.
That moon, however, during the bright fortnight when the sun is situated beyond it,
is continuously filled from the end of the [preceding] half-month by the progression of the days.
O Brahmins, the Sun-god constantly replenishes the moon, which has been diminished by the gods,
with a single ray known as Suṣumṇā.
This body of Soma is nourished by the power of the Sun;
on the full moon day, it appears completely full through the course of the days.
The deities and the brahmins drink that Soma, which consists of nectar, once it is complete after half a month; for this reason, they are called "those who feed on nectar."
Then, when fifteen parts remain— consisting of a mere fraction of a *kalā*—
in the afternoon, the hosts of ancestors wait upon him at the final [moment].
The remaining two parts of that time they drink;
that part consists of the nectar of immortality, meritorious, beautiful, and composed of ambrosia.
On the new moon day, that nectar of *svadhā* flows forth from his rays;
having attained the foremost satisfaction for a month, the ancestors remain in a state of bliss.
There is no destruction of the soma; it is consumed as nectar by the gods.
O best of beings, in this same way there is both decrease and increase caused by the sun.
The chariot of the son of Soma is yoked with eight horses, swift as the wind and born of the waters; with them, he travels everywhere.
The chariot of Śukra is surrounded by ten earth-born horses;
and the chariot of Bhauma is made of gold and is exceedingly beautiful, drawn by eight [horses].
Now, Bṛhaspati’s chariot has eight horses and is fashioned of gold;
the chariot of Mandi consists of darkness and has eight horses made of iron;
likewise, the chariot of Svarbhānu, the enemy of the Sun, is surrounded by six horses.
These nine chariots of the great planets have been fully described;
all these illustrious ones are bound to Dhruva by cords of wind.
The planets, constellations, stars, and celestial mansions are all bound to Dhruva;
they revolve and cause him to revolve by means of the rays of the wind.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the first section of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Above Dhruva is Maharloka, extending for ten million yojanas.
The preeminent among the twice-born, who hold office for a kalpa, are stationed there.
Janaloka is likewise situated two crores [of yojanas] beyond Maharloka;
there reside Sanandana and others, the sons of Brahmā.
From Jaloka is Tapoloka, endowed with thirty million [yojanas];
there the Vairāja gods reside, free from the affliction of burning heat.
Sixty million [yojanas] from Prājāpatya is Satyaloka;
those who are there do not return to death, and that is remembered as the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka).
Here dwells Brahmā, the teacher of the world, the soul of the universe, whose face is turned in every direction;
he remains eternally having drunk the supreme nectar of yoga with the yogis.
Ascetics who are tranquil, lifelong celibates,
practitioners of yoga, ascetics, perfected ones, and reciters of mantras enter the Supreme Lord.
That is the sole gateway for yogis proceeding to the supreme state;
having gone there, they do not grieve—for that is Viṣṇu and that is Śaṅkara.
His city, resembling ten million suns and difficult to approach, is filled with garlands of flames; it is impossible for me to describe it in full.
There, within the city of Brahmā, is the abode of Nārāyaṇa;
there the glorious Hari lies, the master of illusion, composed of illusion, and supreme.
That realm of Viṣṇu is said to be free from rebirth;
the great-souled ones who have taken refuge in Janārdana go there.
Above that seat of Brahmā is a beautiful city composed of light, encircled by fire; there dwells the Blessed Lord Bhava.
Mahādeva, together with the Goddess, being meditated upon by wise men and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of yogins, bhūtas, and rudras.
There, those twice-born ones who are disciplined, celibate students,
devoted solely to me, peaceful, ascetics, and exponents of the Veda, go indeed.
Free from possessiveness and free from ego, devoid of desire and anger,
and disciplined through Brahman, they shall behold that which is indeed remembered as the world of Rudra.
These seven great worlds of the earth have been proclaimed;
and below them, O twice-born ones, are the nether regions beginning with Mahātala.
And Mahātala and Pātāla, adorned with all kinds of jewels,
were filled with various bright palaces and temples of the deities.
And it was joined by Ananta, the wise Mucukunda,
and the powerful King who dwells in both Pātāla and heaven.
O Brahmins, Śaila is Rasātala; Śārkara is indeed Talātala; Sutala is said to be yellow; Nitala has the luster of coral;
Vitala is declared to be white; and Tala is of a color other than white.
O best of sages, that auspicious place known as Rasātala is likewise inhabited by Suparṇa, Vāsuki, and others.
Served by Virocana, Hiraṇyākṣa, Takṣaka, and others,
it is renowned as Talātala, endowed with every splendor.
And likewise, Sutala was crowded with the ancient gods (pūrvadeva), such as Vainateya and others, led by Kālanemi, as well as by other [beings].
And Nitala was [ruled] by the Yavanas and others, as well as by the Tārakas, Agnimukhas, and others;
likewise by the Mahāntakas and other nāgas, and by the asura Brahmāda.
And Vitala is indeed renowned, frequented by the lord of serpents Kambala,
as well as by the hero Mahājambha and Hayagrīva.
It was likewise crowded with Śaṅkukarṇa and those led by Namuci,
as well as other various Nāgas, and the ground itself was most beautiful.
Beneath them, the hells beginning with Māyā are proclaimed;
sinners are cooked in them, and they cannot be described.
Beneath the netherworlds (pātālas) dwells the form of Viṣṇu known as Śeṣa;
likewise, Mādhava exists as Kālāgnirudra, as the soul of yoga, and also as Nārasiṃha.
The infinite Lord Janārdana, who is recited as having the form of a serpent, is the support of all this; he rests upon the fire of time (kālāgni).
Having entered him, the Great Yogin Kāla, arisen from his mouth,
consisting of the flames of poison, himself destroys the world at the end.
Possessing a thousand illusions, peerless, the destroyer, born of Śaṅkara—
this is the Tāmasī form of Śambhu, Time (Kāla), who consumes the worlds.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the first section of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, a compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
"This great fourteenfold cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) has been described."
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the definitive account of this Bhūrloka.
This Jambudvīpa is the foremost, as are Plakṣa, Śālmala,
Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara as the seventh.
These seven great continents are surrounded by seven oceans;
each successive continent is said to be larger than the preceding one, and each ocean likewise larger than the preceding ocean.
The oceans are the Salt-water Ocean, the Sugarcane-juice Ocean, the Wine Ocean, the Clarified-butter Ocean, the Curd Ocean, the Milk Ocean, and the Sweet-water Ocean.
The earth, together with its oceans, is recorded as being fifty crores [of yojanas] in extent;
it is composed of seven islands, in brief, measured in yojanas.
Jambūdvīpa is the most auspicious of all the continents;
in its center stands the renowned Mount Mahāmeru, radiant with the luster of gold.
Its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas;
it enters sixteen thousand yojanas below and is thirty-two thousand yojanas wide at its summit.
At its base, its extent is sixteen thousand [yojanas] on all sides;
this mountain stands as the pericarp of the earth-lotus.
Himavān, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha are its southern [boundaries],
while Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin are the mountain ranges to the north.
Two of them in the middle are one hundred thousand [yojanas] in measure, while the others are each ten less;
they are two thousand [yojanas] in height and of the same extent.
O twice-born ones, Bhārata is the southern region (varṣa); beyond that is remembered Kiṃpuruṣa, and likewise Harivarṣa is another [region] to the south of Meru.
The northern region is Ramyaka, and following that is Hiraṇmaya;
and the Northern Kurus are just as these Bharatas are.
O best of the twice-born, each of these [regions] measures nine thousand [yojanas];
Ilāvṛta is in their center, and in its center stands the lofty Mount Meru.
There, on the four sides of Meru, is Ilāvṛta, extending nine thousand [yojanas] in width; O fortunate ones, there are four mountains there that serve as the buttresses of Meru,
rising ten thousand yojanas high.
Mandara is known to be in the east, Gandhamādana in the south,
Vipula on the western side, and Supārśva in the north.
Among them are the Kadamba, the Jambu, the Pippala, and the Vaṭa;
O great sages, that Jambu tree is the reason for the name of Jambūdvīpa.
Fruits of that Jambu tree, as large as great elephants,
fall and shatter on all sides upon the back of the mountain.
From its juice, the river known there as the Jambūnadī indeed flows forth,
and it is drunk by those who dwell there.
Neither perspiration nor foul odor, neither old age nor the decay of the senses arises for those men of steady mind who drink that [milk] there.
Having reached the mud on that shore and being thoroughly dried by the wind,
it becomes the gold known as Jāmbūnada, the ornament of the Siddhas.
O best of sages, Bhadrāśva is to the east of Meru and Ketumāla is to the west; between these two regions lies Ilāvṛta.
One should know that Caitraratha forest is in the east, Gandhamādana in the south,
Vaibhrāja in the west, and the forest of Savitṛ in the north.
Aruṇoda, Mahābhadra, Asitoda, and Mānasa—
these four lakes are always fit for the gods.
Sitānta, Kumudvān, Kururī, Mālyavat,
Vaikaṅka, Maṇiśaila, and Ṛkṣavān are likewise the best of mountains.
Mahānīla, Rucaka, Sabindu, Mandara,
Veṇumān, Megha, Niṣadha, and Devaparvata—
these are proclaimed as the mountains fashioned by the gods, which serve as the dwellings of the Siddhas.
To the east of the lake Aruṇoda are Kesara Mountain,
Trikūṭaśikhara, Pataṅga, and likewise Rucaka.
Niṣadha, Vasudhāra, Kaliṅga, Triśikha, Śubha,
Samūla, Vasudhāra, and Sānumān are the Kurus.
Tāmra, Viśāla, Kumuda, Veṇu,
Vata, Ekaśṛṅga, Mahāśaila, Gajaśaila, and Piśācaka.
Pañcaśaila, Kailāsa, and Himavat, the best of mountains—
these are the preeminent mountains frequented by the gods.
To the south of the Mahābhadrā lake are Kesara-cala,
Śikhivāsa, Vaidūrya, Kapila, and Gandhamādana.
Jārudhi, Sugandhi, Śrīśṛṅga—the best of mountains—Supārśva, Supakṣa, Kaṅka, and Kapila as well. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.43.31)
Piñjara, Bhadraśaila, and the very powerful Surasa;
likewise Añjana, Madhumān, Kumuda, and Mukuṭa.
Sahasraśikhara, Pāṇḍura, Kṛṣṇa,
the great mountain Pārijāta, and likewise Kapilodaka.
Suṣeṇa, Puṇḍarīka, and likewise Mahāmegha—
these are the kings of mountains, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
To the west of Lake Asitoda are Kesara Mountain,
Śaṅkhakūṭa, Vṛṣabha, Haṃsa, and another, Nāga.
Kālāñjana, Śukraśaila, Nīla, Kamala, Puṣpaka, Sumegha, Vārāha, Viraja, Mayūra, Kapila, and Mahākapila. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.43.36)
Thus, these Kesara mountains to the north of Lake Mānasa are frequented by hosts of gods, gandharvas, and siddhas.
Between these principal mountains, in their respective order,
there exist intermediate valleys, lakes, and forests.
There dwell sages and perfected beings who have realized Brahman—
serene, with their passion stilled, and entirely free from all suffering.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the first division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
"The great city measures fourteen thousand yojanas."
Above Mount Meru is the renowned abode of the God of gods, the Creator.
There dwells the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the soul of the universe and the creator of the universe,
being worshipped by the lords of yogis, the lords of sages, Upendra, and Śaṅkara.
There, the blessed Sanatkumāra indeed worships perpetually the Lord of the lords of gods, the soul of the universe, Prajāpati.
Honored by the Siddhas, Ṛṣis, Gandharvas, and even by the gods,
he sat with his soul absorbed in yoga, having drunk that supreme nectar.
There, in front of Brahmā, stands the radiant and pure abode of Śambhu, the god of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Endowed with divine splendor, beautiful with four gates,
crowded with hosts of great sages, and frequented by those who know Brahman.
There, the Great God, the Lord of the Universe and Sovereign of the Pramathas, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, sports with the Goddess and his attendants.
There, the peaceful sages who know the Vedas, the celibate students,
and the ascetics who speak the truth, worship Mahādeva.
To those sages who discourse upon Brahman,
the Supreme Lord Mahādeva himself accepts their worship upon his head along with Pārvatī.
On that very same excellent mountain, to the east, is the supreme city of Śakra named Amarāvatī, endowed with every splendor.
There, hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas devoted to song attend upon that thousand-eyed Indra;
there, the gods wait upon him by the thousands.
For those who are righteous, knowers of the Vedas, and devoted to sacrifice and oblation,
that is the supreme abode, difficult to attain even for the gods.
To the southern quarter of that Fire of immeasurable splendor lies a divine city named Tejovatī, endowed with wonders beyond compare.
There dwells the Blessed One, the Fire-god, blazing with his own splendor;
it is the abode of those who recite prayers and perform fire-sacrifices, and is difficult for the Dānavas to approach.
On the excellent mountain to the south is the great divine city of Yama,
named Saṃyamanī, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
There the gods and other celestial beings attend upon the god Vaivasvata;
that is the abode in this world for men who are true to their word and performers of meritorious deeds.
To the western part of that city belongs the great-souled Nirṛti’s city named Rakṣovatī, which is surrounded on all sides by Rākṣasas.
There, the Rākṣasas attend upon that god Nirṛti;
those who delight in unrighteousness and whose conduct is characterized by darkness go to him.
On the westernmost of excellent mountains is the great city of Varuṇa, named Śuddhavatī; it is meritorious and endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.
There, served by hosts of Apsarases and Siddhas,
sits Varuṇa, the lord of the immortals; there go those clouds and those in the world who are constantly devoted to pilgrimages and who have subdued their passions.
To the north of that city is the great and meritorious city of Vāyu, named Gandhavatī; there dwells that Prabhajana.
Served by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas, the lord of the immortals remains;
and mortals who are devoted to breath-control (prāṇāyāma) go to that eternal state.
To its eastern quarter lies the supreme city of Soma, radiant and named Kāntimatī; there Soma shines forth in splendor.
There, those who are devoted to enjoyments and do not neglect their own duty—
for them, that prepared abode is provided, endowed with various kinds of enjoyments.
And to the east of that city is the great, meritorious city of Śaṅkara named Yaśovatī, which is very difficult for all to reach.
Therein stands the auspicious and vast abode of Īśāna, whose body is that of Rudra-Viṣṇu;
there resides Ghaṇṭeśvara, surrounded by his hosts.
There, for his devotees who desire worldly enjoyments,
a dwelling was previously ordained by the trident-bearing God of gods, the Supreme Lord.
Having issued from the foot of Viṣṇu and having flooded the lunar orb,
the Gaṅgā indeed falls from heaven all around the city of Brahmā.
O twice-born ones, having fallen there, she became fourfold in the directions:
Sītā, Alakanandā, Sucakṣus, and Bhadranāmikā.
From the mountain to the east, Sītā travels through the atmosphere from one mountain to another;
thence, by way of the eastern continent Bhadrāśva, she reaches the ocean.
In the same way, O best of the twice-born, the Alakanandā comes from the south to Bhārata and flows to the ocean, divided into seven streams.
Having passed beyond all the western mountains, Sucakṣus likewise goes to the western region called Ketumāla and reaches the ocean.
O great seers, having passed beyond Bhadrāśva, the Northern Mountains, and the Northern Kurus,
she flows toward the northern ocean.
Mālyavat and Gandhamādana extend as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains;
situated between them stands Meru, shaped like the pericarp of a lotus.
The Bhāratas, the Ketumālas, the Bhadrāśvas,
and the Kurus are the petals of the world-lotus, situated outside the boundary mountains.
Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa are both boundary mountains;
they extend from south to north, reaching as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha ranges.
Both Gandhamādana and Kailāsa extend from east to west;
eighty yojanas in length, they are situated within the ocean.
Niṣadha and Pāriyātra are these two boundary mountains;
situated on the western side of Meru, they stand exactly as the two [preceding ones] do on the eastern side.
Similarly, in the north are the two mountain ranges of Triśṛṅga and Jārudhi;
these extend from east to west and are situated within the ocean.
O twice-born ones, I have thus described to you here the eight boundary mountains,
beginning with Jaṭhara, which stand in the four directions around Meru, O great sages.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the first division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
In Ketumāla, all men are long-lived and subsist on the fruit of the jackfruit tree (panasa).
And women, with complexions like the petals of a blue lotus, live for ten thousand years.
In Bhadrāśva, the men are white and the women resemble the rays of the moon;
they live for ten thousand years, subsisting on the fruit of the mango tree.
In Ramyaka, men and women, possessing the luster of silver, take their delight;
established in goodness and subsisting on the fruit of the banyan tree, they live for eleven thousand five hundred years.
Golden-hued and possessing a golden luster, all of them subsist on lakuca fruit;
eleven thousand and fifteen hundred men and women live there like those residing in the world of the gods.
In the land of Kuru-varṣa, those with dark complexions and who subsist on milk live for thirteen thousand one hundred and five years.
All those born in pairs always enjoy happiness;
in Candradvīpa, they constantly worship the Great God Śiva.
Likewise, O Brahmins, in Kiṃpuruṣa, the Mānavas are golden-hued;
subsisting on the fruit of the Plakṣa tree, they live for ten thousand years.
Endowed with devotion and full of reverence, they constantly worship the fourfold-formed, four-faced God, having fixed their minds in meditation.
Likewise, in Harivarṣa, those who resemble great silver live for ten thousand years, subsisting on sugarcane juice.
There, human beings who are permeated by Viṣṇu constantly worship the divine Viṣṇu, the eternal Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe.
There, the bright, moon-like celestial chariot of Vāsudeva, fashioned from pure crystal, is situated in the Pārijāta grove.
It has four gateways comparable to the mind, is provided with four arches,
is endowed with ten ramparts, and is difficult to assail and hard to traverse.
It was endowed with pavilions made of crystal, resembling the palace of the king of the gods,
and was adorned on all sides with thousands of golden pillars.
It was provided with golden staircases, adorned with various jewels,
furnished with a divine lion-throne, and endowed with every splendor.
It was adorned with lakes containing sweet drinking water and with rivers,
and it was inhabited by pure people devoted to Nārāyaṇa and intent on the study of the Vedas.
And it was crowded with yogis meditating upon Hari,
the Supreme Person, constantly praising Mādhava with mantras and bowing down to him.
There, kings always perform the glorification of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
And charming, playful women, radiant with youth and ever devoted to adornment, sing and dance. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.45.18)
In Ilāvṛta, the people have the color of lotuses, subsist on the juice of jambū fruits,
and possess a stable lifespan of thirteen thousand years.
In Bhārata, however, women and men are proclaimed to be of various complexions;
they are engaged in the worship of various deities and perform various rites.
O you of excellent vows, their maximum lifespan is recorded as one hundred years.
And they live on various kinds of food, depending on their merit and demerit.
This region is proclaimed to be nine thousand yojanas in extent;
O Brahmins, this is the land of action for those humans who possess the requisite qualification.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Ṛkṣaparvata,
Vindhya, and Pāriyātra— these seven are the principal mountain ranges here.
Indradyumna, Kaśerumān, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, as well as Saumya, Gandharva, and Vāruṇa.
This, however, is the ninth among them, an island surrounded by the ocean;
this island extends for a thousand yojanas from south to north.
In its eastern quarter are the Kirātas, and likewise the Yavanas in the western;
in the center are the Brāhmaṇas, the Kṣatriyas, the Vaiśyas, and likewise the Śūdras.
In this place, human beings subsist through sacrifice, warfare, and trade;
and purifying rivers flow forth, having issued from the mountains.
The Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, the Sarayū, the Yamunā,
as well as the Irāvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāśā, the Devikā, and the Kuhū.
The Gomatī, Dhūtapāpā, Bāhudā, Dṛṣadvatī,
Kauśikī, and Lohitā are indeed those rivers that have issued from the foothills of the Himavat.
Vedasmṛti, Vedavatī, Vrataghnī, Tridivā, as well as Parṇāśā, Vandana, Sadānīrā, and Manoramā.
The Carmaṇvatī, Dūryā, Vidiśā, and also the Vetravatī,
as well as the Śigru and Svaśilpā, are recorded as being situated along the Pāriyātra mountains.
The Narmadā, Surasā, Śoṇa, and the great river Daśārṇā; the Mandākinī, Citrakūṭā, Tāmasī, and Piśācikā.
The Citrotpalā, the Vipāśā, the Mañjulā, the Vāluvāhinī,
and the river born from the foot of Ṛkṣavat— these rivers remove all sins of men.
The Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, and the great river Śīghrodā;
the Veṇyā, Vaitaraṇī, Balākā, and Kumudvatī.
Toyā, Mahāgaurī, Durgā, and Antaḥśilā— these rivers,
born from the foothills of the Vindhya mountains, possess auspicious and merit-bestowing waters.
The Sodāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇā, Varṇā, Matsarī,
Tuṅgabhadrā, Suprayogā, and Kāverī, O best of the twice-born—
these are the rivers flowing toward the south, issuing from the foothills of the Sahya mountains.
The Ṛtumālā, Tāmraparṇī, Puṣpavatī, and Utpalāvatī—
these rivers flowing from the Malaya mountains are all known to have cool waters.
The Ṛṣikulyā, the Trisāmā, the Mandagā, the Mandagāminī,
the Rūpā, the Pālāsinī, the Ṛṣikā, and the Vaṃśakāriṇī—
all these, born from the foot of Śuktimat, remove all the sins of men.
O best of the twice-born, these rivers and their tributaries are hundreds in number;
they are meritorious and remove all sins during rites such as ritual bathing and giving of gifts.
In them dwell these people— the Kurus, Pāñcālas, those from the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) and so forth,
as well as those from the Eastern Country and other regions, and the inhabitants of Kāmarūpa.
The Puṇḍras, Kaliṅgas, Magadhas, and all those from the Deccan;
likewise the Aparāntas, Saurāṣṭras, Śūdras, Ābhīras, and Arbudas.
The Mālakas and the Mālavas who dwell in the Pāriyātra mountains, the Sauvīras, the Saindhavas, the Hūṇas, the Śālvas, and those dwelling in Kalpa; KūrmP_1.45.41.
The Madras, the Rāmas, as well as the Ambaṣṭhas and the Pārasīkas, always drink the water and dwell along these rivers. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.45.42)
Sages have declared that there are four ages in the land of Bhārata—
the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— but nowhere else.
In those eight regions, such as Kiṃpuruṣa and the others, there is no sorrow, no fatigue, no agitation, nor any fear of hunger, O great sages.
The subjects are healthy, free from fear, and devoid of all suffering;
they delight in various states of being, and all possess perpetual youth.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the first section of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
On the peak of Mount Hemakūṭa, there was a place exceedingly beautiful with great summits.
The celestial chariot of the Supreme Lord, the God of gods, is made of crystal.
Then the gods, hosts of Siddhas, and Yakṣas constantly perform worship of the God of gods, the Lord of beings, the wielder of the trident.
That god Giriśa, Maheśvara, the wielder of the Pināka bow, shines there eternally together with the Great Goddess, surrounded by spirits.
There stands Mount Kailāsa, with its beautifully distinct peaks,
the abode of ten million yakṣas and of the wise Kubera;
there also is the great sanctuary of Bhava, the God of gods.
There flows the divine Mandākinī, lovely with its perfectly pure waters,
a river adorned with many kinds of various lotuses.
Its waters are constantly touched by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kiṃnaras; it is exceedingly meritorious and most delightful.
And there are hundreds of other rivers adorned with golden lotuses;
on their banks are the abodes of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin),
frequented by hosts of celestial sages, as well as those of Nārāyaṇa.
And on the peak of Sitānta is the auspicious Pārijāta grove;
there is the vast palace of Śakra, adorned with jewels,
provided with crystal pillars, and equipped with golden gate-towers.
Therein was the highly meritorious and beautiful palace of Viṣṇu, the god of gods and lord of all the immortals, adorned with every kind of jewel.
There dwells the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the world, the eternal one and the best among all the immortals, together with Lakṣmī, being worshipped.
And likewise, O Vasudhārā, there are eight meritorious sites among the Vasus, adorned with jewels, which are invincible to the enemies of the gods.
O Ratnadhārā, on that excellent mountain there are seven meritorious hermitages belonging to the high-souled Seven Sages, which are inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas).
Therein lies the most meritorious and vast abode of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest; it is made of gold, possesses four gates, and is adorned with diamonds, sapphires, and other gems.
There, divine seers, Brahmins, Siddhas,
and other celestial rishis constantly worship the supreme, unborn God, the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Constantly worshipped by them along with the Goddess, the four-faced one remains for the welfare of the worlds as the supreme refuge for those who are peaceful.
Then, upon the peak of Ekaśṛṅga, there was a very great, meritorious lake adorned with great lotuses, containing pure, nectar-like water that was fragrant.
There is the hermitage of Jaigīṣavya, adorned by the lords of yogis;
there the Blessed One dwells eternally, surrounded by his disciples—
high-souled knowers of Brahman who are free from defects, noble, and tranquil.
Śaṅkha, Manohara, Kauśika, Kṛṣṇa,
Sumanas, and Vedanāda were his principal disciples.
All are devoted to yoga, peaceful, their bodies smeared with ashes;
possessed of great heroism, they worship, being solely intent upon the knowledge of Brahman.
For the sake of favoring those ascetics of tranquil minds,
Maheśvara, together with the Goddess, repeatedly manifests his presence there.
And on that best of excellent mountains, there were other hermitages belonging to sages of disciplined minds, as well as lakes and rivers.
Among them, the Brahmins, devoted to yoga, practitioners of silent recitation, with their senses restrained,
delight in being intent upon knowledge, their minds fixed on the Supreme Brahman.
Having established the Self within the self, situated at the inner limit of the crest-lock,
they meditate upon the Lord Īśāna, by whom all this is pervaded.
In the cloud named Sumegha is the abode of Vāsava, which resembles a thousand suns;
there dwells the Blessed Indra, the lord of the gods, together with Śacī.
On Mount Gaja, however, is the palace of Durgā, a mine of jewels;
there dwells the Blessed One, Durgā, the Great Goddess herself.
Being worshipped here and there by various manifestations of power,
she drank the nectar of yoga and directly attained divine bliss.
O twice-born ones, on the peak of Mount Sunīla, which is resplendent with various minerals,
there are cities of the Rākṣasas and lakes by the hundreds.
Likewise, O brahmins, there is a city of a hundred [puras] on the great mountain Śataśṛṅga,
consisting of crystal pillars, belonging to yakṣas of immeasurable splendor.
On the peak of the great-souled Śvetodara mountain, there is a city belonging to Suparṇa,
provided with walls and gate-towers, and adorned with jeweled archways.
There, that glorious Garuḍa, like another Viṣṇu in person,
remained meditating upon that supreme light, the imperishable Viṣṇu who is the Self.
Furthermore, O best of sages, there is another meritorious temple on Śrīśṛṅga belonging to the illustrious Goddess;
it is made of gold, enriched with all kinds of jewels, and features beautiful gateways of precious gems.
Therein resides that supreme power of Viṣṇu, most enchanting,
Lakṣmī of infinite majesty, ever eager to enchant the world.
Worshipped by gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and cāraṇas, she dwells there,
having reflected upon the source of the world, radiant with the rays of her own power.
Right there is the great abode of Viṣṇu, the God of gods;
there are four lakes there, which are the refuge of various lotuses.
Likewise, on the Thousand-Peaked Mountain (Sahasraśikhara) is the city of the eight Vidyādharas,
provided with jeweled staircases and adorned by lakes.
There are rivers of pure water, filled with variegated blue lotuses;
there stands the divine Karṇikāra forest, where Śaṅkara dwells together with Umā.
On the great mountain Pāriyātra is the auspicious city of Mahālakṣmī,
endowed with beautiful palaces and adorned with bells and chowries.
It was beautified here and there by throngs of dancing apsarases,
resounding with the booming of mṛdaṅga and muraja drums, and made to ring out with the music of lutes and flutes.
It was crowded with Gandharvas and Kinnaras, filled with the foremost of Siddhas,
adorned with radiant walls, and teeming with great palaces.
Frequented by the wives of the lords of the Gaṇas and a sight for the righteous,
the Goddess dwells there eternally, devoted to yoga.
The great goddess Mahālakṣmī, bearing the excellent trident,
three-eyed and composed of both the existent and the non-existent, is surrounded by all her powers;
there the sages and Siddhas who discourse upon Brahman behold her.
O best of beings, to the north of Supārśva lies the excellent city of Sarasvatī,
where there are lakes frequented by the Siddhas and enjoyed by the gods.
On the peak of Mount Pāṇḍura, which is crowded with various trees,
there are hundreds of cities of the Sandharvas, filled with celestial women.
In those [cities], excellent women, perpetually intoxicated with passion,
likewise sport joyfully and eternally, devoted to pleasures and amorous dalliances.
On the peak of Mount Añjana is a supreme city of women;
there dwell the Apsarases, such as Rambhā and others, who are eager for amorous delight.
Where Citrasena and others always arrive as supplicants,
that city is rich in all kinds of jewels and endowed with many springs.
O you of excellent vows, there may be many cities of the Rudras— those whose passion has been stilled and whose minds are dedicated to the Lord— even during the month of Kaumuda.
Within them dwell the Rudras, great yogis who move within the interior of Maheśa;
having ascended to the supreme light, they reside in that most excellent station.
On the peak of Mount Piñjara, there are three cities of the Gaṇeśas;
there, on Mount Kapila, resides the ascetic Suyaśas, the lord of Nandīśvara.
And likewise, on the peak of Jārudhi, there is the radiant and meritorious temple of the god of gods, the wise Bhāskara of immeasurable splendor.
In the northern direction of that very place is the unsurpassed abode of the Moon;
there the delightful Lord Śītadīdhiti (the Cool-rayed One) rejoices.
Furthermore, O great sages, on Mount Haṃsa there is another divine abode,
extending for a thousand yojanas and adorned with golden and jeweled archways.
There dwells the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the soul of the universe, praised by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), together with Sāvitrī and accompanied by Vāsudeva and the other deities.
To the southern quarter of that [mountain] is the supreme city of the Siddhas,
where Sanandana and other preeminent sages dwell.
On the peak of Pañcaśaila, not far from there, were the three cities of the Dānavas belonging to that wise preceptor of the Daityas.
On the peak of the Fragrant Mountain, adorned with rivers, lies the holy hermitage of Kardama; there dwells the blessed Ṛṣi.
To the east of that very place, slightly toward the south,
the blessed Sanatkumāra, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, resides there.
On all these mountains and others as well, there are lords of sages,
pure lakes, rivers, and abodes of the gods.
I am indeed unable to enumerate the meritorious signs of accomplishment established by the sages, nor the excellent hermitages situated in the forest.
This detailed description of Jambūdvīpa has been told in brief;
it is not possible for me to describe it in full detail even in hundreds of years.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
[The ocean] surrounds Jambūdvīpa on all sides with a width double that of the continent.
Having encircled the ocean of salt water, Plakṣadvīpa is situated.
And in Plakṣadvīpa, O best of brahmins, there were seven principal mountain ranges,
straight and extensive, with beautiful peaks, frequented by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas).
Gomeda is the first of them; the second is called Candra;
then Nārada, Dundubhi, Soma, and likewise Ṛṣabha;
Vaibhrāja is declared the seventh, who is exceedingly dear to Brahmā.
There, the unborn Lord, the soul of the universe, the witness of all, and the creator of the world, is worshipped by the celestial rishis, gandharvas, and siddhas.
In those regions, the lands were meritorious; there were neither mental afflictions nor physical diseases, and there were no men who committed evil deeds in any way whatsoever.
In those seven regions, there are likewise seven rivers that flow toward the ocean;
in them, the Brahman-sages constantly worship the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Anutaptā, Śikhī, Vipāpā, Tridivā,
Amṛtā, and Sukṛtā are proclaimed by name.
There are indeed innumerable small rivers and very many lakes;
yet in these, there is no condition of a *yuga*, nor are there men who possess long lifespans.
The Āryakas, Kurus, Vidaśas,
and Bhāvins are likewise proclaimed as the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras on that island.
The Blessed Lord Soma is worshipped there by the inhabitants of that region;
and for them, O best of sages, there is union with Soma and conformity to his form.
All are constantly devoted to the Dharma and always possess joyful minds;
they live for five thousand years, free from disease.
Twice the size of Plakṣadvīpa all around,
Śālmali is situated, encircling the ocean of sugarcane juice.
There too, for seven years, there are likewise seven principal mountain ranges,
straight and well-jointed, as well as seven rivers of virtuous course.
Kumuda, Unnata, and the third, Balāhaka;
Droṇa, Kaṅka, Mahiṣa, and Kakudvān—these are the seven mountains.
Yonī, Toyā, Vitṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śuklā, Vimocanī,
and Nivṛtti— these rivers are remembered as the removers of the sins of men.
O best of the twice-born, neither greed nor anger exists among them;
nor is there even the condition of the [degenerate] ages, for people live free from ailment.
There, the social classes constantly worship the eternal Vāyu; for them, there is union with him, as well as similarity of form and residence in the same world. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.47.17)
O twice-born ones, in this island, the Brāhmaṇas are said to be tawny (kapila), the kings likewise ruddy (aruṇa),
the Vaiśyas are recorded as yellow (pīta), and the Śūdras are black (kṛṣṇa).
Kuśadvīpa is situated surrounding the Ocean of Wine on all sides with a circumference twice that of Śālmala.
Vidruma, Hema, Dyutimān, Puṣpavān,
Kuśeśaya, Hari, and Mandara— these are the seven mountains.
Dhūtapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, Saṃmatā,
as well as Vidyudambhā and Mahī— these are the rivers that carry water there.
And there are hundreds of other auspicious rivers with jewel-like waters, O Brahmins;
in them, the gods and others attend upon Brahmā, the Lord.
The Brāhmaṇas are said to be the Draviṇas, the Vipras; the Kṣatriyas are the Śuṣmiṇas;
the Vaiśyas are the Snehas, and the Śūdras are the Mandehas.
All were endowed with wisdom and possessed virtues such as loving-kindness;
all acted according to what was taught, and all delighted in the welfare of living beings.
They worship Brahmā Parameṣṭhin with various sacrifices;
for them there is union with Brahman (sāyujya), similarity of form (sārūpya), and residence in the same world (salokatā).
O Brahmins, Krauñcadvīpa, twice the size of Kuśadvīpa, surrounds it on all sides, encircling the ocean of clarified butter.
Krauñca, Vāmanaka, and the third, Andhakāraka; Devāvṛt, Vivinda, and likewise Puṇḍarīka;
and the seventh mountain is said by name to be Dundubhisvana.
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Saṃdhyā, Rātri, Manojava,
Khyāti, and Puṇḍarīkā are remembered as the principal rivers.
The Puṣkaras, Puṣkalas, Dhanyas, and Tiṣyas were, in order,
the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, O best of the twice-born.
They worship Mahādeva through sacrifices, gifts, and meditative concentrations;
through various vows and fasts, through gold, through Vedic study, and through libations.
For them, union with Rudra (rudrasāyujya) and his formal likeness (sārūpya) are indeed extremely difficult to attain;
yet, by his grace, residence in the same world (salokatā) and proximity (sāmīpya) come to pass.
O Brahmins, Śākadvīpa is situated surrounding the Ocean of Curd, being twice the extent of Krauñcadvīpa on all sides.
Udaya, Raivata, Śyāmāka, Astagiri,
Āmbikeya, Ramya, and Keśarī are the mountains.
Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nalinī, Reṇukā,
Ikṣukā, Dhenukā, and Gabhastī are the rivers.
Drinking the water of these rivers, the humans there live free from disease,
devoid of sorrow, and liberated from passion and hatred.
The Magas, the Magadhas, and likewise the Mandagas—
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras— are situated here in this sequence.
They constantly worship the god Divākara, the sole witness of all the worlds and the god of gods,
with various vows and fasts.
O best of Brahmins, through his grace, they attain union with the Sun, proximity to him, similarity of form, and residence in the same world. KūrmP_1.47.38.
Surrounding Śākadvīpa stands the ocean of milk (kṣīroda-sāgara);
and in its center is Śvetadvīpa, where those devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa dwell.
There, the districts are meritorious and endowed with various wonders;
there, white-complexioned men are constantly born, ever devoted to Viṣṇu.
Therein are neither mental anxieties nor physical ailments, nor is there any fear of old age or death;
[the beings there] are completely freed from anger and greed, and devoid of deceit and envy.
All are eternally nourished, free from fear, and possessed of eternal bliss and enjoyments;
they are all devoted to Nārāyaṇa and have Nārāyaṇa as their ultimate goal.
Some yogins are constantly devoted to meditation with their senses restrained;
some mutter prayers, some perform austerities, and others are possessed of higher knowledge.
Others, cultivated through the yoga of seedlessness and through the state of Brahman,
meditate upon that supreme ether, Vāsudeva, the highest goal.
The supreme, highly fortunate ones who are single-minded and without external support behold the Supreme Brahman known as Viṣṇu, who is beyond darkness.
All of them have four arms and hold a conch, a discus, and a mace;
all are clad in beautiful yellow garments, and their chests are marked with the Śrīvatsa.
Others, devoted to Maheśvara, have their foreheads marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra);
they possess rays produced from their own yoga and have the great Garuḍa as their vehicle.
Endowed with all powers, eternal, blissful, and stainless,
those persons who move within Viṣṇu dwell there.
There, moreover, is another city of Nārāyaṇa, difficult to access and difficult to traverse,
named Nārāyaṇa, which is adorned by Vyāsa and others.
Enclosed by golden walls and adorned with pavilions made of crystal,
it was filled with a thousand splendors, invincible, and most beautiful;
it was joined by palace ramparts and crowded with watchtowers.
With thousands of golden gate-towers adorned with various jewels,
it was provided with white coverings and decorated with diverse ornaments.
It was adorned with various kinds of pleasure groves and flowing streams, surrounded on all sides by lakes, and resounded with the music of lutes and flutes.
It was adorned with many variegated banners and provided on all sides with pathways and staircases embellished with jewels.
Abounding with hundreds of thousands of women, endowed with divine cattle,
crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and adorned with ruddy geese;
it has four gates, is incomparable, and is inaccessible to the enemies of the gods.
In various places it was graced by throngs of dancing apsarases,
who were skilled in the performance of diverse songs and difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Accompanied by lovers who were exceedingly tender, endowed with various charms,
possessing faces like the full moon, and joined by the tinkling sound of their anklets.
With gentle smiles, lips like beautiful bimba fruits, and eyes like those of young, innocent fawns; endowed with every splendor, adorned, and possessing slender waists.
With the gait of noble royal swans, well-attired, possessing sweet voices, skilled in conversation and discourse, and adorned with divine ornaments; KūrmP_1,47.58.
With bodies bent by the weight of their breasts, eyes rolling with intoxication, their limbs variegated with many colors, and devoted to various enjoyments and pleasures; KūrmP_1,47.59.
Adorned here and there with gardens of blossoming flowers,
it is pure, possesses innumerable virtues, and is accessible even to the gods.
In the midst of that glorious and sacred abode of the Lord Śrīpati of immeasurable splendor, there was a place of exceeding brilliance, surrounded by high walls and arched gateways.
That divine station of Viṣṇu is indeed difficult even for yogins to attain;
in its midst lies the one Lord Hari, possessing the luster of a lotus petal,
the source of the entire world, reclining upon the serpent Śeṣa as his bed.
Being contemplated by the lords of yogis, headed by Sanandana,
it is that supreme state beyond darkness, having drunk the nectar of the bliss of one's own self.
Clad in beautiful yellow garments, infinite, possessed of great illusion and mighty arms,
his two feet are eternally grasped by the daughter of the Milky Ocean.
And that goddess, beloved of Hari and worthy of worship by the world, sat constantly at his feet with her mind fixed on him, drinking the nectar of Nārāyaṇa.
Neither the unrighteous nor those who take refuge in other deities go there;
that place named Vaikuṇṭha is venerated even by the gods.
I possess no wisdom for describing that place in its entirety;
indeed, only this much can be said: that it is the city of Nārāyaṇa.
He alone is the supreme Brahman, the eternal Vāsudeva;
the glorious Nārāyaṇa lies there, deluding the world with his māyā.
This world was born from Nārāyaṇa and is established in him alone;
at the end of the kalpa it returns to him, for he alone is the supreme goal.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the first division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Śākadvīpa is situated with a width double that of [Jambūdvīpa].
Resting upon the Ocean of Milk is the continent known as Puṣkara.
O best of Brahmins, there is here but a single mountain, Mānasottara,
which rises fifty-five thousand yojanas high;
it is just as wide and is circular on all sides.
That very island, known as Mānasottara, is situated in the western half;
though it is a single great peak, it is divided into two by its configuration.
On that island, two other auspicious and meritorious regions are recorded,
situated respectively around Mount Mānasa and Mount Anumaṇḍala;
they are known as the region of Mahāvīta and Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
Puṣkara is surrounded by an ocean of sweet water;
on that island stands a great banyan tree, worshipped by the immortals.
In that place dwells Brahmā, the soul of the universe and the creator of all;
right there, O tigers among sages, is the abode of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa.
Here dwells the imperishable Mahādeva, who is half-Hara and half-Viṣṇu;
the Lord, dark and tawny-hued, is being worshipped by Brahmā and the others, by Kumāra and other yogis, as well as by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Yakṣas.
All the subjects there were healthy, possessing a radiance equal to that of Brahmā;
they were free from disease and sorrow, and devoid of passion and hatred.
There, neither truth nor falsehood existed; there were no superior, inferior, or middling [beings];
there were no duties of the castes and stages of life, nor were there rivers or mountains.
O best of the twice-born, beyond Puṣkara stands the great ocean of sweet water on all sides.
Beyond that, the great arrangement of the world is seen:
a golden ground twice as large, and everything indeed like stone.
Beyond that is the mountain which forms the boundary of its own circle;
being both luminous and non-luminous, it is called Lokāloka.
The great mountain Lokāloka is recorded to have a height of ten thousand yojanas, and its width is exactly the same.
Having completely surrounded that mountain on all sides, darkness stands there;
and that darkness is encircled on every side by the shell of the cosmic egg.
These seven great worlds and the seven nether regions (pātālas) have been proclaimed;
thus has this extent of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) been described by me in brief.
Thousands of millions of such eggs are to be known,
because the primordial cause (pradhāna), which is all-pervading and of an imperishable nature, exists everywhere.
Within all these eggs are the fourteen worlds;
in each of those places reside the four-faced Brahmās, the Rudras, Nārāyaṇa, and the others.
O Brahmins, there are seven enclosures, each ten times larger than the preceding one,
situated all around, where the wise go.
The one, infinite, unmanifest, and eternal Great One—
Prakṛti, the imperishable— exists transcending the entire world.
Since the infinite has no end and its number cannot be found, it should be known as the unmanifest; that is Brahman, the supreme state.
This Ananta is recited everywhere and in all places;
its imperishable majesty has also been previously described by me.
He has gone everywhere and exists in all places:
on the earth, in the netherworld (rasātala), in the sky, in the wind, in the fire, in all the oceans, and even in heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, in darkness and in goodness (sattva), this very one of great splendor,
the Supreme Person, sports with his limbs divided into many forms.
Maheśvara is beyond the unmanifest; from the unmanifest arose the cosmic egg, and from the egg Brahmā was born; by him this world was created.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The sages said:
"Regarding those Manvantaras that have passed and those yet to come here..."
Tell us those [teachings] and the Vyāsas who appeared in the Dvāpara age.
The division of the branches of the Veda by the wise God of gods,
as well as the incarnations of the Lord for the sake of dharma in the Kali age— [all this has been told].
O Sūta, you ought to tell us here in brief all this: how many disciples indeed did the God of gods have during the Kali ages?
Sūta said:
First was Manu Svāyambhuva, then Manu Svārociṣa,
as well as Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa.
These six Manus have passed; but now this son of Ravi, Vaivasvata, is the one whose seventh interval is currently underway.
I have thus described to you the intermediate period at the beginning of the Kalpa pertaining to Svāyambhuva; hereafter, listen to that of Manu Svārociṣa.
During the Svārociṣa interval, the Pārāvatas were the Tuṣita gods;
there was a lord of the gods named Vipaścit, the destroyer of the asuras.
Ūrjastambha, Prāṇa, Dānta, Vṛṣabha,
Timira, and Ārvarīvat— these were the seven Ṛṣis.
Caitra, Kiṃpuruṣa, and others were the sons of Svārociṣa.
This second period has thus been described; now hear the subsequent one.
In the third interval as well, O brahmins, the Manu named Uttama appeared;
there, the lord of the gods was Suśānti, the subduer of enemies.
The Sudhāmānas, the Satyas, the Śivas, the Pratardanās,
and the Vaśavartins— these five groups are recorded as consisting of twelve each.
Rajordhva, Urdhvabāhu, Sabala, Anaya,
Sutapas, and Śukra— these were the seven Saptarṣis.
Within the Tāmasa period, there were the gods, the Suras, the Vāharayas,
as well as the Satyas and the Sudhiyas— these being the twenty-seven groups.
Śibirindra was likewise characterized by the performance of a hundred sacrifices;
he became a devotee of Śaṅkara, intent upon the worship of Mahādeva.
Jyotirdharma, Pṛthu, Kāvya, Caitra, Agni, Vanaka,
and Pīvara— these seven sages were also present there during that interval.
And in the fifth [Manvantara], O best of Brahmins, the one known by the name Raivata was the Manu;
and Vasu was the Indra there, the crusher of the Asuras.
The Amitābhas, Bhūtarayas, Vaikuṇṭhas, and Svacchamedhas—
these are the fourteen groups of gods there, fourteen for each.
Hiraṇyaroman, Vedaśrī, Urdhvabāhu,
Vedabāhu, Sudhāman, Parjanya, and the great sage [Parameṣṭhin]—
these were the seven ṛṣis, O brahmins, who existed there during the Raivata Manvantara.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, and Raivata—
these four Manus are remembered as belonging to the lineage of Priyavrata.
O twice-born ones, in the sixth Manvantara, Cākṣuṣa was the Manu;
Manojava was likewise the Indra; now learn also of the gods.
The Ādyas, Prasūtas, Bhāvyas, Pṛthagās, and Divaukasas—
these five groups of eight, possessed of great majesty, are indeed to be depicted.
Sumedhas, Virajas, Haviṣmat, Uttama, Madhu,
Atināman, and Sahiṣṇu— these were the seven auspicious ṛṣis.
O brahmins, the son of Vivasvat, the highly effulgent Śrāddhadeva,
that wise Manu is currently presiding over the seventh interval (manvantara).
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the hosts of Maruts were the gods there;
likewise, Indra, the slayer of enemy heroes, became Purandara.
Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, Jamadagni, Gautama,
Viśvāmitra, and Bharadvāja were the seven ṛṣis.
Viṣṇu’s incomparable power, intensified by the quality of goodness (sattva), abides in the maintenance of the world;
all kings and the inhabitants of heaven are but portions of that power.
O twice-born ones, formerly in the Svāyambhuva interval, Yajña was born as the mind-born son of the Prajāpati Ruci through Ākūti; he arose from a portion of that [Lord].
Then, moreover, when the Svārociṣa interval had arrived,
that god was born in Tuṣitā together with the Tuṣita deities.
In the Auttamamanvantara as well, Viṣṇu,
the Lord of Men (Janārdana), being of truthful nature, became Satya in the city of Satyā, together with the truthful and most excellent gods.
And when the interval of Tāmasa had indeed arrived once again,
Hari himself became Hari in the womb of Haryā through the divine Haris.
In the Raivata interval as well, he was born from the mind in the period of Saṃbhūti;
that one of great splendor appeared together with the mind-born gods.
And during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara as well,
that Puruṣottama Vaikuṇṭha was born of Vikuṇṭhā together with the Vaikuṇṭha deities.
When this Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived,
Viṣṇu was born as Vāmana from Kaśyapa and Aditi.
By that great-souled one, having conquered these worlds with three strides,
the triple universe was given to Purandara, its thorns removed.
O brahmins, these were indeed his seven bodies during the seven Manvantaras, by which the subjects were protected.
Since this entire world has been pervaded by the Great-Souled Vāmana,
he is therefore remembered as Viṣṇu, from the root *viś*, meaning "to enter."
"In the beginning, this Keśava creates everything, protects it, and destroys it;
he is the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the inner self of all beings—so says the Śruti. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.49.37)
Nārāyaṇa stands pervading the entire universe with a single part;
he exists as the all-pervasive one in fourfold forms, both with qualities and without qualities.
One form of the Blessed One is the nature of gnosis, auspicious and stainless;
designated as Vāsudeva, it transcends the qualities (guṇas) and is perfectly partless.
The second is the other manifestation known as Kāla-saṃjñā, which is characterized by darkness (tāmasī) and designated as Śeṣa;
this supreme form of Vaiṣṇavī destroys everything at the end.
Likewise, another [form] characterized by an abundance of *sattva* is designated as Pradyumna;
he, as Viṣṇu, establishes the entire world, for he is the eternal primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The fourth form of Vāsudeva is designated as Brāhmī;
the one called Aniruddha is characterized by passion (rājasī), while Pradyumna is the agent of creation.
He who, having become everything, sleeps together with Pradyumna—
the Lord known as Nārāyaṇa— he is Brahmā, and he performs the creation of beings.
O lords of sages, that body of Nārāyaṇa which is called Pradyumna deludes the entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans.
She alone is proclaimed as the primordial nature (prakṛti), the source of the entire world;
for Vāsudeva is the infinite self, Hari, who is absolute and devoid of qualities.
Having realized that the triad of principles— Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Kāla— is supreme, eternal, and identical with Vāsudeva, one is liberated.
And this one [Vāsudeva], who is undecaying and imperishable Hari, further divided himself fourfold into four parts: Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa was Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa himself;
formerly, Hari indeed became Apāntaratamas by his own will.
Neither the gods nor the sages know the supreme Brahman, which is without beginning or end;
the Lord Vyāsa alone, the master Nārāyaṇa, knows this.
Thus, O best of sages, this majesty of Viṣṇu has been declared to you;
this is the truth, indeed the truth—knowing this, one is no longer deluded.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the first part of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Formerly, while this present Manvantara was occurring, the great and all-pervading Lord...
In the first Dvāpara age, Vyāsa was considered to be Svāyambhuva Manu.
At the command of the Lord Brahmā, the Prajāpati Vedavyāsa divided the Veda into many parts during the second Dvāpara age.
In the third [age] Uśanas was the Vyāsa; in the fourth it was Bṛhaspati;
Savitṛ was the Vyāsa in the fifth, and Mṛtyu is proclaimed [to have been] in the sixth.
In the seventh [Manvantara], Indra was likewise [Vasu]; Vasiṣṭha is held to be [the Ṛṣi] in the eighth;
Sārasvata in the ninth; and Tridhāman is recorded in the tenth.
In the eleventh [manvantara] was Trivṛṣa, and after him Śatatejas;
likewise, Dharma was in the thirteenth, and Tārakṣu in the fourteenth.
Tryāruṇi was indeed in the fifteenth, Dhanañjaya in the sixteenth;
Kṛtañjaya was in the seventeenth, and Ṛtañjaya in the eighteenth.
From him [Vaiśampāyana] came Vyāsa; from Bharadvāja after him came Gautama;
Rājaśravas was the twenty-first, and after him came Śuṣmāyaṇa.
Tṛṇabindu is remembered as the twenty-third [incarnation], Vālmīki as the one following that;
likewise Śakti is the twenty-fifth, and Parāśara is the twenty-sixth.
