Likewise, in the twenty-seventh [Dvāpara], the great sage Jātūkarṇya was Vyāsa;
and when this twenty-eighth Dvāpara arrived, O twice-born ones,
Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana became the son of Parāśara.
He alone is the expounder of all the Vedas and Purāṇas;
he is the great yogi Pārāśarya, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Hari.
Having propitiated the Lord Īśāna and beheld the three-eyed one accompanied by Ambā,
that lord, by his grace, made Vyāsa the compiler of the Vedas.
Then the great sage took four disciples who had mastered the Vedas:
Jaimini, Sumantu, Vaiśampāyana, and Paila as the fourth among them; and me as the fifth.
That great sage received Paila as the reciter of the Ṛgveda,
and likewise Vaiśampāyana as the expounder of the Yajurveda.
He appointed Jaimini as the reciter of the Sāmaveda; likewise, he appointed Sumantu, the best of sages, for the Atharvaveda;
and he employed me to proclaim the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
The Yajurveda was originally one; he divided it into four parts.
From that which became the Cāturhotra, he then performed the sacrifice.

O best of the twice-born, he established the office of the Adhvaryu with the Yajus formulas, the office of the Hotṛ with the Ṛks, the office of the Udgātṛ with the Sāmans, and likewise the office of the Brahman with the Atharvans.
Then that Lord, having extracted the Ṛcas, composed the Ṛgveda;
likewise, he composed the Yajurveda from the Yajus formulas and the Sāmaveda from the Sāmans.
In ancient times, he divided the Ṛgveda into twenty-one branches,
and then he composed the Yajurveda with exactly one hundred branches.
He divided the Sāmaveda into a thousand branches,
and he likewise divided the Atharvaveda into nine.
The Lord Vyāsa divided the Purāṇa into eighteen parts;
this very same Veda, which formerly consisted of four quarters, [was thus expanded] from the Ancient One.
The syllable Oṃ was born from Brahmā; it is the purifier of all defects.
For the Blessed One Vāsudeva, the eternal, is indeed to be known through the Vedas.
He who knows this through the Veda is proclaimed in the Veda as the Supreme; he is the knower of the Veda.
This is the furthermost Brahman, the light, the supreme bliss.
The reality proclaimed by the Vedic words is Vāsudeva, the supreme state;
the sage devoted to the Vedas knows this Veda, which is to be known through the Vedas.
He who is established in the Vedas knows this supreme Veda, the eternal Lord.
He is the Blessed One, the one to be known through the Vedas, the Great Lord whose very form is the Veda.
He alone is the Veda and the object of knowledge; by taking refuge in him alone, one is liberated.
The great sage Pārāśarya understands this imperishable syllable, the Oṃkāra, which is both the eternal Veda and that which is beyond the Veda.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the first division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
"The incarnations of Vedavyāsa have indeed been described for the Dvāpara age."
O you of excellent vows, listen now to the incarnations of Mahādeva in the Kali age.
In the first Kali age of the Vaivasvata interval, the white, most radiant God of gods appeared for the welfare of the brahmins.
On a delightful peak of the Himavat, on Chagala, the best of mountains,
his disciples— endowed with topknots and immeasurable splendor— came to be.
Śveta, Śvetaśikha, Śvetāsya, and Śvetalohita—
these four high-souled Brāhmaṇas were masters of the Vedas.
Subhānu, Damana, and then Suhotra, as well as Kaṅkaṇa;
Lokākṣi was the lord of yogins, and Jaigīṣavya was in the seventh [manvantara].
In the eighth [manvantara] there will be Dadhivāha; in the ninth, the lord Vṛṣabha;
Bhṛgu is declared to be in the tenth, and after him, Ugra is remembered as the next.
In the twelfth [kalpa] Atri is proclaimed, and in the thirteenth Bala;
in the fourteenth Gautama, and after that Vedaśīrṣa.
From him came Gokarṇa, then Guhāvāsa, Śikhaṇḍin,
Jaṭāmālin, Aṭṭahāsa, Dāruka, and Lāṅgalin in succession.
Śveta, and likewise Para, Śūlin, Ḍiṇḍin, and Muṇḍin in sequence;
Sahiṣṇu, Somaśarman, and Nakulīśa is the Lord at the end.
In the Vaivasvata interval, twenty-eight incarnations of the trident-bearing Śambhu are proclaimed for the Lord at the end of the Kali Yuga; among them,
at the sacred site of Kāyāvatāra, there is the Lord of Gods, Nakulīśvara.
There, the God of gods had four disciples who were rich in asceticism; each of the other [deities] likewise had their own eminent sages as disciples.
I shall describe in due order those yogins, the best among the knowers of yoga, who are serene-minded, self-controlled, and have taken refuge in devotion to the Lord.
Śveta, Śvetaśikha, Śvetāsya, Śvetalohita,
Dundubhi, Śatarūpa, Ṛcīka,
Ketumān, Vikeśa, Viśoka, Viśāpa, and Śāpanāśana.
Sumukha, Durmukha, Durdama, Duratikrama,
Sana, Sanātana, Mukāra, and Sanandana.
And Dālabhya, a great yogi, as well as Sudhāman, Virajas, and Śaṅkhapātraja, who were of righteous nature and great majesty.
Sārasvata, Megha, Ghanavāha, Suvāhana,
Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and the sage Pañcaśikha.
Parāśara, Garga, Bhārgava, and likewise Aṅgiras; Balabandhu, Nirāmitra, Ketuśṛṅga, and Tapodhana.
Lambodara, Lamba, Lāmbākṣa, Lambakeśaka,
Sarvajña, Samabuddhi, Sādhya, and likewise Satya.
Śudhāmā and Kāśyapa, Vasiṣṭha and Virajas, Atri and Ugra, as well as Śravaṇa and Śraviṣṭhaka.
Kuṇi, Kuṇibāhu, Kuśarīra, Kunetraka,
Kaśyapa, Uśanas, Cyavana, and Bṛhaspati.
Utathya, Vāmadeva, Mahākāya, Mahānila,
Vācaśravas, Supīka, Śyāvāśva, and Pathīśvara.
Hariṇyanābha, Kauśalya, Lokākṣi, Kuthumi, the learned Sumantu, Varcari, Kabandha, and Kuśikandhara.
Plakṣa, Dārbhāyaṇi, Ketumān Gautama,
Bhallāpī, Madhupiṅga, and Śvetaketu, a treasury of asceticism.
Uśija, Bṛhaduktha, Devala, and Kapila;
Śālihotra, Agniveśya, Yuvanāśva, and Śaradvasu.
Chagala, Kuṇḍakarṇa, Kumbha, Pravāhaka,
Ulūka, Vidyuta, Śādvala, and Āśvalāyana.
Akṣapāda, Kumāra, Ulūka, Vatsa,
Kuśika, Garga, Mitraka, and Ṛṣya.
These disciples are great-souled yogis in all the cycles;
they are stainless, predominantly absorbed in Brahman, and devoted to the yoga of knowledge.
Indeed, for the benefit of the brahmins, they manifest incarnations at the command of the lords of yoga, truly for the purpose of establishing the Vedas. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.51.28)
Those Brahmins who always remember them, bow down to them,
gratify them, and honor them shall attain the knowledge of Brahman.
This interval of Vaivasvata has been declared in detail;
and there shall also be Sāvarṇa and Dakṣasāvarṇa.
The tenth is Brahmasāvarṇi, and Dharmasāvarṇi as well;
the twelfth is Rudrasāvarṇi, and Rocamāna is the thirteenth;
Bhautya is declared to be the fourteenth—these are the future Manus in their proper order.
This first portion has indeed been told to you, uttered by Nārāyaṇa,
and augmented by narratives of the past, the future, and the present.
Whoever should read, or even hear, or cause the best of the twice-born to hear this,
shall be liberated from all sins and rejoices together with Brahmā.
Having bathed in a temple or indeed on the banks of rivers,
one should recite [this] after bowing with devotion to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person.
Salutation to the God of gods, the Supreme Self of the gods,
the Ancient Puruṣa, Viṣṇu in the form of the Tortoise.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the Pūrvavibhāga of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of sixty thousand verses.
